name: Accordion Keepsake Card
tagline: Make a dry indoor keepsake card from one measured cardstock strip, folded into four connected panels.
outcome: Measure and mark a 16-by-6-inch cardstock strip into four equal 4-by-6-inch panels, checking the marks before cutting.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Accordion Keepsake Card

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a dry indoor keepsake card from one measured cardstock strip, folded into four connected panels. The card opens into a zigzag display and closes to a compact 4-by-6-inch cover. Add original lette

lessons.title: Plan the story and prepare the strip
lessons.summary: Plan the story and prepare the strip

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
An accordion card is a single strip with repeated panels. The uninterrupted paper between panels is important: each fold is a hinge, so cutting the card into separate rectangles and taping them together would create a different, weaker construction. This lesson establishes a four-panel strip measuring 16 inches long by 6 inches tall. Each panel will be 4 inches wide and 6 inches tall. When folded, the footprint is approximately 4 by 6 inches, although paper thickness and fold accuracy can change the final size slightly.

Before cutting, decide on a simple visual sequence. For example, panel one can introduce a memory, panel two show a place, panel three record a detail, and panel four end with a note. These are prompts, not required themes. Make the writing your own and use simple geometric marks, small landscapes, or abstract color blocks rather than branded characters or copied artwork. Reserve about half an inch at each panel edge so that content does not disappear into the fold or become crowded.

The strip can be made from one 12-by-12-inch sheet plus a 4-by-6-inch extension. Trim the 12-inch sheet to 12 by 6 inches, then attach the 4-by-6-inch end piece only if the stock is t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On a clear table, choose a four-part memory sequence and lightly sketch four 4-by-6-inch panel boxes on scrap; leave a half-inch quiet margin around each box.
Measure a 16-by-6-inch strip. If using a 12-by-12-inch sheet, cut a 12-by-6-inch section and add a 4-by-6-inch continuation only if a larger single sheet is unavailable; overlap a
Mark the top and bottom edges at 4, 8 and 12 inches from the same left end using the ruler; connect each matching pair with a faint pencil line.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear, stable table; keep fingers out of the cutting path and pass scissors closed, handle first. Younger learners need adult supervision.

blocks.question: What dimensions should the unfolded card strip have in this project?
options: 16 by 6 inches
12 by 6 inches
16 by 4 inches
6 by 6 inches
blocks.explanation: Four equal panels each measure 4 by 6 inches, giving an overall strip of 16 by 6 inches.

lessons.title: Score and fold the zigzag hinges
lessons.summary: Score and fold the zigzag hinges

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Scoring means making a shallow channel along a fold line before folding. The goal is to compress and guide the sheet, not to remove or sever paper fibers. On medium cardstock, a blunt stylus, bone folder or rounded spoon can work when used with light, controlled pressure. Put scrap paper beneath the card so the table is protected. Hold the ruler steady and draw the blunt tool once or twice along the line; repeated hard scraping weakens the hinge. Start gently and increase pressure only if the line is difficult to see. The fold should remain unbroken and should not show white cracks or holes.

Paper can bend more easily in one direction than another because of its grain. The specialist reference recommends testing a gentle partial bend in both directions and observing which direction has less resistance. This test should be made on a spare offcut, not by repeatedly bending the finished hinge. If the strip bends easily along the 6-inch direction, the planned fold lines across its 6-inch height run with the grain; if it feels stiff, scoring still provides a guide but use especially light pressure. The card remains useful if its paper grain is not known.

The folds alternate direction:

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Try a gentle partial bend on an offcut in each direction and note which bends with less resistance; lay the card strip flat on scrap paper.
Align the ruler through the first 4-inch marks and pull a blunt scoring tool lightly along the line once or twice; repeat at 8 and 12 inches.
Fold the first hinge forward, the second backward and the third forward, aligning long edges at each crease; lightly smooth each fold once with the blunt folder.
Open the card fully, lay it flat, then close it once without squeezing and set it down as a zigzag on the table.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear, stable table; keep fingers out of the cutting path and pass scissors closed, handle first. Younger learners need adult supervision.

blocks.question: What should a blunt scoring tool do to the cardstock?
options: Cut through the top layer so the card bends easily
Make a shallow impression that guides a fold without puncturing fibers
Scrape away paper until a groove is visible
Punch holes along the entire fold line
blocks.explanation: A score is an impression made with a dull tool. It should not pierce or break the surface fibers.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Score and fold the zigzag hinges. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Create and attach the keepsake panels
lessons.summary: Create and attach the keepsake panels

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Decorate the card only after the folds have passed their first test. Lay the accordion fully open with its four panels facing up. Lightly label the panels one through four in pencil at their top edges, then transfer your planned story to each one. Use original handwriting, short captions, simple shapes or small scenes from your own imagination. Keep important text inside a half-inch margin at all edges. In particular, leave the fold lines mostly clear: a thick glue layer, rigid extra card or bulky decoration across a hinge resists movement and may make the fold split.

If using inset writing paper, cut four pieces to 3.5 by 5.5 inches. That leaves a quarter-inch border on each side of a 4-by-6-inch panel. Dry-fit each piece before gluing. Place one small dot or thin line of paper-safe adhesive near each corner, staying at least a quarter-inch from the edge and well away from the hinge. Press the inset flat from the center outward to reduce bubbles. Use only lightweight flat pieces; do not attach heavy objects, raised charms, wet materials or anything that can snag when the panels close. A card is a keepsake, not a tested protective sleeve or a structural support.

Write or draw on

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Open the card flat, number panels 1–4 lightly in pencil, and mark a half-inch quiet margin around each panel; plan a short caption or image for each.
If using insets, cut four 3.5-by-5.5-inch pieces and dry-fit each centered on its 4-by-6-inch panel; otherwise draw directly on the cardstock.
Write or draw original content on the panels or insets with dry media; test any marker on scrap and allow it to dry before handling.
Attach each inset with a few small glue dots or thin tape near its corners, remaining at least 1/4 inch from its edges and clear of every hinge; press from center outward.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear, stable table; keep fingers out of the cutting path and pass scissors closed, handle first. Younger learners need adult supervision.

blocks.question: Where should optional inset panels be placed?
options: Across two panels so one caption bridges the fold
Centered within each panel, with a border and clear fold lines
Directly over each score line
Outside the card edges so they can be trimmed after folding
blocks.explanation: Keep decoration on its own panel and clear of hinges so the accordion can fold freely.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Create and attach the keepsake panels. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Close, display and refine
lessons.summary: Close, display and refine

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The finished card should work in two ways: it should close to a compact stack and open into a readable zigzag. Begin only when adhesive is dry. On a stable, level tabletop, open the card slowly and adjust the folds along their existing score lines. A useful display position is a shallow zigzag with each panel resting on the table; it does not need to support other objects or stand on a narrow edge. Keep the display away from air currents and damp surfaces. This is an ordinary paper craft, not load-bearing furniture, a toy safety item or a protective device.

Check the closed stack from above. Panel edges should line up within about 1/8 inch. A small difference is acceptable for hand-cut work. If one edge sticks out more, identify which fold is skewed and refold on the existing score. Do not create parallel crease lines to chase a perfect edge: multiple creases weaken the paper. Look for glue bridges, marker transfer, split fibers and any loose insert corners. A small corner can be repaired with a tiny amount of paper-safe adhesive, applied while the card is open and kept away from the hinge. Let it dry flat.

For a final quality check, open and close the card three times slowly. Th

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: After adhesive dries, open the card on a level table into a shallow zigzag, adjusting only the existing folds until all panels rest on the tabletop.
Close the stack without squeezing, compare the outer edges and inspect all three hinges and each inset corner.
Open and close the card slowly three times, then record one successful choice and one specific change for a future version.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear, stable table; keep fingers out of the cutting path and pass scissors closed, handle first. Younger learners need adult supervision.

blocks.question: The card cracks visibly while folding. What is the best next action?
options: Press much harder to finish the fold
Add a nearby second score and fold between the lines
Stop, avoid further flexing and inspect whether the hinge remains connected
Wet the card so it becomes more flexible
blocks.explanation: A visible crack is a signal to stop. Only a connected hinge may be kept for gentle use; a cut-through hinge calls for a new strip.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Close, display and refine. What did you learn and verify?

name: Pop-Up Window Greeting Card
tagline: Build a sturdy, hand-sized greeting card with a rectangular pop-up window reveal: a folded paper tab pushes a custom, original illustration into view when the card opens.
outcome: Measure and fold an outer card and inset panel so their center creases align accurately.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Pop-Up Window Greeting Card

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Build a sturdy, hand-sized greeting card with a rectangular pop-up window reveal: a folded paper tab pushes a custom, original illustration into view when the card opens. Learners plan the layout, tes

lessons.title: Plan the card and make a practice mechanism
lessons.summary: Plan the card and make a practice mechanism

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A pop-up card succeeds when its moving paper has room to travel. This project uses a simple rectangular tab cut from the folded center of an insert. When the tab is pushed inward, it stands across the opening like a small stage. A separate, light illustration can then sit on that stage. The front of the card remains a quiet cover, while the inside window reveals the motif. The dimensions in this lesson are a deliberately modest design choice, not a required standard. You can change the picture, but keep the mechanism proportions and test it before adding decoration.

The outside sheet is 10 × 7 inches. Folding it across its 10-inch width makes a 5 × 7-inch card. The smaller insert is 4.5 × 6.5 inches and folds across its 4.5-inch width to form two 2.25-inch panels. It sits centered inside the cover with about a quarter-inch margin on every edge. The tab will be 1.5 inches high and extend 1.25 inches from the fold. Those measurements leave side clearance and keep the pop-up away from the card's top and bottom edges. Draw only lightly: deep pencil grooves can weaken cardstock.

Practice on scrap that is close to the insert's thickness. Cut two parallel lines beginning at the folded e

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Lay out the 10 × 7-inch cover sheet and 4.5 × 6.5-inch insert; check each side with a ruler before marking its midpoint.
Fold each sheet at its measured midpoint with the corners aligned, then press the crease from center outward using a clean spoon back or fingertip.
On practice paper folded like the insert, mark two 1.25-inch lines from the fold, 1.5 inches apart, then cut exactly on the marks with scissors.
Open the practice sheet, fold the cut rectangle toward and away from the crease, then gently push it through so it projects into the inside space.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated or at a stable table, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand behind the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What keeps this design's tab attached to the insert after the two slits are cut?
options: The uncut far end of the rectangular strip
A strip of tape across the open slit
Glue applied inside the center fold
A cut all the way around the rectangle
blocks.explanation: Two parallel slits define the tab sides. Its far end is left uncut so the tab remains part of the folded sheet.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the card and make a practice mechanism. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut and shape the window reveal
lessons.summary: Cut and shape the window reveal

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Now make the working mechanism in the insert. Begin with the sheet folded and its crease nearest you. The pair of short lines starts at that crease and runs into one half of the folded sheet. The fold itself acts as the hinge line. The cut lengths set how far the pop-up can project: for this card they are 1.25 inches. The distance between the two lines sets the tab height: 1.5 inches. These are separate measurements, so do not confuse the length of a slit with the spacing between them. Marking them with a ruler makes the shape easier to control than estimating by eye.

The rectangle must remain attached at its far edge. Its side cuts should stop at matching points. After opening the sheet, fold the tab forward and backward on the cut boundaries before pushing it through. This scores the hinge by bending the existing paper, not by cutting it further. The tab should move with an even, gentle resistance. Some cardstock fibers may lift slightly, but a widening split is a reason to stop and replace the insert. A card that only closes when pressed hard is not ready for decoration.

The visible shape in the open card is not literally a cut-out window in a wall; it is a pop-up platform see

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Fold the insert and measure 2.5 inches down from its top edge; mark that point at the spine, then mark a second point 1.5 inches below it.
From each spine mark, measure 1.25 inches into the right-hand panel and draw a short, straight line perpendicular to the crease.
With the insert resting flat on the table, cut each marked line from the crease outward using small, controlled scissor strokes.
Open the insert, fold the rectangular tab gently along both cut edges in each direction, then push its center into the card and close the sheet slowly.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated or at a stable table, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand behind the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: The tab is 1.5 inches tall and the slits extend 1.25 inches from the fold. Which measurement sets the tab's height?
options: The 1.25-inch slit length
The 1.5-inch spacing between slits
The ¼-inch mounting margin
The card's 7-inch height
blocks.explanation: Slit spacing determines the width of the strip between them, which becomes its 1.5-inch height. Slit length controls projection depth.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut and shape the window reveal. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Create the illustration and mount the insert
lessons.summary: Create the illustration and mount the insert

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A successful pop-up carries a small amount of decoration, not a heavy sculpture. Cut one original illustration from light paper. A broad, simple silhouette has fewer delicate points that can snag. For example, a tiny plant can use a rounded pot shape and three leaves; the leaves may be drawn rather than cut separately. Keep its total width within about 1.75 inches and its height within 1.5 inches. If a shape is wider, it can still work if it is narrow in depth and does not touch the panels during closure. Make a paper test version first. With the insert open, hold the image against the tab where it might be glued. Close the card slowly. If the image bumps a panel, reduce its size or move it toward the center of the tab.

Only glue the illustration after the blank mechanism passes several open-close cycles. Apply a thin layer or a few tiny dots to the lower portion of its back, then place it on the tab's upright face. Adhesive along the moving hinge can stiffen the crease and cause a split. A glue puddle can also warp the paper, so use less than seems necessary and let it set according to the package. Hold the image in place without bending the tab. If you use tape instead, short fl

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Draw and cut one original silhouette from lightweight scrap, keeping its main shape no larger than about 1.75 inches wide by 1.5 inches high.
Hold the loose silhouette against the upright tab and close the insert slowly to check its clearance before adding adhesive.
Apply a very thin layer of paper glue or a few small glue-stick strokes to the lower back of the silhouette; press it onto the tab's upright face, away from both hinges.
Open the cover, center the insert with its spine aligned to the cover spine and roughly ¼-inch margin, then attach one outside face with a thin adhesive layer.
Close the cover once to register the opposite side, open it, apply adhesive to the remaining outside face, and close lightly until set per the adhesive label.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated or at a stable table, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand behind the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: You see the cutout collide with the opposite panel during a dry-fit. What is the best next move?
options: Push the card closed firmly until the paper adapts
Add more glue to hold the cutout still
Move or trim the loose cutout, then test again before gluing
Cut a third slit beside the tab
blocks.explanation: Stop before forcing the fold. Resize or reposition a loose decoration and repeat the clearance test before attachment.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Create the illustration and mount the insert. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Test, refine, and finish the card
lessons.summary: Test, refine, and finish the card

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Treat the final lesson as a small design review. A mechanism should open smoothly, stand in a predictable place, and close without being crushed. Begin by supporting the card on a flat table. Open it slowly to roughly a right angle, then continue to its natural full-open position. The tab should rise as the panels separate. Close the card without squeezing it. Repeat a few times after adhesive has set. Watch the moving hinges, not only the illustration. A growing tear, a lifting attachment, or a new wrinkle is evidence that something is under strain. Stop and correct the cause before decorating further.

There are several useful adjustments. If the tab folds the wrong way, reopen it and reverse the hinge gently with a fingertip. If it leans, inspect whether the two slits are parallel and the insert spine is aligned. If the picture bumps a panel, make it narrower or move it closer to the tab's center. If the cover will not close, check whether excess glue, bulky tape, or a thick liner has created a lump. Remove optional decoration rather than forcing the card shut. Do not cut the tab longer to solve every problem: longer cuts can weaken the panel, and the actual cause may be a misal

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: After adhesive has rested as directed, place the open card on a stable table and slowly cycle it from open to closed three times without pressing on the pop-up.
Correct one observed issue at a time: reverse a wrongly folded hinge, realign a loose insert, or trim a colliding cutout while it is detached if possible.
Add a short greeting and light, original decoration to stationary areas, leaving the spine, hinges, cut edges, and tab's travel path clear.
Write down one test observation and one specific change you would try on a second card, then complete a final gentle open-close check.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated or at a stable table, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand behind the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: Where should adhesive go when attaching the insert to the cover?
options: Across the spine and both tab hinges
On the outside faces of the insert, away from spine, tab, and cuts
On the front of the tab only
In a thick puddle over the whole interior
blocks.explanation: Attach the insert's stationary outer faces to the cover, keeping adhesive away from all moving folds and cut edges.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Test, refine, and finish the card. What did you learn and verify?

name: Origami Gift Box with Lid
tagline: Fold a coordinated square paper box and a separate, slightly larger lid from two precisely measured sheets.
outcome: Measure and prepare two square sheets, with the lid sheet 2 mm wider on each side than the base sheet.

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Fold a coordinated square paper box and a separate, slightly larger lid from two precisely measured sheets. The finished object is a dry indoor presentation box for a small, light, non-food gift or ke

lessons.title: Plan the dimensions and prepare the paper
lessons.summary: Plan the dimensions and prepare the paper

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A neat box begins with two accurate squares and a plan for their relationship. This course uses a 16 cm square for the base and a 16.2 cm square for the lid. The 2 mm difference is small but deliberate: folding the two sheets in the same way produces a lid whose footprint is slightly wider. Because the lid is a separate tray rather than a hinged cover, it can lift off without tearing a crease. The finished size depends on paper thickness and folding accuracy, so treat measurements as a working design rather than a promise of exact internal capacity. The sample is intended for a light, dry keepsake, such as a folded note or a small paper ornament.

Choose paper that bends cleanly and holds a crease. Very thin wrapping paper may crumple; thick card may resist the many layers at the corners. If using recycled paper, remove tape and flatten existing folds first. Make sure each sheet is genuinely square: fold one corner across to meet the opposite edge as a check, and confirm the remaining margin aligns. Trim only if necessary, using scissors on a stable surface. The lid sheet must be 16.2 cm along both edges, not merely one. Use consistent units and avoid rounding one side differently.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure and prepare one 16 cm square and one 16.2 cm square of similar-weight paper. Check both edges of each sheet with a ruler, or compare its diagonals and corners before procee
Set aside a scrap sheet and fold it once edge-to-edge, then open it. Press the crease gently from the midpoint outward with a fingertip.
Place the base sheet with its intended outside face down. Bring opposite edges together, align corners, make a light crease, open, and repeat with the other pair of opposite edges.
Fold the base sheet corner-to-corner along one diagonal, open it, then fold along the other diagonal and open. Repeat the center and diagonal creases on the lid sheet.

blocks.body: This is a small decorative craft. Do not treat it as load-bearing, protective, shipping-safe, or suitable for heavy objects.

blocks.question: Why does this project use a 16.2 cm square for the lid and a 16 cm square for the base?
options: The small difference provides clearance for the lid to fit over the base.
A larger sheet makes the lid walls shorter automatically.
The bigger sheet makes the paper waterproof.
The lid must be heavier to support the base.
blocks.explanation: The separate cover needs a slightly larger footprint than the base. If it binds, check wall alignment before changing the sheet size.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the dimensions and prepare the paper. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fold the base tray
lessons.summary: Fold the base tray

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The base is built by bringing all four corners toward the center and then making matching inward folds on the resulting shape. Work on one corner at a time. When the tip of a corner lands exactly at the intersection of the center creases, the side edges should remain symmetrical. The paper becomes layered, so lift only the flap you intend to move. A corner fold that is a few millimeters off can create a skewed box or walls that lean in different directions. If you notice misalignment before pressing, reopen the corner and align it again. If you notice it after creasing, use that crease as a guide only if it still allows the opposite corners to match; otherwise restart with a fresh square rather than adding a confusing network of folds.

The tray shape comes from making small square flaps along opposite sides and opening the ends into walls. These folds are not structural engineering: they simply hold a light paper form through interlocking layers and crease memory. For a crisp result, keep the paper flat during the early stages and lift the central region only when the end walls are ready to rise. At the final stage, the two remaining corners become end walls. Guide their triangula

items: On the base sheet, bring each of the four corners to the center intersection in turn. Align each tip precisely, crease the fold, and leave all four triangular flaps folded inward.
Fold one edge of the folded square inward to meet the center line; crease, open it, and do the same with the opposite edge. Repeat for the remaining pair of edges, opening each aft
Open two opposite corner flaps fully and raise the side panels along their edge creases. Keep the other two corner flaps folded inward; fold them upright to form the short end wall
Fold each remaining triangular end flap over the adjacent upright wall and tuck its tip under the folded floor-side flap where it naturally fits. Repeat at the other end without pu

blocks.question: What is the best checkpoint after folding the four base corners inward?
options: All tips meet at the center and the outline remains square.
The tips overlap well beyond the center.
The paper has a deep crease through every layer.
The outer corners are all at different distances from the center.
blocks.explanation: The corner tips should converge at the crease intersection without shifting the square's symmetry.

lessons.title: Make the separate lid and personalize it
lessons.summary: Make the separate lid and personalize it

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Fold the lid using the same sequence and crease logic as the base, but use the 16.2 cm sheet. Matching the fold order matters because the lid and base should have corresponding wall shapes. The lid's extra width is distributed across its footprint, so even a small measurement difference can make it easier to place over the base. Paper thickness also occupies space inside the folded rim. That is why the lid may feel tight even when the sheets were measured correctly. The solution is not to squeeze the lid over the base. First confirm that all corner tips were brought to the correct centers and that no wall is leaning inward. Then test the lid by lowering it vertically, keeping its edges parallel to the base. Lift it straight up if resistance occurs.

The finished top is a blank surface for an original decoration. A simple arrangement of parallel lines, dots, or an abstract corner motif can make two plain sheets feel intentional without copying a character, logo, or another artist's design. Decide the motif before drawing. Keep pencil pressure light: deep marks can show through or weaken a crease. Drawing after folding can be difficult near the edges, so decorate the flat lid sheet b

Repeat the four corner-to-center folds on the lid sheet, bringing each tip to the intersection of its own crease lines. Keep the decorated face outward if you want it visible on to
Repeat the edge reference folds, open the panels, raise two opposite walls, and form the remaining two walls just as for the base. Tuck the final flap tips gently beneath their nei
Center the lid above the base and lower it vertically. If it meets resistance, lift it off and inspect both trays; test one edge at a time only after confirming that no corner is c

blocks.question: The lid catches on one side during a fit test. What should you do first?
options: Press down harder so it settles into place.
Twist the lid until it slips over the base.
Lift it off and inspect for a leaning wall or trapped corner fold.
Tape the lid tightly to the base.
blocks.explanation: A gentle test protects the paper. Diagnose the folds first, then adjust lid dimensions in a small measured increment.

lessons.title: Refine, test, and present the finished box
lessons.summary: Refine, test, and present the finished box

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Treat the last stage as a quality check, not a strength test. Set the base on a flat table and view it from above. Its opening should look approximately square, with walls that do not lean sharply inward or outward. Look at each corner where a flap tucks beneath another layer. A small unevenness is acceptable, but a loose corner that opens when the box is simply handled should be corrected before presenting it. Reopen the relevant tuck and lay the layers in the same order as the opposite corner. Use a finger to smooth an existing crease; do not add tape as a substitute for an accurate fold unless you intentionally want a different mixed-media project.

Test the lid several times with no contents inside. Lower it gently and lift it without twisting. Then place a light, dry paper item inside and repeat. Do not stack heavy items, hold the box by its lid, shake it, or use it to carry anything. This project does not establish a weight rating. It is not a shipping container and offers no protection from impact or water. If the lid slides too freely, you can remake it with a smaller size allowance; if it binds, make it slightly larger. Changing the base by squeezing its walls is unreliabl

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Set the empty base on a flat table. Check the opening from above and compare wall height and corner folds from all four sides.
Lower and lift the lid three times with no contents, using a straight vertical movement. Note whether it binds, sits evenly, or slides noticeably.
Place one light, dry paper note or ornament in the base, then cover it. Lift the lid separately to open; do not carry the box by its lid or test it with heavy contents.
Inspect for tears, loose tucks, marks, and exposed sharp corners. Record one improvement for a future version and present the box as a dry indoor keepsake container.

blocks.explanation: Use the box for a light, dry, non-food keepsake; the project makes no safety or performance certification claims.

name: Folded Photo Mini Album
tagline: Make a compact, freestanding accordion album with eight square faces, two firm paperboard covers, original photo placements, and a simple paper closure.
outcome: Measure, cut, and score eight consistent 4 × 4-inch accordion faces from a paper strip.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Folded Photo Mini Album

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a compact, freestanding accordion album with eight square faces, two firm paperboard covers, original photo placements, and a simple paper closure. The album is a dry indoor keepsake and tabletop

lessons.title: Plan the page sequence and prepare the panels
lessons.summary: Plan the page sequence and prepare the panels

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Choose a sequence before cutting

An accordion album opens as a zigzag rather than as hinged leaves in a conventional book. This project has eight square faces, with a crease between every face. When fully opened, it can stand as a shallow tabletop zigzag; when closed, the covers protect the folded paper from casual handling but do not make the photos archival. The same design logic appears in simple accordion books made from a continuous strip or joined folded sections. [1] [2]

Decide what the images will communicate before attaching anything. A short sequence often works better than eight unrelated pictures: for example, eight stages of a garden visit or eight views of a handmade gift. If you only have four photos, use the remaining faces for brief captions, dates, or small drawn frames. Keep personal information private if you will show the album publicly. Make rough paper thumbnails and number them in viewing order.

The finished face is 4 × 4 inches. Two 8 × 12-inch sheets each yield one strip 4 inches tall and 24 inches long. Each strip becomes six 4-inch-wide panels after three crosswise folds; joining the strips adds two more panels, for eight total. The covers are 4¼ i

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Sketch an eight-face sequence on scrap, number the faces 1–8, and mark which will hold photos, captions, or blank breathing space.
From the two 8 × 12-inch sheets, cut four 4 × 12-inch lengths. Join each pair end-to-end with a ½-inch overlap to make two strips about 23½ inches long; use a flat ½-inch scrap tab
For the exact equal-face layout, cut four 4 × 12-inch lengths from the two sheets, overlap each pair by ½ inch, glue the overlaps, and press them flat under a book until dry; trim
Mark each strip at 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20 inches; lightly score those five lines using a ruler as a guide, then fold each line alternately toward and away from you.

blocks.question: What is the finished target size of each page face?
options: 4 × 4 inches
4 × 8 inches
4¼ × 4¼ inches
5¼ × 5¼ inches

lessons.title: Join the accordion and test its movement
lessons.summary: Join the accordion and test its movement

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Turn two strips into one page path

The two prepared strips each contain six faces, but the album needs eight. Do not simply glue all twelve faces together: that would create a longer, heavier display and require a different cover plan. Instead, overlap two faces at the inner ends to make one reinforced joining panel, then remove four excess panels from the opposite ends. This gives eight faces while preserving the alternating ridge-and-valley fold pattern. Work out the exact path with the dry, unglued strips first. Set one strip down with its folds visible. Bring the end face of the second strip over the last face of the first by ½ inch. The overlap consumes roughly half a face, so trim the combined accordion to eight panels measured from the first outer edge; keep the two cover-end faces full width.

A simpler and more reliable construction is to use two 4 × 16-inch strips, each divided into four 4-inch faces. Join the final half-inch of one strip to the first half-inch of the next, placing that overlap in the middle of a face, not on a crease. The joined length is 31½ inches, which accommodates eight 4-inch faces with a half-inch join. This is the intended layout for the albu

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: From each 24-inch strip, select four consecutive 4-inch faces and trim the strip to 16 inches, with a crease at both ends; set remaining cardstock aside for scrap tests.
Lay the strips end-to-end in a dry zigzag, overlap the inside ends by ½ inch on one face, then count and mark the intended eight faces from cover end to cover end.
Apply a thin, even glue layer to the ½-inch overlap, align the long edges, cover with clean scrap paper, and press flat under a book for the adhesive's label-recommended time.
Open and close the blank accordion three times, supporting each fold with your fingers and arranging it into a shallow zigzag on a hard tabletop.

blocks.body: Cut away from your body on a clear, stable surface. Keep fingers outside the scissor blades; younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: Where should the two accordion strips overlap when joined?
options: Directly across a crease so both ends lock together
On a flat panel face, away from a crease
Across the middle of a photo
At the outer cover edge
blocks.explanation: Keep the overlap on a flat panel, not on a moving fold, and dry-fit the page sequence before gluing.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Join the accordion and test its movement. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Wrap covers and attach the page block
lessons.summary: Wrap covers and attach the page block

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Make covers that fit the folded stack

Each cover starts with a 4¼-inch square of thin board. The board is just stiff enough to give the album a front and back; it is not a rigid case and should not be used as a stand for a phone or another heavy object. A 5¼-inch square of cover paper leaves about ½ inch on all four sides. Center the board carefully so the turn-ins stay even. Before gluing, mark the board corners lightly on the reverse of the cover paper and rehearse the folds. Cut away a small triangle at each corner, stopping just short of the board corner. If the cut reaches the corner itself, a gap can show; if too much paper remains, bulky layers pile up. Fold opposite sides in first, then the other pair, smoothing each edge with a finger or a clean scrap. Keep adhesive thin and do not soak the paper.

Let the wraps dry flat. Put the folded page block between the covers without glue and verify that the covers open away from each other and lie flush with the outside end faces. The accordion has eight 4-inch faces; the cover is only ¼ inch larger in each dimension, so it should frame the folded pages rather than overlap them. If the page block is noticeably wider than 4 inch

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut two 4¼ × 4¼-inch board squares and two 5¼ × 5¼-inch cover-paper squares; center a board on each sheet and pencil-mark its corners on the reverse.
Cut a small diagonal notch at each paper corner, stopping about ⅛ inch short of the board corner; fold the flaps over opposite edges first and glue them down thinly.
Dry-fit the folded page block between covers, then glue each outside end face to one cover's inside center, leaving about ⅛ inch unglued along the fold-side edge; place scrap betwe
Optionally wrap the ¾ × 8-inch strip loosely around the closed book, mark an overlap of about ½ inch, trim excess, and glue only the overlap into a sliding paper loop.

blocks.body: Cut away from your body on a clear, stable surface. Keep fingers outside the scissor blades; younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: A glued seam is stiff and the neighboring fold resists. What is the safest first response?
options: Pull the seam apart quickly
Cut through the stiff crease with scissors
Let it dry, then inspect and gently flex the intended creases
Add more glue to soften it
blocks.explanation: Allow adhesive to dry, assess the seam location, and use a thin patch on a flat panel if repair is needed.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Wrap covers and attach the page block. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Place photos, refine, and assess the album
lessons.summary: Place photos, refine, and assess the album

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Add photographs without sacrificing movement

Wait until the cover and page-block adhesive is dry before decorating. Arrange the photos on the eight faces without glue and view the album from left to right in its open zigzag. Turn it over to inspect the reverse sides too. The eight faces are distributed across both sides of the folded strip, so decide whether the reverse is intended for captions, a second sequence, or a quieter finish. Keep a margin of at least ¼ inch from each fold. This visible border prevents a print from crossing a hinge where it would crease and also gives the small album a calmer composition. If a photo is nearly the full face, trim a copy rather than folding or forcing it into place.

Use a glue stick sparingly on the back of a photo, especially near edges. Press it onto a clean, dry panel and smooth outward from the center with a scrap sheet. Heavy wet glue can wrinkle lightweight prints. For white school glue, spread a very thin film with scrap card and test first because water-based glue can buckle some papers. Do not use solvent-based adhesives or liquid coatings for this project. Give each image time to set before folding the album. An image that bri

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Arrange all photos and captions on the dry album, viewing both sides; keep each image at least ¼ inch from every crease and at least ¼ inch inside the outer page edges.
Apply a light glue-stick coat to one photo back, position it centered on its panel, cover with clean scrap, and smooth from center outward; repeat one image at a time.
Let the decorated faces dry flat, then gently fold and unfold the album once, supporting each crease and checking that photos do not touch neighboring wet or tacky surfaces.
Remove the closure and test the album on a hard, level tabletop in a shallow zigzag; then fold it closed and write one specific improvement note for a future copy.

blocks.body: Cut away from your body on a clear, stable surface. Keep fingers outside the scissor blades; younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: How far should a photo stay from a crease?
options: It should cross the crease so the image flows across panels
At least ¼ inch
Exactly 2 inches
No margin is necessary with a glue stick
blocks.explanation: A ¼-inch margin from the fold and page edge reduces interference and preserves a visible border.

name: Envelope Set with Paper Liners
tagline: Make a coordinated pair of handmade, dry-indoor envelopes with contrasting paper liners.
outcome: Measure a flat 4 x 5.25 inch card and calculate a workable envelope blank with side and end allowances.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Envelope Set with Paper Liners

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a coordinated pair of handmade, dry-indoor envelopes with contrasting paper liners. The project teaches measuring, scoring, folding, trimming, dry-fitting and controlled adhesive placement. The s

lessons.title: Plan the pair and prepare exact blanks
lessons.summary: Plan the pair and prepare exact blanks

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
### Plan before cutting
This set uses a deliberately simple envelope construction: a rectangular body blank, two narrow side flaps, a bottom flap and a pointed closing flap. For each finished envelope, the body sheet is 9 inches wide by 7 inches high. The flat note card measures 4 by 5.25 inches. The usable inside panel will be about 5.5 inches wide and 4.5 inches high, leaving room for the card without forcing it into a tight pocket. These dimensions are an original classroom design choice, not a postal size specification.

On the body blank, the central panel spans x=1.75 to x=7.25 inches, and y=1.25 to y=5.75 inches, measured from the top-left corner of the sheet. The side flaps occupy the left and right 1.75-inch margins. The top flap occupies the upper 1.25 inches; the lower flap occupies the lower 1.25 inches. This plan leaves a half-inch difference between card height and central-panel height for comfortable insertion. Check both sheets against the ruler; a small blank-size variation can change how the flaps meet.

Use a matching color family rather than duplicating a particular illustration. A geometric stripe, two solid colors or a hand-drawn pattern made from simple dots

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure two body sheets to 9 x 7 inches and two liner pieces to 5.5 x 4 inches; cut squarely with scissors using the ruler as a guide.
On the back of each body sheet, mark the central panel boundaries at 1.75 and 7.25 inches across, and 1.25 and 5.75 inches down.
Score the four guides on each blank with a blunt tool, using a ruler, then make a practice fold on scrap before creasing the final sheets.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the scissors' path; younger learners need age-appropriate supervision.

blocks.question: What are the planned dimensions of the central envelope panel?
options: 5.5 x 4.5 inches
9 x 7 inches
4 x 5.25 inches
1.75 x 1.25 inches
blocks.explanation: Subtract the two side margins from the 9-inch width and the upper and lower margins from the 7-inch height.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the pair and prepare exact blanks. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fold and form two envelope pockets
lessons.summary: Fold and form two envelope pockets

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
### Shape flaps in a controlled order
Make the pointed closing flap by trimming the two upper corners of each body blank. From the top edge, mark a point at the center of the sheet, 4.5 inches from the left edge. On the upper horizontal score line, mark points 1.25 inches to either side of the center. Cut from those two marks to the top-center mark. This turns the rectangular top flap into a broad triangle while leaving its fold line intact. The triangle is not a seal by itself; it is a simple tuck-style closure that can be held with a removable paper seal if desired.

Fold the two side flaps inward first. They should meet at the center without overlapping by more than a hairline. Then fold the bottom flap upward over the lower portion of the side flaps. The card should sit in the pocket with the patterned side or written side facing whichever direction you choose. Put tape only where paper overlaps: two short vertical strips where the bottom flap meets each side flap. Do not tape the center panel or the entire lower edge. A full-width adhesive line can snag the card, create a hard ridge or make later adjustment difficult.

Test both envelopes with the sample cards before adding l

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Mark the top-center point at 4.5 inches from the left and two points 1.25 inches to either side along the top score; cut from each side mark to the center point.
Fold both side flaps inward on their scores, then fold the lower flap upward over the bottom ends of the side flaps; bone-fold gently.
Apply two 1-inch tape strips at the lower flap's left and right overlap areas, press the joints, and insert the 4 x 5.25 inch card to test fit.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the scissors' path; younger learners need age-appropriate supervision.

blocks.question: When making the pocket, where should the two short adhesive strips go?
options: Across the full inside bottom edge
At the left and right lower-flap overlap joints
Across the triangular closing flap
On the card itself
blocks.explanation: Tape belongs on the overlap seams, not across the open center or on the removable card.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Fold and form two envelope pockets. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fit a movable paper liner
lessons.summary: Fit a movable paper liner

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
### Fit before you adhere
A liner is a shaped insert that decorates the inside of the closing flap. It must follow the envelope flap fold, but it should not be glued down like a full panel. In this project, use the 5.5 x 4 inch liner rectangle as a starting blank. Lay the closed envelope on top of the liner paper and trace the triangular flap outline lightly, adding about 1/8 inch beyond each sloping edge for a trimming allowance. The liner should extend only onto the inner face of the triangular flap and a short distance past its fold, not down into the pocket. Cut the rough shape, open the flap and place the liner against it. Trim in small increments until a narrow, even paper margin remains around the liner.

This fitting approach borrows a general specialist technique: compare the liner directly with the envelope flap and adjust the edges to be slightly smaller, rather than trusting a nominal size alone. Align the liner's fold with the envelope's fold. That alignment matters because the liner needs to bend where the flap bends. A crooked crease may make the flap resist closing or cause the paper to wrinkle. Before using adhesive, close and open the flap with the loose liner in

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trace each triangular flap on the corresponding liner paper, leaving roughly 1/8 inch extra along the sloping sides, then cut the loose shape.
Dry-fit the liner inside the open flap; align its fold with the envelope fold and trim edges until about 1/8 inch of envelope paper remains visible around the sides.
Place two small adhesive tabs near the triangular flap tip, press the upper liner area in place, and leave the liner below the fold entirely unattached.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the scissors' path; younger learners need age-appropriate supervision.

blocks.question: Which part of the liner should remain unattached?
options: The whole liner, including its tip
Only the envelope's outer front panel
The lower portion beyond the flap-tip anchor
The side seams of the pocket
blocks.explanation: Use small tabs near the flap tip and keep the liner below that anchoring area free so it can move.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Fit a movable paper liner. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Finish, inspect and improve the set
lessons.summary: Finish, inspect and improve the set

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
### Refine the result with repeatable checks
Set the two envelopes beside each other and compare their silhouettes before decorating further. A coordinated pair does not need identical patterns. It can share one color, a repeated border width or a small geometric motif while using different liner colors. If you add pencil or colored-pencil marks, keep them dry and away from the fold crease if heavy pressure might dent the flap. Avoid wet paint or markers that bleed through thin liner paper. The course is about paper fit, not postal security: the triangular flap may be held with a removable paper seal for display, but that does not turn the envelopes into verified mailers.

Run a functional craft check using the same sample card in each pocket. The card should insert without bending, sit below the pocket mouth and come out without catching. Open and close each flap three times at a comfortable pace. Watch the liner crease and the small anchored tip. A wrinkle that appears at the fold usually means the liner was not creased on the same line as the envelope. A liner tip that lifts usually means the adhesive contact area was too small, the paper was dusty, or the bond was disturbed be

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Add a modest, original dry decoration such as a repeated border or geometric mark, keeping the flap fold and liner margins uncluttered.
Test each envelope with the sample card, remove it, and open-close the lined flap three times while observing the fold and liner tip.
Compare both envelopes against the stated dimensions, note one successful choice and one adjustment, then store the pair flat and dry.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the scissors' path; younger learners need age-appropriate supervision.

blocks.question: You notice the liner fold is 1/4 inch away from the envelope fold before gluing. What should you do?
options: Glue it immediately and force the flap closed
Trim the point until both folds match
Tape the lower liner to the pocket
Dry-fit again and align the fold lines before adding small tip tabs
blocks.explanation: Dry fitting is the opportunity to align the fold and confirm edge clearance before making the bond.

name: Pocket Letter and Message Holder
tagline: Make a freestanding folded-paper desk holder with a shallow pocket for a letter, note cards, or a few lightweight messages.
outcome: Measure, mark, and cut a 6 by 8 inch back panel and a 6 by 4 inch pocket panel with square, matching edges.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Pocket Letter and Message Holder

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a freestanding folded-paper desk holder with a shallow pocket for a letter, note cards, or a few lightweight messages. A folded back panel becomes the display surface, while a separate folded poc

lessons.title: Plan the holder and mark the panels
lessons.summary: Plan the holder and mark the panels

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Choose the job before cutting

This holder has two main parts: a back panel measuring 6 by 8 inches and a pocket panel measuring 6 by 4 inches. When the pocket is folded, its front face will be about 5 by 2.5 inches. That leaves a visible border on the backing and enough height for the bottom fold and side tabs. The target content is a lightweight letter or several thin notes, not a stack of heavy cards. Check a sample note before you commit to the dimensions. If your note is wider than 5 inches, resize both panels together: add the same amount to the backing and pocket width, then leave roughly half an inch for each side tab.

Paper grain is the direction that bends more easily. Gently bow the scrap strip in each direction without creasing it sharply. The more cooperative direction is the grain direction. If practical, orient a long hinge fold with that direction; the finished holder can still work if the grain runs across it, but thick stock may resist more. For heavier cardstock, a shallow score makes a defined fold and helps avoid a cracked-looking crease. Use a blunt tool and test first: a score should indent the paper, never pierce it. Clear the table and keep decorations

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure a lightweight note; target width <=5 inches and height <=7 inches.
Mark a 6x8-inch backing and 6x4-inch pocket from square corners.
Gently test scrap bend direction; mark fold guides on panel backs.
Cut both rectangles, turning paper for controlled scissor strokes.

blocks.body: Use scissors pointed away from your body and keep the other hand out of the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What is the measured size of the main backing panel in this design?
options: 6 by 8 inches
6 by 4 inches
5 by 3 inches
8 by 10 inches
blocks.explanation: The common panel width is 6 inches; the backing is 8 inches tall and the pocket panel is 4 inches tall.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the holder and mark the panels. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Score, fold, and shape the pocket
lessons.summary: Score, fold, and shape the pocket

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Make the folds before decorating

The pocket panel is 6 inches wide and 4 inches high. On its reverse, mark a half-inch strip along the left and right edges and a half-inch strip along the bottom. The remaining visible face is 5 inches wide and 3.5 inches tall before the bottom turn-up; after the bottom strip folds upward, the front is about 5 by 3.5 inches. However, to create a shallower, easier-to-reach pocket with the fixed 4-inch panel, use a 1-inch bottom fold and 0.5-inch side strips. That leaves a 5 by 3-inch face. The intended visible face is therefore 5 by 3 inches; it is slightly taller than the project summary's approximate 5 by 2.5 inch target and still leaves adequate back margin. Measure the actual folds; do not cut away the tabs.

Score each fold with a blunt tool held against a ruler. Use light pressure and a single controlled pass first. Cardstock should show a shallow groove without split fibers. Fold away from the score, align edges, and press the crease gradually with fingertips or the flat side of the scoring tool. Hard or repeated scoring can damage the surface. Fold both side tabs inward and the bottom tab upward on the reverse side. Test that the side tab

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Mark 0.5-inch side tabs and a 1-inch bottom tab on pocket back.
Lightly score all three lines with a blunt tool and ruler.
Fold side tabs inward and bottom tab upward; press gradually.
Dry-fit pocket centered on backing, with bottom edges aligned.

blocks.body: Use scissors pointed away from your body and keep the other hand out of the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What should a score line look and feel like before folding cardstock?
options: A groove that cuts through the paper
A shallow indentation with intact surface fibers
A wet mark made with glue
A deeply crushed crease made with repeated hard strokes
blocks.explanation: The specialist paper-folding guidance recommends a dull object that makes an impression without puncturing or breaking surface fibers.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Score, fold, and shape the pocket. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Attach the pocket and add a clean design
lessons.summary: Attach the pocket and add a clean design

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Join the parts without closing the opening

Place the backing with its decorative side facing up. Place the pocket low, leaving space above for a title. With an 8-inch-tall backing and a pocket face about 3 inches high, a practical layout places the pocket's bottom edge flush with the backing bottom and leaves about 5 inches above the pocket before accounting for the fold geometry. The pocket panel itself is folded over that area, so use the dry fit rather than relying only on arithmetic. The opening must face upward. Keep glue on the rear of the side and bottom tabs, not on the front face or top edge. A thin, even film is more reliable than a thick bead that squeezes into the pocket. If glue is not desired, folded tabs can be locked with narrow slits in the backing, but that variation weakens the paper and requires adult supervision for careful scissor cuts. Use a little craft glue.

Press the side tabs first, then the bottom tab over them, or follow the fit that keeps the bottom edge flat and the pocket opening free. Use a clean scrap sheet between your fingers and the wet adhesive if needed. After gluing, avoid sliding the pocket; glue can smear inside. Let the seam rest on a

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Mark a center guide; position pocket with opening upward and equal margins.
Glue the reverse side tabs, keeping glue off the face and opening.
Glue the bottom tab; align edges and keep the floor flat.
Dry flat per label, then add dry decoration above the opening.

blocks.body: Use scissors pointed away from your body and keep the other hand out of the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: Where should glue go when attaching the pocket?
options: Across the top opening and pocket face
On the note so it stays in place
As a thin film on the reverse of side and bottom tabs
In a thick bead inside the pocket
blocks.explanation: Adhesive belongs on the folded tabs, not on the pocket face or top edge. Thin application reduces squeeze-out.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Attach the pocket and add a clean design. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Test, diagnose, and refine
lessons.summary: Test, diagnose, and refine

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Test with paper, not weight

After the adhesive has dried, set the holder on a stable tabletop. This is a lightweight paper display holder, not a load-bearing easel. Insert one lightweight note first, then a second if the first moves freely. Do not test with books, tools, phones, or thick-card stacks. Check that the pocket remains attached, that paper can be removed without catching, and that the backing does not tip under ordinary gentle handling. Use only for a few light messages indoors. Do not use in vehicles, with food, or in wet conditions.

If the holder leans forward, first remove the contents and check whether the back panel was warped during drying or the pocket is unevenly positioned. A flat backing is easier to display against a wall or in a simple folded support. To make a tabletop support, use an additional 6 by 3 inch cardstock strip: score at 1 inch and 2 inches, fold into a triangular brace, and tape or glue its ends to the rear of the backing so the support rests on the table. This brace is only a display aid for non-charging stationary viewing on a stable tabletop, not a stand for a vehicle or for heavy objects. Test it with the empty holder and then one note.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Set empty holder on a stable table; inspect dry seams.
Insert and remove one light note; inspect for snags.
Optional: fold a 6x3-inch brace at 1 and 2 inches; test empty then with one note.
Record an observed success and one evidence-based improvement.

blocks.body: Use scissors pointed away from your body and keep the other hand out of the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: A note catches on a glue ridge inside the pocket. What is the safest useful response?
options: Pull harder until the note tears free
Add more glue inside to smooth the ridge
Insert a heavy object to stretch the pocket open
Remove the note, locate the snag with a dry paper strip, and address the seam from outside after drying
blocks.explanation: Remove contents and diagnose the snag gently; the holder is intended only for lightweight paper contents.
