name: Paper Corner Bookmarks
tagline: Make a reusable, dry-indoor paper bookmark that slips over a page corner.
outcome: Measure and cut a true 12 cm by 12 cm square, identifying and correcting unequal sides before folding.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Paper Corner Bookmarks

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a reusable, dry-indoor paper bookmark that slips over a page corner. The course teaches a reliable pocket fold using a 12 cm square, checks fit in an actual book, and develops an original, non-ch

lessons.title: Plan a square that will fold cleanly
lessons.summary: Plan a square that will fold cleanly

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A corner bookmark is a small pocket that grips the corner of a page. Its fit depends on two things: the width of the starting square and how accurately the diagonal folds meet. This lesson uses a 12 cm square as a practical starting point. The number is a design choice for this course, not a universal size; books and paper thickness vary. A smaller 10 cm square may suit a slim paperback, while a larger 13–14 cm square may cover more of a broad page corner. Make the first sample at 12 cm so later adjustments have a known reference.

Check the paper before measuring. Thin printer paper is easy to fold but can soften quickly, while very thick card may resist the tucked layers. Uncoated paper in the approximate 90–120 gsm range is a manageable beginner choice. If only thin paper is available, keep the creases crisp and avoid repeated unfolding. Use a spare square for a practice sample instead of trying to rescue a badly crushed sheet.

A square has four equal sides and right-angle corners. Measure two perpendicular edges from the same corner; mark 12 cm on each, then connect the endpoints. Measure the resulting sides before cutting. If you are using paper that already has one straight

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Clear a flat table and place the paper, ruler, pencil, scissors, and optional scrap sheet within reach; choose one 12 cm square and a spare practice square.
On the reverse of a larger sheet, mark 12 cm along one edge and 12 cm along an adjacent edge, then join the marks with a light pencil line.
With the sheet flat on the table, cut slowly along the guide using appropriate scissors, keeping fingers away from the blade path; alternatively ask an adult to cut it.
Measure each side and compare opposite sides; mark the paper’s reverse lightly with an arrow so you can remember which side you want on the outside.

blocks.body: Work seated at a clear table. Keep scissors closed when not cutting, use them only for the paper in this project, and do not walk or gesture while holding them. Pass closed scissors handle-first; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What is the best first check before folding the course’s 12 cm square?
options: Confirm the four sides are close to equal and the corners are square.
Coat the sheet with glue so it cannot move.
Cut a notch in every corner.
Fold it into a rectangle first.
blocks.explanation: Equal side lengths and a stable square shape give the diagonal fold the best chance to align.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan a square that will fold cleanly. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build the diagonal and the pocket
lessons.summary: Build the diagonal and the pocket

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The bookmark’s structure comes from a diagonal triangle and two tucked corners. Work with the square turned like a diamond, with one corner pointing toward you. Fold the far corner down to meet the near corner so the square becomes a triangle. Match the tips precisely before pressing the crease. A crease made while corners are offset will not become centered just because it is pressed harder. Lift and realign once if necessary; repeated hard rubbing can thin or tear paper.

For the next folds, keep the triangle’s long edge nearest you and its point facing away. Bring each lower side corner up to the top point, one at a time, to establish two diagonal guide creases. Open both back out. These guides locate the pocket sides and help the two flaps sit symmetrically. Fold only the top layer’s far tip down to the long lower edge. This creates a horizontal band or pocket lip. Do not fold all layers down together: that would close the pocket instead of forming an opening.

The two side corners now fold upward again and tuck beneath the lip. Insert each tip into the pocket rather than simply laying it on top. Keep the centre seam aligned, then press the layered shape flat. If the first tip

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Turn the square so it looks like a diamond and fold the far corner down to meet the near corner, matching the points before creasing across the middle.
With the triangle’s long edge toward you and point away, fold the left lower corner up to the far point, crease, then repeat on the right; open both side folds again.
Fold only the top layer’s far point down to the midpoint of the long lower edge, creating a flap that lies across the triangle.
Fold the left side corner upward and tuck its tip inside the new pocket; repeat on the right, align the centre, and press the bookmark flat.

blocks.body: Work seated at a clear table. Keep scissors closed when not cutting, use them only for the paper in this project, and do not walk or gesture while holding them. Pass closed scissors handle-first; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: Which fold creates the pocket lip?
options: Glue both side corners flat to the triangle.
Fold only the top layer’s far point down to the long lower edge.
Fold every layer down at once and seal the bottom.
Cut away the triangle’s point.
blocks.explanation: The top layer becomes the lip; the side corners tuck under it to create the open pocket.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build the diagonal and the pocket. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Test fit and decorate without blocking the pocket
lessons.summary: Test fit and decorate without blocking the pocket

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A bookmark that looks neat on the table may still be too loose or too tight on a real page corner, so test before decorating. Open the pocket gently with a fingertip and slide it over one corner of a book page. Hold the book still and turn the page once. The bookmark should remain in place under ordinary page handling without requiring the paper corner to be bent sharply. Do not tug hard or test by shaking the book. This small paper object is a page marker, not a clamp or a device that protects a book.

Fit can vary because page dimensions, paper thickness, and the accuracy of the square all vary. If it slips off a thin page, check that both side tips are tucked and the central folds are even. Try a second page or a small stack of up to ten loose pages. If it remains loose, make a fresh sample using a slightly smaller square, such as 11 cm. If the pocket pinches or creases the page, first make sure the page enters straight; then try a larger 13 cm square on a new sample. Do not cut or force the finished pocket to adjust it.

Choose an original design that works with the folded triangle. A simple border, alternating dots, a small abstract sun, or a leaf made from basic shapes is eno

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Open the pocket gently and place it over one page corner without bending the page; turn that page once at normal speed.
Try the bookmark on a thin page and on a stack of up to ten loose pages; note whether it feels loose, comfortable, or tight.
If the fit is wrong, make a new sample from an 11 cm square for a loose thin-page fit or a 13 cm square for a tight fit; preserve the same fold sequence.
Sketch a flat original motif on the outer face, keeping at least the lower pocket opening and tucked edges free of marks or glued pieces.

blocks.body: Work seated at a clear table. Keep scissors closed when not cutting, use them only for the paper in this project, and do not walk or gesture while holding them. Pass closed scissors handle-first; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: The bookmark slips off a thin page. What should you do first?
options: Shake the book harder to test it.
Glue the page into the pocket.
Inspect whether both tips are tucked and folds are even, then test a fresh 11 cm square if needed.
Fold the page corner sharply so it grips.
blocks.explanation: A loose fit may come from an untucked tip or an oversized square; diagnose gently and adjust a new sample.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Test fit and decorate without blocking the pocket. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Finish, refine, and assess the bookmark
lessons.summary: Finish, refine, and assess the bookmark

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Finish the surface with light, deliberate marks. Pencil first if the design is complex, then add color in a thin layer. Paper can buckle if it is rubbed repeatedly, so build color with a few gentle passes and let the sheet rest flat between passes. Do not coat the bookmark with liquid or claim that a marker or adhesive makes it waterproof. The finished piece is intended for dry indoor use. If using an optional paper accent, test one tiny scrap with the glue stick; if the paper wrinkles, skip the accent and draw the motif instead.

Assemble any accent on the broad front face only. Apply a small swipe of adhesive to the back of the 2 cm accent, press briefly onto the paper, and wipe away residue before it dries only if the label permits and using a dry scrap. Keep adhesive away from the pocket mouth and do not put wet work into a book. Allow full label-directed drying. A dry, flat attachment should not lift when touched lightly at its edge. If it curls, remove it gently before the glue sets or leave it and use the drawn-only version for the next piece; pulling a firmly attached scrap may tear the base.

Run a final usability check: the pocket remains open, both tips stay tucked, the

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Draw the chosen motif with light, controlled strokes on the outer face, or attach one flat paper accent no larger than 2 cm × 2 cm using a small amount of glue stick.
Let any adhesive dry fully according to its label; keep the bookmark out of the book until the accent is dry and flat.
Repeat the gentle page-corner fit test and one page turn, then inspect the tucked tips, opening, and paper edges.
Write down one successful choice and one adjustment you would make on a second bookmark; store the finished piece flat and dry.

blocks.body: Work seated at a clear table. Keep scissors closed when not cutting, use them only for the paper in this project, and do not walk or gesture while holding them. Pass closed scissors handle-first; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: Where may an optional glued accent go?
options: Across the pocket opening, to keep it shut.
Inside the book against the page, while wet.
Across a crease and both tucked tips, using a thick layered stack.
Flat on the broad outer face, away from the opening, using a small amount of glue stick.
blocks.explanation: Decoration belongs on the outside face and should stay flat, small, and clear of the opening.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Finish, refine, and assess the bookmark. What did you learn and verify?

name: Layered Paper Landscape Card
tagline: Build a freestanding-looking but non-structural paper landscape on a folded greeting card.
outcome: Measure and fold a 10 × 7 inch card blank into a 5 × 7 inch card with a clean, aligned crease.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Layered Paper Landscape Card

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Build a freestanding-looking but non-structural paper landscape on a folded greeting card. Cut a sequence of overlapping hills, attach them with thin foam spacers, and control the silhouette so the di

lessons.title: Plan the card and prepare a reliable fold
lessons.summary: Plan the card and prepare a reliable fold

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A layered card succeeds when its quiet parts are measured first. The outer base carries every scene layer, so an inaccurate fold can make the front look off-center even when the hills are beautifully cut. This course uses a 10 × 7 inch blank folded across its 10-inch width at the midpoint: the finished face is 5 inches wide and 7 inches tall. Before cutting anything, decide that the landscape will sit in a 4 × 5.5 inch window, centered on the front with a half-inch margin at both sides and three-quarter-inch margins at top and bottom. Those margins leave breathing room and keep the raised edges away from the card's outside edge.

Check paper grain if the sheet bends easily. Gently bow it in both directions without making a sharp crease; the direction that bends with less resistance is usually along the grain. A fold along the easier direction tends to behave better, but scoring also helps heavier stock. Use a blunt tool and ruler to make a shallow channel, not a cut. If there is no scoring board, place the ruler at the measured fold and draw the blunt tool along it on a protected table. Fold the card so the scored indentation is inside the fold, then press from the center outward.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure a 10 × 7 in rectangle on the card base, check both diagonals visually with the ruler, and trim the edges with scissors if needed.
Find the midpoint at 5 in along the 10 in edge. Place a ruler through the two marks and make one light blunt score, then fold along the line.
On a practice sheet, draw a 4 × 5.5 in window and mark a horizon, a high distant ridge, two middle hills, and a low foreground curve.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and keep the non-cutting hand behind the blade path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What is the finished face size when a 10 × 7 in blank is folded at the midpoint of its 10 in side?
options: 5 × 7 in
5 × 5 in
blocks.explanation: Folding the 10-inch width in half produces a 5-inch width; the 7-inch height is unchanged.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the card and prepare a reliable fold. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Template and cut the landscape layers
lessons.summary: Template and cut the landscape layers

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Cutting four related shapes is easier when each one has a clear job. The back layer establishes the distant skyline. The next layers cover its lower edge, so their bottoms do not need to be perfectly shaped; only the visible upper contour matters. Make each band about 1.5 to 2 inches deep at the tallest point, and extend it slightly past both sides of the 4-inch scene width. That extra width is a trimming allowance, not a final overhang. Keep the template itself at 4 × 5.5 inches, then draw curves across a slightly wider piece of colored paper. Vary the silhouettes: a shallow far ridge, a tall peak near one side, a low rolling middle, and a foreground rise can suggest distance without intricate drawing.

Choose a palette with readable contrast. If adjacent sheets have nearly the same lightness, their edges may disappear when layered. A useful paper-only test is to place the scraps together under the same room light and check whether each boundary remains visible from arm's length. Assign colors before cutting so you do not end up with an attractive stack whose layers blend together. Label each piece on its hidden lower edge or keep them in order on the table. Cut slowly along the c

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut a 4 × 5.5 in window from scrap paper and mark its centerline and intended 1/2 in side margins on the card front using faint pencil ticks.
Cut four colored strips about 4.5 in wide; draw a different hill contour across each strip, with 1.5–2 in depth and gently varied peak positions.
Arrange the four bands back-to-front in the planned color order and dry-fit them against the window, overlapping each lower edge by about 1/4 in.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and keep the non-cutting hand behind the blade path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: Which tool and action make a safe score for this project?
options: A sharp craft knife pressed through the cardstock
A blunt tool drawn lightly along a ruler to indent, not cut, the paper
The scissor point dragged repeatedly across the fold
A metal point pressed until the paper separates
blocks.explanation: A score is a controlled indentation. The instruction specifically avoids a sharp knife or any tool that cuts through the sheet.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Template and cut the landscape layers. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build depth and attach the scene
lessons.summary: Build depth and attach the scene

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Depth comes from controlled spacing, not from using the thickest possible pads. In this sample, the farthest band lies flat. The next band can also lie flat, or receive a small number of foam pads. Lift only one or two selected foreground bands so the edges cast a delicate shadow. If every layer is raised equally, the card becomes bulky and the contour stack may snag when handled. Place pads well inside the side edges and away from the exact curved outline; a pad should support paper, not peek out. Use several small pads distributed across a band rather than one central point, because a long strip can bow between supports.

Assemble from back to front. Attach the farthest ridge to the top of the scene window first, then place the next band so it overlaps the previous lower edge by about a quarter inch. Check the horizon from directly above before pressing the adhesive firmly. Continue toward the foreground. When using glue stick, apply a thin, even coat to the hidden overlap zone; excessive glue can wrinkle light paper. With double-sided tape, use short lengths and keep the liner clean until placement. Attach the completed landscape panel to the card only after the layers look bala

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the far ridge along the top of the window and attach it with a thin adhesive line on the hidden lower area; leave its side overhang untrimmed for now.
Set the second band over the first with about 1/4 in overlap; add three or four thin foam pads across its hidden lower area if a raised edge is desired.
Add the remaining two bands from back to front, alternating flat adhesive and foam only where needed; press each attachment through clean scrap paper.
Trim the side overhangs along the window edges, then attach the finished scene panel to the card using a thin perimeter of adhesive and a few interior dots.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and keep the non-cutting hand behind the blade path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: Why should the hill bands be dry-fitted before adhesive is added?
options: To make the paper permanently waterproof
To check overlap, coverage, color contrast, and contour visibility while repositioning is easy
To determine how much pressure can be applied to the fold
To guarantee the card can support weight
blocks.explanation: Dry arrangement exposes gaps or hidden ridges before adhesive makes changes difficult.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build depth and attach the scene. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Inspect, finish, and refine
lessons.summary: Inspect, finish, and refine

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A finished card should open and close comfortably, show four intentional bands, and remain tidy when viewed from the front and side. Let wet adhesive set according to its label before writing inside or stacking the card. A useful inspection sequence is to check the outer margins first, then inspect the hill contours, then gently open the card to confirm that no foam or glue has bridged the fold. Do not tug a raised edge to test it; that can peel paper fibers even when the attachment is sound. Instead, look for a lifted corner and press it gently through clean scrap paper. If one edge still lifts, add a tiny amount of paper-safe adhesive beneath the edge with a scrap-paper applicator.

Test the card on a clean tabletop. It is a greeting card, not a freestanding structural display or a protective product. Its job is to open, close, and communicate a small landscape. Write a short greeting inside only after glue is dry. Keep lettering simple and original, such as a brief seasonal wish or a note about a favorite walk; do not copy a character, logo, or protected artwork. If the front seems crowded, remove an optional embellishment rather than adding more decoration. A refinement can als

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Allow adhesive to set as directed, then inspect the front from above and from a slight side angle for lifted corners, visible pads, gaps, and uneven margins.
Open and close the card once without forcing it; add a short original greeting inside after the adhesive is dry, then record one successful choice and one possible improvement.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and keep the non-cutting hand behind the blade path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: A raised edge lifts slightly after glue dries. What is the best first response?
options: Pull the edge hard until it tears free, then rebuild the stack
Wet the entire card front until it softens
Gently apply a tiny dab of paper-safe glue beneath the edge and press through clean scrap
Cover the edge with thick foam pads
blocks.explanation: A tiny localized adhesive repair is preferable to pulling, soaking, or adding unnecessary thickness.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Inspect, finish, and refine. What did you learn and verify?

name: Folded Desk Calendar Stand
tagline: Build a compact folded-cardstock easel with a replaceable, hand-lettered month card.
outcome: Measure and mark a 6 × 8 inch cardstock body, with fold lines at 2 and 5 inches from its bottom edge.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Folded Desk Calendar Stand

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Build a compact folded-cardstock easel with a replaceable, hand-lettered month card. A measured triangular brace and a front retaining lip help the stand display light paper on a stable indoor tableto

lessons.title: Plan the silhouette and measure the blank
lessons.summary: Plan the silhouette and measure the blank

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## What you are building

The stand is a single 6-inch-wide by 8-inch-tall back panel that folds into a shallow easel. With the panel lying upright in front of you, the bottom 2 inches become the front foot, the next 3 inches form the angled display face, and the remaining 3 inches fold back as a rear leg. A separate narrow folded strip across the bottom edge becomes a retaining lip. The calendar card measures 4 × 5 inches, leaving a visible border on the 6-inch-wide face. The proportions are a practical design choice for a small, lightweight paper display; they are not a strength rating.

Before cutting, lay out the parts on scrap. The 6 × 8-inch body uses a larger piece than the card so the fold geometry stays simple and the folded foot is broad enough to stand on a flat desk. The rear panel and front foot should rest on the surface together. The middle panel is the viewing plane. A small paper brace behind the fold can limit accidental flattening, but it does not make the model load-bearing. The separate lip merely catches the bottom edge of the paper month card.

Measure from the lower edge of the body and mark fold lines at 2 inches and 5 inches. The spacing matters: it makes

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Clear a flat work area and place the 6 × 8-inch body sheet vertically, with its 6-inch edge across the bottom.
On the body, mark light pencil ticks 2 inches and 5 inches above the bottom edge at both sides, then connect corresponding ticks with the ruler.
Measure a separate 4 × 5-inch calendar card and a 2 × 5-inch brace strip; mark a 0.5-inch fold allowance along one long edge of the brace strip.

blocks.body: Use scissors carefully, cut away from fingers, and keep the supporting hand out of the cutting path. Younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: What are the three body-panel depths, measured from bottom to top?
options: 2-inch foot, 3-inch face, 3-inch rear leg
3-inch foot, 2-inch face, 3-inch rear leg
2-inch foot, 4-inch face, 2-inch rear leg
1-inch foot, 3-inch face, 4-inch rear leg
blocks.explanation: The body is 8 inches high. Scores 2 inches and 5 inches above its lower edge create panels of 2, 3, and 3 inches.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the silhouette and measure the blank. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Score folds and form the easel body
lessons.summary: Score folds and form the easel body

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Make controlled creases

A score is a shallow channel that encourages cardstock to bend along a chosen line. It should compress the surface slightly without puncturing, slicing, or scraping away fibers. A blunt bone folder is convenient, but an empty ballpoint pen or rounded craft stick can work if it is clean and not sharp. Put the sheet on a smooth surface that will not be marked. Align the ruler carefully over a fold line and hold it steady with fingers well away from the scoring path. On a scrap first, draw the tool along the ruler with light, even pressure. Look at both sides. A correct test leaves a visible indentation but no hole or split. Heavy card may need a second gentle pass rather than one forceful pass.

Score the two body lines and the brace's half-inch flap line. Fold each body line slowly, bringing the panels together along the score and using the ruler edge to support a straight crease. Do not snap the card backward and forward repeatedly; repeated flexing can weaken the fold. The 2-inch bottom panel turns forward to make a flat foot. The 3-inch top panel turns backward to become a rear leg. The remaining 3-inch panel between them faces forward as the display p

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Test the blunt scoring tool on scrap, pressing lightly along a ruler until it leaves a shallow line without cutting the paper.
Score both horizontal body lines and the 0.5-inch brace flap line with the ruler held firmly; make a second light pass only if the card resists.
Fold the bottom 2-inch panel forward at its score and the top 3-inch panel backward, pressing each crease once with the blunt tool.
Set the folded body on a level tabletop and check the face angle and contact points before attaching anything.

blocks.body: Use scissors carefully, cut away from fingers, and keep the supporting hand out of the cutting path. Younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: What should a successful cardstock score look and feel like?
options: A deep groove cut through most of the sheet
A shallow indentation that guides a fold without puncturing the surface
A row of holes made with a pin
A crease made by repeatedly bending the card both directions
blocks.explanation: A score is a depression, not a cut or puncture. Test pressure on scrap before scoring the measured parts.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Score folds and form the easel body. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Attach the brace, lip, and removable calendar
lessons.summary: Attach the brace, lip, and removable calendar

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Join paper without blocking the page

The brace is an interior reinforcement for the folded shape, not a structural guarantee. Place the 2 × 5-inch brace strip behind the body so it bridges the rear fold region. Fold its 0.5-inch flap along the score. Position the flap against the back of the display face, roughly centered across the width, and let the remaining strip extend down toward the rear leg. A short length of tape or a thin layer of paper glue can secure the flap. With glue, use only a small amount and press the surfaces together until they stay aligned. Keep glue away from the visible calendar face and the foot. Let the bond set according to its label before testing. For tape, press the tape flat and avoid wrinkles that would make the stand rock.

The retaining lip is a separate 6 × 0.75-inch strip, folded lengthwise at 0.25 inch. The narrow flap is the attachment tab. Center the lip along the bottom of the display face and attach the flap to the front, leaving the remaining 0.5-inch strip projecting upward as a shallow ledge. Make the ledge continuous enough to catch a paper card, but do not cover the card's writing area. Use small tape pieces at the ends and center,

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut the brace strip and fold its scored 0.5-inch flap; place the flap centered on the back of the face with the strip reaching toward the rear leg.
Attach the brace flap using a small amount of paper glue or two short pieces of paper tape, then leave it undisturbed if glue is used.
Cut a 6 × 0.75-inch lip strip, score it lengthwise at 0.25 inch, fold the flap, and attach it across the bottom of the display face with the 0.5-inch ledge projecting upward.
Write a month heading and weekday labels on the 4 × 5-inch card, then slide it behind the lip and center it on the face.

blocks.body: Use scissors carefully, cut away from fingers, and keep the supporting hand out of the cutting path. Younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: Which is an appropriate final use for this stand?
options: Holding a tablet during a video call
Supporting a mug while the glue dries
Displaying its lightweight removable month card on a stable indoor tabletop
Propping a heavy book open
blocks.explanation: The project is a decorative paper easel for a light card only, not furniture or a certified device holder.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Attach the brace, lip, and removable calendar. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Inspect, refine, and plan the next month
lessons.summary: Inspect, refine, and plan the next month

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Check the finished paper model

Let any adhesive reach the set time given on its package before placing the stand upright. Put it on a level indoor table away from edges. Look at it from the side: the foot should lie flat, the rear leg should touch the same plane, and the display face should hold its angle without being propped by a cup or other object. Look from the front: the face should appear centered over the foot, the lip should be level, and the card should not hide the paper joints. These are visual checks, not a load test. Keep the stand restricted to the lightweight paper card. Do not hang a device, press on the face, or test it by adding weight.

A mild wobble can often be corrected by checking whether tape or glue has made a lump under one foot. A warped panel usually needs to be remade from flatter stock. If the angle opens too far, reposition the brace while tape is still removable or add a narrow paper stop tab to limit spreading. Do not use weights, sharp pins, staples, or metal fasteners to force the model into shape. A split fold can be covered with a narrow paper strip adhered across the crease, but if the tear runs through most of the panel, start again with

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: After adhesive sets, place the stand on a level tabletop and inspect the foot, rear-leg contact, face angle, and lip alignment without pressing or loading it.
Correct a small angle or alignment issue by repositioning removable tape or adding a narrow paper stop tab behind the fold.
Decorate the card with an original geometric border or simple color marks, keeping the month title and weekday/date grid legible.
Check the date sequence for the chosen month, remove and reinsert the card once, then store spare cards flat and dry.

blocks.body: Use scissors carefully, cut away from fingers, and keep the supporting hand out of the cutting path. Younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: If a fold feels resistant and the cardstock is whitening, what is the best response?
options: Force it sharply so the panel stays straight
Cut a slit down the fold with a sharp blade
Wet the paper to soften it
Stop, check the score, and gently refold once along the existing line
blocks.explanation: Whitening is a warning that fibers are stressed. Do not force, wet, or cut the cardstock.

name: Paper Woven Greeting Card
tagline: Plan, weave, mount, and finish a one-of-a-kind folded greeting card with a small paper-woven panel.
outcome: Measure and cut a 3.5 by 4.75 inch warp panel with an intact top margin and seven evenly spaced vertical strips.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Paper Woven Greeting Card

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Plan, weave, mount, and finish a one-of-a-kind folded greeting card with a small paper-woven panel. You will learn a controlled over-under weave, adjust strip tension without tearing paper, and turn t

lessons.title: Plan the panel and cut a stable warp
lessons.summary: Plan the panel and cut a stable warp

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A paper weave behaves best when its vertical strips stay attached to a firm margin. That attached section is the warp header: it keeps seven narrow strips in order while the crosswise strips pass between them. For this design, the finished woven field is 3.5 inches wide by 4.25 inches tall. The complete warp starts 3.5 by 4.75 inches, leaving a half-inch header at the top. With seven strips across 3.5 inches, each strip is half an inch wide. The uniform spacing makes an easy first weave and leaves enough paper width to handle without pinching.

Choose two papers with distinct colors or patterns so the crossing is readable. A very thick board is difficult to bend and weave; very thin tissue tears when lifted. Midweight paper is forgiving. Before cutting the actual warp, try one offcut from each paper: bend it gently and slide one strip across another. If it creases sharply or splits, switch to a more flexible sheet. Work on a clear table and mark lightly so guide lines can be erased or hidden. Cut only from the open bottom toward the header, stopping at the line; the uncut half-inch must remain continuous. The header is not a waste margin: it keeps the warp aligned and becomes a hid

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut or select a 3.5 x 4.75 inch warp rectangle and mark a line 0.5 inch below its top edge.
Mark six vertical guide lines at 0.5-inch intervals across the rectangle, then cut upward from the bottom edge to the header line along each guide.
Cut seven weft strips, each 0.5 inch wide and about 4.25 inches long, from the contrasting sheet; set them in order beside the warp.

blocks.body: Cut on a clear, stable surface. Keep fingers behind the scissor blades and point scissors away from the body; close and pass them handle-first.

blocks.question: Why does the warp keep a half-inch uncut header?
options: It keeps the vertical strips connected and aligned
It makes the card waterproof
It replaces the card fold
It guarantees the card can be mailed without packaging
blocks.explanation: The attached header holds the warp strips together while weft passes through them; it is not a weatherproofing or mailing feature.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the panel and cut a stable warp. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build an even over-under weave
lessons.summary: Build an even over-under weave

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The plain weave in this card uses a simple row rule. Row one passes over the first vertical strip, under the next, and repeats across. Row two reverses that order. Every later row alternates again. Think of the row as a path, not a forceful threading task: gently lift one warp strip, slide the weft through the opening, then lower the strip. A blunt fingertip is enough for this wide half-inch spacing. Avoid sharp implements that can scratch the table or pierce the paper. A paper strip should glide with light resistance. If it catches, back it out a little and identify which vertical strip has folded or which opening is too small.

After each row, nudge it toward the previous row until gaps close, but do not pull the ends hard. Paper does not stretch like cloth; extra tension can bow the vertical strips or tear an edge. Keep the left and right ends of each weft row slightly beyond the warp until the panel is complete. Check the pattern every row: if two adjacent rows show the same over-under sequence, the surface may still hold together, but the alternating pattern will be interrupted. You can correct the latest row immediately by sliding it back out and restarting from the opposite

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the warp flat with its header farthest from you; pass the first weft strip over warp 1, under 2, and continue alternating across all seven.
Slide row one upward until it sits just below the header, then weave row two starting under warp 1 and alternating in the reverse sequence.
Repeat the alternating start for rows three through seven, moving each row gently upward and keeping warp strips parallel.

blocks.body: Cut on a clear, stable surface. Keep fingers behind the scissor blades and point scissors away from the body; close and pass them handle-first.

blocks.question: If row one begins over warp 1, how should row two begin for the plain weave?
options: Over warp 1 again
Under warp 1
Skip warp 1 entirely
Tie row two to the card fold

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A loose weave can shift while you mount it, so secure the crossings at the edges before lifting the panel. Use a small amount of glue stick under the exposed weft ends where they meet the outer warp strips. Press with a clean scrap of paper rather than a fingertip if the adhesive is tacky. Glue only the edge overlaps; coating the entire woven surface flattens the texture and can make thin papers ripple. Trim the side overhang so it is even with the outer warp edges. Keep the top header and lower warp ends in place; they are the frame that holds the weave together. A narrow backing mat covers those unfinished edges and creates a clean border.

The card base is a 10 by 7 inch sheet folded in half to make a 5 by 7 inch portrait card. Score the fold lightly with a blunt folder or the back of a spoon before creasing; a ruler helps keep the fold straight. Do not cut or score with a knife. The woven panel sits centered on a 4 by 5.25 inch backing piece, which in turn sits on the card front with approximately half-inch side margins and three-quarter-inch top and bottom margins. Centering is more important than forcing mathematically perfect symmetry if the handmade panel varies slightly. D

Center the woven panel on the 4 x 5.25 inch backing, then center the backing on the card front and glue the backing down after a dry fit.

Cut through the warp to widen the opening

For a clean first project, correct a row before its edges are fixed; after gluing, avoid pulling against the surrounding paper.

Personalize the card with a short title, small geometric marks, or a hand-drawn border on the backing. Keep embellishment light so the paper panel remains the focus. Avoid copying a recognizable character, logo, or another artist's exact design. Leave the inside dry and clear until the adhesive has set; then write a message with a pen that does not bleed through the card stock. This card is a paper keepsake for ordinary dry indoor handling. It has not been tested for water resistance, repea

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: A rolled rose is a continuous spiral, not a stack of separate petals. For this project, six flowers use 12 cm square sheets. The spiral will begin at the outside edge and wind toward a small central tab. Leaving a little extra paper at the center gives you a base to glue down; cutting all the way through would leave the coil without an anchor. A gently wavy outer edge creates a ruffled rim. It does not need to be mathematically even: regular, shallow curves are easier to roll than sharp corners. Choose paper that bends without cracking. Very thin paper curls readily but can tear; heavy cardstock may resist tight turns. Construction paper or light cardstock is a useful middle ground. Practice first on scrap using a strip rolled around a blunt pencil, then open it again. Notice how tight rolling makes a smaller, denser center, while letting the roll relax makes a broader bloom. The goal is consistent gentle tension, not force. Keep all six flower sheets the same size so the bouquet looks intentional, then vary color or the fullness of a few outer curves for an original arrangement. Set a ruler, pencil, scissors, backing discs, and glue within reach before cutting. Place a scrap sheet

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: Rolling from the outside toward the center lets the innermost part become the flower's core. Start by curling the narrow outer tip around a blunt pencil or marker, then continue by hand. Keep the ribbon edge aligned and the roll snug, but do not crush it. A relaxed coil should open slightly when released; that natural spring makes the blossom wider. If the paper has a colored front and plain back, keep the colored side facing outward as you roll. If both sides match, choose one face and use it consistently. The flower does not need an exact number of turns. Its appearance depends on the spiral spacing and how tightly the learner holds it. Hold a new coil over the table while easing your grip so it cannot fall. Let it expand until the outside reaches approximately 4–5 cm across, then gently gather it back if it opens too far. This is a visual guide, not a rigid pass/fail size. The final center tab sits underneath the flower. A small adhesive spot on that tab secures the coil while preserving the open layers above. Use a scrap of card as a glue applicator and apply a thin film rather than a puddle. Excess glue can soak paper, stiffen the petals unevenly, or stick the bloom to the wor

items: Curl the outer tip around a blunt pencil, then roll inward with the colored face out.
Release pressure gradually; let the coil open to about 4–5 cm and tuck the tab underneath.

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: Leaves are folded accents, not structural braces. Cut six green rectangles measuring 3 x 5 cm. Two leaves per stem create a balanced but uncluttered silhouette. Each flower receives a 2 cm cardstock backing disc. The disc spreads the attachment area beneath the rolled paper; it is not a load-bearing plate. First attach a craft stick to the disc with a small amount of glue and let the joint become tacky. Then place the flower's center tab over the disc and press gently from the back. This order keeps glue away from the open spiral layers. If your paper is very light, use less pressure: a hard thumbprint may flatten the rose. The craft-stick stem should remain visible below the flower and should never be used to support a pot, sign, or other weight. Wrap each stick with a narrow green strip cut about 1 cm wide. name: Folded Paper Butterfly Garland
tagline: Make a light indoor wall decoration from eight original, fan-folded paper butterflies arranged along a measured cord.
outcome: Plan an eight-butterfly color sequence and mark a 150 cm display cord with consistent center positions.

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a light indoor wall decoration from eight original, fan-folded paper butterflies arranged along a measured cord. This course teaches a repeatable two-wing method, careful center binding, even spa

lessons.title: Plan the rhythm and prepare your paper
lessons.summary: Plan the rhythm and prepare your paper

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Start with a measured design

This garland uses eight butterflies on a 150 cm cord. Each butterfly is made from two folded panels measuring 10 × 15 cm. A panel’s 15 cm dimension becomes the length of its folded fan; its 10 cm dimension is the direction across the pleats. That distinction matters: folding across the 10 cm width creates a fan about 10 cm tall, while the 15 cm edge determines how many pleats fit. With 8 mm pleats, the long edge gives roughly eighteen to nineteen folds. Small differences are fine; matching the pair is more important than reaching an exact fold count.

Lay out eight pairs of colors before cutting. A useful example is four alternating pairs of warm and cool colors, with one darker pair at each end. You can change the palette, but make the two wings of each butterfly visually compatible. Paper that is extremely thin may droop; very heavy card resists tight accordion folds and makes a thick center. Test one small fold in a scrap before committing your chosen stock.

Use a ruler and pencil lightly. Erase visible guide marks before assembly if the paper surface allows it. Keep the workspace dry and clear, and place scissors where they cannot roll from the

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Clear a dry table, gather the listed supplies, and cut or select sixteen panels measuring 10 × 15 cm. Pair them into eight sets.
Arrange the eight pairs in the intended sequence, then mark the 150 cm cord at the eight center positions listed in the lesson.
Test one accordion fold in a scrap and choose paper that creases without cracking or springing open excessively.

blocks.body: Use scissors only for paper; pass them closed handle-first, cut away from fingers, and store them closed when not in use. Younger learners need adult supervision and age-appropriate scissors.

blocks.question: What are the target dimensions of each wing panel?
options: 5 × 5 cm
blocks.explanation: The course specifies 10 × 15 cm panels so paired fans and spacing measurements remain consistent.

lessons.title: Build two even folded fans
lessons.summary: Build two even folded fans

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Fold the panels into fans

An accordion is a connected series of alternating folds. The goal is not merely to make many creases; the ridges should reverse direction regularly so the paper opens into a compact fan instead of a rolled tube. Start at a short edge of the 10 × 15 cm panel and fold a strip about 8 mm wide toward the back. Turn the paper over and fold the next strip toward the front. Continue to the far short edge. If the final strip is narrower than 4 mm, leave it as a small end tab rather than adding a sliver pleat that will be hard to control. The exact number of pleats varies with paper and hand accuracy.

Use the ruler’s 8 mm marks to establish the first few folds, then work by matching the new edge to the previous crease. This keeps the pattern consistent without drawing eighteen lines on every panel. Press each crease with a fingertip or blunt tool. A sharp crease makes the wings spring open in a controlled way, but excessive force can cut or whiten delicate paper. Keep the fold stack aligned at both ends. If edges begin to drift, pause and reset the next fold instead of making the error progressively worse.

The two panels for each butterfly should be folded in

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Fold the first panel from a 10 cm short edge into alternating pleats about 8 mm wide along its 15 cm dimension; repeat with its partner.
Press each crease gently with a fingertip or blunt folder, keeping the folded edges aligned; leave any final sliver under 4 mm as an end tab.
Pinch each folded panel at its midpoint along the 15 cm length, making the top and bottom fan sections close to 7.5 cm each.

blocks.body: Use scissors only for paper; pass them closed handle-first, cut away from fingers, and store them closed when not in use. Younger learners need adult supervision and age-appropriate scissors.

blocks.question: Why fold a paper strip around the butterfly waist?
options: To make the wings waterproof
To hold the two fans together without a sharp fastener
To make the cord load-bearing
To flatten all pleats permanently
blocks.explanation: The band is a gentle center restraint. It should secure the stack without cutting or flattening it.

lessons.title: Join the wings and form the butterfly
lessons.summary: Join the wings and form the butterfly

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Join without crushing the pleats

Take the two folded fans from one color pair and place their pinched midpoints together, side by side. Their pleat edges should point in the same general direction so that both wings open smoothly. Hold the waist with one hand while the other checks that the top halves and bottom halves are near equal. A butterfly does not need identical upper and lower wings, but the pair should not be dramatically lopsided unless that asymmetry is an intentional design.

Use a 1 × 8 cm paper strip as a soft center band. Wrap it around the pinched waist, leaving the folded wing ends free. Bend the band gently; do not crease it sharply over the fan stack. Tuck its end under the first wrap and press only the overlapping band, not the pleats. The band should hold the assembly when lightly lifted, with no slipping, but it should not cut into or flatten the paper. The band is a practical alternative to wire: it has no sharp ends and keeps the course fully paper-based. If the strip is too short, use a longer offcut; do not pull hard to compensate.

Open the wing portions by separating the pleat layers with fingertips. Fan the top and bottom sections outward until eac

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the two pinched fans together at their midpoints with pleats aligned and the upper and lower sections approximately level.
Wrap a 1 × 8 cm paper band around the waist, tuck its end under the wrap, and press the band gently to secure it.
Separate the folded layers and fan the upper and lower wing sections outward on both sides; shape gently with fingertips.
Fold a 1 × 2 cm paper scrap into a small loop around the cord and tuck its ends beneath the back of the center band.

blocks.body: Use scissors only for paper; pass them closed handle-first, cut away from fingers, and store them closed when not in use. Younger learners need adult supervision and age-appropriate scissors.

blocks.question: A young learner wants to cut the panels. What is the best course-aligned response?
options: Let them cut while the cord is held in the other hand
Use scissors to trim any material, including wire
Provide age-appropriate paper scissors and adult supervision, passing them closed handle-first
Skip supervision because the paper is lightweight
blocks.explanation: The safety notes call for age-appropriate supervision, paper-only cutting, and closed handle-first passing.

lessons.title: Space, inspect, and display the garland
lessons.summary: Space, inspect, and display the garland

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Finish the arrangement and inspect it

Make the remaining seven butterflies one at a time. Reuse the same sequence: pair the fans, align the midpoint, band the waist, open the wings, and attach a loop. Keeping a consistent sequence reduces forgotten parts and gives you a natural inspection pause. Before each butterfly goes onto the cord, compare it with the sample. Does its body band cover the waist? Do the wings open without a split? Can the cord loop move without pulling the paper apart? Repair a loose band on the table rather than discovering it after the cord is hanging.

Place each center at its corresponding cord mark. The marks are about 18.6 cm apart, measured center to center. Slide the paper loops rather than dragging the folded wings. Stand the cord on the table and look from above; spacing that appears regular in a straight line can look uneven when the cord curves. You may adjust colors into a repeating rhythm, but keep the center spacing close enough that the pieces do not bunch together. Leave the 10 cm tails clear for attachment.

For display, use two removable clips or tape tabs appropriate to the wall and the product label. Fasten the cord ends only; do not att

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Repeat the butterfly assembly for the other seven pairs, checking every waist band and paper loop before threading onto the cord.
Slide the butterflies onto the cord and place each body center at one of the eight measured marks, about 18.6 cm apart.
Attach only the cord ends with appropriate removable clips or tape and display the garland indoors on a stable, low-risk wall area.
Inspect all eight butterflies and the display from close range and at arm’s length; remove any damaged or loose piece for repair.

options: Pull harder until the fold finishes
Wet the entire panel and press it flat
Bind the cracked fan tightly with cord
Stop, try lighter paper or wider folds, and replace a badly split panel
blocks.explanation: Cracking indicates unsuitable stock or excessive strain. Change the material or fold width rather than forcing it.

name: Geometric Paper Wall Mosaic
tagline: Plan, cut, arrange, and mount a dry indoor decorative mosaic from colored paper on a light cardboard panel.
outcome: Measure and mark a 30 × 40 cm display panel with a consistent 2 cm perimeter and balanced central design area.

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Plan, cut, arrange, and mount a dry indoor decorative mosaic from colored paper on a light cardboard panel. The original 30 by 40 cm design uses a calm border, three geometric color fields, and a deli

lessons.title: Plan the panel and choose a readable geometry
lessons.summary: Plan the panel and choose a readable geometry

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Lesson 1 — Plan before cutting

This project is a flat paper display, not a tiled surface that can carry weight. Start with a light, flat 30 × 40 cm cardboard panel. The finished design leaves a 2 cm border on every side, giving a central field of 26 × 36 cm. That field is divided into three horizontal bands, each 12 cm high. Use a 2 cm blank channel between bands: the arithmetic is 12 + 2 + 12 + 2 + 12 = 40 cm? Because the field is 36 cm high, instead set band heights to 10 cm, with 3 cm gaps: 10 + 3 + 10 + 3 + 10 = 36 cm. This repeated correction matters: measurements must add up before pieces are glued. The three bands will each contain four 6.5 cm-wide geometric blocks, with 1 cm paper channels between blocks, totaling 4×6.5 + 3×1 = 29 cm; that does not fit a 26 cm field. Use three blocks across instead: 3×8 + 2×1 = 26 cm. The final plan is therefore three bands of 10 cm height, separated by 3 cm channels, and three 8 cm blocks per band, separated by 1 cm channels.

The layout is a guide, not a demand for mathematical perfection. A pale paper background or the cardboard itself can remain visible in the channels. Choose three tile colors plus a contrasting border; repeat each

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure a 30 × 40 cm rectangle on clean cardboard and trim to size with scissors only if the board can be cut safely; otherwise select a pre-cut panel.
Mark a faint 2 cm border, then mark the 26 × 36 cm inner field; divide its height into three 10 cm bands with two 3 cm gaps, and its width into three 8 cm blocks with two 1 cm gaps
Pick three tile colors and one border color; jot a simple band-by-band pattern, repeating each tile color at least twice.

blocks.question: What are the exact dimensions of the inner design field after a 2 cm border on a 30 × 40 cm panel?

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Lesson 2 — Cut and sort the tiles

The design uses a tile vocabulary that is easy to measure and forgiving to assemble. Make 2.5 cm squares and right triangles cut from 5 cm squares. Two right triangles from one square can fill a square-sized area, but the mosaic does not require every square to be perfectly tessellated. Leave the marked 1 cm vertical and 3 cm horizontal channels open; they are intentional breathing room, not mistakes. A practical starter quantity is 80 squares and 20 triangles, with roughly ten spare pieces in each shape. A 21 × 29.7 cm sheet can yield several rows of 2.5 cm squares, but margins and imperfect cuts reduce yield, so cut a few test rows and count before assuming a precise yield.

Use a ruler and pencil to mark the reverse of paper. Cut a short stack of one sheet at a time so scissors stay controllable. Keep fingertips away from the line and rotate the sheet rather than twisting your wrist into an awkward position. Scissors are for paper, not for trimming clothing or other materials. Sorting pieces into shallow paper piles by color and shape reduces hunting and makes dry placement faster. Discard pieces with torn fibers or glue residue; they tend t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On the back of colored sheets, mark 2.5 cm intervals and cut one sheet at a time into squares; make at least 80 squares plus about ten spares.
Mark and cut 5 cm squares from accent paper, then cut diagonally corner to corner to make at least 20 right triangles plus a few extras.
Sort squares and triangles by color in separate labeled paper piles; keep the best edges for the outer edges of each block.

blocks.body: Use scissors only while seated or standing still at the table. Cut away from fingers, keep the other hand behind the cutting path, and pass closed scissors handle-first. Younger learners should have appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: How do the planned three blocks fit across the 26 cm field?
options: Three 8 cm blocks with two 1 cm gaps
Four 8 cm blocks with three 1 cm gaps
Three 10 cm blocks with no gaps
Two 8 cm blocks and one 6 cm block
blocks.explanation: The width check is 8 + 1 + 8 + 1 + 8 = 26 cm.

lessons.title: Dry-fit the composition and attach tiles
lessons.summary: Dry-fit the composition and attach tiles

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Lesson 3 — Arrange, inspect, and glue

Dry fitting means arranging pieces on the panel without adhesive. It is the key decision point because moving a paper tile is easy before it is glued and difficult after. Lay a pale backing sheet in the 26 × 36 cm field if you want a uniform ground; trim it to that exact size. Otherwise let the cardboard show in the channels. Arrange the three 8 × 10 cm blocks according to your sketch. Keep the border clear. In each block, combine squares with triangles and leave one or two small areas of visible ground for contrast. Look at the panel from a few steps away, then rotate it: if one band feels much heavier, redistribute the dark tiles. A photo can help you see balance, but it is optional.

Test adhesive on a spare piece of the same paper. Apply a thin, even film near the edges and center; too much glue can wrinkle lightweight paper, seep into channels, or cause the cardboard to warp. A glue stick can be used instead if its label says it is suitable for paper and card. Work one block at a time and preserve the measured channels. Press with a clean scrap sheet from the center outward, then lift it gently. Avoid rubbing colored paper because ink

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Lay the optional 26 × 36 cm backing sheet in the field, then place the 3 × 3 block layout without glue, keeping each 8 × 10 cm block inside its penciled boundary.
Within each block, arrange squares and triangles in a repeating but varied sequence; keep tile edges inside the block and leave one or two small ground-color openings.
Test a thin coat of water-based paper glue on a spare tile; when acceptable, glue one block at a time and press gently through clean scrap paper.
Let the panel dry flat according to the adhesive label, then gently test one corner tile with a fingertip; add the optional reverse backing only when fully dry.

blocks.body: Use scissors only while seated or standing still at the table. Cut away from fingers, keep the other hand behind the cutting path, and pass closed scissors handle-first. Younger learners should have appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What is the best reason to arrange tiles without glue first?
options: It lets you check balance and fit while pieces can still move
It makes the glue dry faster
It strengthens the cardboard
It makes any paper safe outdoors
blocks.explanation: The composition can be adjusted freely before glue makes pieces difficult to reposition.

lessons.title: Finish, assess, and display lightly
lessons.summary: Finish, assess, and display lightly

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Lesson 4 — Refine and choose a display

After the adhesive has dried, inspect the work in good light. A successful mosaic has an even 2 cm border, three horizontal bands of equal height, two wide horizontal channels, and two narrow vertical channels. The nine blocks may vary internally, but the block edges should respect the pencil plan. Look for glue shine, loose fibers, and edges that extend beyond the panel. Trim a projecting paper edge with scissors only when the scissors can move freely and your fingers are away from the cut. Do not trim the cardboard while the art is held in your hand. Erase faint guide marks only if the eraser does not scuff the paper.

A small amount of handmade variation is not a defect. Correct only a problem that affects readability, adhesion, or safe display. For a lifted tile, slide a small paper scrap under the loose edge, add a minimal amount of the same water-based glue, and press under clean paper while flat. If the board has a mild curve, let it rest flat under light, evenly distributed pressure only if the art surface is protected and dry enough not to stick. If it remains bowed, use it as a tabletop leaner rather than forcing it onto a wall.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect border, channels, block edges, and tile corners in bright light; mark only loose, projecting, or visually confusing areas for repair.
Repair one loose tile at a time with minimal water-based glue under its edge, press through clean scrap, and let the panel dry flat again.
Choose a stable shelf lean or an appropriately rated light-duty hanging method; record final size and one specific improvement for a future version.

blocks.heading: Overview

The spaces between paper planes produce small real shadows, but those spaces only help if the planes align and the scene remains legible. This course uses a stylized sunrise landscape: a pale sky with a round sun, two distant peaks, a rolling middle ridge, and a foreground hill with a winding path. blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: A spacer is a small rail that holds one paper plane away from the next. Even rails matter more than a large number of layers: inconsistent height can tilt an image, create contact points, or make the stack bulge. This project uses approximately 0.125-inch-thick cardstock strips, folded into shallow rails where practical. Fold a 0.5-inch-wide strip lengthwise to create a narrow double-thickness ridge, then test its compressed height; card stock varies, so use the smallest consistent spacer you can make. Alternatively, cut 0.125-inch-thick clean packaging card into rails. Do not use soft, crumbly material or sharp-edged metal. For every interval, prepare two side rails about 6.5 inches long and two short cross-rails about 0.5 inch long. Place the long rails near the left and right edges of the art, inside the 0.375-inch border, and use the short pieces only where a span sags. Keep rails away from important windows. A small spacer at the center top or bottom can help a broad paper edge stay level, but it must not cover the sun, path, or ridge opening. lessons.title: Plan a coordinated three-wheel display

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A pinwheel is a light paper rotor: diagonal slits create four flexible corner tabs, and gathering every other tab at one center makes a shallow vane shape. The paper needs to bend, but its corners should remain connected to the square. A clean square and matching cut lengths help all three wheels look related. This course uses 12 cm squares. That size provides enough material to handle the tabs while keeping the finished display modest; it is a design choice for this project, not a required standard.

Before cutting, choose three colors that contrast with one another. A simple plan is one dominant color, one lighter color and one small accent. Keep decoration light: a heavy sticker on one corner can make the wheel unbalanced, and thick layers may rub at the axle. Draw only faint guide marks so they do not distract from the finished paper. The display base is 18 × 8 cm, with three stems spaced along its long axis. It sits flat on a table and is not meant to support weight.

Set up a calm workspace with enough room for the ruler, paper and scissors. Keep pins out of the work area until an adult-led assembly step. Check that the cardboard is dry and flat. If it rocks, choose another p

blocks.question: Why do the diagonal cuts stop about 2 cm before the center of a 12 cm square?

To make the square larger after cutting.

To make the paper absorb more water.
blocks.explanation: A small uncut central area keeps the four corner tabs attached while allowing them to fold into a rotor.

lessons.title: Cut and shape the paper vanes
lessons.summary: Cut and shape the paper vanes

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A pinwheel begins as a square with four diagonal slits, one from each corner toward the center. The slits must stop short: if they meet, the center separates into loose pieces and there is no connected hub to gather. For a 12 cm square, make the stop point about 2 cm from the exact center along each diagonal. That leaves a compact central zone and four generous tabs. The precise distance is a practical balance: too little uncut paper weakens the hub; too much makes short, stiff vanes. Use the same measurement on all three squares.

Fold one corner tab from each of the four corners toward the center, but do not fold all four corners. Instead gather alternating corners, which makes a pinwheel spiral. Keep the folds soft and aligned so the tips meet without stacking a bulky lump. Do not crease the entire vane flat; a small curved lift helps preserve a little shape. A tiny center mark helps you see where the four points should converge. Keep fingers clear of the scissor path and cut on a flat surface. Younger makers should have an adult cut or directly supervise.

Before moving to the next lesson, inspect the back as well as the front. The center should remain intact, all four slits sh

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On each square, lightly mark the center at 6 cm from each edge and draw diagonal guides from all four corners toward that mark.
Cut along each diagonal from a corner and stop 2 cm before the center; repeat for all four corners.
Bring the first and third corner tabs toward the center, then bring the second and fourth tabs over them, alternating around the square.
Hold the gathered tips together and make a tiny pilot hole at their common center using an adult-controlled hole punch or pin.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers and pass them handle-first. Younger learners need direct adult supervision.

blocks.question: Which corners should be gathered to create the intended pinwheel shape?

Two adjacent corners only.
Every other corner, bringing four alternating tips to the center.
Only the corners with pencil marks.
blocks.explanation: Alternating corners distribute the four vanes around the hub and create the characteristic folded rotor form.

lessons.title: Mount the wheels with free movement
lessons.summary: Mount the wheels with free movement

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Mounting is a balance between holding the paper securely and leaving it enough room to turn. A pin pushed tightly against the folded hub clamps the paper. A small spacer between paper and stem creates a little clearance, while a gentle touch keeps the hub from tearing. In this design, a small bead or short straw ring serves as that spacer. The pin remains a sharp fastener, so an adult handles it or closely supervises an older learner. Keep the work surface clear and place the pin directly into the intended support; do not wave it around or leave it unattended.

The front-to-back sequence is gathered paper hub, spacer, then stem end. The pin passes through the center and into the straw wall at its top. It should be secure enough that the paper cannot slide off, but not driven so deeply or tightly that it grips the paper. Do not use the display as a moving toy or test it near faces. If the straw splits, replace it rather than adding force. A cardboard stem would need enough substance to retain a pin; thin rolled paper can crush, so the course uses a short paper straw and cautious handling.

Nudge one vane lightly and observe whether the wheel moves without rubbing; repeat for the other two wheels.

blocks.question: A pinwheel stops as soon as you release it. What should you inspect first?

Whether a spacer is present and the paper is pinched against the straw.

lessons.title: Arrange, stabilize and refine the display

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A pinwheel display is successful when it stands calmly and the paper faces remain distinct. A flat base matters more than adding weight or height. Put the 18 × 8 cm cardboard foot on a level tabletop and check whether it rocks. Reinforce its underside with paper tape if needed, keeping the tape smooth so it does not catch on the table. Stems should be taped upright near the three marks, with their bottoms aligned along the base. Use short tape bands around the straw and base rather than covering the entire stem. Tape is a positioning aid, not a structural guarantee.

Leave enough spacing for the folded corners to turn without contacting one another. A gentle hand-turn of each wheel can reveal collisions. If the wheels overlap, reposition a stem before pressing the tape firmly. Keep the project indoors, dry and away from table edges. Do not carry it by one straw. The cardboard display is stationary and decorative; it is not a hanging ornament, a toy for rough play, or a support for other objects.

This project makes one flower roughly 16–18 cm (6¼–7 in) across when its outer petals are gently opened. blocks.body:

That leaves a 1.5 cm border on each side. The capital initial is about 7 cm tall and 4–6 cm wide, depending on the letter. Put three accent motifs around it—such as a small diamond, a leaf-like oval, and a tiny sun made from a circle with short rays—but keep their outlines joined to the letter or to a shared border. Invent your own plain geometric motifs; do not trace a protected character or a branded mark.

Draw the panel and letter lightly on scrap first. A simple block letter is easiest because its broad strokes give room for bridges. In letters with enclosed counters, such as A, B, D, O, P, or R, the inner paper island would fall away unless you join it to the surrounding sheet. Add a narrow bridge from that island to the outer letter, then add one or two extra ties to nearby decorative strokes if the composition permits. Sketch one block capital about 7 cm high, add three original geometric accents, and connect every island with bridges at least 5 mm wide.
Mark planned waste areas with a light X and practice a straight line, a broad curve, and a bridge on scrap card.

blocks.question: Why should an enclosed counter in a block letter have a paper bridge to the surrounding design?
options: It keeps the inner paper island attached to the single-sheet artwork.
It makes the paper waterproof.
It removes the need for a backing sheet.
It makes the artwork load-bearing.
blocks.explanation: A bridge preserves continuity between the counter island and the surrounding sheet. It should remain visibly broad enough to handle.

lessons.title: Transfer and prepare the template
lessons.summary: Transfer and prepare the template

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Once the sketch works, make a clean full-size template. Draw it on separate paper at the same 12 × 12 cm scale or trace it from the practice sketch. Mark the outer boundary, the capital, the three accents, and every bridge. Add a small arrow labelled WASTE in each opening that should be removed. This label is especially useful around letters with counters: the paper inside the letter may be waste only if you have intentionally connected it, while the bridge itself must remain. Avoid relying on memory once you begin cutting.

Place the template over the main cardstock and align the boundaries. Use two small low-tack tape tabs outside the artwork, or trace the design lightly through the paper if it remains visible. Test tape first on an offcut: if it lifts fibers, do not use it. A sheet that shifts during cutting can make the blade travel unpredictably, so hold the page flat with the non-cutting hand well away from the cutting path, or tape only the distant corners to the mat. Never put fingers beneath the area where the blade may exit.

Before using a knife, settle the workspace: mat under the whole design, light aimed so pencil lines are visible, scraps bin nearby, and drinks moved

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Redraw or trace the final 12 × 12 cm design on a clean template, marking all waste areas with X and all bridges with short bars.
Align the template on the cardstock, secure only distant corners with tested low-tack tape, then place the sheet on the mat.
Check the blade, handle, lighting, and clear tabletop; rehearse the intended knife direction without cutting, or select scissors-only simplification.

blocks.body: Use a craft knife only on a cutting mat over a stable table. Keep the supporting hand behind the cutting direction and away from the blade path; make controlled cuts away from the body.

blocks.question: What is the best response if a marked scrap does not lift after cutting?
options: Pull hard so the hidden fibers break.
Put the knife down safely, then inspect and finish the cut line with a controlled pass on the mat.
Hold the sheet in the air and cut toward the hand.
Pour water over the cut to loosen it.
blocks.explanation: Resistant waste usually means a short section remains uncut. Revisit the line while the paper is supported; never yank it.

lessons.title: Cut openings without severing the bridges
lessons.summary: Cut openings without severing the bridges

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Start with the smallest inner openings, not the outer silhouette. This leaves the panel stable while details are being made. Keep the mat under the entire cut and use the knife only as a controlled paper-cutting tool. Hold it comfortably, keep the free hand out of the path, and draw the blade through the paper with light, steady pressure. If the paper does not separate, repeat a controlled pass over the same line rather than forcing the blade. Move or rotate the paper to bring the next line into a comfortable direction; do not twist your wrist around an awkward corner.

For a curved opening, divide it mentally into short segments. Stop at each corner or bridge, lift the blade, rotate the sheet on the mat, then continue. Remove only the waste marked X. Ease out a loose scrap from its edge with the blunt end of a tool or a gentle lift after the blade is safely put down. Never tug a scrap that is still attached; a sudden tear can widen the opening into a bridge. Inspect the underside too, because a cut can look complete on top while a small uncut fiber remains beneath.

The retained connections matter more than intricate detail. Leave the 5 mm bridges in place, and preserve the 8 mm m

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut the smallest marked openings first, using short controlled strokes and rotating the paper on the mat for comfortable angles.
After each opening, put the blade down safely, lift the waste gently, and inspect both sides for uncut fibers or tears.
Cut larger internal negative spaces in sections, preserving the 8 mm letter strokes and at least one clear bridge from each accent.

blocks.question: Which order best helps keep the cardstock supported during detailed work?
options: Cut the outside square first, then make every inner opening.
Cut random details and decide which areas are waste afterward.
Cut inner openings first, inspect them, then trim the outside edge near the end.
Glue backing before any cutting.
blocks.explanation: Leaving the outside border intact gives the panel stability while internal shapes are cut.

lessons.title: Finish, mount, and review the artwork
lessons.summary: Finish, mount, and review the artwork

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
When all intended interior waste has been removed, inspect the template and the panel together before cutting the outer edge. Check that no X-marked area remains accidentally attached and that no bridge was cut away. Erase only exposed pencil marks, using light strokes and supporting the paper nearby with a flat hand away from delicate details. If the sheet curls, let it rest under a clean book for several minutes before mounting; do not wet it or use heat. Now trim the outer square to 15 × 15 cm with scissors or a ruler-guided knife on the mat, keeping fingers beyond the cutting line. The earlier 1.5 cm margin should remain around the 12 cm artwork area.

Place the cut panel on contrasting backing and check the effect before gluing. The backing should be visible through the openings, while the broad paper strokes remain the main focus. If the contrast is too low, choose another scrap backing; do not add wet paint or liquid treatments to the finished paper. To mount, lift the panel by its strong border. Apply a thin glue-stick layer to the backing around its perimeter and a few broad areas of solid paper, avoiding bridges and cut edges. Lower the panel from one edge and smooth outw

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Compare the panel with the template, remove remaining marked waste, lightly erase exposed pencil, and rest curled paper beneath a clean book.
Trim the outside to 15 × 15 cm with scissors or a guided cut on the mat, then test the contrasting backing behind the artwork.
Apply a thin layer of glue to the backing, lower the panel into place, smooth gently, and let it dry flat before tabletop display.

blocks.body: Use a craft knife only on a cutting mat over a stable table. Keep the supporting hand behind the cutting direction and away from the blade path; make controlled cuts away from the body.

blocks.question: During knife work, where should the free hand be?
options: Directly in front of the blade to hold a tight corner.
Under the sheet to catch the blade tip.
On top of a marked waste area, pressing beside the knife.
Away from the blade path, holding a distant edge only if needed.
blocks.explanation: Support the page without placing fingers where a slipping blade could travel. Rotate the sheet for awkward angles.
