modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Build a freestanding, open-ended paper lantern from a measured cardstock sleeve and an inner color panel. A controlled set of curved vertical cuts expands when the sleeve is shaped into a cylinder, re

lessons.title: Plan a sleeve that will stand
lessons.summary: Plan a sleeve that will stand

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The lantern is a short, open cylinder with an uncut top band and bottom band. Its design depends on a sleeve that curves smoothly, not on a rigid frame. Begin with the cardstock in landscape orientation: it measures 11 inches wide and 8.5 inches high. Reserve a 0.5-inch overlap at the right edge for the closing seam. The usable circumference is therefore about 10.5 inches. When joined, this makes a cylinder roughly 3.3 inches across; the exact diameter varies slightly because paper bends and the overlap is not a perfect geometric circle. The finished height remains 8.5 inches.

The slots are cut vertically in the sheet while it is flat. They begin 1.25 inches below the top and end 1.25 inches above the bottom. That leaves sturdy continuous bands to hold the shape. Plan nine slots across the 10-inch field between the side margins, spacing them about 1.1 inches apart. The repeated cuts will open into narrow windows as the flat sheet curves. A paper strip underneath makes the windows look colored from inside. Make a test slot in scrap first: cut a 2-inch line, curve the scrap gently, and observe how the slit opens. If the cardstock splits at the end, use wider slot spacing or softer,

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the 8.5 × 11-inch cardstock landscape and label its top edge lightly. Mark a 0.5-inch overlap strip along the right short edge and a 0.5-inch side margin at the left.
Measure 1.25 inches from both the top and bottom edges and draw faint horizontal stop guides across the slot field.
On scrap, cut one 2-inch slot that stops well before the scrap edge; curve the sample gently and inspect the end.

blocks.body: This is an unlit, dry indoor decorative object only. Do not add a candle, flame, bulb, battery, wiring, or any other light source.

blocks.question: Why do the slot cuts stop 1.25 inches from the top and bottom edges?
options: To preserve continuous bands that hold the sleeve together
To create a sealed base for objects
To make room for a battery
To make the cylinder waterproof
blocks.explanation: The top and bottom bands remain continuous so the slotted sheet can curve without separating into strips.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan a sleeve that will stand. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut repeated windows with intact bridges
lessons.summary: Cut repeated windows with intact bridges

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The lantern's visual rhythm comes from nine narrow slots, not from complicated cutouts. On the main sheet, mark slot centers across the open 10-inch field. Place the first center about 0.5 inch in from the field's left edge, then mark roughly every 1.1 inches. Because the sheet and pencil marks are hand-measured, prioritize even spacing and intact margins rather than chasing a mathematically perfect pattern. Each slot is a straight vertical cut about 6 inches long, connecting the two horizontal stop guides. Cut one at a time with the paper resting flat. Keep the blades away from the tabletop, and stop precisely at the guide rather than snipping through the band.

Do not remove a strip of paper: each slot is a narrow opening with paper remaining on both sides. When curved into a cylinder, the bars between slots become flexible ribs. If slots are too close, the ribs become weak. If one cut crosses another or reaches an edge, the neighboring ribs may tear when the sleeve is rounded. Work slowly and gently spread the sheet into a curve only after all cuts are complete. Do not press a sharp crease into the central field. A soft curve lets the openings widen naturally.

Use a small decor

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Mark nine slot centers between the side margins, beginning about 0.5 inch inside the slot field and spacing marks about 1.1 inches apart.
Cut each slot from the top stop guide to the bottom stop guide with scissors, keeping the cardstock flat and the blades within the marked field.
Curve the cut sheet loosely around a cylindrical household object about 3 inches wide, without creasing or forcing it, then remove it.

blocks.body: This is an unlit, dry indoor decorative object only. Do not add a candle, flame, bulb, battery, wiring, or any other light source.

blocks.question: Your nine planned slots would leave very thin paper ribs. What is the best adjustment?
options: Cut all slots wider
Use seven evenly spaced slots
Cut through the top band as well
Add a candle so the slots are visible
blocks.explanation: Slot count can be reduced to suit the sheet. Keeping broad, even ribs is more important than using exactly nine openings.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut repeated windows with intact bridges. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fit the color panel and close the cylinder
lessons.summary: Fit the color panel and close the cylinder

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The inner paper adds color through the windows without blocking the open ends. Cut a strip of colored paper 8 inches high and about 10.5 inches long. This length nearly matches the sleeve's useful circumference, but allow a modest gap rather than forcing its edges together. First wrap the colored strip inside the sleeve without glue. Its top edge should sit about 0.25 inch below the top edge of the outer sleeve, and its bottom edge about 0.25 inch above the bottom. This inset prevents the lining from protruding and lets the structural bands remain visible. Trim the colored strip in small amounts if it overlaps heavily or wrinkles.

Use a few small dabs of glue stick on the colored panel's short edge and position that edge near, but not over, the sleeve seam. Press through a clean scrap of paper so fingers do not snag a slot. The lining only needs to stay in place; it should not be stretched taut across each opening. Next form the outer sleeve into a cylinder and overlap the right 0.5-inch strip inside the left side edge. Apply a thin, continuous glue-stick coat to the overlap, not to the slot field. Align the top and bottom edges before pressing. Hold the seam until it grips, then

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trim the colored paper to about 8 × 10.5 inches and dry-fit it inside the sleeve, inset roughly 0.25 inch from the top and bottom edges.
Apply a few glue-stick strokes to one short edge of the inner panel and attach it inside near the future seam, pressing gently through scrap paper.
Wrap the outer sheet into a cylinder, overlap its 0.5-inch seam strip inside the opposite edge, glue the overlap, and align the top and bottom rims before pressing.

blocks.body: This is an unlit, dry indoor decorative object only. Do not add a candle, flame, bulb, battery, wiring, or any other light source.

blocks.question: Which dimension describes the seam overlap on the 8.5 × 11-inch sleeve?
options: 1.25 inches
3 inches
0.5 inch
8.5 inches
blocks.explanation: A half-inch overlap closes the 11-inch-wide sheet while leaving approximately 10.5 inches of circumference.

lessons.title: Refine, inspect, and display safely
lessons.summary: Refine, inspect, and display safely

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Refinement means checking stability and finish, not adding weight or turning a decorative shell into a working light. Let the glue set for the time stated on its package, using the 15–30-minute range as a planning estimate only. Look at the lantern from the side: it should stand with its bottom rim contacting the tabletop around most of its circumference. Slight waviness in handmade cardstock is normal. If the seam is secure but the sleeve leans, gently adjust the curve by holding opposite sides of the intact top and bottom bands. Do not pinch the slots or flatten the cylinder.

Inspect each slot endpoint. The paper bridges should remain intact, with no spreading cracks. A small lifted edge can be pressed down with a tiny amount of glue stick, then left to dry. Keep decoration sparse: add a repeated dot, line, or abstract leaf shape to the bands, or write a short word in your own lettering. Avoid copied characters, branded figures, or artwork from a source. Test marker on an offcut first; some inks may show through the thin paper. If the outside design competes with the colored liner, erase or cover only while the material permits, or simply stop and treat the contrast as the desig

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Let the joined lantern rest upright until the adhesive has set, following its label and using the estimated drying window only as a guide.
Inspect the bottom rim, seam, inner panel, and all slot endpoints; add only a small paper-and-glue reinforcement where needed.
Add a restrained original pattern to the intact bands using dry coloring tools, then place the lantern on a dry, stable indoor tabletop.

blocks.body: This is an unlit, dry indoor decorative object only. Do not add a candle, flame, bulb, battery, wiring, or any other light source.

blocks.question: The liner wrinkles because its ends are pressed together tightly. What should you do?
options: Pull the outer sleeve wider until the wrinkle vanishes
Add water to soften the paper
Glue every slot shut
Trim a small amount from the liner and dry-fit it again
blocks.explanation: The liner should fit loosely inside. Small incremental trimming is safer than forcing either layer.

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The finished sample is a compact 20 cm wide by roughly 30 cm long indoor hanging. Its 20 × 5 cm cardboard header carries six short strings, each with a target beaded length of 23 cm; about 2 cm at the top and 5 cm at the bottom remain for knots and clearance. Overall hanging length will be about 30 cm. These are design targets, not structural ratings. The hanging is for a stationary decorative display, not a doorway, room divider, or place where people or animals pass through it.

Choose lightweight paper that folds without cracking. On each sheet, draw tapered strips: each triangle is 1.5 cm wide at its broad end and narrows evenly to a point over a 14 cm length. Cut roughly 48 triangles to make six strings of eight beads, plus several spares. At this size, each finished bead should be about 1.5 cm long, but roll tightness and paper thickness vary. Make one test bead before cutting every strip. The wide edge controls bead width; the strip length supplies the wrap, so a longer strip typically makes a fuller bead.

Sort the paper by color or pattern before rolling. Pick a simple sequence, such as alternating warm and cool colors, and mark the plan on scrap paper. This prevents late-

Use the tested template to mark and cut about 48 matching triangles, then sort them into six color sequences of eight.
Set out a protected work area, ruler, blunt rolling tool, small glue dab surface, and separate bead-drying area.

lessons.title: Roll, seal, and dry tapered beads
lessons.summary: Roll, seal, and dry tapered beads

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Work with one triangle at a time. Orient it broad edge toward you and place the rolling tool across the broad base. If a particular printed area should show on the finished bead, face that side outward as you roll. Start with a snug first wrap around the blunt tool. Keep the left and right paper edges aligned so the bead tapers instead of forming a lopsided cone. Roll away from your body with fingertips rather than pressing hard. A gentle, steady pull keeps layers compact without tearing the paper.

When most of the triangle has wrapped, add a small smear of white craft glue along the final pointed tip and finish rolling. Do not coat the whole strip: a wet interior can buckle and glue the bead to the tool. Pinch the tip briefly against the outside layer, then slide the bead off. If it resists, rotate gently rather than yanking. Put it on the non-stick surface with the seam down. Leave it until fully dry before threading. The specialist guidance consulted describes lightweight paper as easier to roll, triangular strips for tapered beads, and a final small adhesive application to secure the point. Your dimensions here are this course's design choice, not a copied pattern.

Make two o

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the broad edge of one triangle against the blunt rolling tool, with the chosen exterior pattern facing outward, and make one snug first wrap.
Roll the strip steadily toward its point, keeping light fingertip tension and guiding both edges evenly.
Apply a small dab of craft glue to the final tip, finish the roll, and press the tip against the bead surface for several seconds.
Slide the bead gently off the tool, place seam-down on the non-stick mat, and let it dry fully before sorting.

blocks.question: What should you do if a bead tip lifts after drying?
options: Coat the entire bead with solvent varnish
Apply a tiny amount of craft glue, press the tip, and dry fully
Pull the cord hard until the tip closes
Use the bead immediately and hide the tip against the header

lessons.title: Thread six balanced strands and finish the header
lessons.summary: Thread six balanced strands and finish the header

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Before threading, sort the dry beads into six groups of eight. Lay each group in order from top to bottom so you can compare color rhythm and total length. Cut six string lengths of 42 cm. Tie a stopper knot about 5 cm from one end of each string; this leaves a short tail beneath the beads and reduces the chance that a bead slides off during handling. Thread eight beads onto each strand, alternating their broad ends upward and downward if you want a varied surface. Keep the pattern intentional. Optional paper spacers can create small breathing gaps, but they are not required. If used, thread only larger, easy-to-handle spacers and keep them away from young children.

Measure the beaded section against a ruler. Aim for 23 cm, with the top bead beginning roughly 2 cm below the header and the bottom knot leaving about 5 cm of bare cord. Since paper beads vary, the count is a guide rather than a guarantee. A strand that is shorter than its neighbors can be adjusted with a spacer or a spare bead; do not stretch the cord to disguise differences. Tie a second secure knot at the upper end, leaving about 2 cm of cord for attaching it to the header.

Wrap the cardboard header with a 22 × 7 c

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut six 42 cm cord lengths and tie a stopper knot 5 cm from one end of each.
Thread eight dry beads onto each cord in the planned color order, then measure the beaded span against the 23 cm target.
Tie a secure upper knot on each strand, leaving about 2 cm of cord above the knot for attachment.
Wrap the 20 × 5 cm cardboard with the 22 × 7 cm paper, fold the excess over the back, and glue the folded edges down.

blocks.question: Which strip shape is used here to make tapered paper beads?
options: A 14 cm triangle, about 1.5 cm wide at its base
A 5 × 5 cm square
A 14 cm narrow rectangle
A circle cut from card

lessons.title: Attach, inspect, and display the finished hanging
lessons.summary: Attach, inspect, and display the finished hanging

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Use the six marks from Lesson 1. Tie each cord's upper tail around the header at its mark. A double knot snug against the back is enough to position a very lightweight strand; this course does not claim a rated load or provide structural wall-mounting instructions. Keep the knots on the rear face so the front looks tidy. Use small pieces of masking tape only as temporary helpers while you level the strands. Once all six are attached, set the header down and compare the bottoms. The final design should be about 20 cm wide and roughly 30 cm from header top to the ends, although bead length and knots create small differences.

Check every bead tip with a gentle fingertip touch. If a tip lifts, remove the strand from display and repair it with a tiny amount of glue; let it dry again. Check that the string is not fraying and that the header has not softened from excess glue. Gently lift the header a few centimeters above a clear tabletop and observe whether any strand slips. This is a simple craft inspection, not a load test or proof of safety. Never pull hard or hang it where failure could injure someone.

For display, choose a dry indoor spot where the object can remain still and out

name: Three-Dimensional Cardstock Cityscape

modules.description: Build a freestanding, tabletop city scene from a folded 24 × 18 cm cardstock base, layered skyline strips, and three-dimensional folded buildings. This original design uses simple scored folds, glued

lessons.title: Plan the skyline and prepare the base
lessons.summary: Plan the skyline and prepare the base

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A cityscape looks dimensional when the viewer can tell which shapes are near and which are far away. In this project, the rear skyline is tallest, the middle row is lower, and a short foreground row overlaps their feet. The three layers sit at different distances on one folded base. Think of the folded base as a shallow display stage: its horizontal floor is 24 cm wide and 9 cm deep, while its upright back is 24 cm wide and 9 cm tall. Together these use one 24 × 18 cm sheet folded across its 9 cm midpoint. Keep all constructions light. A paper city gains its apparent depth from overlap, not from strength or a heavy pile of decorations.

Begin with a tiny plan before cutting. Draw a 24 cm-wide rectangle and mark three skyline bands. Give the rear strip a varied roofline between 7 and 12 cm high, the middle strip 5–9 cm high, and the foreground strip 3–6 cm high. Leave at least 1 cm between the tallest rear roofs and the top edge of the back panel. Vary widths so the buildings do not look like identical boxes: a narrow tower can sit beside a broad low block, while a stepped roof or sloping paper roof gives a different silhouette without requiring a complicated mechanism. The sample d

items: On scrap, draw a 5 cm line with a ruler and score it gently with the blunt tool; fold along the groove, then make a second test with less pressure if fibers break.
Measure a 24 × 18 cm rectangle on the base sheet, trim it with scissors, and mark a fold line 9 cm from one short edge.
Score the 9 cm line, fold the shorter panel upward, and press the crease with the side of a ruler; set the L-shaped base on the table.
Sketch three skyline outlines on scrap within the planned height bands, label rear/middle/front, and mark a 1 cm glue tab below each building strip.

B. It makes the building waterproof

lessons.title: Cut and fold the three skyline rows
lessons.summary: Cut and fold the three skyline rows

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The city’s repeated shapes should feel related, but they do not need to be identical. Make the rear skyline from a strip about 24 cm wide and 13 cm high, the middle from a strip 24 cm wide and 10 cm high, and the foreground from a strip 24 cm wide and 7 cm high. On each, reserve the bottom 1 cm for a continuous attachment tab. These are maximum sample envelopes; roof shapes can dip below them. Draw the skyline across the remaining height, keeping broad wall sections between roof steps. Avoid very thin towers or long spikes because their edges can curl and catch. You can create a simple original visual language with repeated window squares, one striped roof, and one paper sign. Do not copy a recognizable character or existing artwork.

Each skyline strip attaches at a different distance along the floor. Fold its 1 cm tab backward so it will lie flat on the base when the wall stands up. A parallel fold is a fold whose two crease lines run alongside one another; in this model, the tab hinge and the upright wall cooperate to raise a paper surface. Repeat for a 24 × 10 cm middle strip and a 24 × 7 cm foreground strip; use different roof rhythms and leave at least two wide wall areas on each.
Score each 1 cm bottom tab along a straight ruler line and fold it backward, away from the drawn building face.
Arrange the three dry strips on the floor at approximately 0.5 cm, 3.5 cm, and 6.5 cm forward of the rear crease, with tabs flat and faces upright.

blocks.question: Why test scoring pressure on scrap cardstock first?
options: A. To make the paper absorb more glue
B. To find pressure that makes a crease without cutting or tearing fibers
C. To soften scissors
D. To measure the base width
blocks.explanation: A shallow, controlled score guides a fold while avoiding damage to the sheet.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut and fold the three skyline rows. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Decorate and assemble the layers
lessons.summary: Decorate and assemble the layers

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A successful paper scene is readable before it is detailed. Add decoration in a few clear scales: large blocks establish buildings, medium rectangles suggest windows or doors, and only a handful of small marks add texture. Keep most windows away from cut edges because edge-mounted pieces lift more readily. For a balanced sample, use windows roughly 0.8 × 1.2 cm, one or two door shapes about 1.5 × 2.5 cm, and roof accents no wider than the building beneath them. These details are suggestions; simple drawn lines work just as well. Make each layer’s contrast distinct: the far layer can be pale, the middle layer medium, and the foreground layer darker. If you only have one color, alternate blank walls with patterned ones.

Decorate the building faces while they lie flat. Put the paper sign on one building and a repeated window arrangement on another, but leave a small clear margin around every tab and fold. Apply glue sparingly to the tab, not to the entire floor. Too much adhesive can wrinkle light paper or squeeze into a visible shiny bead. Place the rear layer first and hold it upright while the glue begins to grab. Then add the middle and front strips. This front-to-back sequence a

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut or draw windows, doors, and roof accents while each strip is flat; place windows at least 5 mm from cut edges and keep tabs undecorated.
Apply a thin, even layer of glue to the rear tab, align it near the back crease, and hold its wall upright until it stays in place.
Glue the middle tab about 3 cm forward of the rear row and the front tab about 3 cm ahead of the middle row, holding each face upright until stable.
Let the assembled rows rest undisturbed for the adhesive’s label time, then inspect the base from the front and both sides without pulling on buildings.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table and cut away from fingers; younger learners need direct adult supervision. This course does not require a craft knife.

blocks.question: Which assembly order best preserves access and visible depth?
options: A. Front row, then middle, then rear
B. Glue every row together as a flat stack
C. Rear row, then middle, then foreground
D. Attach the roof details before making any folds
blocks.explanation: Attaching rows rear-to-front makes tab placement easier and allows each closer row to overlap the one behind it.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Decorate and assemble the layers. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Finish, test, and refine the display
lessons.summary: Finish, test, and refine the display

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Finishing is a design decision, not a contest to fill every blank surface. Add one or two details that clarify place: a simple paper footpath, a row of trees, or a sign written in your own words. Keep the floor mostly open so the viewer can distinguish it from the building faces. A few low paper trees can be cut from scrap and glued flat to the floor; they are scenery, not supports. To make a modest freestanding tower, fold a separate 4 × 8 cm piece into a narrow rectangular column: score at 2 cm, 4 cm, and 6 cm across its width, fold into a square tube, and glue its 2 cm overlap tab. Keep the tower short—no taller than 8 cm—and attach it only if its base can sit flat behind a row without pushing the back panel. It is optional; omit it if the scene already feels crowded.

Inspect the model against observable criteria rather than an imagined perfect example. Are the rear, middle, and front rows visibly separate? Is the base flat on a tabletop? Do the walls stand without being held? Are any tabs unglued? Is glue completely dry? A tiny lean can be corrected by placing a narrow folded-card brace behind the wall, attached to the wall and floor with paper-safe adhesive. Make the brace no

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Add only selected finishing details, such as a footpath or two simple trees, and keep scenery flat and within the base outline.
Check the base on a level table, then inspect every wall and tab visually; press only the base lightly if you need to confirm it does not rock.
View the scene from front and side at tabletop distance, note one specific improvement, and move the finished model by supporting its floor from underneath.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table and cut away from fingers; younger learners need direct adult supervision. This course does not require a craft knife.

blocks.question: A paper wall leans after the glue has set. What is the safest suitable repair?
options: A. Put a heavy book on its roof
B. Attach a small folded-card brace behind the wall
C. Heat the joint with a flame
D. Pull the wall until the tab tears straight
blocks.explanation: A modest paper brace is a targeted repair for a leaning wall; do not use heat or heavy loads.

name: Cardboard Desk Caddy
tagline: Plan and build a small, dry-use desk caddy from clean corrugated cardboard.
outcome: Measure and mark a 20 cm by 14 cm base and three compartment dividers with consistent reference edges.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Cardboard Desk Caddy

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Plan and build a small, dry-use desk caddy from clean corrugated cardboard. Three open compartments organize lightweight stationery while folded walls and glued tabs keep the caddy together. The sampl

lessons.title: Plan the footprint and map the pieces
lessons.summary: Plan the footprint and map the pieces

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
### What you are building
The caddy has an open rectangular base measuring 20 cm wide by 14 cm deep. The back wall is 8 cm high; the front wall is 5 cm high so contents remain visible. Two side walls are 8 cm high. Inside, one divider runs front-to-back and one runs left-to-right across only the left bay. This makes three open areas: a broad right-hand bay for pens or a small notebook, and two smaller left-hand bays for an eraser, clips or sticky notes. These dimensions are design choices for this course, not a tested load rating.

Check your cardboard before drawing. Corrugated board has a wavy middle between flat paper faces. A crushed or damp region bends unpredictably, so place the base and walls on the flattest area. Orient the main corrugations vertically in the walls where practical; the walls stay visually straight, but this craft is still only a lightweight tabletop organizer. A liner sheet or board can hide the base's cut edges, but it does not make the caddy waterproof.

The sample wall strips include 1 cm joining tabs along their bottom edges. A tab is folded inward and glued to the base. This is easier to position than trying to butt-glue two raw edges. The outer shell

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Clear a tabletop, place scrap board over it, and inspect the carton for dampness, dirt, staples or crushed folds. Choose the flattest area.
On paper, sketch a 20 × 14 cm base with 20 × 8 cm back, 20 × 5 cm front and two 14 × 8 cm side panels; add a 1 cm tab to the lower edge of each wall.
Mark the base and four wall strips on cardboard with a ruler, measuring each dimension from a common square corner; label each piece and mark the tab fold line.

blocks.body: Work on a clear, stable tabletop; keep drinks and food away because this dry craft is not food-contact certified.

blocks.question: What are the sample outside dimensions of the base?
options: 20 cm wide by 14 cm deep
20 cm by 8 cm
14 cm by 8 cm
20 cm by 5 cm
blocks.explanation: The base is 20 × 14 cm. Wall panel heights and joining tabs are separate measurements.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the footprint and map the pieces. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut, score and pre-fold safely
lessons.summary: Cut, score and pre-fold safely

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
### Controlled cuts and folds
Cutting quality starts with support. Keep the cardboard flat on a sacrificial board and move it as needed so the cut stays comfortable. Scissors are suitable for many single-wall cartons. Use several small, controlled snips rather than twisting the blades through a thick corner. If the material resists, stop. For learners who need a knife cut, an adult should take over and use a stable cutting mat, a metal straightedge and light repeated passes rather than one forceful stroke. Keep the non-cutting hand behind the guide and away from the blade path.

The bottom tab fold line should be scored, not cut through. On a scrap, press a blunt scoring tool along a ruler with moderate, even pressure. The goal is a shallow groove that compresses the surface enough to guide a fold while leaving the paper liner intact. A cut that severs the liner can make the tab detach. Test the fold direction: the tab turns inward, toward the inside of the caddy. Make a small crease gradually rather than snapping the board sharply.

Cut pieces slightly outside the pencil line if your scissors tend to drift, then trim back to the line with small snips. Smooth sharp paper points by

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut out the base and four wall strips with scissors on the supported board, turning the cardboard rather than twisting your wrist; ask an adult to handle any stubborn knife cuts.
On each wall strip, use a blunt tool and ruler to press a shallow score exactly 1 cm from the bottom edge, then fold the tab inward slowly.
Place the four walls around the base without glue, tabs pointing inward, and check that the corners meet and the base remains rectangular.

blocks.body: Work on a clear, stable tabletop; keep drinks and food away because this dry craft is not food-contact certified.

blocks.question: Why make a shallow score along the 1 cm tab line?
options: To cut the wall into two separate pieces
To guide a controlled fold while leaving the liner connected
To make the caddy waterproof
To increase the caddy's certified load rating
blocks.explanation: A gentle score compresses the fold path; it should not sever the paper liner.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut, score and pre-fold safely. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Assemble the shell and fit the dividers
lessons.summary: Assemble the shell and fit the dividers

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
### Build the open shell
Assemble the outer walls one at a time. Apply a thin, continuous film of glue to the tab, not a large bead that squeezes into the interior. Hold the wall upright against the base edge. Use a paper right-angle corner or the square corner of a folded sheet to check the wall is close to vertical. Temporary masking tape can hold the outside seam while the glue begins to set. Follow the product label for full curing time; do not assume a surface that feels tacky is ready for handling.

The front wall is intentionally lower than the back. Confirm it is at the front before gluing. The two side walls and back are 8 cm high. If the base bows, lay it flat on the table and press gently along the tab from inside; do not place heavy objects on the assembly. Once the four walls are attached, let the shell rest. A small gap at a joint is not a reason to flood it with glue; a narrow paper patch can bridge the seam after the first bond dries.

Fit dividers only after measuring the actual interior. Measure from inside face to inside face at the position where each divider will sit. A snug divider can stand with small glue tabs folded at its ends; do not force it between wall

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Glue the back wall tab to the base, align it flush with the 20 cm edge and hold it upright with paper tape while checking the corner.
Attach the two side walls and lower front wall in turn, checking the 14 cm and 20 cm edges and maintaining the lower front orientation.
Leave the shell undisturbed for the adhesive label's required setting time, then measure inside widths and lengths where the dividers will sit.
Cut a front-to-back divider to the measured inside depth and about 8 cm high, then add small folded tabs or plan edge-gluing; position it roughly 7 cm from the left inside wall.
Measure the left bay between front and back inside faces; cut a cross divider about halfway along that bay, test fit and glue its ends or tabs in place.

blocks.body: Work on a clear, stable tabletop; keep drinks and food away because this dry craft is not food-contact certified.

blocks.question: What is the best way to size the dividers?
options: Use the full outside base dimensions
Cut them all to 20 cm long
Measure between the inside faces at each exact position
Force an oversized piece into the shell
blocks.explanation: Measure the actual interior after the shell is assembled, then trim gradually.

lessons.title: Finish, inspect and refine for real use
lessons.summary: Finish, inspect and refine for real use

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
### Finish without hiding defects
Wait until all structural glue has fully dried according to its label. Remove temporary tape slowly so it does not peel the outer paper layer. Inspect every corner and the divider joints before adding decoration. Pressing on a joint while it is damp can shift it and make a weak bond appear finished. If a joint has lifted, re-glue it in a thin layer and support it with tape or a paper brace until dry.

Optional facing paper can cover a plain exterior. Measure each face separately; cardboard thickness means the inside and outside panels are not all identical. Cut paper a little smaller than the face so it does not wrap over openings or cover a joint that still needs inspection. Spread a thin layer of glue across the paper, smooth from the middle outward, and let it dry flat. Do not coat the caddy with household chemicals, varnish or wet finishes. Keep this object dry and indoors. No decoration should obstruct the compartments or leave small loose pieces where a child or pet could swallow them.

Test with lightweight objects such as a few pens, one eraser and a small stack of sticky notes. Add items gradually and observe whether the base stays flat, t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Wait for full adhesive cure, remove temporary tape carefully and inspect seams, tabs and divider intersections before decorating.
Optionally measure and glue paper facing to individual exterior faces, keeping it clear of the open top and any questionable seam.
Place a few lightweight stationery items in the bays, then observe the base, walls and dividers without pressing or adding weight deliberately.
Write one observation, one proposed dimension change and one limit for safe use; store the caddy dry indoors.

blocks.body: Work on a clear, stable tabletop; keep drinks and food away because this dry craft is not food-contact certified.

blocks.question: A pair of scissors cannot cut through a thick corner. What should a beginner do?
options: Twist the scissors harder while holding the panel in the air
Stop, support the work and ask an adult to make a safe cut if needed
Bend the cardboard until it tears
Use a kitchen knife on the lap
blocks.explanation: Stop when resistance is high. The course specifies adult-handled knife cuts on a suitable mat, away from the body.

name: Notebook with a Replaceable Cover
tagline: Make a reusable wraparound sleeve for a small, ordinary notebook.
outcome: Measure a closed notebook's height, width and thickness and use those measurements to plan a removable sleeve with usable pocket depth.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Notebook with a Replaceable Cover

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a reusable wraparound sleeve for a small, ordinary notebook. The sleeve slides off without adhesive, has two inward-folded pockets that hold the notebook covers, and can be replaced when its pape

lessons.title: Measure the notebook and plan the sleeve
lessons.summary: Measure the notebook and plan the sleeve

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A removable cover works by wrapping around the notebook rather than sticking to it. The sheet must travel across the back, around the front and back covers, and into two inside pockets. If it is too short, the pocket edges will pull out. If it is much too long, the pockets will overlap awkwardly or buckle. Measure the actual notebook while it is closed and resting naturally; do not squeeze it thinner. Note height H, cover width W, and thickness T. Measure the thickness at the spine and at the fore-edge. If these differ, use the larger thickness so the paper does not have to stretch. The sample project uses H=8.5 in, W=5.5 in and T=0.5 in, but your measurements take priority.

For the sheet's short dimension, use H plus 0.5 in for top and bottom clearance, giving 9 in in the sample. For its long dimension, use 2W + 2T + two pocket depths P + 0.5 in of fitting ease. Set P to about 2 in for a flexible notebook cover. Sample arithmetic is 11 + 1 + 4 + 0.5 = 16.5 in. A 12 x 18 in sheet therefore leaves room to trim and square the edges. Divide the sample long dimension into zones: a 0.5 in fitting allowance at the outside edge, a 2 in pocket, a 5.5 in front panel, a 1 in spine zone (the

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Close the notebook and measure H, W and T at the spine and fore-edge; write down the larger thickness reading.
Calculate short sheet dimension as H+0.5 in and long dimension as 2W+2T+2P+0.5 in, with P about 2 in; sketch panel zones on scrap.
Make a paper mock-up of the panel sequence and slide the closed notebook into the proposed pockets before marking the cardstock.

blocks.body: Cut cardstock on a clear, stable surface with scissors pointed away from your body; keep fingers out of the cutting path and store scissors closed when not in use.

blocks.question: What is the best first step before choosing cardstock dimensions?
options: Measure the closed notebook's height, width and thickness
Assume all notebooks of the same page size have the same thickness
Cut a 12 x 18 inch sheet immediately
Fold the cardstock several times until it fits
blocks.explanation: Use the real closed notebook dimensions. Sample numbers are illustrative and should not override measuring.

lessons.title: Mark, score and fold the sleeve blank
lessons.summary: Mark, score and fold the sleeve blank

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Lay the cardstock with its longer dimension horizontal. Choose which face will be visible on the outside; make light pencil marks on the inside face so they can be erased later. Square one short edge to the ruler and use it as your starting edge. For the sample notebook, mark the panel boundaries in order from the left: first a 2 in pocket flap, then a 5.5 in front panel, then a 1 in spine allowance (about 2T for the sample's 0.5 in thickness), then a 5.5 in back panel, and finally a 2 in pocket flap. For another notebook, substitute the measured plan from Lesson 1. The additional 0.5 in fitting margin may be trimmed from the far edge after the test fit. For another notebook, replace these numbers with the calculated dimensions. Verify the sum with a ruler before making any crease. A single wrong boundary shifts every later panel.

Place a ruler along each pencil line and hold it firmly without placing fingers in the path of the scoring tool. Run a blunt folder along the ruler with steady, moderate pressure. Test on scrap first. A good score appears as a shallow straight indentation; a deep groove or cut means too much pressure. Fold the cardstock toward the inside so the crease li

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Mark the panel boundaries on the inside face, measuring each segment from the same squared edge and checking the total twice.
With a ruler held flat, make one controlled pass along each fold line using a blunt folder; test the pressure on scrap first.
Fold the two pocket flaps inward, open them, then wrap the untrimmed blank around the notebook and seat both covers in the pockets.

blocks.body: Cut cardstock on a clear, stable surface with scissors pointed away from your body; keep fingers out of the cutting path and store scissors closed when not in use.

blocks.question: Why does the project score a fold before creasing stiff cardstock?
options: To cut partway through the sheet so it bends freely
To make a shallow guide that helps the fold form in a controlled line
To make adhesive stick to the inside
To permanently attach the notebook cover
blocks.explanation: Scoring creates a guided indentation. Use a blunt scoring tool, not a sharp blade.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Mark, score and fold the sleeve blank. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Shape the pockets and finish the edges
lessons.summary: Shape the pockets and finish the edges

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Keep the notebook closed while checking the sleeve. Remove it before trimming. First inspect the top and bottom edges. The sample has half an inch of total height clearance, so if centered it leaves roughly a quarter inch at each end. Mark parallel trimming lines only where the sheet extends beyond that allowance. Do not cut away the pocket depth or the panel widths. Cut slowly with scissors on the table, advancing the paper rather than reaching across the cutting path. If the sheet is too small already, do not trim it further; remake the sleeve with a larger blank.

Return the notebook to the sleeve. Put the front cover fully into its pocket, then do the back cover. Smooth the wrap from the spine outward with your palm. A pocket should grip through its depth and friction, not through a tight pinch. Open the notebook a few pages and close it again. The sleeve should stay seated and should not drag pages, cover the writing area, or spring away from the fore-edge. If the paper springs open, check that the spine allowance includes the notebook thickness. A temporary paper clip can hold a test fold while you assess it, but remove clips before normal use so they cannot scratch or snag.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Remove the notebook, mark the top and bottom margins, and trim only excess paper with scissors while keeping fingers away from the blades.
Reinsert the closed notebook, seat each cover fully inside its pocket, and smooth the spine and panels by hand.
Erase remaining inside-face marks and optionally decorate flat panels with light dry media; let optional media dry before reinstalling.

blocks.body: Cut cardstock on a clear, stable surface with scissors pointed away from your body; keep fingers out of the cutting path and store scissors closed when not in use.

blocks.question: The notebook slips out of one pocket, but the rest of the wrap fits. What is the most targeted next change?
options: Make the entire wrap much tighter
Glue the notebook cover to the pocket
Increase the shallow pocket depth on a fresh blank
Trim more from the pocket edge
blocks.explanation: Change the dimension linked to the symptom. Keep the notebook removable and make the pocket deeper.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Shape the pockets and finish the edges. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Test the fit and refine for replacement use
lessons.summary: Test the fit and refine for replacement use

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful test is gentle and repeatable, not a stress test. Open the notebook to a comfortable writing position, turn several pages, and close it. Watch the top and bottom edges and both pocket corners. Then slide the notebook out and back in once, using the normal insertion path. Do not yank on a pocket or pull sharply at a crease. The sleeve is intended to organize and personalize stationery on a desk; it is not impact protection. If you carry the notebook in a bag, treat the sleeve as decorative and keep sharp objects away from it.

Look for four fit signals. The back panel should sit over the back cover without a large gap. The spine should not be crushed or visibly rounded by a tight wrap. Each pocket should cover enough of its notebook cover to stay seated when the notebook is opened gently. Finally, the top and bottom edges should not extend so far that they catch on pages. A mark at a fold may mean the score was too deep or that the grain direction resisted the fold. Paper grain is not always obvious on a purchased sheet; when unsure, test a small offcut by gently bending it in both directions and choose the direction that bends more smoothly for the principal folds. Do not

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Open, page through, close, and remove/reinsert the notebook gently while watching pocket corners and fold lines.
Diagnose any gap, bulge or slip by comparing it to the recorded panel measurements, then select one adjustment for the next blank.
Record final H, W, T, pocket depth and any adjustment on a project note stored with the notebook.

blocks.body: Cut cardstock on a clear, stable surface with scissors pointed away from your body; keep fingers out of the cutting path and store scissors closed when not in use.

blocks.question: Which tool and approach are appropriate for scoring this beginner cardstock sleeve?
options: An exposed craft knife pressed deeply along the ruler
A sharp kitchen knife used freehand
A powered cutter with its guard removed
A blunt folder or rounded plastic-ruler edge, tested on scrap
blocks.explanation: A blunt scoring tool is sufficient. Test pressure on scrap and keep the paper surface intact.

name: Fold-Out Homework Planner
tagline: Build a compact, freestanding paper planner that opens into four labeled panels: this week, next week, projects, and notes.
outcome: Measure and lay out a four-panel planner body with four equal 5 by 8 inch panels and a clear fold allowance.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Fold-Out Homework Planner

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Build a compact, freestanding paper planner that opens into four labeled panels: this week, next week, projects, and notes. The folded body is 8 by 5 inches; the display base is a light, non-load-bear

lessons.title: Plan the panels and prepare the fold strip
lessons.summary: Plan the panels and prepare the fold strip

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: The finished planner is built around a simple accordion: four panels connected in a zigzag so the pages can spread across a desk and fold into a compact stack. An accordion is made from one long sheet or from joined sheets folded in alternating directions; the alternating folds are what let the strip open and close without tearing at a single hinge [1]. This design uses two 8.5 by 11 inch sheets. Cut four panels exactly 5 by 8 inches from them, then join the short edges with narrow paper tabs. The resulting panel sequence is four panels wide, approximately 20 inches open, and 8 inches tall. The 8.5-inch sheet width leaves a 3-inch remainder, which becomes joining tabs and test strips rather than waste. Set aside a 1/4-inch unprinted margin along each panel edge that will be joined; writing too near a hinge can disappear into the fold. The planner is deliberately small enough to sit on a desk, not large enough to serve as a wall chart. Before gluing anything, mark each panel lightly: This Week, Next Week, Projects, and Notes. The headings are original functional labels, not a copied artwork or branded design. Keep dates and task text in pencil or erasable ink if the plan may change.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure and cut four 5 by 8 inch panels from the two sheets, keeping the edges square.
On the reverse, mark a 1/4-inch joining tab on the short edge of panels 1, 2, and 3; lightly score each tab at its base and fold it under.
Dry-fit the four panels in order, alternating which side of each panel faces up, and label their positions lightly.

blocks.body: Use scissors slowly, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand outside the cutting path. A young learner should have adult supervision; use pre-cut pieces if appropriate.

blocks.question: Why are the three panel creases folded in alternating directions?
options: A. To make a zigzag that opens and collapses as an accordion.
B. To make every panel permanently stand upright.
C. To make the paper waterproof.
D. To shorten the planner by cutting material away.
blocks.explanation: An accordion uses alternating creases so adjacent panels can fold into a compact stack and reopen.

lessons.title: Join, crease, and label the planner
lessons.summary: Join, crease, and label the planner

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: Good paper folds are controlled bends, not cuts. Use a blunt tool and modest pressure to compress the fibers along a straight line; pressing too hard can sever the sheet, while folding without a guide can produce a wandering hinge. The three joins between four panels are alternating hinges. Lay the joined strip face down. At the first joint, fold away from you; at the next joint, fold toward you; continue alternating. In profile this makes a zigzag. A dry fold test before adding any decoration shows whether the hinges are truly alternating. Keep the hinge band free of thick marker, stickers, or glued layers because extra thickness concentrates bending force. A thin paper tape strip can reinforce the reverse of a join, but tape should not cover both faces at once or create a stiff ridge that prevents the fold. Apply a small amount of adhesive under each tab, smooth from the center outward, and leave the assembly flat until the glue sets according to its label. If glue squeezes into a hinge, lift the panel gently while it is still workable and wipe excess onto scrap paper; do not force a dried, glued hinge. For decoration, use original shapes, a color key, or simple boxes. Do not dra

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Apply a thin film of glue under each 1/4-inch tab, overlap the neighboring panel by the tab width, and press flat on scrap paper.
Mark three fold lines at the panel joints with the blunt scorer, then fold them in alternating directions to form a zigzag stack.
Add four headings and simple writing guides, keeping at least 1/2 inch clear around each fold and outer edge.

blocks.body: Use scissors slowly, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand outside the cutting path. A young learner should have adult supervision; use pre-cut pieces if appropriate.

blocks.question: Where should headings and writing stay clear of decoration?
options: A. Directly over each fold line.
B. Within a 1/2-inch margin around folds and outer edges.
C. Only on the cover boards.
D. Under the glued joining tabs.
blocks.explanation: Clear margins prevent writing from being hidden by folds, covers, or join tabs.

lessons.title: Make covers and a tabletop easel
lessons.summary: Make covers and a tabletop easel

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: Covers protect the folded paper from casual desk handling, but this thin cardboard construction does not turn the planner into a rigid book or a protective device. Cut two cover boards measuring 5 1/4 by 8 1/4 inches. These are slightly larger than a 5 by 8 inch panel, leaving a narrow margin on each side. Wrap each board in a 9 by 6 inch piece of paper: center the board, fold the paper over each long edge, and fold the short ends like a neat parcel. Trim only where folded layers would pile up at a corner; keep a small overlap so cardboard is not exposed. Glue the cover to the outside face of the first and last planner panels, leaving the hinge line clear. Close the planner and check that both covers align before the glue sets. For display, make a separate easel from thin cardboard: a 6 by 8 inch support panel with a triangular rear leg cut from a 3 by 6 inch rectangle. The support acts as a backboard; the folded planner rests against it. The rear leg should touch the tabletop and lean against the backboard, making a broad triangle. Use a 1-inch strip of paper tape along the hinge between leg and backboard, with half the tape on each part. A shallow 1/2-inch bottom lip, made by fol

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut two 5 1/4 by 8 1/4 inch cover boards and wrap each in a centered 9 by 6 inch cover-paper piece, folding and gluing the margins to the back.
Attach one cover to the outside of the first panel and one to the outside of the last, leaving the first and last creases free.
Cut a 6 by 8 inch backboard, a 3 by 6 inch leg, and a 1/2 by 6 inch lip strip from thin cardboard; join the leg to the backboard with paper tape as a hinge and attach the lip at th

blocks.body: Use scissors slowly, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand outside the cutting path. A young learner should have adult supervision; use pre-cut pieces if appropriate.

blocks.question: What is the correct response if the easel rocks on the table?
options: A. Place a heavy object on the top edge.
B. Use it near the table edge so it can lean outward.
C. Stop, check the level surface, and reposition or widen the rear leg.

modules.description: Build a compact tabletop board that holds three changeable task cards under a clear reusable writing surface. A paper backer, folded cardboard easel, and simple card pockets make it easy to sort work

lessons.title: Plan the board and prepare its parts
lessons.summary: Plan the board and prepare its parts

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The finished board uses a 20 × 15 cm front panel. Three 6 × 7 cm task cards sit across the lower half, each held by a shallow pocket. A clear sleeve lies over the upper writing strip, so you can write a date or one short priority and wipe it away. The cards carry longer task names; the categories are Next, Doing, and Done. This separation keeps the board readable without forcing every note into tiny handwriting.

The plan deliberately leaves a 1 cm margin on each side. Place the three 6.5 cm-wide pockets with approximately 0.25 cm gaps and minimal side margins; the row then uses about 20 cm of the 20 cm panel width. Leave about 1 cm between the pocket row and the top writing window. Dry-fit the full row before attaching anything. Try the paper pieces in position before taping anything. If a card fits too tightly, it will snag; if the pocket is too wide, the card can slouch or slide out when the board is lifted. A good fit lets a card move with two fingers but keeps it upright when the board rests on the table.

Measure twice and cut once. Mark dimensions lightly in pencil on the back of the material. Keep the ruler flat and check that its zero mark begins at the panel edge rather t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut a 20 × 15 cm white cardstock front panel and a 22 × 17 cm cardboard backer. Mark corners with a ruler and pencil.
Cut three task cards, each 6 × 7 cm, from cardstock. Write Next, Doing, and Done at the top of separate cards in pencil for layout only.
Cut three pocket faces 6.5 × 3 cm. Fold a 0.5 cm tab along each short side and along the bottom, leaving the top open.
Arrange the three 6.5 cm pocket faces in a row on the lower panel with approximately 0.25 cm gaps and minimal side margins; check the full row fits the 20 cm panel, then place the

blocks.body: Use blunt-tip scissors on a clear tabletop, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand behind the cutting path. Younger learners need an adult nearby.

blocks.question: What is the planned size of each removable task card?
options: 6 × 7 cm
2 × 7 cm
blocks.explanation: The course specifies three 6 × 7 cm cards and pockets arranged across a 20 cm-wide panel.

lessons.title: Create the reusable writing face and card pockets
lessons.summary: Create the reusable writing face and card pockets

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A clear sheet protector can serve as a wipe-clean barrier over paper. The specialist classroom example referenced below uses cardstock inside a protector as a reusable writing surface; this course adapts that simple material idea into a compact task board. Actual marker compatibility varies by sleeve finish and marker formulation, so test a hidden corner with the exact marker you plan to use. Write a small mark, wait a minute, and wipe it with a dry soft cloth. If the mark smears permanently or leaves color behind, do not put the sleeve on the board; switch to a known dry-erase-compatible reusable sleeve.

Cut no more clear plastic than necessary. Ideally, use the intact sealed edge as a top or side edge and trim only the open edge if the sleeve is too large. Avoid tiny loose scraps, and discard them safely. Put white cardstock behind the writing area to improve contrast. Tape the sleeve along its non-opening edge, with a hinge-like strip rather than a strip across the whole face. The sleeve should lie flat, but it must still open enough to replace the backing sheet if you want to change the heading.

For the task pockets, fold the tabs away from the visible face. Secure only the t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Test the marker on a discreet corner of the clear sleeve: make a 1 cm line, wait 60 seconds, then wipe with the dry fabric square.
Cut the sleeve to cover an approximately 20 × 4 cm top strip, preserving a sealed edge if possible; slide a white cardstock strip behind it.
Attach the writing window at its upper edge with paper tape, placing tape on the backer and folding it over as a hinge; secure the other edge with two small side tabs if needed.
Attach one test pocket using only its folded side and bottom tabs; insert and remove a task card five times before adding the other two.

blocks.body: Use blunt-tip scissors on a clear tabletop, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand behind the cutting path. Younger learners need an adult nearby.

blocks.question: Why test marker erasability on a small hidden sleeve corner first?
options: It makes the plastic stronger
It reveals whether that marker and sleeve combination wipes clean before the main face is used
It measures the board's load capacity
It removes the need for dry wiping
blocks.explanation: The course requires a small test with the exact materials and says to stop if residue remains.

lessons.title: Assemble the board and make a tabletop easel
lessons.summary: Assemble the board and make a tabletop easel

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Once the writing strip and test pocket work, attach the remaining two pockets at the measured positions. Keep the top openings aligned. Insert the matching cards before pressing the tabs down firmly; this checks that no tape or glue blocks the channel. Add simple original visual cues if useful, such as a small pencil-drawn dot pattern on each card. Avoid relying on color alone to communicate status, and do not copy branded characters or artwork. Plain words and shapes make the board personal and easy to revise.

The backing easel is a folded cardboard brace, not a frame or a shelf. The 20 × 7 cm strip is creased at 2 cm and 5 cm from one end, producing three panels measuring 2, 3, and 2 cm. Tape the first 2 cm panel near the lower rear of the board, then fold the middle section outward and attach the far 2 cm tab to the backer near its bottom edge. The exact angle is not a safety rating; it is only a way to lean the light board on a tabletop. If the material crushes, substitute a second cardboard strip or use the board flat. Do not add heavy objects, suspend it, or place it where a bump could send it falling.

Try the stand on a clean, level table. The board should rest with its lo

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Attach the other two pockets in the planned row, using their folded tabs and checking each card fit before pressing tape or glue firmly.
Center the front panel on the cardboard backer, leaving an approximately 1 cm border, and attach it with tape around the back or glue on the outer margins.
Cut a cardboard brace 20 × 7 cm. Mark fold lines 2 cm and 5 cm from one short end, then crease gently with the ruler edge without cutting through the cardboard.
Tape one 2 cm end tab to the rear lower area of the board; fold the center outward and tape the far tab to the backer so the brace forms a triangular support.
Place the board on a stable tabletop and observe it from the front; test gentle writing pressure with one finger on the clear strip.

blocks.body: Use blunt-tip scissors on a clear tabletop, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand behind the cutting path. Younger learners need an adult nearby.

blocks.question: Which repair is appropriate if a pocket binds a card?
options: Force the card through repeatedly
Seal the opening with tape
Ease the side tabs outward and test the card again
Apply solvent to the pocket
blocks.explanation: A tight pocket is corrected by adjusting its side tabs, then checking that the card moves freely.

lessons.title: Use, test, and refine your task system
lessons.summary: Use, test, and refine your task system

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful board is not the one with the most decoration; it is the one whose next action is obvious. Put only actionable tasks on the cards. “Read chapter” is vague, while “Read pages 12–16 and write two questions” gives a clear endpoint. Keep each card to one task or one short task sequence. Move a card from Next to Doing when work starts, and to Done when the stated endpoint is met. A task that grows should be split into smaller cards rather than squeezed into tiny writing.

Before daily use, write a sample priority on the clear window and erase it with the dry cloth. Do not use wet cleaners, abrasive pads, or a marker that has not passed the test. If the writing ghosts, stop and verify the marker on the spare corner again. A faint mark may mean the surface is unsuitable or the marker was left too long; erase promptly and switch to a tested compatible combination. Replace a scratched or cloudy sleeve rather than pressing harder.

Check the physical build after moving the board between desks. Paper pockets and tape can loosen, especially if cards are pulled sharply. Repair a loose tab with a small tape patch, keeping the opening free. If the stand feels weak, use the board flat unt

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Write one short sample priority on the clear strip, wait a minute, and erase it using the dry fabric square.
Write three actionable tasks on the removable cards, place them in Next, Doing, and Done, then move one card through the sequence to model completion.
Inspect the board edges, pocket tabs, clear window, and brace; record one observed flaw and make one small revision or state why a flat layout is safer.

blocks.body: Use blunt-tip scissors on a clear tabletop, cut away from fingers, and keep the other hand behind the cutting path. Younger learners need an adult nearby.

blocks.question: What should you do if the cardboard easel rocks under light writing pressure?
options: Stack a heavy object behind it
Use the board flat or add a light paper shim under the brace
Stand on the board to test strength
Use it in a moving vehicle
blocks.explanation: The safe response is to use a flat layout or adjust the brace lightly; the stand is not load-bearing.

name: Cardboard Drawer Dividers
tagline: Measure one drawer and build a removable, four-cell grid from clean corrugated cardboard.
outcome: Measure a drawer's usable inside width, depth, and height, then select divider dimensions with clearance for easy removal.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Cardboard Drawer Dividers

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Measure one drawer and build a removable, four-cell grid from clean corrugated cardboard. You will test the fit before joining the panels, adjust a snug slot without forcing it, and choose sensible us

lessons.title: Measure the drawer and choose a layout
lessons.summary: Measure the drawer and choose a layout

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A good divider begins with the drawer, not with a guess about a standard size. Open it fully and measure the clear inside width at the front, middle, and back. Some drawers taper or have runners that intrude. Use the smallest usable width. Measure inside depth at both sides and use the smaller value. Measure the inside height from the floor to the lowest obstruction, such as a handle screw or overhanging rail. The sample design in this lesson fits a drawer whose usable space is approximately 12 inches wide, 9 inches deep, and at least 2 1/2 inches high. These are example dimensions, not a claim about every drawer. For another drawer, repeat the arithmetic and make a paper test.

The sample uses two intersecting panels, creating four compartments. Leave a small clearance so the grid lifts out instead of scraping the walls. With a 12-by-9-inch clear drawer, make the long panel 11 7/8 inches long and the cross panel 8 7/8 inches long. Each panel is 2 1/4 inches tall, leaving about 1/4 inch below a 2 1/2-inch drawer rim. Mark the drawer floor with removable paper guides if helpful, but do not write on the furniture. Think about what will go into each cell: a compartment for pens needs

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure inside width at the front, center, and back; measure depth on both sides and clear height at the lowest obstruction.
Subtract 1/8 inch from the smallest width and depth to set panel lengths; choose a height about 1/4 inch below the drawer's clear height.
Sketch a top view with one long panel crossing one short panel at their midpoints; note which items will occupy each of the four cells.
Inspect a flat cardboard area and mark the flute direction on its edge with an arrow; try a shallow score and fold on the scrap only.

blocks.body: Cutting is the sharpest-risk task. A teen or adult should handle the craft knife; younger learners can mark lines while an adult cuts. Follow the tool maker's age and use guidance.

blocks.question: Your drawer measures 12 inches wide at the front but 11 7/8 inches at its narrowest usable point. What is the best approach for the sample clearance?
options: Cut the panel to 12 inches so it fills the front exactly.
Use the narrowest measurement and leave a little clearance, then dry-fit.
Measure the drawer exterior and subtract one inch.
Make the insert intentionally wider and bend it into place.
blocks.explanation: Measure the usable inside dimensions at multiple points. The sample subtracts a small clearance from the narrowest measurement and verifies fit before joining.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Measure the drawer and choose a layout. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Mark and cut two matching panels
lessons.summary: Mark and cut two matching panels

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Accurate, square panels make the later joint easier to align. Lay the cardboard on a mat with a broad flat area. Identify its flute direction before deciding where to put the long edges. In a folded cardboard structure, fold orientation affects how readily a crease collapses; maker education material demonstrates a difference between folds made in line with flutes and folds made across them. Here, we avoid depending on a folded load-bearing corner: the panels remain flat and support one another through their slots. The flute observation is still useful when you orient the pieces and when you practice any optional paper-tab fold. Do not interpret a clean fold as proof of load capacity.

Mark the long panel as 11 7/8 inches by 2 1/4 inches and the cross panel as 8 7/8 inches by 2 1/4 inches for the sample drawer. Use a straightedge and pencil. Mark each outline on the same face, then label the parts “long” and “cross.” Before cutting, verify the lengths against the written drawer measurements. A frequent mistake is to measure the second panel from the first panel's edge rather than from zero on the ruler; independently check each end-to-end dimension. Make cuts on a stable mat with t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Mark one 11 7/8 × 2 1/4-inch rectangle and one 8 7/8 × 2 1/4-inch rectangle, labeling each before cutting.
Secure the board on a cutting mat and cut each outline with the blade moving away from the body, using repeated light passes along a straightedge.
Place each cut panel flat in the drawer in its planned direction, without joining them, and verify the 1/8-inch target clearance.
Use an offcut to test a shallow score with a blunt tool, stopping before the outer liner is pierced.

blocks.body: Cutting is the sharpest-risk task. A teen or adult should handle the craft knife; younger learners can mark lines while an adult cuts. Follow the tool maker's age and use guidance.

blocks.question: For the sample 2 1/4-inch-high panels, how deep is each half-height slot?
options: 2 1/4 inches
3/16 inch
1 1/8 inches
1/4 inch
blocks.explanation: The opposing slots each extend halfway through the panel height, so their depths add to the full 2 1/4-inch panel height.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Mark and cut two matching panels. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut the complementary slots and join the grid
lessons.summary: Cut the complementary slots and join the grid

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The grid is made by two slots that meet at the center. One slot opens upward from the bottom edge of the long panel. The other opens downward from the top edge of the cross panel. Each slot stops halfway through the panel height, so the panels interlock with their top edges level. On the sample 2 1/4-inch-tall panels, the slot depth is 1 1/8 inches. A slot should be only as wide as the cardboard is thick, with a small allowance for a hand-cut fit. Measure the actual board thickness at a clean cut edge rather than relying on the nominal “about 1/8 inch.” A practical starting slot width is that measured thickness plus about 1/16 inch. If the board is 1/8 inch thick, the starting slot is 3/16 inch wide. Test this width first on the scrap.

Mark the long panel's center at 5 15/16 inches from either end. Mark the cross panel's center at 4 7/16 inches from either end. Center the slot on each mark. Cut the long-panel slot from its lower edge upward 1 1/8 inches. Cut the cross-panel slot from its upper edge downward 1 1/8 inches. Keep the slot sides parallel; a tapered or angled slot can make the intersection lean. A ruler helps mark the slot, but the blade cut should be controlled and sup

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure cardboard thickness at a clean edge, then test a slot on scrap at thickness plus about 1/16 inch.
Mark the center of the long panel 5 15/16 inches from an end and mark a centered slot 3/16 inch wide, 1 1/8 inches up from its bottom edge.
On the cross panel, mark its center 4 7/16 inches from an end and a matching-width slot 1 1/8 inches down from the top edge.
Cut each slot carefully on a mat with controlled passes, stopping precisely at its half-height endpoint; then slide the parts together by hand.

blocks.body: Cutting is the sharpest-risk task. A teen or adult should handle the craft knife; younger learners can mark lines while an adult cuts. Follow the tool maker's age and use guidance.

blocks.question: You are about to cut a slot, but the cardboard slips and the blade catches. What should you do?
options: Pull harder so the blade finishes the cut quickly.
Hold the moving cardboard close to the cut line.
Stop, retract the blade, stabilize the work on the mat, and get appropriate adult help if needed.
Try cutting while holding the panel in the air.
blocks.explanation: Stop if the board moves or the blade catches. Retract the tool, resecure the workpiece on a mat, and use appropriate supervision rather than forcing a cut.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut the complementary slots and join the grid. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Test, label, and refine the organizer
lessons.summary: Test, label, and refine the organizer

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
An empty-drawer test is part of the build, not a decorative final step. Lift the assembled grid by its panels and lower it into the drawer without scraping. It should sit on the bottom, leave a little wall clearance, and have no panel pressing against the drawer front or back. Look from above: the crossing should be close to square, and each cell should retain a useful opening. If the grid leans, remove it and inspect the slots. One slot may be off-center, too wide, or cut at a slight angle. Correct the cause rather than trying to bend the panel into place while it is trapped in the drawer.

Next, test a few light, dry supplies such as capped pens, erasers, sticky notes, and paper clips in a small dish or envelope. Paper clips can fall through gaps at the bottom because the design uses no base; that is a feature of a removable grid, not a defect to hide. Keep loose tiny items in a small paper envelope or an existing container placed in a cell. Do not add liquids, sharp blades, food, fragile items, heat sources, or a heavy stack of books. The dividers are not furniture and have no tested load rating. If the cells are too small for the intended contents, revise the layout or move the

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Lower the empty joined grid into the drawer and inspect wall clearance, panel height, squareness, and ease of removal.
Place a few light dry desk items into the four cells, leaving room to remove them without bending the panels.
Use a small paper envelope for tiny loose pieces and add optional labels or a short paper-tape tab only if needed.
Record one fit observation and one next improvement, then remove the insert and store it flat when not needed.

blocks.body: Cutting is the sharpest-risk task. A teen or adult should handle the craft knife; younger learners can mark lines while an adult cuts. Follow the tool maker's age and use guidance.

blocks.question: The slots bind even though the drawn marks look centered. What is the most useful next check?
options: Compare the opening to actual board thickness and the scrap slot test.
Bend the panels hard until the joint closes.
Add a heavy object on top to push the pieces together.
Cut a long slit through the entire panel height.
blocks.explanation: Use the real thickness and scrap test as a guide. Widen a binding slot in small increments while keeping its walls parallel.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Test, label, and refine the organizer. What did you learn and verify?

name: Reading Journal with Pocket Inserts
tagline: Make a soft-cover reading journal from ordinary paper, with three removable folded pocket inserts for reading cards, quotes, and next-read notes.
outcome: Measure and prepare a 5 x 7 inch paper journal cover and four folded writing sheets with consistent grain-free, square edges using a ruler and pencil.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Reading Journal with Pocket Inserts

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a soft-cover reading journal from ordinary paper, with three removable folded pocket inserts for reading cards, quotes, and next-read notes. The inserts are sized for a finished 5 x 7 inch journa

lessons.title: Plan the journal and make its pages
lessons.summary: Plan the journal and make its pages

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Start with the finished object in mind: a closed journal 5 inches wide and 7 inches tall, small enough to sit beside a book but large enough for short reading notes. Four 10 x 7 inch inner sheets fold once to make eight leaves, or sixteen writing surfaces. The cover is also 10 x 7 inches before folding. Place the long 10-inch edge horizontally and fold in half so the final spine is 7 inches tall. A folded sheet is called a leaf; the nested leaves make a small signature. This simple paper model is for ordinary desk use, not for archival preservation or heavy handling.

Measure carefully before cutting. A small mismatch between sheets can be trimmed later, but a cover that is substantially smaller than the pages may catch their corners. Use a blunt scoring tool and a ruler to establish the fold before pressing it. Scoring means making a shallow crease line, not cutting through the sheet. On scrap, compare a direct fold with a lightly scored fold; the scored line should guide the crease without tearing fibers. Keep pencil marks on the inside edges where they can be erased. If the paper is already exactly the desired size, do not trim it just to match an example.

Check the stack befor

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On four inner sheets, mark a 10 x 7 inch rectangle and trim each with scissors; repeat for one cover sheet of the same size.
With each sheet horizontal, mark the midpoint at 5 inches along the long edge, lightly score from top to bottom, then fold the two halves together.
Nest the four folded inner sheets, place the folded cover around them, and tap the spine and open edges gently on the table to align.

blocks.body: Cut away from your body on a clear, stable tabletop. Keep fingers behind the scissor blades and close scissors when setting them down; younger learners need adult supervision.

blocks.question: What size does a 10 x 7 inch writing sheet become when folded once across its 10-inch dimension?
options: 5 x 7 inches
10 x 3.5 inches
4 x 6 inches
3 x 5 inches
blocks.explanation: The sheet is 10 inches wide and 7 inches tall; folding the width in half produces a 5 x 7 inch leaf.
