name: Fabric Storage Basket for Light Items
tagline: Sew a small lined, softly structured fabric basket for light desk or craft items such as paper clips, fabric scraps or folded notes.
outcome: Measure and cut matching cotton panels and stabilizer using a consistent half-inch seam allowance.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Fabric Storage Basket for Light Items

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Sew a small lined, softly structured fabric basket for light desk or craft items such as paper clips, fabric scraps or folded notes. Two boxed corners give the base depth, while a lining conceals most

lessons.title: Plan, mark and prepare the panels
lessons.summary: Plan, mark and prepare the panels

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The sample basket uses four matching rectangles, each 10 inches wide by 6.5 inches tall: two for the outside and two for the lining. At each lower corner of every rectangle, mark a square 1.5 inches on each side. When the side seams are sewn at a half-inch allowance and the opposing corner edges are joined, the base is about 7 inches wide by 3 inches deep. The finished wall height is roughly 4.5 inches, depending on seam turn and pressing. The finished measurements are approximate because fabric thickness and sewing accuracy affect them. This is a useful light-duty desk size, not a rigid bin.

Choose a stable woven cotton that does not stretch when gently pulled diagonally. Prewash only if appropriate for the fabric and dry it fully. Press wrinkles flat with heat that the fabric can tolerate; do not assume every scrap tolerates an iron. If you use fusible interfacing, follow that specific product's temperature and pressing instructions rather than a generic setting. A small test on an offcut can reveal scorching, adhesive residue or poor bonding before the full panels are involved. Keep the interfacing within the fabric edges so it does not stick to the iron or pressing surface. A

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure and cut two outer and two lining rectangles, each 10 x 6.5 inches; square the corners and label the pairs on the wrong side.
On all four pieces, mark a 1.5-inch square in both lower corners and cut out the eight squares.
Fuse or baste optional interfacing to the wrong side of the two outer panels, following the product's own instructions and testing first on a scrap.
Sew a short test seam on scraps, then verify a balanced straight stitch and an approximately half-inch seam allowance with the ruler.

blocks.body: Keep fingers clear of the needle path; stop with the needle down before repositioning fabric, and switch off/unplug the machine before changing its needle or clearing a jam.

blocks.question: Why are the same-size squares removed from both lower corners of every panel?
options: They provide fabric edges that can be joined to form a shallow base
They make the top opening elastic
They reduce the basket's finished height by exactly half
They create ventilation holes
blocks.explanation: A corner notch is opened flat and its opposing edges are sewn together, converting a flat panel into a three-dimensional base.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan, mark and prepare the panels. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Sew and shape the outer shell
lessons.summary: Sew and shape the outer shell

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The outer shell is made from two panels with their printed or right sides facing one another. Sew the two long side edges and the bottom edge, leaving the top open. Keep the half-inch seam allowance consistent, and backstitch a few stitches at the start and finish of each seam to discourage unraveling. The lower corner cutouts interrupt the bottom edge; sew only along the remaining straight portions, stopping and starting at the cutout corners. Do not sew across the open notch yet. A slow, steady pace gives a beginner more control than trying to steer quickly around thick intersections.

To form a boxed corner, open one cutout so its two raw edges meet. The side seam should align exactly with the center of the little flattened end; pin or clip through both layers. Measure the seam line 1.5 inches from the point where the cutout edges meet, then sew across that line. The 1.5-inch measurement is the distance across the flat corner from edge to edge, not the half-inch seam allowance. This joined edge becomes the depth of the base. Repeat for the other outer corner and both lining corners in the next lesson. Avoid catching folds in the seam: feel the layers flat before sewing and keep

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the two outer panels right sides together and sew both sides and the bottom's straight segments at a half-inch allowance, securing seam ends; leave the top open.
Flatten each outer cutout with its side seam centered, align the raw edges and sew a straight 1.5-inch corner seam across the flat edge.
Turn the outer shell right side out, shape corners with fingers or a blunt tool and place it on a level table to inspect the base.
Trim bulky corner allowances carefully to about 1/4 inch only after verifying the stitching, and press the shell if material care permits.

blocks.body: Keep fingers clear of the needle path; stop with the needle down before repositioning fabric, and switch off/unplug the machine before changing its needle or clearing a jam.

blocks.question: What is the sample corner seam measurement across the flattened 1.5-inch notch?
options: One-half inch
One and a half inches
Three inches
Six and a half inches
blocks.explanation: Do not confuse the 1.5-inch corner seam across the flat notch with the half-inch allowance at the panel edges.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Sew and shape the outer shell. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build the lining and join the basket
lessons.summary: Build the lining and join the basket

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Make the lining in the same sequence as the outer shell, but leave a turning opening in the bottom. Place the two lining panels right sides together. Sew the side edges and the bottom segments, stopping with a gap about 3 inches long at the center of the bottom seam. Secure the stitching on both sides of the gap. The gap is not a defect: it is the route through which the joined basket will be turned right side out. Then form and sew the two boxed corners exactly as for the outer shell. Keep the opening away from those corners so it remains accessible and does not weaken a high-stress junction.

Keep the outer shell right side out. Leave the lining wrong side out and slip the shell inside it. The right sides of the outer and lining should face each other, and their top raw edges should align. Match side seams first, then distribute any small easing evenly around the opening. Pin or clip at the seam intersections and at a few points between them. Stitch all the way around the top edge at a half-inch allowance. Before turning, check that you have joined the full circumference and not accidentally sewn the mouth closed through extra folds. Trim only bulky seam allowance if desired, tak

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Sew the lining side seams and bottom segments right sides together at a half-inch allowance, leaving a centered, secured 3-inch bottom opening; sew both boxed corners as before.
Place the right-side-out outer shell inside the wrong-side-out lining; match top edges and side seams, then clip around the rim.
Sew around the complete top circumference at a half-inch allowance, avoiding folds; secure the beginning and end of the seam.
Pull the outer shell through the lining gap, ease the corners gently, tuck lining inside, then close the gap by machine or hand with raw edges folded inward.

blocks.body: Keep fingers clear of the needle path; stop with the needle down before repositioning fabric, and switch off/unplug the machine before changing its needle or clearing a jam.

blocks.question: Why should the lining bottom include a secured three-inch opening?
options: It lets the basket be hung
It creates a drainage outlet
It gives room to turn the joined basket right side out
It makes the boxed corners longer
blocks.explanation: The turning gap is a temporary construction opening and must be closed after turning.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build the lining and join the basket. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Finish, inspect and choose a sensible use
lessons.summary: Finish, inspect and choose a sensible use

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Shape the lining fully into the basket and roll the top seam so it sits at the very edge. Smooth the rim between fingers, then use a few clips to hold it evenly. A narrow topstitch, around 1/8 inch from the edge, is an optional finish. Sew slowly and keep the stitch line parallel to the rim. If you are uncertain about topstitching, practise on scraps; a hand-sewn slip stitch or simply pressing a clean rim can be a suitable beginner finish. Topstitching does not transform a soft basket into a rigid or load-rated container. It only helps the layers behave as one at the edge.

Inspect the whole basket in good light. Check the outer side seams, the lining closure, the top seam and both bottom corners. Gently tug each seam with fingers; do not load-test by hanging it or pulling on a handle because there is no handle and this project is not designed for lifting. Place it on a level table and press lightly on the base. A small amount of fabric flex is normal. A strong lean, open stitches or a corner that separates needs repair before use. Test the basket with a few light items, such as fabric clips or folded notes. Keep objects dry and comfortably below the rim so the basket remains stabl

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Roll the top seam to the edge, smooth and clip the rim, then optionally topstitch about 1/8 inch from the edge after practising on a scrap.
Inspect all seams and the lining-gap closure in good light; gently finger-check for openings, skipped stitches or fraying.
Set the basket on a level indoor table and test it with a few light, dry items such as paper clips or folded notes.
Record the final approximate size and care limits, then select a dry indoor location suited to light items only.

blocks.body: Keep fingers clear of the needle path; stop with the needle down before repositioning fabric, and switch off/unplug the machine before changing its needle or clearing a jam.

blocks.question: A learner finds the interfacing bubbling after pressing. What is the safest next move?
options: Increase heat to the maximum and press directly on the adhesive
Pull the layers apart while hot
Keep sewing and assume the basket will become rigid
Stop, let it cool, then follow the product directions or omit the stabilizer
blocks.explanation: Interfacing products vary; use their specific directions and do not increase heat blindly.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Finish, inspect and choose a sensible use. What did you learn and verify?

name: Braided Friendship Bracelet
tagline: Make a slim, three-color friendship bracelet from embroidery floss using a controlled three-strand braid, measured to a real wrist, with braided tie ends and a practical fit check.
outcome: Measure a wrist and choose a braid length that leaves usable tie tails without making the finished band uncomfortably tight.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Braided Friendship Bracelet

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a slim, three-color friendship bracelet from embroidery floss using a controlled three-strand braid, measured to a real wrist, with braided tie ends and a practical fit check. This is a fiber cra

lessons.title: Plan the fit and prepare the strands
lessons.summary: Plan the fit and prepare the strands

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A braid gets shorter than its loose strands because each leg travels diagonally around the other two. For this sample, begin with three equal 90 cm strands. That length is generous for a narrow bracelet with two braided ties, but the braid itself should be measured against your wrist rather than guessed from the strand length. Floss thickness and how firmly you pull both change the amount consumed. Keep the strands equal; an unequal leg tends to run out early or produce a lopsided band.

First measure the wrist where the bracelet will sit. Wrap a paper strip comfortably around the wrist, not tight, mark where its end meets, then measure the strip flat. Subtract about 1 cm from that circumference for the main band. The small allowance lets the bracelet sit neatly while the two ties meet without the band squeezing. For instance, a 16 cm wrist suggests a main braided section near 15 cm. This is a starting sample, not a universal size: leave a finger-width comfort check and adjust before finishing.

Choose three colors with visible contrast, such as deep blue, pale blue, and warm cream. The color order will repeat as a simple diagonal braid, not form a complex woven motif. Lay out the

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Wrap a paper strip gently around the wrist, mark the overlap, and measure the strip flat in centimeters. Write down the number.
Subtract approximately 1 cm from the wrist measurement to set the initial main-band target; record it as a flexible target, not a tight fit rule.
Cut one 90 cm strand in each of three colors with blunt-ended scissors, cutting away from your fingers.
Arrange the strands A-B-C in your preferred order, align their ends, and tie one overhand knot about 8 cm from the ends.

blocks.body: Use blunt-ended scissors on a clear, stable tabletop. Cut away from the body, keep fingers outside the blades, and close the scissors before setting them down.

blocks.question: What is the next move after crossing the left strand over the center?
options: Cross the right strand over the new center
Cross the left strand under both others
Pull all three strands sideways at once
Tie a knot after every crossing
blocks.explanation: The repeated sequence is left over center, then right over the new center. The center changes position after each crossing.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the fit and prepare the strands. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Anchor and learn the three-strand rhythm
lessons.summary: Anchor and learn the three-strand rhythm

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The braid is made by moving an outside strand across the center, alternating sides. With three strands lined up left, center, and right, move the left strand over the center; the former center becomes left and the moved strand becomes center. Then move the right strand over the new center. Repeat left, then right. Saying “left over, right over” quietly can help a beginner avoid repeating one side. Keep the strands flat rather than twisting them before each crossing. The braid should show a neat sequence of diagonal color segments.

Anchor the starting knot to a clean tabletop with a small piece of low-tack tape. Place the knot just beyond the tape edge so the three working strands can descend freely. Tape only the knot, not the full thread length. Use light, even tension: after each crossing, draw the working strand down until the braid looks settled, then stop. Pulling hard makes a narrow, rigid cord and consumes length quickly; leaving slack creates gaps. Your first 2–3 cm are practice. Inspect them before deciding whether to continue.

A useful checkpoint is a consistent width and a repeatable crossing order. The center strand changes after every move, so track the strands by th

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Tape the starting knot to a stable tabletop, placing the knot just beyond the tape so the strands hang free.
Separate the strands left, center, and right. Move the left strand over the center, then move the right strand over the new center.
Repeat the left-over, right-over sequence for 2–3 cm, snugging each crossing with light, similar tension.
Pause and compare the sample width and color sequence; if needed, undo only the last one or two crossings and restart the rhythm.

blocks.body: Use blunt-ended scissors on a clear, stable tabletop. Cut away from the body, keep fingers outside the blades, and close the scissors before setting them down.

blocks.question: A 16 cm wrist is being used for the sample. What initial main-band target does the course suggest?
options: Exactly 8 cm, regardless of style
About 15 cm, then check fit before finishing
90 cm
No measurement is useful
blocks.explanation: The sample subtracts about 1 cm from the wrist circumference for an initial band target, but the unfastened comfort check is essential.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Anchor and learn the three-strand rhythm. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build the measured bracelet band
lessons.summary: Build the measured bracelet band

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Continue the same alternating sequence, checking the work every few centimeters. Measure the braided section from the base of the starting knot, not from the loose tie tail. Stop when the main band reaches your chosen target. A sample plan for a 16 cm wrist is approximately 15 cm of braid, followed by two short ties. The measurement is approximate because thread type and braid tension influence the final fit. Never stretch the braid while measuring; set it down naturally and measure without pulling.

A simple color braid looks its best when the crossings are orderly, but minor handmade variation is normal. Focus on three observable qualities: all three colors appear along the band, the braid has similar width from end to end, and there are no loose loops large enough to catch easily. If a strand frays, smooth it between clean fingers and continue only if it remains strong. Do not use glue, heat, or chemicals to seal the fibers. This design is secured by knots and braiding alone.

Before ending the main section, place the band gently around the wrist without fastening it. Check that the ends approach each other without stretching and that the band is not tight. If it feels short, ad

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Continue alternating left-over-center and right-over-center, keeping the strands untwisted before each move.
Every 3–4 cm, lay the bracelet flat and check its width and tension without pulling it taut.
Measure the main braid from the starting knot to its working end; stop near the wrist target recorded in Lesson 1.
Test placement by resting the braid around the wrist without tying; confirm it is comfortable and leaves ends that can meet.

blocks.body: Use blunt-ended scissors on a clear, stable tabletop. Cut away from the body, keep fingers outside the blades, and close the scissors before setting them down.

blocks.question: The band feels tight and pinches during the try-on. What should the learner do first?
options: Pull the ties harder so the band settles
Leave it on until the fibers loosen
Remove it immediately and adjust or remake it looser
Apply adhesive to the inside
blocks.explanation: Comfort takes priority. Remove a tight bracelet and lengthen or remake it; discontinue wear if irritation continues.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build the measured bracelet band. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Braid the ties, finish, and inspect
lessons.summary: Braid the ties, finish, and inspect

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
When the main band reaches its target, gather all three strands and make a small overhand knot close to the braid end. Leave the thread legs beyond it long enough to braid into a tie. Divide the legs into three groups of one strand and braid about 4–5 cm using the same alternating sequence. Tie a secure overhand knot at the tie tip. Repeat at the starting end: carefully remove the temporary anchor, preserve the starting tails, and braid them for a similar length. The finished object has a central band and two flexible ties that can be crossed and knotted.

Check the knots by holding the bracelet over the table and applying a gentle hand pull. This is a craft inspection, not a strength rating. If a knot loosens under this light check, retie it rather than relying on glue. Trim only the very ends after confirming the knot stays seated. Leave a short fringe, about 5–8 mm, so the knot cannot unravel immediately; keep scissors away from the skin and braid. Ask another person to help tie the bracelet if reaching around your wrist is awkward. Do not tie it so firmly that it is difficult to remove.

For the final fit check, slide one finger beneath the band and ensure it moves without pinc

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Gather the three working strands at the end of the band and tie a small overhand knot close to the braid, leaving thread beyond it.
Braid the three tails for about 4–5 cm and secure the tip with an overhand knot; repeat with the starting tails.
With the bracelet off the wrist, gently test each end knot by hand, then trim loose tips to leave about 5–8 mm of fringe.
Try the bracelet on loosely, slide one finger beneath the band, and inspect the skin for discomfort; remove it if anything pinches or irritates.

blocks.body: Use blunt-ended scissors on a clear, stable tabletop. Cut away from the body, keep fingers outside the blades, and close the scissors before setting them down.

blocks.question: Why should the three initial strands be approximately equal in length?
options: Equal strands help all three legs reach the finishing stage together
Equal lengths make the bracelet waterproof
Unequal strands make knots impossible
It is only for matching colors
blocks.explanation: All three strands contribute repeatedly to the braid. Similar starting lengths reduce the chance that one color runs short first.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Braid the ties, finish, and inspect. What did you learn and verify?

name: Knotted Adjustable Cord Bracelet
tagline: Make a simple two-color cord bracelet with a hand-knotted center band and an adjustable square-knot slider.
outcome: Measure a comfortable bracelet loop and select working cord lengths from the stated plan.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Knotted Adjustable Cord Bracelet

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a simple two-color cord bracelet with a hand-knotted center band and an adjustable square-knot slider. You will measure a comfortable loop, practice the knot rhythm, finish the loose ends without

lessons.title: Measure and prepare the cord
lessons.summary: Measure and prepare the cord

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A comfortable bracelet begins as a loop that can pass over the hand, not merely as a strip matching the wrist. Cord thickness and knot bulk change how a finished band feels, so use the paper strip to record your own measurement rather than relying on a standard size. This project uses four strands for the center band: two inner core strands remain nearly straight while two outer working strands travel around them. The sample lengths are deliberately generous for a short beginner band. If you have a very large wrist, very thick cord, or want a longer woven section, add working length before cutting; joining a short cord halfway through is harder to make neat.

Lay colors out so you can identify them. The two color-A strands are folded at their midpoint, producing four tails when arranged side by side: A, A, B, B is a convenient order, with the two middle strands serving as the core. A neat center depends on keeping that core parallel and maintaining similar tension on left and right knots. Tape the folded midpoint to the work surface, not to your skin. Leave the cord flat and untwisted. Before making the full band, make a sample knot and check that the cord slides without fuzzing or

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Wrap the paper strip around your wrist where you want the bracelet to sit, mark the overlap without tightening, then measure the marked length in centimetres. Add 2 cm and write th
Cut one 150 cm color-A piece and one 110 cm color-B piece; fold the A piece in half and align its two ends. Arrange the four tails as A, A, B, B, with the two middle strands design
Tape the folded midpoint to the table and make one loose practice half-knot around the two center strands, then untie it. Check that the cord bends smoothly and that each working e

blocks.body: Keep scissors closed and pointed away from your body when not cutting; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: Why add about 2 cm to the paper wrist measurement when planning the loop?
options: A. To leave room for cord bulk and comfortable movement.
B. To guarantee the bracelet fits every wearer.
C. To make the slider knots longer automatically.
D. To hide uneven knots beneath the sleeve.
blocks.explanation: The allowance accommodates cord thickness and movement, but the wearer still checks the fit on their own hand.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Measure and prepare the cord. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Knot a flat center band
lessons.summary: Knot a flat center band

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The center band is made from repeated square knots. A square knot is a pair of opposite half-knots: the first half makes a loop on one side, and the second half reverses the direction so the finished sequence lies flatter. Repeating only the same half-knot makes a spiral or corkscrew. That twist is not a disaster, but it changes the look and can make a narrow bracelet less comfortable. Keep the two core strands straight and close together. The working cords should travel around them without crossing the cores. Pull the two working ends outward with similar force, then slide the new knot upward until it rests against the previous one. Tightening too hard compresses the design and can make the cores disappear; leaving every knot loose produces gaps and a band that shifts.

For this sample, aim for a center band about 4 cm long, then assess whether the available core tail length will still allow the bracelet to close at your measured loop target. Cord and hand sizes vary, so treat 4 cm as a design target rather than a mandatory number of knots. Count the completed pairs, not just individual half-knots. Pause every few pairs to compare the band edges. The left and right edges should lo

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: With the four strands facing you, take the far-left working strand over both center strands and under the far-right working strand; pass the far-right strand behind the center pair
Reverse the direction: bring the far-right working strand over the core pair and under the far-left strand; pass the far-left strand behind the cores and up through the right loop.
Repeat complete pairs until the band measures about 4 cm, pausing after every two pairs to inspect its edges and core alignment. Stop sooner if your recorded loop target would be e

blocks.body: Keep scissors closed and pointed away from your body when not cutting; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What helps a square-knot band lie flat rather than corkscrew?
options: A. Tighten every knot as hard as possible.
B. Start every half-knot on the same side.
C. Reverse the starting side for each half-knot and keep the cores parallel.
D. Pull the core strands out after each pair.
blocks.explanation: A square-knot pair combines opposite half-knots, with the core strands kept straight through the sequence.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Knot a flat center band. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Shape the loop and make the slider
lessons.summary: Shape the loop and make the slider

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The adjustable closure is a short sleeve of square knots tied around the two bracelet ends where they overlap. The base ends point in opposite directions, and the slider knots encircle both at once. The sleeve should hold the ends together while still allowing them to move when you deliberately push it. Place the bracelet loop on the table with the knotted band outward. Bring the two base tails together in opposite directions to form a loop, then compare its circumference with the target you wrote down. Remember that the center band contributes length too. Adjust overlap until the complete loop can pass over your hand and sits comfortably at the wrist. Tape the tails temporarily so they do not shift as you knot.

Use the 60 cm slider cord as a separate working piece. Center it beneath the two parallel tails and make alternating half-knots around both. Each half-knot is snugged against the previous one, but the bracelet tails themselves must not be trapped so tightly that they cannot slide. A sleeve around 2.5–3 cm long is a useful starting point. Keep the slider cord ends available on both sides. Finish those ends by tying them together on the underside with a compact double overha

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Curve the band into a loop, cross the two long core tails in opposite directions, and slide the overlap until the full bracelet loop matches your target circumference. Hold the cro
Center the 60 cm slider cord under the two crossed tails. Make a half-knot around both tails from the left, then the reversed half-knot from the right; repeat until the sleeve is a
On the underside, tie the two slider-cord ends together with a secure double overhand knot. Tie a compact stopper knot at each bracelet-tail tip, or add an optional bead with a kno

blocks.body: Keep scissors closed and pointed away from your body when not cutting; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: The slider is too tight to adjust. What is the safest useful correction?
options: A. Pull the bracelet tails forcefully through it.
B. Undo one slider pair and rebuild it with lighter tension.
C. Cut one of the core tails shorter.
D. Apply an unknown liquid lubricant.
blocks.explanation: Rebuilding the tight pair with less tension restores movement without adding an unverified substance.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Shape the loop and make the slider. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fit, test, and refine the finish
lessons.summary: Fit, test, and refine the finish

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A finished bracelet should adjust smoothly and remain comfortable during ordinary gentle movement. Test the sleeve by holding the bracelet body rather than pulling hard on the decorative band. Push the sleeve to enlarge the loop, pass it over your hand, and bring it back down to the wrist. Use two fingers to nudge the tails in opposite directions; this should change the loop size without the sleeve unraveling or the end stops entering the sleeve. Do not perform a strength test by yanking. Knotted cord jewelry is not designed to carry weight or protect the wearer.

Inspect the top, underside, and cut ends in good light. Look for a missing reversal, an exposed loose loop, fuzzy abrasion, a tail that is too short to grip, or any rough component touching skin. A consistent band has compact knots with similar spacing. The slider should be short enough to move easily and long enough to hold the two tails aligned. If it drifts during gentle adjustment, add one balanced pair of slider half-knots. If it is too tight, undo one pair and rebuild with lighter tension. If the band itself spirals, correct the square-knot alternation; making the slider tighter will not solve a twisted center band.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Hold the bracelet by its woven band and move the slider in both directions using gentle fingertip pressure; enlarge the loop, pass it over your hand, and reduce it to wrist fit.
Inspect both faces and all cord ends in bright light. Check for an alternating flat band, no loose loops, smooth skin-facing knots, and short but grippable tails beyond the slider.
Wear the bracelet briefly for a comfort check, remove it, and write one observed strength and one specific next-version change. Store it dry and flat.

blocks.body: Keep scissors closed and pointed away from your body when not cutting; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What should keep the bracelet tails from passing completely through the slider?
options: A. A sharp metal pin pressed into the cord.
B. Adhesive melted into the cord with a flame.
C. The slider knot tightened until it cannot move.
D. Compact stopper knots or securely knotted suitable beads.
blocks.explanation: Knotted stops retain the tails while preserving the slider's intended movement.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Fit, test, and refine the finish. What did you learn and verify?

name: Yarn-Wrapped Decorative Letter
tagline: Make a freestanding tabletop initial from a broad cardboard letter form, wrapped with two coordinated yarn colors and finished with a folded cardboard easel.
outcome: Plan and cut a readable block initial with a 20 cm height and a minimum 2.5 cm stroke width.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Yarn-Wrapped Decorative Letter

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a freestanding tabletop initial from a broad cardboard letter form, wrapped with two coordinated yarn colors and finished with a folded cardboard easel. This is a dry indoor decorative object, no

lessons.title: Plan a readable shape and prepare the cardboard
lessons.summary: Plan a readable shape and prepare the cardboard

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A wrapped letter is easiest to read when its strokes are broad enough to receive yarn without forcing dense bundles around narrow corners. This lesson uses a 20 cm-high block capital A, with an overall width of 16 cm and strokes about 2.5 cm wide. The open triangular center creates a more demanding area than a solid letter, so you will wrap each leg separately and finish the crossbar as a distinct section. Keep the sample dimensions consistent; if you choose another initial, preserve the broad strokes and make a paper plan before cutting.

Corrugated cardboard has a fluted inner layer. Its strength and flexibility change with the direction of the flutes, so use two matching layers if your board feels floppy. Tape the layers together around the edges rather than saturating them with glue. The letter will sit on a small folding rear support; it does not need to carry any object.

Before cutting, check whether the shape has narrow bridges or sharp inside corners. A point that is too tight can become hidden under yarn, while an undersized opening may disappear. Round internal corners slightly on the template, and keep the A's triangular opening at least 5 cm wide at its broadest point.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On paper, draw a block A 20 cm high and 16 cm wide. Use 2.5 cm-wide legs and crossbar, and leave a triangular opening at least 5 cm wide at its broadest point.
Trace the template onto cardboard, mark BACK on one face, and cut the outline on a stable surface with scissors. If using a knife for thick board, have an adult cut on a mat, away
On the back, lightly mark three zones: left leg, right leg, and crossbar. Mark a 5 cm-wide band across the lower third for color B.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and body. Use scissors only on a stable surface; thick board should be cut by an adult with a guarded craft knife and cutting mat, or simplified to thinner laminated board.

blocks.question: Why is the sample A designed with strokes about 2.5 cm wide?
options: To make the cardboard heavy enough to hold a phone
To give adjacent yarn passes room to cover the face without fragile narrow bridges
To guarantee the letter is waterproof
To remove the need to inspect the cut edges
blocks.explanation: The chosen sample width accommodates yarn rows and reduces fragile narrow areas; it does not certify strength or protection.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan a readable shape and prepare the cardboard. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Anchor, tension, and wrap the first leg
lessons.summary: Anchor, tension, and wrap the first leg

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Yarn coverage comes from orderly adjacent passes, not from pulling as hard as possible. Excess tension can bend a thin cardboard stroke or make yarn slide toward a corner. Hold the letter flat on the table and pull only enough to remove slack. Keep the yarn ball beyond the work area so it can feed freely. Cut manageable lengths of roughly 1.5 to 2 m; a very long strand tangles and drags over the face, while a tiny strand creates too many joins.

Start on the back with a short tail held by paper tape. Bring the working strand around an outer edge, across the face, around the opposite edge, and back. Each pass should sit snugly beside the previous one. On a diagonal leg, angle each pass so it follows the stroke rather than making a horizontal stripe across the whole letter. The cardboard edges will have some exposed areas because the yarn bridges from front to back; this is normal for this flat relief design.

When you approach an inside corner, pause and inspect the yarn path. A sharp tug can narrow the triangular opening or stack yarn into a lump. Turn the letter in your hands instead of twisting your wrist around a tight strand. If rows spread, nudge them together gently with a fi

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut a 1.5–2 m piece of color A. Tape its 5 cm tail to the back near the lower end of the left leg, then bring the strand around the edge to the face.
Wrap the strand around the left leg in adjacent angled passes, turning the letter to follow its slope. Keep tension gentle and stop at the color-band boundary.
When the strand ends, tape it on the back. Start a fresh length beside the tail with its own taped end, overlap the yarn for one pass, then continue to the band boundary.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and body. Use scissors only on a stable surface; thick board should be cut by an adult with a guarded craft knife and cutting mat, or simplified to thinner laminated board.

blocks.question: Where should a yarn join and its taped tail go when possible?
options: Across the open center of the A
In a thick knot on the front
On the back of the cardboard
On the easel foot beneath the table
blocks.explanation: Back-side joins keep the decorative face clear and help preserve the letter shape.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Anchor, tension, and wrap the first leg. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Complete the color band and join the sections
lessons.summary: Complete the color band and join the sections

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The second leg mirrors the first in technique, not necessarily in exact yarn angle. Treat the center opening as a boundary: yarn should travel around a stroke, never across the open triangle. Use one section at a time and stop at the pencilled band edges. The color change is most secure when both tails are taped on the back and the new yarn begins beside the old color rather than over a thick bundle.

The crossbar is a separate bridge between the legs. Its intersections can become crowded because wrapped yarn from both legs already occupies the surface. Lay the crossbar strand so it follows the horizontal bar. If a pass must cross a wrapped leg to reach the back, keep that crossing behind the letter, not across its face. Trim a strand only after checking that the tail is taped; a cut end can unravel several rows.

The two-color band is intentionally simple. It makes a clear design feature without relying on a character, logo, or copied artwork. You may reverse the colors or omit the band, but keep a consistent plan and make color joins on the back. A small amount of cardboard showing on the side edges is acceptable for this flat decorative piece; do not apply so much glue that it b

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Wrap the right leg of the A with color A, following the diagonal and stopping at the matching color-band edge; tape each yarn join on the back.
Wrap the 5 cm band on both legs and the crossbar with color B, then resume color A above the band. Place every color join on the back and tape its tail.
Wrap the crossbar with color A, following its horizontal stroke and covering the central overlap. Inspect the front before trimming any remaining tails.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and body. Use scissors only on a stable surface; thick board should be cut by an adult with a guarded craft knife and cutting mat, or simplified to thinner laminated board.

blocks.question: What is the safest response if the board bows under the yarn?
options: Pull harder so the rows cannot slip
Unwind recent passes and wrap more loosely, reinforcing the back if needed
Heat the cardboard until it flattens
Add water to soften it
blocks.explanation: Gentle tension prevents distortion; a matching cardboard backing can help if the board itself is too flexible.

lessons.title: Fit a tabletop easel and refine the finish
lessons.summary: Fit a tabletop easel and refine the finish

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A small rear easel lets the initial stand for viewing without claiming that it can hold anything. Cut a 12 × 10 cm rectangle from cardboard. Score a fold line 4 cm from one short edge by pressing gently with the closed scissor handle or a blunt tool; do not cut through. The short 4 cm flap is the attachment tab. Fold the remaining panel into a shallow angled brace. Dry-fit the letter against the brace on a level table before taping or gluing. The angle should let the letter stand without sliding, but the assembly remains a lightweight display object.

Test the support with the letter alone. Do not lean on it, put a phone on it, or display it near a table edge. A support that tips can be repositioned or widened using a second folded strip. The letter's back may be uneven because yarn wraps around edges, so attach the tab to a relatively flat area. Paper tape is reversible and adequate for light display; if using craft glue, apply sparingly and follow its cure instructions.

Finish by trimming fibers with scissors while the letter rests flat. Keep the scissors away from wrapped strands you intend to retain. Check the support seam and all yarn ends. A clean finish means secure tails,

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut a 12 × 10 cm cardboard rectangle, mark a fold 4 cm from one short edge, and crease gently without cutting through the board.
Fold the large panel into a shallow triangular brace, position its 4 cm tab on the letter back, and test the letter upright on a level tabletop before fastening.
Secure the tab with paper tape or a small amount of labeled craft glue. Trim stray fibers and inspect yarn ends, edges, and support; display away from heat, moisture, and table edg

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and body. Use scissors only on a stable surface; thick board should be cut by an adult with a guarded craft knife and cutting mat, or simplified to thinner laminated board.

blocks.question: When is the easel ready for display?
options: After it holds the letter alone on a level table without sliding during a brief untouched check
After it can carry a phone and a book
After it is hung from a ceiling
Before the fold is tested, to avoid handling it
blocks.explanation: Check the easel with the letter alone on a stable tabletop; do not use it as a stand for devices or other items.

name: Small Woven Wall Hanging
tagline: Make a small woven wall hanging on a reusable cardboard loom.
outcome: Lay out and cut an evenly spaced, even-count set of slots on a cardboard loom using stated measurements.

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a small woven wall hanging on a reusable cardboard loom. This original two-color design includes plain weave, a short raised ridge, and fringe. Learn to measure a stable warp, weave without drawi

lessons.title: Plan the weave and prepare a small loom
lessons.summary: Plan the weave and prepare a small loom

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A loom is a temporary frame holding the warp steady while you pass weft across it. Warp means vertical threads; weft is the yarn woven horizontally. This is a target: yarn thickness and packing affect the result.

Mark a centered 14 cm span on each short edge and lay out 20 matching positions about 7 mm apart. Their alignment matters more than perfect spacing; matching notches keep warp lines parallel. If your marks drift or your count is odd, redraw before cutting.

Tape the cord start at the back, bring it over a top notch, down the front, around the matching bottom notch, then behind the board to the next position. The front should show 20 straight lines. Tension should prevent sag without bowing the board. A bowed board means loosen and reset. The MassArt museum guide defines warp as up-and-down strings and weft as yarn woven across them; these terms help identify whether a problem comes from the frame or a row. The sample uses a continuous warp path and shallow paired notches, chosen for a beginner's small project. Keep the board flat on a table while marking and cutting, and count each position aloud or mark it off so a missed notch does not create a gap. Compare top and bott

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure and mark 20 matching positions across both short edges.
Cut 6 mm shallow notches at each mark.
Wrap cord through matching top and bottom slots; tape ends behind.
Seat every cord in its notch and secure the tail.

blocks.body: Cut cardboard on a stable table with scissors pointed away; younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: Which threads run vertically on this loom?
options: Weft
Warp
Fringe
Ridge
blocks.explanation: Warp is vertical; weft crosses it.

lessons.title: Build a level plain-weave foundation
lessons.summary: Build a level plain-weave foundation

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Plain weave repeats a simple path: over one warp, under the next, then reverse the relationship on the next row. Leave an 8 cm starting tail to tuck later; do not knot weft onto an edge warp, because a bulky knot can pull that edge inward.

After pulling a row through, shape it into a shallow arch rather than a taut straight line. If one area curves, ease its high spots rather than forcing the full row down.

For this original design, weave color A for a 2 cm band, color B for 3 cm, then return to A. Measure from the first packed row; yarn varies, so row counts are only a guide. Correct a loose or skipped row while it is recent. Cedar Dell's cardboard-loom instructions also highlight alternating over-under paths and edge pull-in; use that principle by leaving slack at turns and checking width regularly. [Source: Cedar Dell Forest Farm, accessed 2026-11-24.] A consistent gentle packing pressure is more useful than speed. If the warp becomes loose or the frame bows, pause and correct the setup before adding more rows. Keep the needle blunt and pass it through open gaps rather than forcing it through yarn. A color join should have a tail, not a tight knot. This makes the back easier t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Weave color A over-under across all warp lines; leave an 8 cm tail.
Shape a shallow arch, pack gently, then reverse the sequence.
Weave color B for a 3 cm band, leaving a tail.
Return to A; weave toward 14 cm high and check regularly.

blocks.body: Cut cardboard on a stable table with scissors pointed away; younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: The center is narrowing after several rows. What is the best immediate response?
options: Pull every remaining row tighter
Cut the edge warps and hide them
Undo the newest tight rows and reweave them with a shallow arch
Glue the textile to the loom
blocks.explanation: The arch adds turn slack and protects width.

lessons.title: Add texture and shape the finished field
lessons.summary: Add texture and shape the finished field

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A small raised ridge adds texture without a complicated loom. Use contrasting yarn across a central 5 cm section, then make a return pass over that same group. In this sample the ridge is about 1 cm high. Avoid many passes: excess bulk can distort the textile and make release difficult.

The blunt needle should pass freely through warp gaps. If threads crowd, open a path with fingertips instead of forcing the needle. Keep tails long enough to weave into the back. Small floats on the reverse are acceptable, but avoid loose loops that can snag.

Continue until the woven field is about 19 cm tall, leaving roughly 2 cm of open warp at top and bottom for finishing. Actual dimensions vary with yarn and packing. Look for a rectangle with nearly parallel sides, readable bands, and no large gaps. A loose section can be nudged with a fingertip. If too tight, unpick a few rows and rebuild with a longer arch. At this stage, inspect the whole surface in good light, checking the reverse for skipped warps and the front for an uneven ridge. Do not hide major tension problems with fringe. Measure top, center, and bottom widths; small handwoven differences are normal, but a large change signals corr

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Weave two return passes of color B across the central 5 cm.
Resume full-width A, leaving about 2 cm open at top.
Tuck yarn tails beneath nearby back stitches with blunt needle.
Measure width at three points and height at both sides.

blocks.body: Cut cardboard on a stable table with scissors pointed away; younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: Why use a non-stretchy cotton cord for the warp when available?
options: It helps keep vertical tension more consistent while weaving
It makes the hanging fireproof
It guarantees an exact finished size
It replaces the need for a loom
blocks.explanation: A stable warp is easier to tension consistently.

lessons.title: Release, finish, mount, and inspect
lessons.summary: Release, finish, mount, and inspect

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Removal changes the warp from frame-held threads into a finished textile. Support the woven surface while loosening tape. Free loops one at a time; never yank. For this design, preserve the top loops and slide a light dowel through them; the alternative of cutting and tying all loops is not used here.

The 24 cm dowel extends beyond the roughly 15 cm textile. Tie a 45 cm hanging cord near its ends to form a shallow loop. Use an appropriate indoor wall hook according to its instructions, or display the piece against a wall on a stable shelf. The support is for a light decorative work only.

Inspect by brushing fingertips lightly over both faces. A row that shifts markedly needs better tucking; slight height variation is normal. Check for long loose loops, sharp tool parts, and splinters. Record actual measurements rather than claiming the target exactly. Keep the textile dry and away from heat. The MassArt guide notes that releasing loom loops takes patience; ask for help instead of pulling hard on a stuck section. [Source: MassArt museum guide, accessed 2026-11-24.] If a loop catches, ease the cardboard away while supporting the textile. The dowel should be smooth and light. Test t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Loosen tape and free loops gradually while supporting the textile.
Slide dowel through top loops; pair and knot bottom warp ends.
Tie the hanging cord near both dowel ends; inspect for splinters.
Record dimensions and inspect both faces before dry indoor display.

blocks.body: Cut cardboard on a stable table with scissors pointed away; younger learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: Which finish is appropriate for this small display object?
options: Suspend a heavy planter from the warp
Use the dowel and loop only for light indoor decorative display
Place the textile over a heater to dry it quickly
Seal the finished work with an unknown chemical coating
blocks.explanation: The dowel supports light decoration only.

name: Tassel Bookmark Set

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a coordinated set of three flat yarn bookmarks, each with a slim paper-free yarn stem and a neat, removable tassel at its top. This project teaches measured cardboard winding, secure yarn joins,

lessons.title: Plan the set and prepare a simple form
lessons.summary: Plan the set and prepare a simple form

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A coordinated set looks intentional when every stem has the same length and tassels share a shape. This design uses a 20 cm stem and a tassel about 5 cm long, for roughly 25 cm overall. The tassel stays outside a book while the narrow stem sits between pages. These are design targets: adjust for a larger book, but keep the page-contact section slim. Choose smooth medium-weight yarn for a first attempt. Bulky yarn makes thick stems; fuzzy yarn hides knots. Keep spare yarn for ties and corrections. Even tension matters more than pulling hard. If tight wraps bend the card, loosen them.

Use a flat cardboard form at least 22 cm long and 5 cm wide. Mark the 20 cm stem span and a separate 5 cm tassel span. The longer span standardizes strands; the shorter one makes compact tassels. Smooth edges prevent snags. Replace cardboard with rough or damaged edges rather than sanding it and creating dust. Select one color or three related colors before cutting. Estimate the full set and keep some yarn in reserve. The quantities are practical estimates, not exact consumption guarantees.

Decide whether each stem will be one color or joined from color sections. The join is repairable, but should sit

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Choose three colors or one repeated color, then set aside about 7 m of yarn in total.
Mark a 20 cm height and a separate 5 cm height on clean cardboard; cut or select a form with a 5 cm width.
Place the ruler, scissors, yarn and book on a clear table; anchor the cardboard with removable tape if it slides.

blocks.body: Cut yarn over a clear, stable tabletop. Keep fingers outside the scissor blades, close scissors between cuts, and use age-appropriate scissors with adult supervision where needed.

blocks.question: What is the target finished stem length in this course?
options: 10 cm
20 cm
25 cm
30 cm
blocks.explanation: The 20 cm winding height standardizes stems; tassel length adds about 5 cm to the overall hanging length.

lessons.title: Build straight, slim bookmark stems
lessons.summary: Build straight, slim bookmark stems

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A stem is a flat bundle of parallel yarn strands, not a rigid core. Overbuilding may feel sturdy but makes a ridge between pages. Wind 6–8 strands along the 20 cm span. Keep passes beside one another rather than crossing into a dense knot. Tie scrap yarn around both ends before lifting the bundle. The ties should hold strands without crushing them. Cut the loops at both ends, keeping the ties in hand; the released strands form a straight stem. If one loop remains, lay the bundle flat and cut that loop separately rather than tugging it toward a blade.

Make three stems. For a coordinated multicolor set, join color sections with a 20 cm strand tied around the full bundle ends. A square knot is a compact, repairable connection. Pull gently in opposite directions to test it. If it slides, undo and retie with longer tails. Do not add glue: it can stiffen the stem and conceal a loose tie. If a join remains bulky, use fewer strands or make separate single-color bookmarks. That is a valid design choice, not a failed project.

Keep unfinished stems in a loose bundle so they do not tangle. Compare their lengths against the ruler before attaching tassels. Small variations are easy to correct

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: For each stem, wind yarn along the 20 cm form in parallel passes until there are 6–8 strands; tie a 20 cm scrap around each end of the bundle.
Cut the looped bundle at the middle of each end, then lift it off the cardboard while holding the ties.
Make three stems, then join color sections end-to-end with a snug square knot in a 20 cm joining strand, or leave the stems as individual single-color pieces.

blocks.body: Cut yarn over a clear, stable tabletop. Keep fingers outside the scissor blades, close scissors between cuts, and use age-appropriate scissors with adult supervision where needed.

blocks.question: Why should the stem use a modest number of parallel strands?
options: It makes the yarn waterproof
It makes the tassel fuller
It helps the bookmark remain flexible and less bulky between pages
It removes the need for secure knots
blocks.explanation: The bookmark needs to sit in a book without creating an unnecessary ridge, so keep the stem flat and light.

lessons.title: Make and attach three compact tassels
lessons.summary: Make and attach three compact tassels

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A tassel has a tied head, a narrow neck and free fringe. The top tie holds loops together and its tails attach the tassel to the stem. The neck tie gathers the fringe about 1 cm below the head. Make three tassels using about 24 wraps each around the 5 cm form. Yarn thickness changes apparent fullness, so compare bundles side by side. If they look sparse, add the same number of wraps to each before tying; changing only one makes an uneven set.

Slide a 20 cm tie under the bundle near its top edge and knot it securely. Hold that knot as you lift the bundle, then cut loops at the opposite end. Gather the fringe and double-knot a second tie around the neck. It should define the shape without cutting into fibers. Lay fringe flat and trim only longer ends in tiny cuts. Never cut close to a knot. If one tassel becomes too short, shorten its partners only if the resulting set still looks balanced; otherwise remake it.

Attach the top tie tails around the stem end with a square knot. Hide tails by weaving them through nearby strands with fingers or an optional blunt tapestry needle. First perform a gentle pull test while knots remain accessible. A sound tassel hangs in line with the stem an

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Wind yarn around the 5 cm cardboard section about 24 times, keeping the passes side-by-side; slide a 20 cm tie under the top edge and knot it.
Hold the top knot, lift the yarn from the form, and cut the loops at the opposite end.
Gather the strands and double-knot a second 20 cm tie around the neck about 1 cm below the head; trim the fringe evenly in small cuts.
Tie the tassel’s top tails around the upper stem end with a square knot; weave the tails into the stem and perform a gentle pull test.

blocks.body: Cut yarn over a clear, stable tabletop. Keep fingers outside the scissor blades, close scissors between cuts, and use age-appropriate scissors with adult supervision where needed.

blocks.question: When should you cut the tassel loops off the cardboard?
options: After placing a secure top tie and holding its knot
Before wrapping any yarn
After gluing the bundle to the book
Only after cutting the top tie
blocks.explanation: Secure the top with a tie first, then cut the free loops while maintaining control of the bundle.

lessons.title: Finish, inspect and test the set
lessons.summary: Finish, inspect and test the set

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Finishing is an inspection, not a race to trim every loose end. Hold each bookmark at the join and pull gently in opposite directions. Slight fiber movement is normal; a knot should not slide open and strands should not detach. Inspect both sides of each tassel: top tie secure, neck centered, fringe reasonably even. If ends are long, trim a little at a time with the tassel lying on the table. Keep fingers outside the blades. Do not cut so close that a tie weakens.

Test in a closed paperback. Put the stem between pages near the outer edge and leave the tassel outside at the top. Close the cover gently. Pages should close without force or a pronounced bulge, and the bookmark should remain easy to remove. Never wedge the tassel into the spine. If the join creates a ridge, move it outside the closed pages or remake the stem with fewer strands. This checks practical fit only; books and bindings vary, and the yarn is not archival or protective.

Compare all three pieces side by side. Correct a loose knot or a mismatched stem before adding any optional decoration. Uneven color blocks may be intentional; weak connections are not. Keep finished bookmarks dry and store them flat to reduce t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect each stem and tassel, then gently pull on opposite sides of every join and top knot.
Lay each tassel on the table and snip only visibly long fringe ends in small increments, comparing all three side by side.
Place one stem between pages near the outer edge of a paperback, leave the tassel outside, and close the book gently.
Compare the three bookmarks, make one final safe correction if needed, and store them flat and dry.

blocks.body: Cut yarn over a clear, stable tabletop. Keep fingers outside the scissor blades, close scissors between cuts, and use age-appropriate scissors with adult supervision where needed.

blocks.question: A knot slips during the gentle pull test. What is the safest useful response?
options: Pull harder until it either holds or breaks
Cover the slipping knot with a thick layer of glue
Ignore it because the tassel is decorative
Undo it, retie with longer tails around the full bundle, then test gently again
blocks.explanation: A secure repair uses a longer tie around the complete bundle, followed by a gentle retest.

name: Pom-Pom Bag Charm
tagline: Make a soft, two-color yarn pom-pom and attach it to a short, finished-loop bag charm.
outcome: Measure and cut a 12 cm by 8 cm cardboard wrapping template and explain how template width affects the pom-pom's starting size.

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a soft, two-color yarn pom-pom and attach it to a short, finished-loop bag charm. The project teaches controlled wrapping, secure center tying, careful trimming, and a simple sewn connection. The

lessons.title: Plan the silhouette and prepare the wrapping template
lessons.summary: Plan the silhouette and prepare the wrapping template

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Choose colors and set up

This charm uses a rounded yarn puff with a short loop held by a commercial split ring. It is intentionally small enough to hang from a bag zipper, but it is not designed to carry weight or to be pulled as a handle. Choose two smooth yarns that feel similar in thickness. A strong contrast makes the accent easier to see; two close shades create a quieter result. If you have only one yarn, the project still works. Keep color B for the loop or use color A throughout.

Measure a rectangle 12 cm long by 8 cm wide on clean, dry cardboard. Cut on the marked lines to form a flat wrapping template. The 8 cm width sets the initial yarn bundle span. The finished pom-pom becomes smaller when its loops are cut and its outline is rounded, so do not expect an 8 cm finished ball. For this design, the target after shaping is approximately 7 cm across. This is a practical target, not a tolerance test; the exact result depends on yarn thickness and trimming.

Before wrapping, cut a 45 cm length of strong sewing thread or floss for the center tie. Set it where it cannot be tangled into the yarn. Put scrap paper underneath the work to catch fibers. Keep the cardboard edges s

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Choose one or two smooth yarn colors of similar thickness, then measure 12 cm by 8 cm on clean cardboard and cut out the rectangle.
Set out about 18 m of color A, 8 m of color B, the 45 cm center tie, the ring, scissors, and scrap paper; keep the tie separate from the wrapping yarn.
Sketch a quick placement note: color A first, color B as an accent band, then a folded loop through the split ring.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a stable, well-lit work surface; cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What does the 8 cm width of the cardboard template primarily determine?
options: The approximate starting span of the wrapped bundle
The finished charm's guaranteed diameter
The required length of the split ring
The exact number of yarn turns
blocks.explanation: The template sets the starting bundle span. The sample pom-pom is trimmed to about 7 cm, but results vary with yarn and shaping.

lessons.title: Build an even two-color yarn bundle
lessons.summary: Build an even two-color yarn bundle

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Wrap with an even hand

Lay the cardboard template flat. Hold the end of color A against the card with a thumb and wrap over it so the first few turns trap the tail. Continue winding from one long edge around the back and over the front, keeping each pass beside the previous one. Count one complete circuit as one turn. Aim for about 60 turns of color A across the 8 cm span. Then add roughly 30 turns of color B. You may cluster those 30 turns in one broad band or space them in smaller groups for flecks. Both choices are original design variations, not different construction methods. If your yarn is significantly thicker than ordinary medium-weight yarn, use fewer wraps and judge the density by coverage rather than forcing all 90 turns onto the card.

The goal is an even cushion, not a compressed board. Pull enough to seat each strand, but do not stretch the yarn or bend the cardboard. Too few wraps create a sparse puff whose center tie may show. Too many wraps make the center difficult to cut and can leave a lumpy shape. Let the yarn sit naturally and keep the bundle near the center of the template. If a strand slips off the edge, pause and put it back; do not tug sharply on the

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Hold the color A tail on the template and wrap about 60 complete turns evenly across its width, trapping the starting tail beneath the first wraps.
Add about 30 turns of color B as one broad accent or several spaced groups, keeping the overall bundle centered and similar in thickness on both sides.
Cut the wrapping yarn, tuck its end under neighboring turns, and position the 45 cm tie under the bundle at its midpoint, perpendicular to the wraps.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a stable, well-lit work surface; cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: Why should the center tie be firm before cutting the loops?
options: It makes the yarn dry faster
It keeps the bundle together as loops become loose strands
It creates a sharper ring closure
It prevents every possible snag during use
blocks.explanation: Cutting releases looped yarn; the tight center tie prevents the bundle from separating.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build an even two-color yarn bundle. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Tie, release, and shape the pom-pom
lessons.summary: Tie, release, and shape the pom-pom

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Secure before cutting

Bring the tie ends over the center of the wrapped bundle and knot them firmly. A doubled strand or floss is useful because the center must stay cinched after the loops are cut. Pull steadily until the bundle feels held together, but stop before the tie snaps. If the knot slips, retie it now while the bundle is still supported by the card. Leave both tie ends long; they will help anchor the charm loop. Do not cut close to the knot.

Slide the tied bundle off the cardboard carefully. The folded loops will still be intact. Using sharp scissors, cut through the loops along both long sides of the bundle, one side at a time. Keep your fingertips behind the cutting edge. A few inner loops can remain concealed, so rotate the bundle and inspect the center before moving on. The cut strands will spread into a rough, bow-tie shape around the firm knot. If you see the center open or strands begin to pull free, stop; tighten and reinforce the tie before trimming further.

Now round the shape gradually. Snip only the longest protruding strands, rotating the puff as you work so you do not hollow one face. Aim for about 7 cm across, but let the yarn's actual density guide

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Tie the center tie tightly around the midpoint with a secure double knot, keeping the two ends long for the later loop attachment.
Slide the tied bundle off the cardboard, then cut through the folded loops along both long sides, rotating the bundle to find any hidden loops.
Rotate the puff and trim the longest points in small snips until it is roughly 7 cm across, preserving the center tie and color detail.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a stable, well-lit work surface; cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: You notice the center knot loosening as you cut. What is the best next action?
options: Pull hard on loose strands to tighten the shape
Continue cutting and cover the gap with more yarn later
Stop and add a fresh strong tie at the midpoint before continuing
Glue the surface strands over the knot
blocks.explanation: Pause cutting and reinforce the center while the bundle can still be gathered securely.

lessons.title: Add the ring loop and inspect the finished charm
lessons.summary: Add the ring loop and inspect the finished charm

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Make a neat attachment

Cut about 12 cm of color B for a narrow hanging loop. Fold it in half to form a loop with two loose ends. Pass the folded end through the split ring. Then pass the two loose ends through the folded loop and pull gently to make a hitch around the ring. This simple attachment is suitable for a decorative charm. It is not intended for heavy loads, forceful pulling, or use where a loop might catch.

Use the center tie tails to anchor the loop to the pom-pom. Thread one tail at a time through the blunt tapestry needle and pass it through the firm center of the puff, avoiding broad surface loops where the tie could slip. Position the ring loop against the knot, then tie the center tails around its two loose ends with two firm knots. If the tails are short, sew them back through the center for several centimeters and knot them securely. Do not pull so hard that the yarn bundle is cut or distorted.

Before clipping any excess, tug the ring loop gently while holding the puff. This is a light inspection, not a strength certification. If the attachment moves, reinforce the center connection; if the center tie itself shifts, retie or remake the pom-pom. Trim excess t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut about 12 cm of color B, fold it in half, pass the folded end through the split ring, then pass both loose ends through the fold and snug the hitch.
Use the long center tie tails to sew through the pom-pom's firm center, position the ring loop at the knot, and tie the tails around the loop ends with two firm knots.
Inspect the center and ring, lightly test for movement, trim excess ties only after the joint is stable, then remove clippings and make tiny shaping corrections.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a stable, well-lit work surface; cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the cutting path. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: How should the charm loop be anchored to the pom-pom?
options: Tie it around one loose outer strand
Tape it to the outside of the puff
Clip the center tie tails off and leave the loop unattached
Sew the long center tie tails through the firm center and knot them around the loop ends
blocks.explanation: The center is the bundle's gathered anchor point; outer strands are not a reliable attachment base.
