name: Braided Fabric Coaster
tagline: Make a small, flat, three-strand braid from woven fabric strips, then coil and hand-stitch it into a colorful 4-inch decorative coaster.
outcome: Select stable, clean woven fabric scraps and prepare three consistent strips approximately 1 inch wide and 30 inches long.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Braided Fabric Coaster

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a small, flat, three-strand braid from woven fabric strips, then coil and hand-stitch it into a colorful 4-inch decorative coaster. The project teaches strip preparation, even braiding, controlle

lessons.title: Choose fabric and prepare a balanced braid
lessons.summary: Choose fabric and prepare a balanced braid

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A successful coaster begins with a braid that is neither lumpy nor hard as a rope. Use stable woven fabric such as cotton poplin, quilting cotton or a light-weight shirt fabric. Avoid stretchy knit, slippery satin, thick denim and cloth with loose decorative loops: they behave differently in a small braid and make consistent tension harder. Wash and dry reused fabric first if its history is uncertain, then let it lie flat. The sample design uses three strips, each about 1 inch wide and 30 inches long. That length is a starting point, not a guarantee: strips may shrink or fray, and a larger or more compact braid changes how much is needed. Prepare a few extra inches when possible.

The strips need not be perfectly straight, but dramatic width changes create bumps. Measure at several points and trim obvious flares. Slightly fraying edges are acceptable if the fabric remains stable; if a strip sheds threads continuously, choose a different piece. A short test braid lets you feel the fabric and practice crossing without committing your full strips. Keep strips in a safe tray when not handling them. Scissors are for fabric and paper only, and the ruler should stay flat so the cutting li

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Choose three clean woven fabric pieces in coordinated colors; reject cloth that stretches easily, sheds heavily or has thick seams.
Measure and cut three strips about 1 inch wide by 30 inches long, keeping each end square; set aside short offcuts for testing.
Braid the short test strips by crossing the left strip over the center, then the right over the new center, alternating sides; keep the crossings snug but flexible.

blocks.body: Cut on a stable surface, direct scissor points away from the body, and close or put scissors away when not cutting. Younger learners need adult supervision.

blocks.question: Which fabric is the best starting choice for this beginner braid?
options: A stable woven cotton with little stretch
A very stretchy knit
Slippery satin in three thicknesses
Fabric with loose decorative loops
blocks.explanation: Stable, similar-weight woven fabric makes consistent crossings easier, though small differences can be corrected by testing.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Choose fabric and prepare a balanced braid. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Braid the full length with steady tension
lessons.summary: Braid the full length with steady tension

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Start the main braid by aligning the three strip ends. Keep approximately 2 inches at the start unbraided; these tails make it easier to anchor the center and can be tucked later. Hold the meeting point between thumb and forefinger, or clip it to a stable work surface. Cross the left strand over the middle, then cross the right strand over the new middle. Repeat, alternating sides. The strand that crosses becomes the new middle, so pause to identify it before the next movement. A calm rhythm prevents accidental double-crossings.

Do not pull the braid taut like a shoelace. Fabric compresses, and excessive tension makes a stiff cord that resists a flat spiral. On the other hand, loose crossings create visible holes and an unstable edge. After every few crossings, lay the braid on the table and see whether it curves gently. A curve is useful evidence: the eventual coaster must turn around a center without sharply kinking. Try to keep the braid's width close to its unbraided starting width. A thumb-width change or more is a cue to stop and correct the latest few crossings.

When a strip runs short, overlap it with a new strip of similar width by about 1 inch and continue braiding the

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Align the three full strip ends and leave about 2 inches as starting tails; hold them with a clip or fingers.
Cross left over center, then right over the new center; repeat while keeping each crossing snug and the braid flexible.
Pause every few inches to lay the braid down, check its curve and width, and correct the most recent crossings if needed.

blocks.body: Cut on a stable surface, direct scissor points away from the body, and close or put scissors away when not cutting. Younger learners need adult supervision.

blocks.question: What should you do if the braid feels rigid and makes a sharp kink when curved?
options: Pull each strand harder
Loosen the most recent crossings and test the curve again
Tie a knot at the kink
Cover the kink with glue
blocks.explanation: Even but gentle tension lets the braid bend around the center. Correct the recent section before continuing.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Braid the full length with steady tension. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Shape a centered coil and join its rows
lessons.summary: Shape a centered coil and join its rows

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A round coaster is built by turning the braid around itself and stitching neighboring rows together. First place the 4-inch paper guide beside the work. Form the starting tails into a small, flat center about 1/2 inch across. The center can be a tiny folded bundle rather than a perfect spiral; what matters is that it lies level and does not form a knot. Pin or clip the center so it cannot unwind. Thread a hand needle with about 45 centimeters of thread, double it if the fabric is dense, and knot the end. Keep the needle pointed away from fingers and rest it safely when pausing.

Make several small stitches through the center bundle to hold it together. Then curve the braid around the center, matching the outer edge of each new row to the inner edge of the previous row. Sew through the adjoining braid edges, not across the full face: small overcast or whip stitches that catch both neighboring ridges make an unobtrusive join. Space them about 1/4 inch apart as a guide. Pull thread only until the rows touch. If stitches are pulled tight, the coil cups; if they are too loose, the rows separate. Pins are temporary guides, not part of the final object, so remove them before your hand rea

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Shape the beginning tails into a flat center about 1/2 inch wide, then pin or clip the bundle temporarily.
Thread the needle with about 45 cm of thread and sew several small stitches through the center to anchor the braid; secure the thread with a small knot.
Curve the braid around the center and hand-stitch adjacent ridges every roughly 1/4 inch, catching both rows without pulling them tight.

blocks.body: Cut on a stable surface, direct scissor points away from the body, and close or put scissors away when not cutting. Younger learners need adult supervision.

blocks.question: Why are joining stitches spaced along both neighboring braid ridges?
options: To turn the coaster into a waterproof object
To make the coaster safe for hot cookware
To keep the rows connected while allowing the coil to lie naturally
To hide every color in the braid
blocks.explanation: The purpose is structural joining of this small craft object, not a performance or safety certification.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Shape a centered coil and join its rows. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Finish the edge and inspect the coaster
lessons.summary: Finish the edge and inspect the coaster

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
When the coil reaches approximately 4 inches across, decide whether another partial turn would make it too large or crowded. A small handmade variation is preferable to forcing an awkward last row. Leave enough braid for an edge tail, usually 2 to 3 inches. To finish, fold the raw end inward so loose cut edges are hidden within the braid. Lay this folded tip along the outside curve, following the circle rather than pointing straight outward. Stitch it to the neighboring row at several points, then weave the thread tail through a few concealed stitches and trim it. Keep the needle and pins accounted for.

Set the coaster on a level table and check it from the side. Press gently with a flat palm; do not iron unless the fabric care label and adult supervision permit it, and do not use high heat to make a structural correction. A small unevenness can often be improved by easing the outer row and redistributing a few joining stitches. A severe dome or ripple usually means tension or spacing changed earlier; undo only the affected section and resew rather than stretching the fabric. If the edge tail protrudes, tuck it more deeply and add a stitch. Avoid glue: it can make a stiff spot and

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Stop coiling at about 4 inches across, leaving roughly 2–3 inches of braid for the finish; check whether an extra turn would buckle.
Fold the raw braid end inward, lay it along the outside curve and sew it down at several points; bury and trim the thread tail.
Set the coaster on a level tabletop, inspect for rocking, gaps, loose ends and protruding pins, then record its measured diameter.

blocks.body: Cut on a stable surface, direct scissor points away from the body, and close or put scissors away when not cutting. Younger learners need adult supervision.

blocks.question: The coil begins to dome as you sew. What is the best first repair?
options: Pull the outer row tighter
Press it under a heavy object and keep stitching
Add glue under the raised area
Release a few tight stitches in that section and resew with more slack
blocks.explanation: A dome commonly comes from tight joining or crowded spacing. Fix the affected section instead of forcing the whole coil.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Finish the edge and inspect the coaster. What did you learn and verify?

name: Basic Embroidered Initial Patch
tagline: Design and stitch a small, original single-letter patch from woven cotton.
outcome: Plan a legible 4 cm-high block initial inside a 6 cm square patch with a consistent 5 mm margin.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Basic Embroidered Initial Patch

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Design and stitch a small, original single-letter patch from woven cotton. You will stabilize the cloth in a hoop, outline a block initial with backstitch, add a simple border, finish the raw edge wit

lessons.title: Plan the patch and prepare the fabric
lessons.summary: Plan the patch and prepare the fabric

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A readable patch starts with a simple shape, not with elaborate lettering. This project uses a 6 cm square finished face. Keep the letter inside a centered 4 cm-high area, leaving a 5 mm clear margin at the edges so the outline does not collide with the border stitching. A block initial with straight or gently rounded strokes is easier to outline than a thin script. Draw your own letter on paper; avoid copying a logo, character, or existing artwork. For a first attempt, choose a letter with broad strokes and few tight corners.

The front fabric is cut larger than the finished patch so you can hoop it and later trim it. Woven cotton is easier to control than jersey because its threads cross at right angles and do not stretch as readily. Place the cloth smoothly in the hoop. Tighten the hoop only enough to hold it flat; excessive force can mark or distort cloth. If you have no hoop, lay the cloth over a firm, flat surface and use a relaxed hand rather than pulling the fabric taut by force.

Use a ruler and light marks. A washable pencil should be tested on a scrap because fabrics and marking tools differ. Draw a 6 cm square boundary, then indicate a smaller centered guide area. Trace

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On paper, draw a block initial about 4 cm high and no wider than 4 cm; simplify narrow gaps and sharp inside corners.
Cut a 10 cm × 10 cm front square and place it in a 10–13 cm hoop with the marked face centered and gently flat.
Lightly mark the 6 cm finished square, centered 4 cm letter area, and letter outline with a tested removable marker.

blocks.body: Keep the needle pointed away from your body and set it in a needle minder or closed container whenever you pause; count it before and after work.

blocks.question: Why does the course use a 10 cm square of front cloth for a 6 cm finished patch?
options: It leaves room to hoop the cloth and trim an even allowance after stitching.
It makes the patch strong enough to carry a small object.
It guarantees the fabric will not fray.
It lets you embroider without a needle.
blocks.explanation: The larger square is a working blank. The planned finished face is about 6 cm, and extra fabric is needed for hooping and edge finishing.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the patch and prepare the fabric. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Practice and stitch the initial
lessons.summary: Practice and stitch the initial

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Embroidery floss is made of several fine plies twisted together. For this small initial, separate the floss and use two plies for the main outline. Hold the cut length near its middle, tease apart two strands, and draw them out slowly; pulling the full bundle can knot it. A working length of roughly 45 cm is manageable. Longer lengths rub against fabric more often and can fray or tangle. Thread the needle without putting it in your mouth. A small knot at the tail can secure this beginner method; leave a short tail and later weave the end under nearby stitches. If the back grows bulky, use smaller knots or secure the tail under several existing stitches.

Practice on the scrap first. A backstitch makes a nearly continuous line: bring the needle up, make a short forward stitch, bring the needle up one stitch-length ahead, then go backward into the end of the previous stitch. Keep stitches around 2–3 mm on the letter and shorten them around curves. The needle should enter the same endpoint as the preceding stitch so gaps stay small. Do not tug until the cloth dimples. The thread should lie on the surface with enough ease that the cloth remains flat.

Start on a straight outer stroke,

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut about 45 cm of floss, separate two plies slowly, thread the needle, and secure the tail with a small knot or a few securing stitches.
On the practice scrap, make a 3 cm backstitched line using roughly 2–3 mm stitches and gentle, even tension.
Outline the initial with backstitch, shortening stitches to about 1–2 mm at tight turns and securing each thread end beneath nearby stitches.

blocks.body: Keep the needle pointed away from your body and set it in a needle minder or closed container whenever you pause; count it before and after work.

blocks.question: Which stitch is used for the continuous outline of the block initial?
options: Running stitch with large gaps
Backstitch, with each return entering the preceding stitch endpoint
A single long thread laid on top
Blanket stitch across the letter interior
blocks.explanation: Backstitch forms the initial outline. Shorten the stitch near tight turns and keep tension gentle.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Practice and stitch the initial. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Add a border and finish the patch edge
lessons.summary: Add a border and finish the patch edge

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A narrow border frames the initial and provides a guide for the finished edge. With the front still in the hoop, mark or imagine a small running-stitch rectangle about 6 cm square around the design. Use optional contrast floss, or keep one color for a restrained look. Running stitch is made by bringing the needle up and down at regular intervals. Spacing near 3 mm is a useful starting point. This guide line is decorative and helps you locate the future trim; it is not a structural seam. Leave the design undisturbed if it already fills the available space.

Remove the hoop and inspect both sides. Trim the front cloth to a square approximately 7 cm × 7 cm, leaving about 5 mm beyond the planned 6 cm finished boundary. Turn the allowance to the back as you stitch around the perimeter. Blanket stitch creates a repeated edge loop; its even spacing helps keep the folded edge contained. Begin with the needle emerging near a corner. Take the next bite through the folded allowance and pull the thread through the loop so the loop sits along the edge. Repeat with stitches about 4–5 mm apart. This is a decorative craft finish and does not certify the patch for heavy wear or load.

At corners, p

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Add an optional 6 cm square running-stitch border, about 3 mm per stitch, keeping it outside the initial and inside the planned trim.
Remove the hoop and trim the front to approximately 7 cm × 7 cm, retaining about 5 mm of allowance beyond the 6 cm finish line.
Fold the allowance to the back and work blanket stitches 4–5 mm apart around all four edges, catching the fold and keeping tension gentle.

blocks.body: Keep the needle pointed away from your body and set it in a needle minder or closed container whenever you pause; count it before and after work.

blocks.question: Your test line dimples the fabric. What is the best adjustment?
options: Pull harder so the stitch becomes flatter
Use six strands for every stitch
Ease thread tension and re-center or loosen the hoop
Wet the fabric immediately
blocks.explanation: Puckering signals excessive tension or hoop distortion. Relax the stitches and adjust the hoop before continuing.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Add a border and finish the patch edge. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cover the reverse and inspect the finished patch
lessons.summary: Cover the reverse and inspect the finished patch

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The backing hides most of the embroidery tails and makes the reverse more comfortable against a garment. Use the 7 cm × 7 cm soft cotton square. Center it over the back of the patch, with its raw edges tucked under the perimeter finish. Hand-baste with loose temporary stitches about 5 mm inside the blanket-stitched border, or catch it discreetly under a few edge loops. The backing should lie flat without pulling the patch into a bowl. Its purpose is to cover and soften, not to make the patch waterproof, protective, or strong enough to carry weight.

Remove temporary basting if you used it, and inspect the letter from arm's length. A recognizable initial should have continuous strokes and adequate openings. Check that the reverse has no long thread tails that can catch. Clip only loose ends, leaving a small tail so knots do not unravel. If a small opening is visible at the edge, add a few hand stitches with matching thread. If a section is noticeably bulky, undo and re-secure the thread rather than cutting through a knot.

Remove washable marks only according to the marking product's label. Test on a scrap, use minimal water if specified, and air-dry the patch fully. Do not assume a

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Center the 7 cm backing square on the reverse and secure it with loose basting or discreet hand stitches just inside the edge finish.
Inspect the front, back, corners, and edge; secure loose tails and add a few matching stitches where a gap remains.
Remove marks only as directed by the marker label, air-dry fully, then decide whether to attach by hand sewing or keep as a sample.

blocks.body: Keep the needle pointed away from your body and set it in a needle minder or closed container whenever you pause; count it before and after work.

blocks.question: You need to pause while a threaded needle is still in use. What should you do?
options: Leave it in the cushion of a chair
Hold it between your lips
Set it on the floor nearby
Place it in a needle minder or closed container and keep it away from children and pets
blocks.explanation: Pause by securing the needle in a designated holder or closed container and count it before and after work.

name: Mini Embroidery Hoop Artwork
tagline: Plan and stitch an original 4-inch botanical mini hoop featuring a curved stem, paired leaves, and a small sunburst.
outcome: Measure and transfer a compact original design inside a 4-inch hoop with a consistent margin.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Mini Embroidery Hoop Artwork

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Plan and stitch an original 4-inch botanical mini hoop featuring a curved stem, paired leaves, and a small sunburst. Learn to prepare fabric, control thread, use backstitch and satin stitch, finish th

lessons.title: Plan the motif and prepare the cloth
lessons.summary: Plan the motif and prepare the cloth

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Make a small design that can actually be stitched

This project uses an original, simple botanical arrangement: one gently bending stem, three pairs of narrow leaves, and a three-ray sunburst near the top. It is a study in line and shape, not a copied illustration. Draw it first inside a 3-inch circle on paper. The hoop opening is 4 inches across, so this leaves roughly a half-inch visual margin around the motif. Keep each leaf about 3/8 inch long and 1/4 inch wide; shapes that are too tiny are hard to fill cleanly. Make the central stem curve gradually rather than turning sharply.

Test your chosen marking method on scrap before drawing on the good cloth. Transfer marks should be faint and removable by a method compatible with the fabric. Do not scrub aggressively or use an untested cleaner. Plain woven cotton is forgiving because the needle passes between threads; stretchy or very loose cloth can distort under hoop tension. Cut an 8-inch square so there is enough cloth outside the hoop to hold and later finish. If the edges fray, leave them alone during stitching and trim only after the design is complete.

A hoop holds the fabric under even tension, not crushing force. The cl

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Draw a 3-inch circle on paper and place a curved stem, six simple leaves, and a three-ray sunburst inside it; use the sample leaf dimensions of about 3/8 by 1/4 inch.
Cut one 8 x 8 inch piece of woven cotton and test the marker, pencil, or tracing approach on a scrap corner.
Transfer the motif faintly, centering its 3-inch boundary on the fabric; mark only essential contours.
Loosen the hoop screw, place fabric over the inner ring, set the outer ring on top, and tighten the screw by hand while smoothing cloth evenly around the rim.

blocks.body: Keep needle and scissors pointed away from the body; pause and place them in a tray or pincushion before moving or reaching.

blocks.question: Why does the sample design use a 3-inch circle inside a 4-inch hoop?
options: To leave a visible margin around the motif
To make the cloth stretch as tightly as possible
To ensure every leaf is exactly the same length
To make the hoop safe to use as a toy
blocks.explanation: A 3-inch motif boundary leaves about a half-inch margin within a 4-inch opening, supporting clear composition.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the motif and prepare the cloth. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Stitch the stem and sunburst outlines
lessons.summary: Stitch the stem and sunburst outlines

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Control the line before adding filled color

Use two separated strands from the six-strand floss for the stem and sunburst outline. Separate strands by holding the desired two together and gently drawing them away from the remaining four; do not yank the whole bundle through the cloth. Cut a working length of about 18 inches (46 cm). Longer thread twists and knots more readily, and repeatedly pulling a long length through fabric adds friction. Thread the needle and leave a short tail. The first few backstitches can secure that tail under the line on the reverse; avoid a bulky knot, especially on this small work.

Backstitch makes a continuous line from short segments. Bring the needle up at the beginning of a line, make one forward stitch, then bring the needle up a stitch-length ahead and return to the previous stitch endpoint. Continue by making each new stitch meet the end of the last. Use about 1/8-inch stitches on the curved stem and shorter stitches around the sunburst rays. Small regular stitches turn more smoothly than long chords that cut across the curve. The specialist tutorial describes backstitch for lines and recommends shorter lengths around curves; treat those di

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut about 18 inches of floss, separate two strands, thread the needle, and begin at the base of the stem while holding the tail under the first stitches.
Backstitch along the curved stem using roughly 1/8-inch segments, bringing each new stitch up ahead and returning to the previous endpoint.
Use shorter backstitches to outline the three sunburst rays, then secure the thread by passing under several nearby reverse stitches and trimming the tail.
Inspect the line from the front and gently tap the cloth; loosen and re-center the hoop if the fabric has puckered or shifted.

blocks.body: Keep needle and scissors pointed away from the body; pause and place them in a tray or pincushion before moving or reaching.

blocks.question: What is the best response if the hoop fabric looks oval after tightening?
options: Pull one edge as hard as possible
Loosen the ring and smooth the fabric evenly from opposite sides
Cover the distortion with a dense layer of stitches
Use a screwdriver for maximum tightness
blocks.explanation: Release the clamp and redistribute fabric evenly; a hoop should hold cloth flat with slight give, not warp it.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Stitch the stem and sunburst outlines. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fill the leaves with controlled satin stitches
lessons.summary: Fill the leaves with controlled satin stitches

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Fill compact shapes without bulky ridges

Choose a second floss color for the leaves. A single strand gives a delicate fill; two strands provide more coverage but can crowd a narrow shape. Try both on the scrap and select the one that lies flat. For each leaf, stitch straight across its width with short parallel satin stitches. Start at one edge and place the next stitch close beside the last, keeping the stitch direction consistent. The thread should cover the marked interior without being pulled hard. On a 1/4-inch-wide leaf, that may mean only a small number of stitches; judge coverage visually rather than cramming in an exact count.

Bring the needle up at one edge and down at the opposite edge, then return to the first edge for the neighboring pass. Keep the needle entering just outside the previous thread so the fabric does not show as a broad gap. Avoid crossing stitches in an X pattern: crossed strands create lumps and an uneven surface. For pointed tips, shorten the final stitches as the shape narrows. There is no need to fill beyond the pencil outline. It is better to have a tiny sliver of cloth showing at a sharp tip than to distort the leaf by forcing a long, wide st

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Test one-strand and two-strand satin stitches on scrap, then choose the strand count that covers a 1/4-inch shape without ridging.
Fill each leaf with parallel stitches crossing its width; shorten stitches gradually toward the pointed end.
Secure the color change under several reverse stitches, trim the tail, and repeat the fill for the remaining five leaves.
Look at the design under good light and compare the leaf edges with the transfer guides; remove visible marks only with the tested method.

blocks.body: Keep needle and scissors pointed away from the body; pause and place them in a tray or pincushion before moving or reaching.

blocks.question: How does the backstitch form a continuous curved line?
options: Make long stitches that cross the entire curve
Tie a knot at every marked point
Bring each new stitch up ahead and return to the previous endpoint
Pass the needle only on the reverse side
blocks.explanation: Backstitch overlaps the endpoint of the prior stitch; shorter segments help it follow a bend.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Fill the leaves with controlled satin stitches. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Finish the hoop back and review the artwork
lessons.summary: Finish the hoop back and review the artwork

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Turn stitched cloth into a display piece

Remove the fabric from the hoop before trimming. Keeping it stretched for long storage can leave a ring or crease, so treat the hoop as a frame only when you are ready to display. With the cloth face down on a clean surface, inspect the reverse for loose tails, loops, or a needle left in the work. Trim only loose ends, not stitches. Return the stitched center to the inner ring, center the motif, then fit the outer ring and tighten gradually. Smooth the fabric around all sides rather than tugging only one direction. The hoop should hold the cloth flat without distorting the round motif.

For a simple dry finish, trim excess cloth to about 1 inch beyond the hoop's outer edge. Fold this allowance toward the back of the inner ring in small, even pleats. Use the hoop rim to trap the folded cloth, or sew a running line around the allowance and gently draw it closed if you prefer a gathered back. Do not use glue as the default: it can stain, stiffen, or complicate later adjustment. Keep the screw accessible and do not cover it with a bulky wad. This is an indoor decorative object; it is not certified for food contact, child play, or structural

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Loosen the hoop and remove the fabric; inspect the reverse and trim only loose tails with small scissors pointed away from your hand.
Rehoop the stitched center with the design centered in the 4-inch opening, smoothing the fabric evenly before hand-tightening.
Trim the excess to about 1 inch beyond the hoop rim, fold the cloth allowance toward the reverse in small pleats, and trap it beneath the inner ring or secure with a loose running
Review the piece against the completion checklist, record one successful choice and one next-time experiment, then store it flat and dry when not displayed.

blocks.body: Keep needle and scissors pointed away from the body; pause and place them in a tray or pincushion before moving or reaching.

blocks.question: A narrow leaf fill bunches when using two floss strands. What should you try first?
options: Pull harder until the ridge disappears
Add several crossed stitches over the ridge
Switch to a tested single strand or reduce fill density
Apply glue to flatten the leaf
blocks.explanation: Use the scrap test to select a strand count that lies flat; parallel coverage should not be forced.

modules.description: Make a freestanding, openwork macrame sleeve that decorates a small, dry-bottomed tabletop nursery pot. Four cords form a flat square-knot panel, then its edges are joined into a removable tube. The s

lessons.title: Measure the pot and prepare a flat panel
lessons.summary: Measure the pot and prepare a flat panel

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Begin with fit, not guesswork

This project wraps a small upright pot with an openwork panel. It is not a cradle: the pot remains on its own tabletop base, and the cord tube merely decorates its sides. The sample design is intended for a straight-sided pot about 8 cm across and 8 cm tall. Measure the pot's circumference by wrapping a narrow paper strip around its widest point, marking where the ends meet, then measuring the marked length. For a 25 cm circumference, plan a relaxed finished panel width of about 27 cm. The extra 2 cm makes a removable sleeve rather than a tight cage. Height is about 6 cm, leaving the bottom and rim visible. If your pot tapers, measure both the top and lower circumference; make the panel fit the larger measurement and check whether the smaller area will stay visually centered.

Cord shortens as knots consume length. Four 180 cm strands are a practical starting allowance for this small panel, not a universal formula. Chunkier cord or a larger pot can use more. Keep the active knotting area on a table, and use a small temporary overhand tie at the center of all four folded strands to create eight working tails. Arrange them in a row: two outer working

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure the pot circumference with a paper strip at the widest point and measure its height; record both dimensions. For the sample pot, use about 25 cm around and 8 cm high.
Cut four 180 cm cords, fold each at its midpoint, align the folds, and tie a loose temporary overhand knot at the midpoint. Lay the eight tails in order on the table.
Make one square knot with the four leftmost tails: cross the left outer cord over the two middle cords and under the right outer cord; pass the right outer cord behind the middle c
Continue across the eight tails by making one more square knot with the four remaining tails; keep each knot about 2 cm wide and the row level.

blocks.body: This sleeve is a decorative wrap for a tabletop pot, never a suspended or load-bearing plant hanger. Do not hang it from a hook or rely on it to support a pot.

blocks.question: For the sample pot with a 25 cm circumference, what relaxed finished panel width is the target?
options: About 27 cm
Exactly 25 cm and tightly stretched
About 10 cm
About 40 cm
blocks.explanation: The design adds about 2 cm to the measured circumference so the sleeve is relaxed and removable.

lessons.title: Build an open square-knot mesh
lessons.summary: Build an open square-knot mesh

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Repeat with measured spacing

A square knot is two linked halves. In the first half, one outer working cord crosses in front of the central filler pair while the opposite outer cord travels behind and comes through the loop. The second half reverses the crossing. The two directions together make a flat knot. If you repeat only one half, the cord forms a spiral; that may be an intentional texture in another project, but it will twist this sleeve panel. Practise slowly enough to see which cord is in front. Do not pull until the loop closes completely before checking the crossing, because a reversed pass is harder to identify once compressed.

With the supplied eight tails, a full row uses two square knots, one with each separate group of four tails. The next row is staggered: use two knots, each straddling the gap between neighboring knots in the row below. To do that, leave the two far outer tails idle and use the six interior tails as groups of four, sharing boundaries. With eight tails, these two knots occupy the center and leave a balanced open edge. The pattern repeats as a three-knot row, then a two-knot row. Aim for a 1.5 cm gap between rows; use a paper gauge or ruler rath

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: For row two, leave the two outside tails unused and tie two square knots across the six interior tails, with each knot centered under a gap in row one.
Alternate three-knot and two-knot rows, leaving about 1.5 cm between rows, until the panel measures approximately 6 cm high and 27 cm wide for the sample pot.
Lay the panel flat and compare both long edges, checking knot faces for twists and measuring from the top row to the bottom row at both sides.

blocks.body: This sleeve is a decorative wrap for a tabletop pot, never a suspended or load-bearing plant hanger. Do not hang it from a hook or rely on it to support a pot.

blocks.question: What makes the two halves of a square knot lie flat rather than spiral?
options: Pull only the left cord each time
Reverse the crossing direction for the second half
Tie a single overhand knot
Wet the cords before tightening
blocks.explanation: A square knot is formed by two opposing half-knots. Repeating one direction makes a spiral.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build an open square-knot mesh. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Shape the panel into a removable sleeve
lessons.summary: Shape the panel into a removable sleeve

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Join edges without making a handle

The panel becomes a tube when its two short ends meet. This seam is a decorative closure only. It should hold the panel's shape around a tabletop pot while remaining easy to open. Bring the ends together around the empty pot or paper template and align top edge with top edge. A gentle overlap of roughly 1 cm is enough. Use two paper clips to hold the overlap temporarily, one near the top and one near the bottom. Clips are setup aids, not permanent hardware; remove them before use. If the panel edges meet with a wide gap, the panel is too short for the pot. If they overlap by several centimeters, it is too wide. Open the seam and adjust with a short cord tie rather than cutting the panel apart.

Use an offcut or a spare 30 cm cord to secure the seam at two points. Thread the cord through existing open spaces along the edge; do not pierce or force through a knot. Tie a small bow or a pair of snug half-hitches that can be undone by hand. Keep the tie ends short enough not to dangle, but leave enough to untie without scissors. Two attachment points, separated vertically, reduce seam gaping while keeping the wrap adjustable. The seam should not pin

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Wrap the panel loosely around the empty pot or paper template, align the short ends, and overlap them by about 1 cm; hold the edges with two temporary paper clips.
Use a 30 cm offcut to lace through existing openings at two seam points, one near each end; tie adjustable bows or hand-untieable half-hitches, then remove the clips.
Slide the empty sleeve onto the pot, center it on the sidewall, and verify that its lower edge sits above the pot base and any saucer.

blocks.body: This sleeve is a decorative wrap for a tabletop pot, never a suspended or load-bearing plant hanger. Do not hang it from a hook or rely on it to support a pot.

blocks.question: A seam gap is too wide. What is the best next step?
options: Hang the pot by the sleeve to stretch it
Cut through the nearest knot
Untie the seam and revise panel width or spacing
Glue the sleeve shut
blocks.explanation: A removable laced seam makes it possible to revise the panel rather than force or permanently alter it.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Shape the panel into a removable sleeve. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Finish, inspect, and refine safely
lessons.summary: Finish, inspect, and refine safely

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
## Test the object in its real setting

Before trimming, decide whether a few visible tails are an intentional finish or need tidying. A small knot panel can look clean with short, consistent tails. For this course, leave about 3 cm at the ends of the seam tie so the closure remains easy to undo. If the main strands have exposed ends at the top or bottom, make a small overhand stopper knot at each pair and trim only excess cord after checking the knot is secure. Keep scissors away from the working mesh. Cutting too close to a knot can release the cord; if uncertain, leave a slightly longer tail and tuck it along the back. Do not add glue or coatings. This keeps the sleeve reversible and avoids unverified chemical or moisture claims.

Test with the pot empty first. Place the pot upright on its normal stable surface, then slide the sleeve over it. Look from the side and above. The top and bottom margins should be balanced, the seam should sit at the back, and the mesh should not bunch into a narrow band. Turn the container by hand, rather than pulling on the sleeve. Check that it remains centered and that the container still rests on its own base. Then remove the sleeve and inspect f

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trim only excess seam-tie tails after confirming the knots remain easy to undo; leave roughly 3 cm on each tie end and keep scissors clear of the mesh.
Test the sleeve on the empty pot on a stable tabletop; check that it slides on and off, sits centered, and never reaches beneath the pot base or across drainage openings.
Inspect the cord for dampness, loose knots, snagging, and uneven rows; record one successful feature and one specific adjustment for a next version.

blocks.body: This sleeve is a decorative wrap for a tabletop pot, never a suspended or load-bearing plant hanger. Do not hang it from a hook or rely on it to support a pot.

blocks.question: Where should the sleeve's bottom edge sit during the tabletop fit check?
options: Under the pot, supporting its weight
Across drainage openings to catch water
Tight around the pot base
Above the pot base and any saucer
blocks.explanation: The lower edge stays clear of the base and saucer because cord is not a water-catching or load-bearing component.

name: Beaded Stretch Bracelet
tagline: Design and make a comfortable, balanced stretch bracelet from round beads and elastic cord.
outcome: Measure wrist circumference and choose a finished inside circumference with a stated ease allowance.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Beaded Stretch Bracelet

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Design and make a comfortable, balanced stretch bracelet from round beads and elastic cord. You will measure your wrist, check bead-hole fit, create a repeatable color pattern, tie and inspect a secur

lessons.title: Measure, choose, and plan the repeat
lessons.summary: Measure, choose, and plan the repeat

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A stretch bracelet should slide over the hand without requiring a hard pull, then sit comfortably rather than gripping the wrist. Begin with a relaxed wrist measurement instead of choosing a size from a generic chart. Wrap a soft tape around the wrist where the bracelet will rest, snug but not tight, and record the circumference to the nearest 2 mm. For a first sample, add about 10 mm of ease to that wrist measurement. This is a design starting point, not a universal fit rule: a smaller hand opening, bead shape, and personal preference can change comfort. You will compare the relaxed inside length with your own wrist later.

This course uses nominal 6 mm round beads in a single strand. Its pattern is four groups of seven main beads, with four accent beads spaced between the groups, giving 28 main beads plus four accents: 32 total. If all measure exactly 6 mm across, the bead run is about 192 mm before the knot area is closed; the knot occupies a small portion of the flexible loop, and real beads and spacing change the result. For that reason, count and measure the actual laid-out string rather than treating the arithmetic as a guaranteed finished size. The sample suits a wrist whos

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure the wrist at the intended wearing position, then record the circumference in millimeters.
Set a first relaxed target about 10 mm longer than the wrist measurement and arrange 28 main beads with four accents between four groups.
Pass the chosen cord through a spare bead hole once, then slide it back and forth gently.

blocks.body: Keep small beads and cord away from infants and pets; promptly collect dropped pieces because they can be choking hazards.

blocks.question: What is the best first check when choosing cord for a batch of beads?
options: Choose the thickest cord sold for bracelets
Test a spare bead and confirm the cord slides without scraping
Stretch the cord until it becomes thinner
Coat the cord with oil so it slides
blocks.explanation: The hole must accept the cord freely; if it catches, change to compatible cord or beads rather than forcing it.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Measure, choose, and plan the repeat. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Lay out and string a balanced bracelet
lessons.summary: Lay out and string a balanced bracelet

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A pattern is easiest to evaluate while it is still on the tray. Lay the beads in the sequence you intend to string them, with the four accent beads at roughly equal intervals. This sample places one accent after each group of seven main beads. Turn beads so their best-looking faces are visible, and rotate any with a hole that appears rough to the discard pile rather than hiding a defect in the design. If the pattern looks uneven, correct it now; once beads are strung, changing the order takes more time and can tangle a long elastic tail.

Cut about 35 cm of cord, leaving ample tails for handling and a knot. If the cord instructions recommend pre-stretching, gently draw a section between your hands once or twice without yanking. The goal is to remove some initial slack, not to test the breaking point. Anchor one end with a loose overhand stopper knot or low-tack tape; do not tape over the working length. String each bead onto the free end in the layout order. Keep a short tail behind the beads so a bead cannot slip off. Do not use powder, oil, or liquid to make beads slide; those substances may affect the cord, adhesive, or skin contact.

After the last bead, bring the two cord ends

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut approximately 35 cm of elastic cord and secure one end with a loose stopper or low-tack tape.
String beads in the inspected tray order, alternating the four accent positions with groups of seven main beads.
Bring cord ends together with the beads relaxed, compare the loop to the target, and change bead count before tying if needed.

blocks.body: Keep small beads and cord away from infants and pets; promptly collect dropped pieces because they can be choking hazards.

blocks.question: Your relaxed loop is too small and requires force to pass over the hand. What should you do?
options: Pull harder several times to stretch it permanently
Wear it only on a smaller part of the wrist
Rebuild with a longer measured bead layout and fresh knot
Add extra glue to the knot
blocks.explanation: A too-small bracelet should be resized before use, not forced over the hand.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Lay out and string a balanced bracelet. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Tie, tuck, and inspect the elastic knot
lessons.summary: Tie, tuck, and inspect the elastic knot

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The knot is the bracelet's most important joining point. A square knot can slip if its halves are not alternated correctly, so first practice on two short scrap lengths of the same cord. For the bracelet, bring the ends together while the bead loop is relaxed. Cross the right end over the left and pass it under; snug gently. Then cross the left end over the right and pass it under. This alternating sequence forms a flat square knot. Keep the knot centered and avoid pulling so hard that the elastic necks down or whitens. If the knot looks like two identical half-hitches stacked in the same direction, untie it before cutting anything and repeat the alternating sequence.

Some craft references describe additional secure knot forms and optional adhesives. Whatever knot method you choose, learn it on scrap and follow the specific elastic maker's directions. This lesson teaches an alternating square knot because it is readily observable and easy to diagnose; do not assume a knot is secure merely because it appears compact. After tying, hold each side of the loop and apply only gentle hand tension. The knot should remain closed, the cord should not creep, and beads should not gap widely.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Practice an alternating square knot on scrap elastic until you can identify the two opposing crossings.
Tie the relaxed bracelet ends right-over-left and then left-over-right, snugging each half without pulling hard.
Apply gentle hand tension; if stable, optionally add a tiny amount of label-approved elastic jewelry adhesive and wait for full cure.
Tuck the knot into a bead only if it slides in without force, then trim excess tails after inspection and cure.

blocks.body: Keep small beads and cord away from infants and pets; promptly collect dropped pieces because they can be choking hazards.

blocks.question: Which sequence makes the square-knot halves alternate in this course?
options: Right over left, then left over right
Right over left twice
Tie one overhand knot and cut both tails immediately
Tie a knot while stretching the loop as far as possible
blocks.explanation: Alternating the crossing direction makes the two halves oppose each other; practice on scrap and test gently.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Tie, tuck, and inspect the elastic knot. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Check the fit and refine the finish
lessons.summary: Check the fit and refine the finish

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A finished-looking bracelet still needs a calm fit and quality check. Lay it flat and confirm that the pattern is balanced around the loop. Roll it gently between your fingers to look for a bead that catches, a knot that protrudes, or a section where cord is visible through a large gap. Then stretch the loop only enough to pass over the hand in a controlled way. If it requires force, stop. Do not repeatedly pull a too-small bracelet over the hand to prove that the elastic is strong; instead, remove beads and retie with a comfortable circumference. If it spins or slides excessively, decide whether the wearer accepts a loose fit or make a smaller version, again correcting before knotting.

For a safe first wear, inspect the elastic each time. Elastic can fatigue from repeated stretching, sharp bead holes, heat, sunlight, chemicals, and age. This course cannot promise a service life. Remove the bracelet before vigorous activity, sleeping, or tasks where it could snag. Do not wear a bracelet with fraying, a nick, a loose knot, a cracked bead, or exposed adhesive. Keep it dry and clean with a soft dry cloth; do not soak it or apply household cleaners. If a repair is needed, remove the d

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect the full loop under good light and gently rotate it to find cracked beads, cord gaps, rough edges, or an exposed knot.
Try the bracelet over the hand once with controlled gentle movement and check that it rests comfortably.
Record wrist measurement, relaxed finished circumference estimate, bead count, and one improvement idea.
Store the bracelet loosely in a dry place and plan to inspect it before each wear.

blocks.body: Keep small beads and cord away from infants and pets; promptly collect dropped pieces because they can be choking hazards.

blocks.question: A cord catches on one bead and develops visible fuzz. What is the safest response?
options: Push harder with a needle
Hide the fuzzy section inside a bead
Use household glue to coat the cord
Stop, remove the bead, and replace any damaged cord
blocks.explanation: Fuzz is a warning of abrasion. Replace the cause and the weakened cord before finishing.

name: Beaded Keychain with a Pattern
tagline: Plan and string a compact repeating-color pattern onto a short beaded keychain.
outcome: Draft a repeating bead-color pattern and calculate how many beads fit a measured strand.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Beaded Keychain with a Pattern

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Plan and string a compact repeating-color pattern onto a short beaded keychain. You will measure the usable strand, practice a secure thread finish inside bead tips, attach a split ring, and inspect t

lessons.title: Choose a repeat and size the strand
lessons.summary: Choose a repeat and size the strand

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Plan the repeat before threading so the finished object can be checked. This sample uses three colors in A–B–C order, four times, with an accent at each end: 14 beads total. The bead section is planned near 8.5 cm, but bead shapes and spacing vary. Measure your row rather than treating that dimension as guaranteed.

Arrange six beads snugly and measure them. Six nominal 6 mm beads occupy about 36 mm; fourteen similar beads would be roughly 84 mm. Use this only as an estimate. Lay out the full sequence, compare it with a ruler, and change length only by adding or removing a complete three-bead repeat. A partial unit breaks the pattern. Cut about 45 cm / 18 in of smooth, non-stretch thread to leave room for the row and knots.

Write a color key and draw the accents and four repeats. Choose original colors and geometry, not branded characters or logos. Inspect each bead for cracks, rough edges, or blocked holes. Thread must pass freely, including the extra pass needed near a knot. Never force a needle or pull thread with pliers. If the materials do not fit, substitute compatible beads or thread. A useful plan has a count, measured sample, and repeat that can be followed without memory

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Sort and inspect beads; measure six in a row.
Write A–B–C; lay four repeats and two accents.
Cut 45 cm thread; tape one end with 12 cm tail.

blocks.body: Beads and findings are choking hazards. Keep them away from children under three and anyone likely to mouth small objects; supervise older children and store parts closed.

blocks.question: What sequence is used in the sample design between the two accent beads?
options: A–B–C repeated four times
A–A–B–C repeated twice
A–B repeated six times
Any order, as long as there are 12 beads
blocks.explanation: The sample has four A–B–C units, followed by an accent bead at each end.

lessons.title: String the repeat with even tension
lessons.summary: String the repeat with even tension

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
String slowly over a tray, with the paper sequence beside the beads. Begin with an accent, add four A–B–C units, then add the final accent. Compare colors after each unit; an early correction takes less time than undoing the whole strand. A blunt tapestry needle may help only if it passes easily. Never force a sharp needle through a blocked bead.

Keep the taped tail anchored and leave enough thread to tie. Slide beads together with light, even tension. They may touch, but the line should remain flexible. Pulling too hard can curl the strand and stress knots. Excess slack leaves gaps that may snag. When strung, lay the row by a ruler and recount: accent, four A–B–C units, accent, 14 beads total.

The row should be near 8–9 cm, but your measured bead fit matters more than an exact target. If too long or short, change a whole unit and update the plan. Do not cut thread or omit a color to force a dimension. Keep spare beads over the tray during changes. Do not finish either end until count, order, and length are satisfactory. Success looks straight, evenly spaced, and still easy to revise. A short check at each repeat prevents a larger correction later. Keep the written color key visi

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: String accent, four A–B–C units, final accent.
Slide beads together gently without stretching thread.
Count beads and measure the row before finishing.

blocks.body: Beads and findings are choking hazards. Keep them away from children under three and anyone likely to mouth small objects; supervise older children and store parts closed.

blocks.question: Your chosen beads will not pass freely over the thread. What is the safest next action?
options: Push a sharp needle hard through the hole
Select beads with compatible clear holes or a suitable thread
Pull the thread with pliers until it passes
Widen the bead hole with a heated wire
blocks.explanation: A bead should accept the selected thread without force; substitute a compatible material rather than enlarging a hole.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on String the repeat with even tension. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Tie the ends and add the key ring
lessons.summary: Tie the ends and add the key ring

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A bead tip is a metal cup that hides a thread knot and ends in an attachment loop. Tie a firm overhand knot, pass the tail through the tip hole, and seat the knot in its cup. It must be too large to pass back through. If it slips, make a larger or second knot and test gently before closing. Specialist instructions describe this knot-in-tip method and gentle plier closure.[1]

Close the cup with smooth-nose pliers and small pressure. Keep fingers clear. Its sides should meet while the loop stays open. Do not crush the loop or rely on glue as the anchor. Repeat at the other end, maintaining mild tension so the final bead does not sit far from its tip. Trim excess tail only after the knot is tested. Replace a cracked, twisted, or sharp finding; do not patch it.

Attach the split ring by rotating its coils sideways just enough to feed the bead-tip loop around. Pulling ring ends apart can distort it. If the loop does not fit, use a larger ring; do not lever it with a sharp tool. Inspect visually and with a gentle hand check. This craft has no load rating. The loop should be seated without an escape gap, and no sharp metal should touch the hand. The metal cup should conceal thread withou

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Tie an overhand knot; seat it inside first tip.
Close cup gently with smooth-nose pliers.
Knot and close second tip while aligning beads.
Rotate split ring coils and feed loop fully on.

blocks.body: Beads and findings are choking hazards. Keep them away from children under three and anyone likely to mouth small objects; supervise older children and store parts closed.

blocks.question: How can you tell that a knot is a suitable anchor inside a bead tip before closing it?
options: It is hidden, so no test is needed
It has been covered in glue
A gentle check does not pull it through the bead-tip hole
It is tied as far from the bead tip as possible
blocks.explanation: Test knot size before closing the metal cup, and remake any knot that passes through.

lessons.title: Inspect, refine, and set safe limits
lessons.summary: Inspect, refine, and set safe limits

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Inspect the piece on a clear table. Trace the sequence and compare it with the key: accent, four A–B–C units, accent. Look for cracked beads, exposed tails, large gaps, kinks, and opened tips. Check by gentle hand pressure only. Do not hang a heavy object to prove strength. This is a decorative keychain for light keys, not climbing, lifting, restraint, or protective equipment.

Repair the actual fault. Correct a swapped bead by opening an intact finish and sliding beads off in reverse order. Retie and retest a slipping knot before closing the tip. Replace sharp or damaged findings rather than hiding them with tape or glue. Replace cracked beads with smooth matching beads. Keep parts over the tray and recount after repair. Update the pattern note if the count or order changes.

Record final count, approximate length, and one specific change for another version. A useful improvement changes one feature and says how to compare results. Avoid dangling additions that snag. Store spare beads closed and away from children and pets. CPSC advises keeping small balls and toys with small parts away from children under three because of choking risk.[2] This is not a toy or certified child prod

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trace pattern; inspect beads, tails, and tips.
Check attachment gently by hand; do not load it.
Record count, measured length, and one specific revision.

blocks.body: Beads and findings are choking hazards. Keep them away from children under three and anyone likely to mouth small objects; supervise older children and store parts closed.

blocks.question: What is the preferred way to put the split ring onto the bead-tip loop?
options: Pull both ring ends directly apart
Rotate the coils sideways and feed the loop around
Cut a gap into the ring with scissors
Glue the loop to the outside of the ring
blocks.explanation: A split ring is fitted by rotating the coils apart slightly and advancing the loop between them.

name: Clip-On Beaded Bag Charm
tagline: Design and assemble a removable, colorful bag charm with a small beaded focal cluster suspended from a clip.
outcome: Plan a balanced charm arrangement within an approximate 90 mm overall length, including clasp and connector.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Clip-On Beaded Bag Charm

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Design and assemble a removable, colorful bag charm with a small beaded focal cluster suspended from a clip. Learn how to plan a compact composition, make consistent bead links, connect findings witho

lessons.title: Plan a compact, balanced layout
lessons.summary: Plan a compact, balanced layout

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A good charm begins with a size limit and a clear visual hierarchy, not with every bead in the box. This sample aims for roughly 75–90 mm from the top of the clasp to the lowest bead. That is a design target, not a tested universal fit: bags, handles and user preferences differ. The clasp is about 25 mm long, the connector chain is 45 mm, and the three bead dangles should hang approximately 18–25 mm below the chain. Lay out pieces before opening any rings. A cluster can feel balanced when one slightly larger focal bead is near the center and two smaller or differently colored beads flank it. Similar length on the side dangles keeps the set tidy, while a center dangle 4–6 mm longer adds a gentle point. Avoid very long strings: they swing more and are more likely to catch on nearby objects.

Check each bead hole against an eye pin before committing. The pin should pass through without force, but the bead should not slide over a factory eye. If a bead is too small for the wire, choose a compatible bead or pin rather than drilling the bead. Put the intended clasp, chain, rings and beads on the mat in the order they will hang. Measure the proposed span with the ruler. Include the approx

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the 25 mm clasp, 45 mm chain, four 5–6 mm rings and three proposed bead combinations on the mat; arrange them in a top-to-bottom line.
Test each bead hole with an unused eye pin and select a center focal bead plus two side beads; use no more than two accents per dangle.
Measure the laid-out chain and dangles, then sketch the order and note the colors and approximate finished span.

blocks.body: Work over a stable, uncluttered tabletop with good light. Wear eye protection while cutting wire and direct the cut end into the bead mat, away from faces.

blocks.question: What should you do if a bead hole is too tight for the eye pin?
options: Force the bead over the pin
Drill the bead with a household drill
Choose a bead and pin that fit without force
Glue the bead to the outside of the pin
blocks.explanation: The bead must slide over the straight pin smoothly. Do not enlarge holes or force a mismatch.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan a compact, balanced layout. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build three neat bead dangles
lessons.summary: Build three neat bead dangles

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A dangle is a bead held on a pin with a closed loop at its free end. Eye pins already have one formed loop, so they reduce the number of loops a beginner must shape. The bead sits against the eye; a small accent, if used, sits above it. Leave a short length of straight pin beyond the top bead so there is enough metal to bend and form a loop. The exact usable tail depends on bead height and pin length. This sample uses a nominal 50 mm pin and beads no taller than about 10 mm, leaving room to trim excess after measuring. A consistent bend just above each bead helps the three loops look alike. Round-nose pliers make a curved loop; flat-nose pliers hold the stem steady. A simple loop must close so the cut end meets the stem without a visible gap. If you cannot close it without distorting the loop, remake the dangle with a fresh pin rather than hiding the gap.

Work slowly and keep the wire end pointed down toward the mat when cutting. Small cutoffs can spring away, so eye protection and a clear work area matter. Make one dangle first and inspect it before repeating the technique. Compare its overall drop to your sketch. The two side dangles can be close in length; the center can be a l

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Thread the center focal bead and any planned accent onto one eye pin, keeping the bead against the factory eye.
Mark a point about 6–8 mm above the top bead, make a right-angle bend with flat-nose pliers, and trim the pin leaving roughly 8–10 mm of tail for loop formation.
Grip the tail near its end with round-nose pliers, curve it over the plier jaw, and bring its cut end back toward the stem to make a small loop.
Repeat the same bead order and loop process for the two side dangles, making their drops similar and the center drop about 4–6 mm longer if desired.

blocks.body: Work over a stable, uncluttered tabletop with good light. Wear eye protection while cutting wire and direct the cut end into the bead mat, away from faces.

blocks.question: Which method is used to open a jump ring while preserving its shape?
options: Pull the two ends directly apart
Twist the ends sideways past one another
Pry at the clasp gate with a screwdriver
Cut through the ring and squeeze it shut
blocks.explanation: Use pliers on opposite sides and twist sideways; replace a ring that no longer closes neatly.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build three neat bead dangles. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Connect the chain and clasp
lessons.summary: Connect the chain and clasp

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Open jump rings by twisting their ends sideways, like sliding one end past the other, rather than pulling the ends apart. Pulling the ends outward makes the ring oval and harder to close. Use two pairs of pliers when available: one holds each side of the ring. Keep the opening small, make the connection, and reverse the sideways twist until the ends meet. Do not lever against the clasp body or use its moving gate as a handle. Some clasp eyes are fixed and some swivel. In either case, attach only through a closed connecting eye designed for that purpose. If the clasp eye is too small for the chosen ring, select a compatible finding; do not force parts together.

The sample assembly uses a ring to connect one end of the chain to the clasp eye, then one ring for each bead dangle to a separate chain link. If the chain links are too small to accept a ring without force, use a different chain or a compatible connector. Space the dangles across three neighboring links so they can move without all stacking on one point. A jump ring can be reused only if it remains round enough and its ends meet cleanly; repeated opening weakens or distorts it. A ring with a gap, kink or sharp edge should b

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Use two pliers to twist one jump ring sideways just enough to pass through the clasp eye and the first chain link; close the ring by reversing the twist until its ends meet.
Attach each dangle loop to a separate nearby chain link using one jump ring per dangle; close every ring fully before moving to the next.
Rotate each connection gently with pliers and check the clasp gate and swivel action without pulling on the beads.

blocks.body: Work over a stable, uncluttered tabletop with good light. Wear eye protection while cutting wire and direct the cut end into the bead mat, away from faces.

blocks.question: What is the safe response to a sharp projecting wire end on a dangle?
options: Attach it and cover the point with tape
Wear it only on a soft bag
Bend it with fingers while wearing the charm
Set it aside and remake the dangle with a fresh pin
blocks.explanation: A sharp or open loop is a stop condition. Replace the pin rather than hiding the defect.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Connect the chain and clasp. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fit, inspect and refine
lessons.summary: Fit, inspect and refine

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The final lesson is a careful fit check, not a strength certification. Choose a sturdy bag ring or handle loop that is intended to accept a small clip. Keep the bag on a table while attaching the clasp. Close the gate fully, then move the bag a short distance by its normal handle and observe whether the charm catches, scrapes, or pulls the attachment point. Do not swing the bag as a stress test. If you see stitching stretch or a thin handle bend, remove the charm immediately. A charm that is attractive on the table may be awkward on a particular bag, so placement is part of the design. The dangles should hang clear of zippers, wheels, hinges, and places where fingers can be pinched. If they knock against a hard surface during ordinary handling, shorten the chain or choose smaller beads.

Inspect the findings in good light. Look for gaps at ring seams, a clasp gate that does not return, a rough cut wire end, cracked beads, and chain links that have opened. Replace a defective part rather than adding glue or wire wraps that were not designed into the assembly. Check again after the first ordinary use and periodically afterward. Store the charm detached, dry, and away from small child

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: With the bag stationary on a table, clip the charm onto a sturdy closed ring or purpose-made handle loop and confirm the clasp gate closes fully.
Lift the bag only by its normal handle for a short ordinary movement; observe whether the charm snags on zippers, fabric or nearby objects.
Inspect every ring seam, dangle loop, clasp gate, bead and chain link in bright light; record the final length and any planned change.

blocks.body: Work over a stable, uncluttered tabletop with good light. Wear eye protection while cutting wire and direct the cut end into the bead mat, away from faces.

blocks.question: The charm visibly pulls the bag's thin fabric loop. What is the best next action?
options: Remove it and find a sturdier compatible attachment point or shorten the design
Add more beads so the charm hangs straight
Clip it to the zipper slider instead
Swing the bag to see if it holds
blocks.explanation: This is decorative only. Remove it when the attachment visibly deforms or the charm snags.
