name: Paper-Bead Necklace
tagline: Turn lightweight scrap paper into a coordinated strand of tapered beads, then string and finish a lightweight decorative necklace.
outcome: Plan and cut at least 18 matching triangular strips with a 12 mm wide base and 180 mm length, keeping the point centered.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Paper-Bead Necklace

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Turn lightweight scrap paper into a coordinated strand of tapered beads, then string and finish a lightweight decorative necklace. You will plan a repeatable bead size, roll and seal each bead with or

lessons.title: Plan the palette and prepare the strips
lessons.summary: Plan the palette and prepare the strips

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: A paper bead is a rolled strip whose widest end becomes one end of the bead and whose narrowing tip produces a tapered profile. This course uses a repeatable triangle rather than an improvised wedge: each strip is 180 mm long, 12 mm wide at its base, and narrows evenly to a centered point. That length is a starting design choice, not a universal rule. The base width largely controls the finished bead’s length along the mandrel, while the strip length and paper thickness affect how many layers build around the core. Thin paper usually rolls more readily than heavy card. Choose a palette before cutting. A page with a dominant color near its outer edge can create a strong accent as it wraps; test a scrap because the visible pattern changes as layers overlap. Plan for 18 beads: 14 main-color beads and four accent beads. Make two extra strips if the page allows, since the first rolls are useful practice. Avoid paper with metallic foil, sticky residue, or a plastic coating; these materials may resist glue and curl unpredictably. Arrange the triangles point-to-point in your mind before assembly. The sample necklace will use a symmetrical center: nine beads on each side of the midpoint, wi

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Choose one lightweight, uncoated paper and a coordinated palette; plan 14 main-color beads, four accents, and reserve up to two practice strips.
Mark and cut triangles about 180 mm long with a 12 mm base and a centered narrow point; keep the point intact.
Dry-arrange nine positions on each side of the center, with two accent beads nearer the center on each side; reserve a strip for a trial roll.

blocks.body: Work at a stable, well-lit tabletop. Use scissors pointed away from the body and ask an adult to assist if cutting control is uncertain.

blocks.question: For the course’s sample bead, what strip shape and measurements should you begin with?
options: A 180 mm long triangle with a 12 mm base and centered point
A 12 mm square
A 180 mm rectangle with no point
A triangle cut from thick laminated card
blocks.explanation: A centered-point triangle about 180 mm long with a 12 mm base forms the specified taper when rolled from its wide end.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the palette and prepare the strips. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Roll tapered beads with open centers
lessons.summary: Roll tapered beads with open centers

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: Use a smooth, blunt 2–3 mm mandrel as a temporary core. The cord must pass through the resulting channel, so check one trial bead against the actual cord before making the whole batch. Place the paper’s chosen outside face against the mandrel-facing direction that will leave it visible on the exterior; with printed paper, make a second practice roll if the pattern seems to reverse or disappear. Start at the wide base and roll toward the point. Keep your fingers close to the winding edge and turn the mandrel rather than pulling the paper sideways. This helps keep the layers centered. For the first turn, wrap the broad base around the mandrel once without glue. A dry first turn gives your fingers a clean grip and prevents sticky glue from grabbing the core. Next apply a very thin line of water-based glue to the remaining strip, leaving the pointed tip for final tacking. Roll steadily with even tension. The bead should feel snug, not crushed; pressure that dents the paper may close the hole or create a lopsided cylinder. When only the final tip remains, use a tiny dab of glue and smooth it down. Too much adhesive can make a hard ridge and can glue the bead to the mandrel. Slide the be

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Square the wide base across the blunt 2–3 mm mandrel and make one snug dry turn, keeping the mandrel visible at both ends.
Apply a very thin line of water-based glue to the remaining strip, leaving the point for a tiny final dab; roll toward the point with even pressure.
Tack the tip with a tiny dab, gently twist and ease the bead off while supporting it, then test the actual cord through without force.

blocks.body: Work at a stable, well-lit tabletop. Use scissors pointed away from the body and ask an adult to assist if cutting control is uncertain.

blocks.question: What should you do if the cord cannot pass through a freshly rolled bead?
options: Push a sharp knife through the center
Gently reopen the channel with the same blunt mandrel while glue is workable
Pull the cord hard until it breaks through
Fill the hole with more glue
blocks.explanation: Use the smooth blunt mandrel while the adhesive is still workable.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Roll tapered beads with open centers. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Make a consistent batch and let it dry
lessons.summary: Make a consistent batch and let it dry

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: Once the practice bead has the right size and its center accepts the cord, repeat the same hand position and rolling direction for the remaining pieces. Consistency does not mean machine-perfect shapes. It means each bead has a visible taper, a serviceable central hole, and no loose flap. If a bead is noticeably longer than the sample, check whether its base was wider; if it is rounder or bulkier, the strip may have been longer or the paper heavier. Record that observation and adjust the next strip rather than squeezing a completed bead into shape. Keep glue in a small dish only if the product label allows decanting, and use a small amount. Apply the exterior coat as a thin film with the soft brush, rotating the bead by its mandrel or by gently touching its dry ends. A thick coat can bridge the threading hole, remain tacky, or wrinkle paper. Do not coat the hole shut. This class uses plain water-based craft glue for tack and a modest surface film; no nail polish, solvent varnish, resin, or waterproofing claim is part of the project. Treat the result as a dry decorative accessory. Dry beads separated on the mat so their wet surfaces do not touch. Follow the glue label and allow addi

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Repeat the proven roll for the batch, checking taper, seam and open channel; set aside damaged beads and preserve a balanced count.
Brush a thin exterior film of water-based glue without flooding either opening; place beads separately on the mat.
Dry undisturbed at room temperature according to the glue label; allow the estimated 45–90 minutes or longer as needed and check for tackiness.

blocks.body: Work at a stable, well-lit tabletop. Use scissors pointed away from the body and ask an adult to assist if cutting control is uncertain.

blocks.question: Why is the first wrap made dry before applying glue?
options: It waterproofs the inner paper
It makes the bead food-safe
It anchors the strip while keeping fingers clean for controlled rolling
It eliminates the need for drying
blocks.explanation: The dry first turn anchors the strip and keeps fingers clean while establishing a straight channel; glue is still needed afterward.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Make a consistent batch and let it dry. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Arrange, string, tie, and inspect
lessons.summary: Arrange, string, tie, and inspect

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: The sample target is approximately 42 cm measured around the strand, excluding any optional extender. Actual bead widths vary, so make the layout on the tabletop before tying. Put a cord length of about 60 cm through a blunt threading aid if needed; avoid needles with sharp points. Center the cord and arrange the beads symmetrically: place the four accent beads as two mirrored pairs near the center, then distribute the main-color beads outward. Keep small gaps rather than forcing a tight pack. A little cord visible between beads lets the strand curve and reduces abrasion at the paper tips. Measure the arranged strand against a ruler or tape. If it is short, add a few beads or slightly increase the gaps; if too long, remove beads evenly from both ends. Do not pull hard to compress paper. Thread one bead at a time, supporting its sides and guiding cord through the opening without scraping the seam. If a bead catches, stop and check alignment; pushing forcefully can split a damp or thin bead. Tie the cord ends in a secure double overhand knot sized to remain outside the nearest bead. Leave enough tail to adjust and test the knot before trimming. A caregiver should help with knots or c

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Center about 60 cm of cord and lay out dry beads symmetrically, with mirrored accent pairs near the center; adjust small gaps or bead count toward 42 cm before tying.
Thread one dry bead at a time without scraping; tie the ends in a double overhand knot outside the last bead, adjust, inspect the knot, then trim tails.
Inspect dryness, open channels, smooth tips, secure seams and knot, balance, and a freely curving strand near 42 cm; keep dry and remove for sports or sleep.

blocks.body: Work at a stable, well-lit tabletop. Use scissors pointed away from the body and ask an adult to assist if cutting control is uncertain.

blocks.question: Which finishing approach matches this course’s safety and care limits?
options: Coat the beads with nail polish for waterproofing
Use resin to make them skin-safe
Spray varnish indoors
Use a thin film of water-based craft glue and keep the necklace dry
blocks.explanation: A thin film of water-based craft glue is the specified finish, but it does not make the necklace waterproof or establish skin safety.

name: Felt Flower Brooch
tagline: Make a compact, layered felt flower brooch with an original five-petal silhouette, a stitched center, and a securely sewn pin backing.
outcome: Draft a balanced five-petal flower from specified felt dimensions and identify the front and backing layers before cutting.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Felt Flower Brooch

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a compact, layered felt flower brooch with an original five-petal silhouette, a stitched center, and a securely sewn pin backing. The course teaches planning, cutting, hand stitching, attachment,

lessons.title: Plan the flower and prepare the work area
lessons.summary: Plan the flower and prepare the work area

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The sample brooch is about 6.5 cm across, small enough to sit on a lapel without needing a long stem or wire. Its five rounded petals are made as two identical layers, each cut from a 12 cm square. A separate 2.8 cm felt circle forms the center, and a 3.2 cm disc hides the rear stitching. The pin-back is approximately 25 mm long. These are design dimensions for this course, not a commercial pattern; you can change the colours while keeping the dimensions consistent. A layered design is forgiving because the rear petal layer can hide small gaps in the front one, while an opaque back disc conceals thread ends and attachment stitches.

Before cutting, consider where the brooch will be used. Felt is soft and the brooch is decorative; it is not a structural clasp for heavy objects and it does not protect clothing from sharpness or snagging. Choose medium-weight felt that does not stretch readily when gently pulled. Very thin felt may curl or show every thread, while thick felt can be hard to pierce repeatedly. Work on a clear, well-lit table with a small container for scraps. Keep the needle parked safely whenever you set it down. Make a paper petal first and arrange five copies in a ci

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Draw a 2.4 cm wide by 3.2 cm long rounded petal on paper, with the narrow base at one end; cut it out and trace five copies around an imaginary 6 cm circle.
Clear a table, set out felt, thread, pin-back, scissors, ruler, needle, and a pin cushion or needle minder; park the closed brooch pin in a dish until needed.
Cut one 12 x 12 cm square of petal felt and two scraps large enough for circles measuring 2.8 cm and 3.2 cm; mark the circle sizes on paper templates first.
Thread the needle with about 80 cm of thread and tie a secure knot; sew a short running stitch through a felt offcut, with stitches about 3–4 mm long.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the scissor blades' path. Use scissors suited to felt and ask for help if cutting feels difficult.

blocks.question: Why do the two sets of five petals use the same template?
options: To make both layers align predictably when offset
To make the center circle unnecessary
To ensure the pin-back cannot rotate
To create a flower that can support heavy objects
blocks.explanation: Identical petal templates create a consistent silhouette; offset placement supplies the layered appearance.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the flower and prepare the work area. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut and layer the petals
lessons.summary: Cut and layer the petals

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The flower uses ten petal shapes: five in a rear layer and five in a front layer. Each layer is cut from the same 12 cm square using the same template, so the finished outline remains reasonably symmetrical. Felt has no woven grain to align, but its surface can still look different when brushed in opposite directions. If the felt has a nap, keep all templates oriented the same way. Trace lightly; deep pencil grooves are unnecessary and may remain visible. Cut with long, controlled scissor movements rather than many tiny bites. A slightly imperfect edge is acceptable because the second layer adds visual depth, but dangling fibres should be trimmed rather than pulled.

To assemble the shape, arrange five rear petals radially, with their narrow bases meeting in the middle. The petal tips should form a loose star. Add the other five over them, rotating the second layer so each upper petal sits between two lower petals. This alternating placement is called offset layering; it exposes both colours or surfaces and distributes the silhouette evenly. Before stitching, look down at the flower from directly above. If one side looks heavier, move individual petals rather than forcing the shape

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trace and cut five petals for the rear layer and five for the front layer using the paper pattern; keep the template orientation consistent if the felt has a nap.
Arrange five petals in a radial ring, bases touching at the center and tips facing outward; place the second five between the first five.
Using a few small stitches near the center, tack through the overlapped petal bases; keep the stitches within the circle area that the center will cover.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the scissor blades' path. Use scissors suited to felt and ask for help if cutting feels difficult.

blocks.question: What is the safest response if the pin-back will not close after attachment?
options: Bend it forcefully until it catches
Stop wearing it and replace damaged or unsuitable hardware
Cover the catch with extra felt
Use it as a safety pin substitute
blocks.explanation: A clasp must operate normally and remain closed; do not force or disguise faulty hardware.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut and layer the petals. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Stitch the center and attach the backing
lessons.summary: Stitch the center and attach the backing

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The center is a separate 2.8 cm circle stitched onto the flower. Place it over the petal junction and check that a narrow rim of petals remains visible all around. A simple running stitch around the circle creates a clean border and catches the petal layers beneath. Pass the needle through the center circle and the overlapped bases, not through a petal tip. Keep the stitches about 3–4 mm apart and pull only until the thread lies flat. This is an accessible beginner method; decorative French knots or beads are optional embellishments and are not needed for a secure result. Avoid adding beads if they might loosen or if small parts are unsuitable for the wearer.

The backing disc is larger than the center and sits at the rear of the flower. First secure the pin-back to the 3.2 cm disc while it is separate from the flower. Position the clasp horizontally, near the upper half of the disc, with its hinged end and catch unobstructed. Sew through its sewable loops or holes using repeated passes and small locking stitches. Do not pierce a solid metal section or force the needle through hardware. Test the attachment while the clasp is closed: it should not rotate freely or lift off the felt.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Center the 2.8 cm circle over the flower junction and stitch around its edge with 3–4 mm running stitches through the circle and petal bases.
Place the closed 25 mm pin-back on the 3.2 cm backing disc, horizontally and slightly above its center; sew through only its designed loops or holes with repeated passes.
Position the disc on the rear of the flower with the clasp oriented for access; sew around the disc edge, catching the petal bases and keeping the needle away from the visible fron
Tie off between the backing and flower, pass the tail under several stitches, then trim it; close the pin and inspect the edge before setting the needle aside.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the scissor blades' path. Use scissors suited to felt and ask for help if cutting feels difficult.

blocks.question: Where should the temporary petal tacking stitches sit?
options: Across the outer petal tips
Outside the flower perimeter
Near the center, under the planned center circle
Directly through the pin catch
blocks.explanation: Keep temporary stitches inside the center area that will be covered by the felt circle.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Stitch the center and attach the backing. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Inspect, refine, and decide how to wear it
lessons.summary: Inspect, refine, and decide how to wear it

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A finished-looking flower is not automatically ready to wear. Inspect the face, edge, backing, and pin separately under good light. The front should have a centered circle and a readable five-lobed outline. The perimeter should not contain long threads or cut notches that could continue tearing. On the back, the disc should sit flat, the pin should open and close without snagging felt, and attachment stitches should remain intact when the flower is handled gently. Do not perform a hard pull test or treat this small accessory as load-bearing; use a light fingertip check only. If a stitch loosens, repair it before wearing. If the hardware itself is damaged, replace it rather than bending metal with force.

Try the brooch on a doubled scrap of medium-weight woven cloth, not on skin. Open the clasp carefully, pass the point through the cloth, close the catch, and check that the flower does not droop excessively. The clasp is small and sharp, so keep it closed whenever it is not being attached. Avoid delicate knits where a pin can snag loops, thin fabrics that may tear, or locations where the point could press against the body. Remove the brooch before laundering or sleeping. The back d

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect the front, five petal tips, center seam, rear disc, thread ends, and clasp under bright light; gently touch the seams without pulling hard.
Test the closed brooch on doubled scrap woven fabric; check that it fastens without catching a knit or pressing against the body, then remove it from the test cloth.
Choose one modest refinement for a future version and write down what you observed, the change, and how you would compare the next result.

blocks.body: Cut away from fingers and keep the other hand outside the scissor blades' path. Use scissors suited to felt and ask for help if cutting feels difficult.

blocks.question: The back disc seam has appeared on the flower's front. What is the best fix?
options: Pull the thread tighter until it disappears
Add a bead over the hole
Cut the visible stitch and leave the seam open
Remove that stitch and take a shallower bite through the back and petal bases
blocks.explanation: A shallow rear stitch can catch the layers without passing through the exposed center.

name: Fabric Bow Hair Clip
tagline: Make a soft, hand-sewn bow from a woven fabric rectangle and attach it securely to a small metal hair clip using a stitched fabric bridge.
outcome: Measure and cut two woven-fabric pieces to the specified dimensions, keeping grain and edges aligned.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Fabric Bow Hair Clip

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a soft, hand-sewn bow from a woven fabric rectangle and attach it securely to a small metal hair clip using a stitched fabric bridge. This design avoids hot glue and lets you remove the clip for

lessons.title: Plan the bow and prepare the fabric
lessons.summary: Plan the bow and prepare the fabric

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
This project makes a compact bow about 9–10 cm wide, depending on how full you arrange the loops. The main rectangle is 18 cm wide by 12 cm high. Its width creates the visible bow surface; its height folds into a padded loop rather than a flat ribbon. A separate 7 cm by 4 cm piece becomes a narrow center band and a small fabric bridge. These are starting dimensions for this design, not a universal pattern. A slippery satin or stretchy knit can shift under hand stitching, so begin with a medium-weight woven cotton. A small-scale print or solid is easier to align than a large motif. Keep the reverse side in mind because some of it may show at the loop edges.

Before cutting, smooth the fabric on a table without stretching it. Mark the rectangles with a ruler and removable chalk. Check each pair of opposite edges: if they are not square, the eventual tube can twist and the loops may look uneven. Cut along the marked lines with fabric scissors. On a paper scrap, sketch a 9 cm-wide bow and mark its center. This rough plan helps you judge whether the clip is proportionate; the clip should not be wider than the bow. You can vary the color, but keep the quantities and construction consiste

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure and mark one 18 × 12 cm main rectangle and one 7 × 4 cm center rectangle; cut both on a stable tabletop.
Fold the main rectangle in half lengthwise with its visible sides facing inward; match the long raw edges and secure with two clips or pins.
Thread the needle with about 50 cm of thread, knot the end, and sew a small running stitch along the aligned long edge, about 6 mm from the edge.

blocks.body: Keep the needle in a pincushion or dish when not stitching; do not leave it loose in fabric or on a chair. Count it before and after the project.

blocks.question: Why does the main rectangle fold with its visible sides facing inward before the long seam is sewn?
options: It conceals the seam allowance inside the turned tube.
It makes the fabric waterproof.
It prevents the clip spring from moving.
It removes the need to turn the tube.
blocks.explanation: The visible sides face each other so the long raw seam is enclosed when the sewn tube is turned right side out.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the bow and prepare the fabric. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Turn the tube and form balanced loops
lessons.summary: Turn the tube and form balanced loops

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The sewn rectangle becomes the soft body of the bow. After stitching, turn it right side out carefully. Do not pull abruptly on one corner: the seam is only a row of hand stitches, and a hard tug can open it. Use a blunt pencil end or a chopstick with no splinters to ease the end outward; never push with a sharp point. Flatten the tube so its seam sits along one edge rather than directly across the front. Finger-pressing is usually enough. If you use an iron, choose a low setting for the fabric and keep fingers away from the hot soleplate.

To make the bow, bring the two short ends toward the middle with a slight overlap of about 1 cm. The overlap will be hidden under the center band. This creates two loops. Arrange each loop so its folded edge faces outward and both sides have approximately the same height. Pinch the center into three small accordion folds, alternating front and back. Each fold should be about 5–7 mm deep. The goal is not perfect mathematical symmetry; it is a stable, centered shape with similar loop size. Use a temporary thread wrap to hold the pinch before taking permanent stitches. If one side looks larger, loosen the temporary wrap and redistribute the fabric

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Turn the sewn tube right side out by easing one end through the opening; use a blunt tool only if needed.
Flatten the tube with the seam along one edge, then bring the short ends toward the center so they overlap by about 1 cm.
Pinch the center into three alternating accordion folds, each about 5–7 mm deep, then temporarily wrap thread around the pinch and knot it.

blocks.body: Keep the needle in a pincushion or dish when not stitching; do not leave it loose in fabric or on a chair. Count it before and after the project.

blocks.question: After pinching the bow center, one loop looks fuller. What is the best time to correct it?
options: Pull hard on the small loop after the clip is attached.
Undo the temporary wrap and redistribute folds before sewing the band.
Cover the larger loop with extra glue.
Cut the larger loop shorter while it is gathered.
blocks.explanation: Balance the loops while the center is held only by temporary thread, before permanent stitching and band attachment.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Turn the tube and form balanced loops. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Make the center band and stitched clip bridge
lessons.summary: Make the center band and stitched clip bridge

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The center piece has two jobs: it visually tidies the gathered bow and helps retain the metal clip. First make a narrow band. Fold the 7 × 4 cm rectangle lengthwise, visible sides together, and stitch the long edge about 5 mm from the raw edge. Turn it right side out. Flatten it with its seam on one edge. Wrap it around the bow center without stretching it tight. A band that is too tight can squash the loops; one that is too loose will rotate. Leave a small overlap at the back and trim only after confirming the fit. Fold the raw end under about 5 mm and hand-stitch the overlap closed.

For an attachment that can be removed, do not glue the bow to the clip. The band holds the bow center, while a short fabric bridge is stitched across the back of the band around the clip's fixed central spine. Slide the clip through this bridge so the spring and opening jaws remain unobstructed. The bridge must be snug enough that the clip does not slide sideways, but loose enough to remove without force. Do not sew through the metal, moving hinge, or spring. The clip should open and close freely after insertion. Make small stitches through fabric only, knotting thread on the concealed underside. If

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Fold the 7 × 4 cm piece lengthwise with visible sides inward and sew the long edge about 5 mm from the raw edge.
Turn the strip, flatten it with the seam at one edge, wrap it around the gathered bow center, and mark the back overlap.
Trim the band to leave about 8 mm overlap, fold the raw end under 5 mm, and whip-stitch the overlap on the back of the bow.
Cut a 2 cm length from the remaining band fabric, fold its long edges inward, and stitch it as a narrow bridge across the back center band, leaving a tunnel sized for the clip spin

blocks.body: Keep the needle in a pincushion or dish when not stitching; do not leave it loose in fabric or on a chair. Count it before and after the project.

blocks.question: Where should the removable fabric bridge hold the clip?
options: Across the hinge and spring so the clip cannot open.
Around the fixed central spine, leaving hinge, spring, and jaws clear.
Through a hole cut in the metal.
Over the outer tip of one jaw only.
blocks.explanation: The bridge is stitched to fabric and passes over the clip's fixed spine; moving parts remain exposed and free.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Make the center band and stitched clip bridge. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Attach, inspect, and refine the accessory
lessons.summary: Attach, inspect, and refine the accessory

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Slide the closed clip's fixed spine through the fabric bridge from the side that leaves the opening lever accessible. Look at the underside before wearing: the bridge should sit over the central spine, not over the hinge or spring. Open and close the clip several times while holding it away from your face. If the mechanism catches fabric, remove the clip and widen or reposition the bridge. The accessory is not ready while any moving part is covered or restricted.

Once the clip moves freely, shape the loops with fingertips. Pull the fabric gently from the outer edges to make the loops round, but do not tug on the band or individual stitches. Compare the two loops from above and from the side. Small differences are normal in a hand-made object; the practical standard is that the center stays centered and neither loop collapses when the bow is set down. Inspect every seam for skipped stitches, loose tails, or fraying. Secure any loose thread with two small backstitches and bury the tail under the band. Then perform a gentle retention test: hold the clip over a table, support the bow with one hand, and apply a light, steady tug to the fabric for several seconds. Stop if the bridge str

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Slide the clip's fixed central spine through the fabric bridge, keeping the hinge, spring, and jaws uncovered.
Fluff each loop with fingertips and compare the bow from the front and side; adjust the center folds if needed.
Inspect seam edges, knots, thread tails, clip edges, and spring; then do a gentle tabletop retention test by tugging the bow lightly while supporting the clip.

blocks.body: Keep the needle in a pincushion or dish when not stitching; do not leave it loose in fabric or on a chair. Count it before and after the project.

blocks.question: The center band makes the loops look flat. What is the safest correction?
options: Tighten the band further so the fabric cannot move.
Add a sharp pin under the band and wear it that way.
Unpick the overlap, refit the band snugly without compression, and stitch it again.
Pull the loops hard until the band stretches.
blocks.explanation: The band should cover the gathers without crushing them. Adjust its length at the stitched overlap.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Attach, inspect, and refine the accessory. What did you learn and verify?

name: Ribbon-Wrapped Headband
tagline: Make a comfortable, neatly wrapped headband from a plain plastic band, two complementary ribbons, and a small bead accent.
outcome: Measure a plain headband and estimate ribbon length with a practical allowance for overlap and finishing.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Ribbon-Wrapped Headband

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a comfortable, neatly wrapped headband from a plain plastic band, two complementary ribbons, and a small bead accent. You will plan ribbon coverage, wrap with even overlap, finish the ends cleanl

lessons.title: Plan the fit, colors, and ribbon path
lessons.summary: Plan the fit, colors, and ribbon path

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Start with the base rather than cutting ribbon immediately. Inspect the headband from end to end. Flex it only slightly in the way it is normally worn; if it whitens, creaks, splits, or has a rough molded seam, replace it. The sample design uses a 12 mm wide band whose outer curve measures about 14 cm. Your band may differ, so measure its outer path from one tip, over the crown, to the other tip.

Choose woven ribbon that bends around the curve without fraying excessively. A width close to the band width gives full coverage with a manageable edge. Satin can be slippery; grosgrain or cotton ribbon is easier to control for a first project. The 1.5 m allowance covers a roughly 14 cm band plus overlapping wraps and end tabs. It is an estimate, not a universal formula. Ribbons wrapped diagonally consume much more length than a straight length along the band.

Make a quick layout plan. Decide whether the main ribbon covers the entire base and whether the narrower accent appears as a short 3 cm section near the crown or as a center band over the bead. Keep the bead low-profile and centered; a heavy or sharp ornament can snag hair or press uncomfortably. Before committing, wrap a 10 cm tri

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure the band's outer curve and width; note both values and inspect the plastic for cracks or sharp seams.
Select a 10–12 mm woven main ribbon and cut a 10 cm test strip; wrap a short section at roughly a 45-degree angle.
Sketch a simple color map and mark the crown location; reserve the small bead for a flat, accessible spot.

blocks.body: Work seated at a clear table. Keep scissors pointed away from your body and close them when setting them down.

blocks.question: Why measure the actual headband before cutting the main ribbon?
options: The band length and curve affect the needed ribbon allowance.
All headbands use exactly the same ribbon length.
Measurement determines whether the bead is washable.
It makes ribbon stretch to fit.
blocks.explanation: Measure the outer curve and width, then use the sample length as a starting allowance rather than a guarantee.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the fit, colors, and ribbon path. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Prepare and anchor the ribbon
lessons.summary: Prepare and anchor the ribbon

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Before starting, bring the ribbon and band to a clean, dry table. Cut the main ribbon to about 1.5 m for the sample size. Do not assume you must use every centimetre; an exact allowance depends on band shape and how steeply you wrap. Keep the remaining ribbon until both ends are finished. For clean ends, cut a short 2 cm length from your ribbon and fold it over the tip as a cap. This hides the cut edge and softens the area that touches hair. The cap should cover only the end; it must not form a hard lump.

The first anchor determines whether the wrap creeps. Place the ribbon tail on the inner side of one tip, with about 2 cm extending beyond the end. Fold that tail over the tip and secure it with a tiny hand stitch or a small dab of compatible craft adhesive. Keep stitches shallow and away from the outside surface. With adhesive, use only the amount needed to wet the ribbon fibers, press the ribbon flat, and respect its label and drying instructions. Adhesives do not all bond identically to slick plastic, so a hidden test is useful.

Use clips to hold the first turn while you check the placement. Pull enough to remove slack, but do not stretch the ribbon or bend the plastic. Work d

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut about 1.5 m of main ribbon and two 2 cm end-cap pieces; test any chosen adhesive on a hidden area and scrap.
Fold one end-cap piece over the first headband tip, keeping its cut edge tucked inward; tack it with a stitch or tiny adhesive dab.
Anchor the main ribbon tail on the inner face with about 2 cm folded over the tip, then add the first wrap across the tail.

blocks.body: Work seated at a clear table. Keep scissors pointed away from your body and close them when setting them down.

blocks.question: A test wrap leaves narrow strips of plastic visible at both edges. What is the best correction?
options: Pull harder so the ribbon narrows.
Increase overlap or select slightly wider ribbon.
Cover the whole band in a thick glue layer.
Ignore the gaps because they strengthen the band.
blocks.explanation: Coverage is corrected by ribbon width or wrap spacing, not excessive tension or glue.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Prepare and anchor the ribbon. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Wrap evenly and add the accent
lessons.summary: Wrap evenly and add the accent

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Wrap from the first tip toward the crown, maintaining a consistent diagonal. At each turn, overlap the previous edge by about one-third of the ribbon width. That coverage helps conceal the base without creating the heavy stacked ridge produced by half-width overlaps. Keep the ribbon edges aligned and smooth the fabric with a fingertip before making the next turn. The inside curve is tighter than the outside curve, so small gathers can form along the inner edge. Ease them flat as you go instead of pulling them to one side.

Work in short stretches of two or three turns. After each stretch, look at both edges and gently flex the band in its ordinary direction. The ribbon should follow the curve without loosening. Do not twist the plastic or try to stretch the ribbon around the curve. If the spiral begins to drift, unwind to the last straight, even section and correct it now. A clip can temporarily hold a section while your hands reposition.

At the crown, add the narrow accent only if the base coverage is smooth. A 3 cm accent panel can be made by laying the narrow ribbon across the top and tucking its ends underneath a main-ribbon turn. Alternatively, keep a single main color and sa

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Continue diagonally along the band, overlapping each turn by about one-third of ribbon width and smoothing before the next turn.
Pause at the crown and optionally tuck a 3 cm accent-ribbon panel beneath a main-ribbon turn, keeping both cut ends underneath.
Continue toward the second tip, gently flexing the band to its usual shape after each short section.

blocks.body: Work seated at a clear table. Keep scissors pointed away from your body and close them when setting them down.

blocks.question: Which pattern best matches a controlled beginner wrap?
options: Leave a gap after every turn.
Pile turns over one another until the band is bulky.
Overlap each turn by about one-third of the ribbon width and check in short stretches.
Stretch the ribbon tightly around the plastic.
blocks.explanation: The planned overlap balances concealment and low bulk; short checks make corrections manageable.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Wrap evenly and add the accent. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Finish the tip, attach the bead, and inspect
lessons.summary: Finish the tip, attach the bead, and inspect

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
When you reach the second end, stop with enough ribbon to fold roughly 2 cm over the tip. Check the outer surface one last time: the final spiral should meet the end cap without leaving a gap. Fold the ribbon tail onto the inner side and secure it with a few small stitches or a tiny amount of suitable adhesive. Then add the second end cap over the tip. Keep the cap's fold smooth and low profile. If you use adhesive, let it set for the full time on its label before testing. Do not use the accessory while any area is tacky or has a strong persistent odor.

Attach the bead only after the ribbon is secure. Place it at the crown and check its contact from several angles. With a sew-on bead, pass the needle through the ribbon layers and the bead holes, making several snug passes; tie off on the inner face and bury the thread tail between layers. Do not pull so tightly that the band puckers. If your bead has no holes, use only an adhesive explicitly suitable for both surfaces, and let it cure. A flat fabric tab is a good no-bead alternative.

Finally, inspect for smoothness and comfort. Run fingers along the inner edge, not over a hot glue nozzle or fresh adhesive. Look for exposed thread

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Fold the final ribbon tail over the second tip, secure it on the inner face, and cover the tip with the second 2 cm cap.
Center the flat bead at the crown and attach it with several snug stitches through the ribbon layers, or omit it if attachment would be unstable.
Inspect both edges and ends, test the accessory briefly for comfort, and record any repair needed before regular wear.

blocks.body: Work seated at a clear table. Keep scissors pointed away from your body and close them when setting them down.

blocks.question: Hot adhesive accidentally contacts your skin while finishing the headband. What should you do first?
options: Pull the molten glue off immediately.
Rub it with a cloth while it is hot.
Continue crafting and inspect later.
Cool the affected skin under cold water; do not pull off the molten glue, and seek medical advice as needed.
blocks.explanation: Hot-melt adhesive is a burn hazard. Follow the safety guidance and seek medical care for serious or concerning injuries.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Finish the tip, attach the bead, and inspect. What did you learn and verify?

name: Air-Dry-Clay Pendant
tagline: Make one original, rounded-rectangle air-dry-clay pendant with a deliberately pressed line motif, a reinforced hanging hole, painted details, and a light brush-on finish if desired.
outcome: Plan a pendant approximately 38 mm wide by 48 mm tall and 6–7 mm thick, with an opening positioned safely inside its top edge.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Air-Dry-Clay Pendant

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make one original, rounded-rectangle air-dry-clay pendant with a deliberately pressed line motif, a reinforced hanging hole, painted details, and a light brush-on finish if desired. This is a decorati

lessons.title: Plan the silhouette and set up a clean work area
lessons.summary: Plan the silhouette and set up a clean work area

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A pendant succeeds when the shape is simple enough to cut cleanly and thick enough to handle. This project uses a rounded rectangle about 38 mm wide and 48 mm tall. The sample is 6–7 mm thick, which gives the hole area more material than a thin sheet would. These are design targets, not a guarantee of durability: air-dry clay can chip or break if dropped, bent, or snagged. Sketch first and decide where the cord opening belongs. Center it across the width and place its center about 7 mm below the top edge. With a 5 mm opening, that leaves roughly 4.5 mm of clay above the hole. Keep the side edges similarly generous.

Set up a dry, uncluttered surface. Keep food, drinks, pets, and small children away. Clay dries while exposed, so divide the work into manageable stages and cover unused clay according to its package. Roll between two same-height guides; they help make the slab even, which lowers the chance that one thin corner dries or breaks differently from the rest. Pressing a texture is a design choice, not a requirement. This course uses one shallow, winding line with a blunt tool, leaving a broad smooth border so the pendant remains legible and easy to paint. A successful plan ha

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Draw a 38 x 48 mm rounded rectangle on paper and mark its centerline and a 5 mm hole centered 7 mm below the top edge.
Clear and cover a dry tabletop; place the template, guides, straw, rolling tool, and blunt cutter within reach.
Wash and dry hands, then condition the clay by gently pressing and folding a walnut-sized portion until it feels even, not sticky or crumbly.

blocks.body: Read the clay, paint, and sealer labels and follow their ventilation, cleanup, and age guidance. Avoid sanding dust; if the dry clay needs substantial sanding, stop and use a damp cloth on a tiny area or leave the texture as-is.

blocks.question: Why use two 6 mm rolling guides for this pendant?
options: They help keep the slab evenly thick.
They make clay waterproof.
They guarantee the pendant cannot break.
They replace the drying period.
blocks.explanation: Guides make it easier to avoid thin spots, but they do not change the material's limitations or drying needs.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the silhouette and set up a clean work area. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Roll, cut, texture, and open the pendant
lessons.summary: Roll, cut, texture, and open the pendant

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The slab should have an even body before its decorative details are added. Place the clay between the 6 mm guides and roll from the middle outward, turning the clay now and then so pressure does not favor one direction. Lift it by sliding the mat or a thin card underneath instead of pulling one corner. Lay the paper template over the slab and cut slowly around it. Round the corners with small, controlled cuts or a damp fingertip if the clay label permits water. Avoid repeatedly stretching the shape; stretched clay can narrow the hanging margin and distort the hole position.

Make the opening before the clay becomes firm. A straw removes a neat plug, while twisting it gently helps avoid a ragged exit. Support the slab with a finger close to, but not directly under, the hole. Check the front and back; if a raised lip appears, smooth it with a rounded tool without thinning the rim. The pressed-line motif should be shallow. A deep groove may become a weak line or collect paint, and a sharp pointed tool can tear the surface. Use the blunt end of a clean tool to press a single curved route that begins below the hole and ends before the lower edge. Leave a plain border at least 5 mm wide.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Roll the clay between the 6 mm guides until the sheet is roughly 6–7 mm thick, rotating the mat between passes.
Place the template on the slab and cut the rounded rectangle, then smooth the perimeter with a fingertip or rounded tool.
Use the straw at the marked position to make a through-hole; lift out the clay plug and smooth both openings without widening the rim excessively.
Press one shallow curved line and up to five small dots into the face, leaving at least a 5 mm border and avoiding the hole rim.

blocks.body: Read the clay, paint, and sealer labels and follow their ventilation, cleanup, and age guidance. Avoid sanding dust; if the dry clay needs substantial sanding, stop and use a damp cloth on a tiny area or leave the texture as-is.

blocks.question: Where should the cord hole be planned?
options: At the extreme top edge so it is easy to find.
Centered across the width with a generous clay margin.
Anywhere after the pendant has fully dried, using force.
Across a deep groove so the pattern lines up.
blocks.explanation: Planning an opening while the clay is fresh and retaining surrounding material helps avoid an unnecessarily weak edge.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Roll, cut, texture, and open the pendant. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Dry slowly, inspect, and add color
lessons.summary: Dry slowly, inspect, and add color

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Air-dry clay changes as moisture leaves it, and the outside can feel dry before the center is ready. Set the pendant flat on a clean, breathable surface in a room with ordinary airflow, away from direct sun, heaters, ovens, and damp areas. Follow the clay package for turning or drying. If it allows turning, wait until the piece is firm enough to lift without bending, then turn it once so the underside can dry. Avoid sealing or painting a cool, damp-feeling center. The maker's stated drying guidance takes priority over a fixed calendar estimate. Thickness, climate, and product formula change the time. The finish step is optional; a dry, undecorated pendant can still meet the project goal.

Inspect both faces and edges under ordinary light. A hairline surface mark may be a cosmetic flaw, but a crack reaching the hole, a soft center, or a warped body is a reason not to thread or wear the piece. A fine nail file may reduce a tiny rough edge only when the clay is fully dry; use light strokes, avoid breathing dust, and stop if material sheds. Painting works best in thin coats. Lay in a base color, allow it to dry, then accent the pressed line with a second color. Do not flood the groove

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the pendant flat on a clean, breathable drying surface and leave it undisturbed away from heat, direct sun, and moisture.
When firm enough to lift without bending, turn it once only if the clay maker recommends turning; continue drying until the product is dry throughout.
Inspect both sides, the hole rim, and all edges; optionally smooth only a tiny dry burr with very light strokes while avoiding dust inhalation.
Paint one thin base layer, let it dry per its label, and add small accents along the pressed line without filling the hole.
Optionally brush on a thin layer of compatible craft sealer over dry paint, following label ventilation and drying directions; leave it unsealed if uncertain.

blocks.body: Read the clay, paint, and sealer labels and follow their ventilation, cleanup, and age guidance. Avoid sanding dust; if the dry clay needs substantial sanding, stop and use a damp cloth on a tiny area or leave the texture as-is.

blocks.question: The pendant feels cool and slightly soft the day after shaping. What is the best next step?
options: Paint it thickly to hold the shape.
Put it in an oven on low heat.
Wait longer in a suitable indoor place, following package guidance.
Thread the cord and hang it to dry.
blocks.explanation: A dry-looking surface is not enough; wait until the clay is firm throughout and follow its label.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Dry slowly, inspect, and add color. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Thread, evaluate, and refine the finished object
lessons.summary: Thread, evaluate, and refine the finished object

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Assembly is deliberately simple: a length of soft cord passes through the opening and ties with a plain knot. Thread only after the clay, paint, and optional finish have dried fully. If the cord catches, do not force it against the hole rim; use a narrower cord or gently pull the end through with a paper loop. Tie the ends securely but leave a comfortable amount of space so the pendant lies at the intended position. Keep the knot away from the clay edge, and do not use a metal jump ring as a lever. Before wearing, inspect the hole and cord under good light. This is a handmade decorative accessory, not a tested load-bearing component. Avoid sports, sleeping, bathing, and situations where a necklace could snag. Remove it if the cord frays, the clay cracks, or paint irritates skin.

Refinement means learning from the object rather than forcing it to meet an unrealistic durability claim. Record whether the hole stayed round, whether the pendant warped, and whether the pressed line remained visible after paint. A photograph can help compare the original template and finished dimensions. If the pendant has a crack or loose fragment, do not wear it; keep it as a display sample or discard

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut about 60 cm of soft cord, fold or taper its end, and pass it through the dry hole without scraping the rim.
Tie the cord ends with a secure simple knot, adjust the pendant to sit centered, and trim only excess cord if needed.
Record the finished dimensions and inspect the hole, paint, and edges; store the pendant dry and separate from heavy or abrasive objects.

blocks.body: Read the clay, paint, and sealer labels and follow their ventilation, cleanup, and age guidance. Avoid sanding dust; if the dry clay needs substantial sanding, stop and use a damp cloth on a tiny area or leave the texture as-is.

blocks.question: What should you do if a crack reaches the cord hole?
options: Cover it with several coats of paint and wear it.
Add a metal ring and pull harder.
Glue it and describe it as tested.
Do not wear it; keep it for display or remake it.
blocks.explanation: A compromised opening should not be treated as safe by hiding or loading the crack.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Thread, evaluate, and refine the finished object. What did you learn and verify?

name: Handmade Bead Organizer
tagline: Make a dry-use tabletop organizer from a shallow reused box, a fitted cardboard grid, and labeled paper tabs.
outcome: Measure a shallow box and calculate divider lengths from its actual interior rather than relying on the sample dimensions alone.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Handmade Bead Organizer

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a dry-use tabletop organizer from a shallow reused box, a fitted cardboard grid, and labeled paper tabs. The 20 × 15 cm tray has six compartments arranged in two rows of three, each about 6.2 × 6

lessons.title: Plan the tray around the box you actually have
lessons.summary: Plan the tray around the box you actually have

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful organizer begins with the container, not with a guessed grid. Boxes sold as the same nominal size can have different inside dimensions because board thickness and folded corners take up space. Work in centimetres and measure the clear interior at the floor, from inside wall to inside wall. Our sample outside size is about 20 × 15 × 4 cm, but the working dimensions are the measured interior. Aim for two rows and three columns. Leave a little room for the insert so it can lift out without scraping; the example leaves roughly 2 mm clearance at the long and short edges.

This lesson establishes a sorting rule before any beads are poured. Choose six useful categories, such as color families, bead type, or project kits. A category should be specific enough that a cell is not a mystery pile but broad enough to fit the quantity. For a starter organizer, keep one category per cell. Do not mix tiny findings with larger beads if the tiny pieces disappear beneath them. Labels are a retrieval aid, so write words that will still make sense next month.

The work surface should be dry, uncluttered, and away from food. Place a shallow scrap of paper beside the box as a temporary catch shee

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Empty the box, open its lid, and measure the clear inside length and width at the floor. Record both measurements in centimetres; measure again near the top if the walls taper.
Plan two rows and three columns. Subtract about 4 mm total clearance from each interior dimension for the floor panel, then divide the usable area into thirds; sketch the layout on
Choose six sorting labels and assign one to each cell on the sketch. Keep categories distinct, for example seed beads, large beads, metal findings, and three color groups.
Place the closed box and scrap-paper catch sheet on a stable table. Keep loose beads closed away from the work area until assembly is complete.

blocks.body: Beads are small parts and can pose choking or aspiration hazards. Keep them away from children under three, pets, and anyone likely to put small objects in their mouth; supervise older children and count/contain pieces before and after work.

blocks.question: Why should you measure the inside floor of your box before cutting the insert?
options: The inside space can differ from the outside size because board thickness and folded corners take room.
The measurement tells you whether the beads are genuine.
It guarantees that the box is child-proof.
It removes the need to test the divider grid.
blocks.explanation: The panel and divider lengths must match the actual interior. Outside dimensions include the board thickness and do not describe the clear space.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the tray around the box you actually have. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut a removable floor and divider pieces
lessons.summary: Cut a removable floor and divider pieces

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The insert has two parts: a floor panel that rests inside the box and a set of upright strips that interlock to form six pockets. Cardboard thickness matters. Thin cereal-box board is easy to cut but can buckle; two layers crossed at right angles make a stiffer floor. A thicker corrugated board holds shape better, although its flutes may make narrow cuts less tidy. Use the cleanest, flattest material available. Test a short offcut before committing to the panel.

For the sample 19.6 × 14.6 cm floor, cut one long divider to the interior length and two cross-dividers to the interior width. Their exact fitted lengths should be measured inside the box, with tiny clearance so the walls do not bow. The grid is created with half-depth slots: one centered slot in each cross-divider and two matching slots in the long divider, spaced to create three columns. Interlock the strips with slots facing opposite directions. Slot width should match the actual board thickness; too narrow crushes and bends the strip, while too wide makes a wobbly joint. Start slightly narrower and widen gradually with small scissor snips.

Never cut a slot by forcing scissors through a thick stack. Make repeated short

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trace a floor panel using the measured interior dimensions minus about 4 mm in each direction; cut it from stiff board and test it inside the empty box.
Cut one long divider strip to the measured inside length and two cross-divider strips to the measured inside width. Make their height about 3 cm, below the box rim.
Mark one half-height slot at the midpoint of each cross-divider. On the long divider, mark two half-height slots at positions one-third and two-thirds of its length; cut each slot
Slide the strips together with slot openings facing opposite directions, then set the grid on the floor panel inside the box.

blocks.body: Beads are small parts and can pose choking or aspiration hazards. Keep them away from children under three, pets, and anyone likely to put small objects in their mouth; supervise older children and count/contain pieces before and after work.

blocks.question: What is the safest response if a bead spills while working?
options: Blow it away from the table so it cannot be seen.
Stop, collect it with a folded card or soft brush, and check the floor before continuing.
Sweep quickly with a bare hand while moving the box.
Leave it for later because the lid is nearby.
blocks.explanation: Pause the activity, control the spill with a dry tool, and check the surrounding floor. Small beads can present choking or aspiration hazards.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut a removable floor and divider pieces. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fit, label, and sort the cells
lessons.summary: Fit, label, and sort the cells

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A grid that looks square on the table may change shape when placed in the box. Fit matters more than perfect geometry: the insert should stay located but come out with a gentle lift. Put the floor panel down first, then lower the interlocked grid into the center. Inspect each corner and intersection. A small gap at the wall is acceptable, but an opening large enough for the smallest bead to slip beneath a divider defeats the purpose. Adjust the panel position or replace a short divider. Avoid adhesive as the first fix because glue can create rough ridges and makes cleaning harder.

Labels need to remain readable after the lid is opened. Cut six small paper tabs and write with a pencil or marker. Attach each to the outside-facing rim of its compartment using a small piece of paper tape, or tuck the tab under the top edge. Keep all sticky surfaces away from the bead area. Use a short word and, if helpful, a simple size or color description. A symbol alone may be forgotten, so pair it with a word. This paperboard is not a moisture barrier; store the organizer indoors, away from dampness.

Sort a small quantity first. Pour or transfer just a few pieces onto a scrap sheet, then pick the

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the floor panel in the box and lower the grid onto it. Check each outside edge and each crossing for gaps, rocking, or bowed walls.
Write six clear labels and attach them to the outer top edge of each cell using a small piece of tape or a tucked paper tab.
Transfer a small test quantity of each category from a catch sheet into its matching compartment, leaving room below the divider tops.
Sort the remaining planned beads in small batches, then return unused stock to its original closed container and recount any spilled pieces.

blocks.body: Beads are small parts and can pose choking or aspiration hazards. Keep them away from children under three, pets, and anyone likely to put small objects in their mouth; supervise older children and count/contain pieces before and after work.

blocks.question: How should the cross-divider slots fit the long divider?
options: They should be extremely wide so the grid can wobble freely.
They should be cut through the whole height of every strip.
They should be centered and about half the strip height, snug to the board thickness.
They should be filled with wet glue before test fitting.
blocks.explanation: Centered half-height slots let the strips cross at the same level; a snug width reduces wobble without crushing the board.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Fit, label, and sort the cells. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Test the organizer and refine the system
lessons.summary: Test the organizer and refine the system

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Testing is a gentle inspection, not a durability certification. Begin with the box stationary on a stable table. Lift out the insert and check that it has not caught on a rough edge. Reinstall it and make sure labels remain attached. Close the lid without pressing down. If the lid touches the beads or will not close naturally, remove some contents or make a lower grid. Never use force to flatten the tray. A lid may reduce incidental spills when the box is carried carefully, but it is not sealed and should not be trusted around young children or used to transport loose beads through a busy area.

For a basic retention check, move the closed box a few centimetres across the tabletop, stop, then open it over the catch sheet. Look for beads that crossed a divider, escaped the box, or became hidden under the panel. Do not shake or drop the tray. If anything crossed, empty the affected cells, find the gap or bowed strip, and correct the insert before storing more. Inspect the scissors and scraps are removed, and check the area and floor for dropped pieces. Store the tray dry, with its lid on, out of reach of children under three and pets.

Think of the category system as something that c

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Lift out the empty insert once, inspect its edges and slot joints, then return it to the box and close the lid without pressing.
With the box closed on the stable tabletop, slide it a few centimetres, stop, and open it over the catch sheet to inspect for movement.
Review the six labels and category amounts. Rewrite unclear labels or divide an overfull category into a separately labeled container.
Close the organizer and store it dry on a stable indoor shelf out of reach of young children and pets; check the work area and floor for stray beads.

blocks.body: Beads are small parts and can pose choking or aspiration hazards. Keep them away from children under three, pets, and anyone likely to put small objects in their mouth; supervise older children and count/contain pieces before and after work.

blocks.question: The closed tray shifts a few centimetres and one bead crosses a cell boundary. What should you do next?
options: Shake the box harder to see if more beads move.
Ignore it because the lid proves the cells are sealed.
Fill every cell to the top so beads cannot move.
Empty affected cells onto the catch sheet, locate the gap, and adjust the grid before re-testing gently.
blocks.explanation: Treat movement as a fit problem. Correct the divider or panel and repeat only the mild tabletop check.

name: Decorative Jewelry Display Card Set
tagline: Design and build a small, coordinated set of reusable paperboard display cards: a pierced-earring card, a necklace card with edge slots, a ring card with a paper retaining band, and a small accessory tag.
outcome: Plan a four-card family on a measured grid, naming each item and reserving clear space for its attachment method.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Decorative Jewelry Display Card Set

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Design and build a small, coordinated set of reusable paperboard display cards: a pierced-earring card, a necklace card with edge slots, a ring card with a paper retaining band, and a small accessory

lessons.title: Plan the card family and make reliable templates
lessons.summary: Plan the card family and make reliable templates

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A coordinated set looks intentional when its cards share a visual rule, not when every card is identical. This course uses four original sample sizes: an earring card 2.5 × 3.5 in (6.4 × 8.9 cm), necklace card 2.75 × 4.25 in (7 × 10.8 cm), ring card 2.5 × 3.5 in, and accessory tag 2 × 3 in (5.1 × 7.6 cm). The extra height on the necklace card gives a chain space to drape without requiring a large sheet. These are practical starting dimensions, not a universal fit; unusually wide or heavy pieces need a larger, sturdier presentation method.

Choose one palette of two colors plus the board color. Plan a border about 1/4 in (6 mm) inside each edge and leave the central attachment area visually quiet. Put a title or maker note near the top, not beneath the jewelry. Make templates from scrap first. A template lets you compare all four silhouettes and check whether the intended item fits before you cut the good board. Mark each template with its name, top edge, and attachment locations. For the necklace, plan two small openings near the top corners with enough paper between opening and edge; for earrings, a level pair of holes. Avoid crowded decorations around openings because openings we

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Draw four rectangles on scrap to the listed sample sizes; label each card and its top edge.
Choose two accent colors and sketch a 1/4-in border plus one simple original motif on each template.
Mark earring holes and necklace openings on the templates, measuring each from the same top and side edges.

blocks.body: Use scissors and a hand punch slowly on a stable table. Keep fingers away from the cutting and punch jaws; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: Why should you make full-size scrap templates before cutting the final board?
options: To check size, visual balance, and opening placement before using the chosen board.
To prove the card can carry any necklace weight.
To make the final card waterproof.
To replace the need to measure the final board.
blocks.explanation: Templates are planning aids. They help confirm intended dimensions and positions before material is committed.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the card family and make reliable templates. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut, decorate, and finish clean card faces
lessons.summary: Cut, decorate, and finish clean card faces

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Before cutting the chosen board, inspect it for bends, greasy spots, tears, or deep folds. A smooth area makes pencil marks easier to erase and gives small holes a better chance of remaining intact. Transfer templates by tracing their outlines on the reverse of the board. Measure the top and bottom widths rather than trusting a single edge; a slightly trapezoid card is more noticeable when several cards sit together. Cut with ordinary scissors in short controlled strokes. Rotate the board, not your wrist at an awkward angle, and stay just outside the pencil line. Trim toward the line in a second pass. Cutting once with a large hurried bite can crush or split the edge.

Decorate while the cards are still flat and before adding openings. Use light marks and a limited palette. On the display face, make the top label legible and keep the lower half quiet. A small abstract leaf, dot cluster, geometric arch, or hand-drawn border is an original motif; avoid copying a known character, logo, or artwork. Add any maker note or item name in a consistent position. If using marker, test it on a scrap first because some inks may bleed through thin board. Use only a little adhesive for paper accen

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trace each template on the reverse of the board and cut just outside the outline with short scissor strokes.
Add the shared border, one simple original motif, and a short item label while the card faces are flat.
Place a clean scrap over any newly glued accent and leave the card flat until the adhesive label allows handling.

blocks.body: Use scissors and a hand punch slowly on a stable table. Keep fingers away from the cutting and punch jaws; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What is the safer way to make earring openings in the card?
options: Push the earring post through the card several times to widen it.
Mark positions and use a small hand punch over scrap backing, keeping fingers clear.
Hold the card in one hand and jab a pin toward the palm.
Cut a long slit with a craft knife.
blocks.explanation: Measure first, use a hand punch where available, and keep hands outside the cutting path. A supervised pushpin alternative is made over scrap on a table.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut, decorate, and finish clean card faces. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Make attachment points for earrings, necklace, and ring
lessons.summary: Make attachment points for earrings, necklace, and ring

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Attachment openings should be sized and positioned for the item while leaving enough paper around them. On the earring card, use the template marks to make two small holes approximately 3/8 in (1 cm) apart, centered left-to-right and about 1 in (2.5 cm) below the top. The spacing is a sample; check it against the pair of earrings or paper stand-ins. A small hand punch is preferable to forcing a sharp object through the board. Place scrap board under the work so the punch exits into a backing surface, and keep fingertips clear. If no punch is available, have an adult create the holes with a pushpin on the table over scrap, never toward a hand.

For the necklace card, mark two openings about 1/2 in (1.3 cm) from the side edges and 3/4 in (1.9 cm) below the top. A small punched hole plus a short scissor snip toward the nearest edge creates a slot through which a lightweight chain can be seated. Stop the slit before it reaches the card's outer corner. If the chain is too thick for this shape, use two folded paper tabs on the back instead of enlarging the slot until it weakens the edge. Keep any chain clasp and excess length on the back only if it rests without pulling the card out of s

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On the earring card, transfer the paired marks about 3/8 in apart and 1 in below the top, then punch over scrap board.
On the necklace card, mark two points 1/2 in from each side and 3/4 in below the top; punch each point and snip a short path to its nearest edge with scissors.
Fold a 1 × 3 in paper strip into a shallow bridge with 1/2-in end tabs and tape the tabs to the back of the ring card.

blocks.body: Use scissors and a hand punch slowly on a stable table. Keep fingers away from the cutting and punch jaws; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: A necklace sample makes the card bow on the tabletop. What should you do?
options: Hang it from a wall hook to remove the bow.
Add a large amount of tape and claim it is reinforced packaging.
Remove the sample and use a lighter display or present the item beside the card.
Cut away most of the card so the chain hangs freely.
blocks.explanation: A tabletop bend means the test load or attachment is inappropriate. Stop the test and choose a lighter or separate display approach.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Make attachment points for earrings, necklace, and ring. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Add the accessory tag and test the finished set
lessons.summary: Add the accessory tag and test the finished set

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The fourth piece is a small accessory tag for a lightweight charm, hair clip, or other item that can rest on a short paper loop. It is not a hole-punched tag intended to hang from a heavy object. Cut a paper strip about 1/2 × 2 in (1.3 × 5 cm), fold it into a loose loop, and secure both ends on the back of the 2 × 3 in tag. If the accessory has a suitable narrow attachment point, it can rest through the loop; otherwise, present the item beside the tag rather than forcing it into a fit. This preserves the card and avoids claiming the tag can carry weight.

Now test each card on a stable tabletop. Place one lightweight sample or paper stand-in on it and look from the front and side. Check three things: the card stays flat, the item is visible, and no opening is enlarging. A card that tips, bows, hides the label, or begins to split has failed this small presentation test. Remove the item and revise the attachment or make a replacement. Do not compensate by piling on tape, adding a hook, hanging it from a wall, or treating it as protective packaging. If the sample is too heavy for the card, use a separate tabletop stand designed for the actual load or simply display the card empty.

Fi

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Fold a 1/2 × 2-in paper strip into a loose loop and tape both ends to the back of the accessory tag.
Test each card with one lightweight sample or paper stand-in while the card rests flat on a stable tabletop.
Erase guides, compare the four margins, write optional item notes on the back, and store the cards flat and dry.

blocks.body: Use scissors and a hand punch slowly on a stable table. Keep fingers away from the cutting and punch jaws; younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What sample dimensions are specified for the necklace card?
options: 2 × 3 inches
2.5 × 3.5 inches
3 × 5 inches
2.75 × 4.25 inches
blocks.explanation: The necklace card sample is 2.75 × 4.25 inches; it is a design starting point rather than a universal standard.
