name: Removable Paper Phone-Case Insert
tagline: Make a dry, removable paper illustration fitted beneath a clear phone case.
outcome: Measure and record the usable interior dimensions of a clear case to the nearest millimetre or 1/16 inch, using a paper test template before decorating.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Removable Paper Phone-Case Insert

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a dry, removable paper illustration fitted beneath a clear phone case. The insert is a decorative, replaceable layer, not a protective component. You will trace the actual case opening, leave dev

lessons.title: Measure the case and make a paper template
lessons.summary: Measure the case and make a paper template

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A good insert follows the inside of the case, not the outline of the phone alone. Clear cases often have raised lips, rounded corners and camera cut-outs that are not represented by a phone’s rectangular body measurement. Work with the phone powered down. Remove the case only if it comes off normally; set the phone aside on a clean, dry surface. Never force a case that is cracked, brittle or unusually tight.

The project’s starting point is a paper template. A typical sample for a compact phone might have a central panel about 7.2 × 14.8 cm, but treat that only as a sketching reference. Your case may be smaller or larger, and its interior walls may taper. The traced template is the authority. Place the case interior-side up on scrap paper and trace the flat back area rather than the outside rim. Mark the top, bottom and camera side so you cannot accidentally rotate the piece later. Estimate the camera clearance conservatively: draw the camera shape as an exclusion zone and keep the paper outside it, rather than cutting a hole that could shift over the lens.

Record the usable width at the top, middle and bottom, and usable length along both sides. If the case narrows, use the narro

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Power the phone down, remove the case only by its normal release method, and wipe loose dust from the case interior with a dry soft cloth.
Lay the case on scrap paper, trace only the flat inner back panel, mark TOP and the camera side, then sketch the camera and other openings as no-paper zones.
Measure usable width at three heights and usable length at both sides; record the smallest values and draw a first paper test piece about 1 mm smaller around the outer edges.

blocks.body: Power the phone down before removing the case for tracing. Follow the device and case maker’s directions; never pry a tight case with a knife or other tool.

blocks.question: Why should the first cut be a paper test template traced from the actual case?
options: It proves the insert will protect a phone from drops.
It accounts for the case’s own taper, rounded corners and opening positions.
It makes it safe to force a tight case over the phone.
It lets you use glue to hold paper permanently against the phone.
blocks.explanation: A case can have a shaped interior that differs from the phone body. A test template lets you tune the paper before decorating.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Measure the case and make a paper template. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Refine the outline and plan original artwork
lessons.summary: Refine the outline and plan original artwork

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Use the test piece to learn where the case’s real boundary differs from the traced line. Cut the test outline with short snips, turning the paper rather than twisting your wrist into the case shape. Rounded corners should be gentle arcs, not sharp points; sharp corners catch and fold more easily. Do not cut a camera opening yet. Instead, leave a generous clear margin around its trace. The finished paper can be made narrower there by trimming the outside contour or by cutting a rounded notch only if your template proves it is necessary. Avoid tiny slits and narrow bridges that can tear.

Before decorating, place the template inside the case without the phone. It should settle under its own weight and lift out using the temporary tab. Check the entire perimeter in bright light. If a section rides up, identify whether the problem is a long edge, a corner radius or an opening boundary. Remove the paper before trimming. Take off only a small sliver—around 0.5 mm at a time—then test again. This iterative approach preserves a snug-looking outline without wedging paper into the case. If your first template becomes too small, make another from the original trace rather than taping scraps on

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut the test template from scrap paper in short strokes, rounding its corners and leaving the camera area as an uncut, generously clear region.
Set the template into the empty case, lift it out, and trim only the areas that visibly curl or press against the rim, removing about 0.5 mm per trial.
On a fresh sheet of final paper, trace the accepted template and lightly draw three broad offset bands and dots inside a 5 mm edge margin, avoiding all shaded no-paper zones.

blocks.body: Power the phone down before removing the case for tracing. Follow the device and case maker’s directions; never pry a tight case with a knife or other tool.

blocks.question: During the empty-case check, the insert curls at one side. What is the best next action?
options: Push the paper under the case rim with a pointed tool.
Add a bead of liquid glue to the case interior.
Remove it, trim the tight edge by a small amount, and test again.
Install the phone and press harder until the rim closes.
blocks.explanation: The paper should rest flat without being wedged. Remove it before making small edge adjustments.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Refine the outline and plan original artwork. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut and finish the removable insert
lessons.summary: Cut and finish the removable insert

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Transfer the approved outline to the final sheet using a light pencil line. Check orientation one more time: TOP should point toward the case’s camera end. Cut on a flat, protected tabletop. Keep fingers behind the scissor blades and rotate the paper to follow curves. Do not cut toward the hand holding it. When the outline is complete, compare it to the test template before erasing guide marks. Small differences are normal, but a pronounced bulge, narrow point or sharp corner should be corrected now. If you are unable to cut a smooth camera-side outline, leave a larger outside clearance rather than attempting a complicated aperture.

Color the design with dry pencils or markers while the paper is flat. Avoid pressing so hard that the paper dents, and stay inside the edge margin. Some markers can bleed through thin stock; test a small mark on a spare offcut first. Let any marker ink dry fully according to its packaging before touching the case. The design is intentionally flat: do not add beads, foam tape, folded paper, wet glue, glitter or a coating. A removable insert works because it is held gently between the case back and the phone; extra thickness can lift the case lip or pres

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trace the accepted outline onto final paper, label TOP lightly on the back, and cut the perimeter with controlled short scissor strokes on the tabletop.
Test each coloring medium on an offcut, then color the bands and dots with light, dry strokes; allow marker ink to dry fully before handling.
Inspect front and back, remove loose graphite and paper dust, then leave the finished insert flat under a clean book if it has a slight dry curl.

blocks.body: Power the phone down before removing the case for tracing. Follow the device and case maker’s directions; never pry a tight case with a knife or other tool.

blocks.question: Which layout decision best protects access to the phone’s camera and connectors?
options: Draw a broad no-paper zone from the case’s own opening trace and keep the insert clear of it.
Cover the camera with clear paper because it is transparent.
Cut small slots after the case is installed on the phone.
Use a wider insert and let the case edge push it away from the openings.
blocks.explanation: Trace openings as exclusions while the case is off the powered-down phone. When uncertain, leave more clear space.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut and finish the removable insert. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fit, inspect and refine safely
lessons.summary: Fit, inspect and refine safely

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The first assembly check is performed with the phone still powered down and the case separate. Put the insert into the empty case, align its TOP mark, then inspect the openings from the case’s inner side. The camera, flash, microphone, speaker, button, port, vent and charging-interface locations must remain clear. Do not rely on a view through the transparent case alone; paper may shift during assembly. If a boundary looks uncertain, remove the paper and enlarge the clearance from the outer edge, or remake it. Never push a paper edge into a small device opening.

If the paper lies flat, return the phone to the case using the maker’s ordinary fitting method. Do not force a corner over the device. Inspect around the entire rim: it should seat as it did before the project. A lifted lip, unexpected button pressure or visible bulge means the insert is too large, too thick or misplaced. Remove the phone and paper, then diagnose the specific interference. Reduce the perimeter in very small steps or use thinner paper. If the case no longer seats normally, stop using the decorated insert. Do not try to improve retention with glue, tape, a tighter case or added layers.

For a final check, co

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the paper in the empty case with its TOP mark aligned, then inspect every device opening and keep the paper boundary well clear of each one.
Refit the powered-down phone by the case maker’s normal method and verify that the rim seats evenly without bulging, lifted corners or new button pressure.
Record the final template width and length, photograph or sketch the abstract layout for personal reference, and remove the insert if fit changes during ordinary handling.

blocks.body: Power the phone down before removing the case for tracing. Follow the device and case maker’s directions; never pry a tight case with a knife or other tool.

blocks.question: A marker test on the offcut feathers through the paper. What should you do?
options: Keep coloring and place the wet side against the case.
Seal it with household spray while the phone is nearby.
Press harder so the color becomes opaque.
Stop that marker and use tested dry pencil or fresh paper.
blocks.explanation: Only use dry media that behaves well on the chosen paper. Let any ink dry fully before fitting.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Fit, inspect and refine safely. What did you learn and verify?

name: Cardboard Phone Stand
tagline: Build a dry-use tabletop phone stand from corrugated cardboard.
outcome: Measure a phone's width and thickness and translate those measurements into a cradle opening and retaining lip with stated clearance.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Cardboard Phone Stand

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Build a dry-use tabletop phone stand from corrugated cardboard. A folded wedge base supports a separate slotted cradle and low toe. Measure your cased phone, test the fit while disconnected, and refin

lessons.title: Measure, choose a profile, and plan the pieces
lessons.summary: Measure, choose a profile, and plan the pieces

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful stand starts with a fit, not a guess. This design has two parts: a folded easel base resting on the table and a separate front cradle with a shallow slot and toe. The base forms a low wedge; the cradle supports the phone's lower edge. The phone is not locked in, so use the stand only on a level, still tabletop.

Measure the phone with its usual case. Record width and thickness. For the example, a phone 76 mm wide and 10 mm thick uses an 82 mm slot and 14 mm depth. Calculate width plus 6 mm and thickness plus 4 mm for other devices. This leaves clearance for easy insertion; the toe is only a low stop, never a clamp. The phone should lift out freely.

Begin with a 260 x 180 mm base blank and mark a fold 90 mm from one short edge. That panel is the foot. Use a paper mock-up to choose the back profile and wedge angle before cutting cardboard. Cardboard flute direction and thickness vary, so test scoring on an offcut. The score should guide a fold without splitting the liner. Select clean, dry board with intact corners; avoid tape, staples, crushed or oily areas. A full-size paper template makes corrections inexpensive and records your measurements. The design is a tabletop dis

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure case-on phone width and thickness; calculate slot width +6 mm and depth +4 mm.
Sketch and cut a paper wedge template; mark 260 x 180 mm blank and 90 mm foot.
Test a shallow score and fold on a clean cardboard offcut.

blocks.body: Use only for stationary, non-charging viewing on a stable tabletop. Never use in a vehicle, near an edge, or where movement could cause a fall.

blocks.question: Your case-on phone measures 76 mm wide. Which example cradle slot width provides the planned 3 mm clearance on each side?
options: 76 mm
82 mm
90 mm
70 mm
blocks.explanation: The course uses phone width plus 6 mm, distributing clearance equally on both sides.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Measure, choose a profile, and plan the pieces. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut parts and form the easel base
lessons.summary: Cut parts and form the easel base

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Transfer the checked paper layout to cardboard only after confirming dimensions. Mark lightly. A straight blank helps the foot sit flat, while a controlled hinge lets the base form a wedge. This single-wall example is small, but its performance is not rated for a load; place the phone gently and remove it before moving the stand.

Use scissors if they cut the board without crushing it. If the board is too thick, an adult can use a craft knife on a cutting mat. Make light repeated passes instead of forcing one deep cut. Keep the straightedge stable and fingers behind it; cut away from the body. Stop if the blade catches or wanders. Never hold cardboard in one hand while cutting.

For the hinge, press a shallow groove with a blunt tool. It should be an indentation, not a slit through the opposite liner. Bend slowly toward the scored side and inspect both faces. The foot lies flat while the tall panel leans back; the rear edge meets the table to complete the wedge. Tape temporarily, then check for rocking on a level surface. If it rocks, inspect the board and fold; do not wedge loose objects underneath. A paper brace may be added inside after the profile is confirmed, but let its adhe

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure case-on phone width and thickness; calculate slot width +6 mm and depth +4 mm.
Sketch and cut a paper wedge template; mark 260 x 180 mm blank and 90 mm foot.
Test a shallow score and fold on a clean cardboard offcut.
Mark the 260 x 180 mm blank and 90 mm hinge from a straight edge.

blocks.body: Use only for stationary, non-charging viewing on a stable tabletop. Never use in a vehicle, near an edge, or where movement could cause a fall.

blocks.question: What should a score line do when forming the base hinge?
options: Cut through both liners so the panels separate cleanly
Crush the whole panel flat with repeated hard pressure
Make a shallow controlled groove while leaving the back liner connected
Be made after the base is glued shut
blocks.explanation: A shallow score guides a fold while preserving the uncut liner as a hinge.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut parts and form the easel base. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build the cradle and join the stand
lessons.summary: Build the cradle and join the stand

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
For the example cradle, cut a 110 x 38 mm rectangle. Mark a centered slot 82 mm wide by 14 mm deep for the 76 x 10 mm phone. Leave material at both ends; widen the cradle if a larger slot would make its tabs fragile. Form a 10 mm forward toe at the bottom by scoring and folding a narrow strip. It should gently meet the lower edge, not cover the screen or press a button.

The cradle is not a spring clip. Never force a device into a tight slot. If loose, use a narrow folded-card shim attached to the stand; if tight, trim the inner edges a little at a time. Remove the phone before adjustments and retest after each one. Keep ports, vents, camera and controls clear.

Center the cradle across the base front, align its lower edge with the table, and temporarily tape it in place. Check that the phone can lean against the back. Remove the phone before joining. Apply a thin layer of paper craft glue to the cardboard contact and let it set according to its label, or wrap the joint with paper tape. Avoid thick lumps that tilt the cradle. Do not test while glue is wet. This is for stationary, non-charging tabletop viewing only, never a vehicle or a use where movement could cause harm.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure case-on phone width and thickness; calculate slot width +6 mm and depth +4 mm.
Sketch and cut a paper wedge template; mark 260 x 180 mm blank and 90 mm foot.
Test a shallow score and fold on a clean cardboard offcut.
Mark the 260 x 180 mm blank and 90 mm hinge from a straight edge.

blocks.body: Use only for stationary, non-charging viewing on a stable tabletop. Never use in a vehicle, near an edge, or where movement could cause a fall.

blocks.question: The knife catches and tears the cardboard liner. What is the safest next step?
options: Push harder to finish before the blade slips
Stop, set the knife safely aside, and use lighter passes or scissors; seek adult help if a knife is required
Hold the cardboard in the other hand and pull it toward the blade
Use a flame to seal the ragged edge
blocks.explanation: Stop on a catch. Reposition the work on a cutting mat and use a safer cutting method with supervision.

lessons.title: Fit-check, refine, and finish the paper edges
lessons.summary: Fit-check, refine, and finish the paper edges

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Wait until adhesive is fully dry. Set the empty stand on a stable, level table and confirm it does not rock. Then place the disconnected phone gently in the slot while keeping it close to the tabletop. Do not push, shake the table, or try a heavier object. The phone should rest against the back, lift out freely, and leave its camera and controls unobstructed. Remove it before any adjustment.

Observe the result rather than forcing a fit. If it slides forward, the toe may be too low or the wedge too upright. Adjust one feature, such as adding a folded-card toe, then repeat the empty-base check. If pinched, trim the slot slightly. If it leans sideways, recenter the cradle or inspect for a warped base. Record the change so you know which adjustment helped.

Cover only rough stand edges with paper strips or paper tape. Keep decoration on the stand, away from every phone opening and contact area. Avoid wet paint, liquid coatings, and claims that the stand protects a phone. Remove the phone before moving the stand. Dampness and repeated bending can weaken cardboard; stop using it if a hinge cracks, joint loosens, or cradle sags. Save the template with the measured dimensions and chosen p

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure case-on phone width and thickness; calculate slot width +6 mm and depth +4 mm.
Sketch and cut a paper wedge template; mark 260 x 180 mm blank and 90 mm foot.
Test a shallow score and fold on a clean cardboard offcut.
Mark the 260 x 180 mm blank and 90 mm hinge from a straight edge.

blocks.body: Use only for stationary, non-charging viewing on a stable tabletop. Never use in a vehicle, near an edge, or where movement could cause a fall.

blocks.question: Which use matches the design's stated limits?
options: Stationary viewing on a stable tabletop, with the phone disconnected from charging
Holding a phone while driving
Supporting a phone while charging overnight
Protecting a phone during a fall
blocks.explanation: The stand is only for stationary, non-charging viewing on a stable tabletop.

modules.description: Make a reusable felt organizer for a fully unplugged charging cable. A long padded-looking strip folds around a loosely coiled cable and closes with a sewn-on button and a reinforced button loop. The

lessons.title: Measure the coil and plan a relaxed fit
lessons.summary: Measure the coil and plan a relaxed fit

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Start with the cable disconnected at both ends. A wrap should hold a loose coil together without forcing a sharp bend or squeezing the cable. Lay the cable on a clean table and form a relaxed coil about 3.5 in (9 cm) across. Do not wind it tightly around fingers or a small object. Measure the approximate circumference around the outside of the coil with a strip of paper, then add roughly 1.5 in (4 cm) for ease. This measurement is a planning aid, not a universal fit guarantee: cable stiffness and connector size vary.

The sample strip is 4 × 8 in (10 × 20 cm), with rounded short ends. Its length wraps around a coil up to about 3.5 in (9 cm) across with room for a small overlap, but the actual button position will be adjusted during fitting. If your measured relaxed coil needs more length, extend the paper template in 1/2 in (1 cm) increments. Keep the body wide enough to bridge the coil without covering the connector ends. A paper mock-up lets you find this out before cutting felt.

Plan a button at one short end and a thread loop at the other. The closure should be easy to open with two fingers; it must not pull the cable into a tight bundle. Mark a centerline and the planned butt

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Unplug the cable at both ends, lay it on the table, and form a relaxed coil about 3.5 in (9 cm) across. Measure the loose coil circumference with a paper strip.
Draw a 4 × 8 in (10 × 20 cm) rounded-end paper rectangle. If the measurement suggests the wrap will not overlap comfortably, lengthen it in 1/2 in (1 cm) increments.
Wrap the paper around the coil loosely, mark where the two ends meet, then mark a proposed button center and a loop position on the template.
Mark a stitch guide about 1/8 in (3 mm) inside the template edge and round the corners smoothly; label the template with the final length and width.

blocks.body: Disconnect the cable from the phone, charger, battery pack, and every power source before measuring, fitting, or storing it. Do not make or test the wrap around a connected cable.

blocks.question: Before measuring a cable for this storage wrap, what should you do?
options: Disconnect it from every device and power source.
Leave one end plugged in so the cable stays straight.
Wrap the cable around a pencil tightly.
Put the wrap on first and then unplug it.
blocks.explanation: The wrap is for storage of a fully disconnected cable only. A connected cable must never be used as the fitting form.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Measure the coil and plan a relaxed fit. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut, layer, and practise the seam
lessons.summary: Cut, layer, and practise the seam

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Place the paper template on felt and trace it twice. Check that both pieces have the same orientation and that the felt is not folded or stretched while tracing. Cut just outside the line with fabric scissors, making steady small snips around curves rather than turning the scissors sharply. Matching outlines help the perimeter stitch lie flat. If your two pieces differ slightly, trim the larger one to match before sewing; do not compensate by pulling thread tightly.

Use a small felt offcut to practise the blanket stitch. Thread a manageable length of floss, around 18 in (45 cm), through the needle and knot the tail. Keep the needle under control and place the offcut on the table. Bring the needle from the back to the front near the edge, then pass it through both layers a short distance along the edge. Guide the working thread through the loop so a small bar rests along the edge. The precise hand motion can feel unfamiliar; practise several stitches before moving to the actual wrap. Aim for stitches roughly 1/4 in (6 mm) apart and roughly the same distance from the edge.

Pull only until the loop sits neatly on the felt. Excess tension puckers the edge and makes the wrap stiff; lo

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trace the adjusted template twice onto felt and cut both pieces just outside the outline using small controlled snips.
Thread about 18 in (45 cm) of floss through the needle, knot the tail, and practise several blanket stitches on a felt offcut, spacing them about 1/4 in (6 mm) apart.
Stack the two cut shapes evenly and place four to six clips around the edges, away from the first sewing area.
Mark or visually follow a seam path about 1/8 in (3 mm) from the edge, then confirm the needle and thread move freely through both layers.

blocks.body: Disconnect the cable from the phone, charger, battery pack, and every power source before measuring, fitting, or storing it. Do not make or test the wrap around a connected cable.

blocks.question: Why make and fit a paper template before cutting felt?
options: Paper makes the felt permanently waterproof.
It lets you check overlap and relaxed fit before committing felt.
It proves the finished wrap protects the cable from damage.
It removes the need to measure the cable.
blocks.explanation: A paper mock-up is adjustable and helps verify the intended dimensions before cutting the two felt layers.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut, layer, and practise the seam. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Sew a balanced edge and attach the button
lessons.summary: Sew a balanced edge and attach the button

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Begin at a long straight edge, away from the future button and loop. Hide the starting knot between felt layers by bringing the needle out through one layer, then begin catching both layers. Work around the wrap with the blanket stitch, keeping each stitch about 1/4 in (6 mm) from the next and about 1/8 in (3 mm) from the cut edge. Those are visual targets, not rigid rules. On a curve, take slightly smaller steps so the felt edge does not bunch. Keep the loop at the edge of each stitch facing the same direction. Even spacing and steady, moderate tension are more useful than speed.

If you reach the end of your thread, finish with a small knot tucked between layers where practical, then thread a fresh length and anchor it through nearby stitches. Avoid leaving a long loose tail that could catch on the cable. At the end of the perimeter, secure the final loop and bury the tail between layers before trimming. Check both faces for loose loops and puckering. If a stitch is missed, unpick just a few stitches with the needle tip rather than cutting felt; a small gap can be resewn.

Fit the wrap around the disconnected coil before adding the closure. Mark the overlap that allows easy openi

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Start on a straight edge by hiding the knot between layers, then sew a blanket stitch around the perimeter with approximately 1/4 in (6 mm) spacing.
At curves, shorten stitch spacing slightly; when thread is nearly used, secure it through nearby stitches and begin a fresh manageable length.
Finish the perimeter by securing the last loop, burying the thread tail between felt layers where possible, and trimming excess thread with scissors.
Fit the sewn body loosely around the still-disconnected coil, mark the overlap, and sew a flat button at the marked point using several passes through its holes.

blocks.body: Disconnect the cable from the phone, charger, battery pack, and every power source before measuring, fitting, or storing it. Do not make or test the wrap around a connected cable.

blocks.question: What is the useful target when tightening each blanket stitch?
options: Pull until the felt edge curls tightly.
Leave a large loop that catches a fingertip.
Seat the loop neatly along the edge without puckering.
Pull so hard the thread cuts into the felt.
blocks.explanation: The thread should hold the edge neatly, not distort the felt or leave snagging loops.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Sew a balanced edge and attach the button. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Make the loop, test, and care for the wrap
lessons.summary: Make the loop, test, and care for the wrap

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Make the loop from a short length of floss or from a narrow strip of felt folded and stitched into a loop. For this sample, a floss loop is simplest: make a loop just large enough to pass over the button with light finger pressure. Anchor both ends on the opposite wrap end with repeated stitches, then knot and bury the tails. Avoid tying a loop so tight that the button must be forced through it. If the loop is too loose, it may slip off in a bag; shorten it by re-sewing the anchor rather than twisting it around the cable.

Test the closure on the empty wrap first. Open and close it several times while watching the button stitches and felt around the anchor. Then coil the unplugged cable loosely and close the wrap. The cable should remain relaxed, with no sharp fold, trapped connector, or pressure from the closure. Open the wrap and remove the cable; inspect it for new kinks, flattening, cuts, discoloration, or other damage. If anything looks wrong, stop using the wrap and assess the cable separately. Never test charging while the cable is wrapped or leave the wrap on during use.

The project is for dry, indoor storage. Keep it away from liquids and heat. Do not wash it while a cabl

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Form a floss loop at the free end, anchor both ends with repeated stitches, and size it to pass over the button with light finger pressure.
Close and open the empty wrap several times, checking the button holes, loop anchors, and surrounding felt for movement or tearing.
Loosely coil the disconnected cable, place the wrap around it, and close the loop without compressing the coil or trapping a connector.
Remove the cable, inspect the organizer and cable separately, then record one improvement and store the wrap dry with the cable fully disconnected.

blocks.body: Disconnect the cable from the phone, charger, battery pack, and every power source before measuring, fitting, or storing it. Do not make or test the wrap around a connected cable.

blocks.question: During fit testing, the wrap makes the coil visibly flat. What is the best response?
options: Use the wrap anyway and pull the loop harder.
Add a second button to clamp it more firmly.
Charge the cable inside the wrap to see if it warms up.
Remove the wrap and revise the length or closure position for a relaxed coil.
blocks.explanation: A storage organizer should not flatten or kink the cable. Revise the fit and do not test charging inside the wrap.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Make the loop, test, and care for the wrap. What did you learn and verify?

name: Fabric Earbud Pouch
tagline: Sew a compact, lined, soft fabric pouch for carrying a disconnected pair of earbuds and their loosely arranged cable.
outcome: Measure and cut two coordinated fabric rectangles to a stated finished-size plan, adding consistent seam allowance.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Fabric Earbud Pouch

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Sew a compact, lined, soft fabric pouch for carrying a disconnected pair of earbuds and their loosely arranged cable. This original envelope-style design closes with a fold-over flap and a short lengt

lessons.title: Plan the pouch and prepare the pieces
lessons.summary: Plan the pouch and prepare the pieces

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The sample pouch is sized around a small set of wired earbuds or a compact pair of disconnected earbuds. It is intentionally a soft organizer, not a rigid case. The outer rectangle and lining are each 6.5 by 8.5 inches. Once the side seams and bottom seam use a 1/2-inch allowance, the body is approximately 5.5 inches wide and 7.5 inches tall before folding. The top 2.5 inches become the flap, leaving a pocket about 5 inches deep. These are design targets: fabric thickness, stitch placement, and turning can change the final result slightly. Before cutting, loosely coil the disconnected cable without cinching it and compare its bundle with the planned interior. If the earbuds or case are larger, enlarge both rectangles equally; keep the 1/2-inch seam allowance and add the desired extra room to the body dimensions.

Use stable woven cotton that does not stretch much. Very thick denim or layered quilting may be difficult to turn by hand, while slippery or stretchy fabric can shift. The ribbon loop is a simple closure aid, not a carrying handle. It is positioned at the center of the pouch front and the flap tucks behind it. Choose two fabrics with enough contrast to identify the lining

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure and mark one 6.5 x 8.5 in rectangle on each fabric, adding no extra allowance beyond those stated cut dimensions.
Cut the two rectangles with fabric scissors and set aside the 3 in ribbon loop piece.
On the wrong side, mark a 1/2 in seam guide along both long sides and one short bottom edge of each rectangle; leave the top short edge unsewn.

blocks.body: Work at a clear, stable table with good light. Cut away from your body, keep fingers out of the scissor path, and close scissors when setting them down.

blocks.question: What are the cut dimensions for each main fabric rectangle in this sample design?
options: 6.5 x 8.5 inches
5.5 x 5 inches
8.5 x 12 inches
3 x 3 inches
blocks.explanation: Both outer and lining rectangles are cut 6.5 by 8.5 inches; the 1/2-inch seams and 2.5-inch flap are included in the design plan.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the pouch and prepare the pieces. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Practice the stitch and join the layers
lessons.summary: Practice the stitch and join the layers

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A backstitch creates a continuous-looking seam by placing each new stitch back into the end of the previous visible stitch, then bringing the needle forward a short distance. For this pouch, aim for stitches about 1/8 inch long and keep them close to the marked 1/2-inch seam line. Small, even stitches help the seam hold together; pulling very hard is not helpful because it gathers the fabric. A specialist sewing tutorial describes backstitch as suitable for seams and emphasizes even stitches with enough tension to lie flat without puckering.[1] Practice on a scrap if the motion feels unfamiliar. A thread length of roughly 18 inches is manageable; longer thread tangles more readily. Knot one end, sew, and secure the end with two small stitches before trimming.

Put the outer and lining rectangles right sides together, meaning the attractive sides face each other. Align the bottom and side edges. Pin or clip within the seam allowance, removing each pin as you approach it; never sew over a pin. Sew the two side seams and bottom seam while leaving the top completely open. Start and end with a few compact securing stitches. The seam allowance is the cloth between the cut edge and stitch

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Thread the needle with about 18 in of thread, knot one end, and practise 1/8 in backstitches on a scrap or marked practice area.
Place the rectangles right sides together, align bottom and side edges, and pin or clip the three edges while leaving the top edge open.
Backstitch along both long sides and the bottom, about 1/2 in from the raw edge; secure each start and finish with two small stitches.

blocks.body: Work at a clear, stable table with good light. Cut away from your body, keep fingers out of the scissor path, and close scissors when setting them down.

blocks.question: How should the two fabric rectangles face when sewing the side and bottom seams?
options: Wrong sides together so seams are exposed
Right sides together, with the top edge left open
Fold both pieces into quarters first
Sew all four edges shut
blocks.explanation: Put the attractive sides together and sew three edges; keep the top opening available for turning and finishing.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Practice the stitch and join the layers. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Turn, shape, and finish the opening
lessons.summary: Turn, shape, and finish the opening

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Before turning, examine the seam intersections at the bottom corners. Trim only bulky thread tails. Do not cut the stitching or clip deeply into the seam allowance. To help corners turn neatly, you may carefully snip a tiny diagonal from the excess allowance near (not through) the stitching, but this is optional and should be skipped if uncertain. Turn the joined work through the open top, easing fabric with fingers or the rounded end of a clean pencil. Never push with a sharp point. Press with fingers so the side seams sit near the edges. The folded top edge naturally separates into the outer side and lining side.

The planned front is the outer fabric with the flap extending from the back. Lay the pouch flat with the opening at the top. Fold the upper 2.5 inches of the back layer forward to form the flap. This creates a useful pocket approximately 5 inches deep. Confirm this by placing a loose paper mock-up or a dry, disconnected earbud bundle inside; do not force the contents into the pocket. Mark the center of the front about 1 inch below its opening. Fold the short ribbon into a loop with its ends together, and place the ends at the center mark. Keep the loop small enough to c

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Turn the pouch through the open top and ease the corners outward with fingers or a blunt pencil end.
Fold 2.5 in of the back top edge forward as a flap and mark the front center about 1 in below the opening.
Fold the 3 in ribbon in half into a loop and stitch its two ends at the front center mark, catching only the front outer layer where practical.
Turn the raw top edges inward about 1/2 in, align outer and lining folds, and close the opening with small backstitches through both folds.

blocks.body: Work at a clear, stable table with good light. Cut away from your body, keep fingers out of the scissor path, and close scissors when setting them down.

blocks.question: What is the useful response if hand stitches make the fabric pucker?
options: Pull the thread harder to flatten it
Switch to a sharp awl and enlarge every hole
Remove a few tight stitches, smooth the fabric, and resew with gentler tension
Cut across the seam to release the tension
blocks.explanation: The backstitch should lie flat. Ease the tight section and resew with consistent, moderate tension.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Turn, shape, and finish the opening. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Check fit, refine, and care for the pouch
lessons.summary: Check fit, refine, and care for the pouch

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A finished pouch is useful only if it opens easily and its seams are intact. Put the flap up, place the dry, disconnected earbuds or a loose cable coil inside, and close the flap by tucking its edge under the ribbon loop. Do not wind the cable tightly or compress earbuds to make them fit. If the bundle barely fits, enlarge the pattern on a later version rather than stretching the current pouch. For a larger pouch, add the same amount to the width of both fabric rectangles and enough height for the content plus the 2.5-inch flap; keep the 1/2-inch seam allowance unchanged.

Check the outside, inside, and all corners in good light. Tug gently on the ribbon loop and top seam using only enough force to see whether stitches move. This is a home craft check, not a load rating. The loop is only a closure catch and must not be used to hang the pouch or carry a heavy object. Repair any loose stitch with matching thread and secure the ends. Keep the fabric dry and clean it only according to the fabric's known care instructions. Remove contents first. Do not promise that cloth protects electronics from impacts, liquid, heat, or static.

Reflect on one design choice: fabric contrast, pocket de

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place a dry, disconnected earbud bundle loosely inside, fold the flap, and tuck its edge beneath the ribbon loop.
Inspect the inside and outside, then gently test the top seam and ribbon attachment for loose stitches.
Write down one successful choice and one measured change for a second version; then secure all needles and tools.

blocks.body: Work at a clear, stable table with good light. Cut away from your body, keep fingers out of the scissor path, and close scissors when setting them down.

blocks.question: Which statement describes a safe use of this finished pouch?
options: Leave earbuds connected and charge them inside
Use the ribbon loop to hang a heavy key bundle
Treat it as a waterproof protective case
Store dry, disconnected earbuds loosely and remove them before use
blocks.explanation: The pouch is a soft organizer for dry, disconnected items. It is not a certified protective or charging enclosure.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Check fit, refine, and care for the pouch. What did you learn and verify?

name: Desktop Cable Labeling Kit
tagline: Make a compact, reusable paper-and-tape kit for identifying desktop cables at both ends.
outcome: Trace a selected disconnected cable visually and record a confirmed destination without guessing.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Desktop Cable Labeling Kit

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a compact, reusable paper-and-tape kit for identifying desktop cables at both ends. You will map cable destinations, create wrap bands and visible flag tags, and keep a matching index card. The l

lessons.title: Map the desktop before making labels
lessons.summary: Map the desktop before making labels

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful cable label answers a small question quickly: what does this cable serve, and where does it go? This project makes a reusable desktop kit with two label styles. The first is a wraparound band for flexible cables. The second is a flat flag tab that stands slightly away from a thicker lead, so its text remains easy to see. Neither style repairs, tests, supports, or changes an electrical cable. Start with cables that are disconnected from both devices and outlets; never label a damaged cord or work at an energized connection. If a cord is hot, frayed, cracked, or has a loose plug, stop and ask a responsible adult or qualified repair service rather than decorating it.

Choose a compact set of up to six desktop accessories: for example, a monitor signal lead, keyboard lead, mouse lead, and a few disconnected charging/data cables. Do not infer a cable’s function from color alone. Trace it visually from one end to the other while disconnected, and write a plain-language destination such as “monitor” or “desk hub.” Avoid private account names and sensitive information. A short code plus destination is easier to scan than a sentence. Use one consistent format, such as “K1 / keyboar

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Choose four to six disconnected, undamaged desktop cables and list each visible destination in pencil.
Assign short unique codes K1–K6 and write a matching code-and-destination line on the index card.
Measure one cable’s jacket circumference loosely with a paper strip, then mark a 25 × 70 mm wrap-band sample and an 20 × 80 mm flag sample.

blocks.body: Disconnect selected cables from both devices and outlets before handling. Never attach labels to live, hot, damaged, frayed, cracked, or loose-plug cords.

blocks.question: What should you do before handling a cable for this project?
options: Disconnect it from both devices and outlets, and check that it is undamaged.
Leave it powered so its destination is easier to identify.
Wrap tape over a damaged section to keep the label steady.
Unplug it by pulling the cord sharply.
blocks.explanation: Disconnecting and inspecting first keeps the craft separate from energized equipment, repair, and damaged-cord handling.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Map the desktop before making labels. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut readable bands and flags
lessons.summary: Cut readable bands and flags

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The paper should stay small enough not to snag, but large enough for a code you can read at arm’s length. For a wrap band, reserve roughly 35 mm of the 70 mm length for writing and the remaining length for going around the cable with a modest overlap. A cable’s circumference varies, so the 70 mm sample is adjustable. For a flag, divide the 80 mm strip into a 20 mm attachment section, a 25 mm text panel, and a 35 mm return/overlap section. Fold the attachment area around the jacket gently, then bring the adhesive-backed ends together beyond the cable. The text panel projects outward; it should not press into an adjacent cable or device.

Use a ruler and pencil to draw templates on one sheet, then cut on the lines over a stable surface. Rounded corners are optional and can reduce sharp paper points, but make the curve shallow so no text is lost. Write codes after cutting so each label can be aligned horizontally. Use dark, plain lettering; avoid decorative symbols that could be mistaken for a port or voltage rating. If you need a color cue, use a small colored mark consistently and keep the written code as the reliable identifier. Color alone is not sufficient because lighting, visio

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut one 25 × 70 mm wrap sample and one 20 × 80 mm flag sample; adjust lengths from the paper mock-up if necessary.
Write the assigned code and short destination on each label’s outward-facing panel in consistent dark lettering.
Round only the outer corners if desired, leaving at least 3 mm clear around all writing.

blocks.body: Disconnect selected cables from both devices and outlets before handling. Never attach labels to live, hot, damaged, frayed, cracked, or loose-plug cords.

blocks.question: Why put the same short code at both ends and in the index?
options: It makes the cable carry more electrical current.
It lets you match the ends and check the destination consistently.
It certifies that the cable is compatible with every device.
It allows you to ignore visible damage.
blocks.explanation: Matching identifiers support organization only; they provide no electrical test or safety certification.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut readable bands and flags. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Attach labels gently and consistently
lessons.summary: Attach labels gently and consistently

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Attach the labels only after the sample fit looks right and the cable remains disconnected. The aim is identification without squeezing, bending, or coating the jacket. For the wrap band, place the text panel outward, loop the blank around the cable, and join the paper ends with a short piece of low-tack tape. Put tape on paper-to-paper overlap rather than directly on the jacket wherever the design allows. Leave enough slack that the label can rotate slightly and be removed without pulling. If it slides along a very smooth cable, use a longer paper overlap and secure the paper ends together; do not tighten the loop.

The flag uses a gentle loop at its narrow attachment end. Bring the paper ends together with tape so the cable is held by a loose paper ring, and orient the written tab outward. The flag should not catch on nearby objects. If your desk is crowded, use the lower-profile wrap band instead. Put the same code on both ends of a cable when both ends are accessible and disconnected. If one end is attached to equipment, do not unplug it solely for this craft unless the equipment owner can safely power down and disconnect it; instead label the accessible disconnected end only,

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Test a tiny removable-tape patch on an inconspicuous jacket area and peel it slowly after a short wait.
Wrap the band around the disconnected cable with the text outward and overlap the paper ends loosely; secure paper-to-paper with low-tack tape.
Attach the flag’s narrow loop gently, orient its text tab outward, and compare code with the index before repeating at the other accessible disconnected end.

blocks.body: Disconnect selected cables from both devices and outlets before handling. Never attach labels to live, hot, damaged, frayed, cracked, or loose-plug cords.

blocks.question: A tape test leaves a tacky mark on the cable jacket. What is the best response?
options: Scrape it with scissors until the jacket is clean.
Apply solvent to dissolve the adhesive.
Stop using tape on that cable and place a removable ID on a nearby organizer.
Cover the mark with permanent glue.
blocks.explanation: A reaction is a reason to stop, not to use tools or chemicals on the cable.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Attach labels gently and consistently. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Audit, refine, and store the kit
lessons.summary: Audit, refine, and store the kit

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A labeling kit is only useful when the record and the physical tags agree. Audit each selected cable from the index to one label, then to the other label if present. Read the text aloud or compare each character; a single swapped digit can make the system misleading. If a cable’s destination is uncertain, mark it “unconfirmed” on the card and remove its labels until the identity can be established safely. Do not guess from connector shape alone. The project does not ask you to power equipment or discover unknown wiring.

Inspect the physical fit. Paper should not clamp the jacket, curl into a connector, cover existing warning text, catch on a moving chair, or obstruct ventilation. A tag near a device should remain on the cable itself and outside the device opening. If a label is damp, frayed, or dirty, replace it. Do not laminate with heat, coat in liquid, or add a protective finish. Those changes are outside the simple dry-paper design and can create material or heat hazards. A small envelope or folded paper pocket can store unused blanks and the index card away from moisture.

Make the project easy to maintain by leaving room on the index for a date or a short update note. When a

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trace each code from the index to its physical label and compare the destination word at both ends.
Inspect every label for slack, legibility, connector clearance, and absence of residue or visible jacket change.
Store spare blanks and the index card in a dry paper pocket and note the date of the audit.

blocks.body: Disconnect selected cables from both devices and outlets before handling. Never attach labels to live, hot, damaged, frayed, cracked, or loose-plug cords.

blocks.question: Where should a label sit?
options: Over the connector contacts, where it cannot slip.
Across a device vent to make the code visible.
Around a cable jacket, clear of connectors, strain relief, and openings.
On a camera lens so the cable name is nearby.
blocks.explanation: Labels belong on the cable jacket with generous clearance, not across device functions.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Audit, refine, and store the kit. What did you learn and verify?

name: Decorative Phone-Case Sticker Layout
tagline: Plan and apply an original, balanced sticker composition to a removable smooth phone case.
outcome: Measure a removable case and mark a decoration-safe zone that excludes the camera, ports, vents, buttons, and charging interface.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Decorative Phone-Case Sticker Layout

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Plan and apply an original, balanced sticker composition to a removable smooth phone case. You will measure a safe decoration zone, test a paper layout, apply stickers without covering functional open

lessons.title: Measure the case and define a safe canvas
lessons.summary: Measure the case and define a safe canvas

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A strong layout begins with the empty space that must remain usable. Work with the case detached from the phone so you can see its openings clearly and avoid getting cleaning water near a device. This project assumes a removable case with a smooth, intact back. Stickers often adhere more reliably to a clean, dry, smooth surface than to a greasy, damp, or dusty one; surface preparation guidance also stresses allowing the surface to dry completely before application [1]. Follow the case maker’s own care directions. Do not assume every plastic or flexible finish behaves alike.

For the sample build, imagine a back panel about 150 mm tall and 75 mm wide. The exact phone-case shape may differ, so measure yours rather than forcing these numbers onto it. Keep a clear margin around the perimeter, and trace camera and other openings onto the paper template. Expand those traced shapes into no-decoration zones. Curved edges and corners are especially poor places for tiny sticker tips because handling may catch them. The finished arrangement should feel intentional from arm’s length, not crowded with equal-sized marks everywhere. Decide on one focal sticker, a few supporting shapes, and a smal

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Detach the case, set the phone aside, and measure the back panel’s height and width in millimetres.
On paper, draw the measured outline and copy the camera, flash, port, button, vent, and charging-interface locations; add a 5 mm no-sticker buffer around openings and a 4 mm edge m
Choose one focal sticker, three to five supporting shapes, and two to four small accents, then mark their approximate positions on the paper template.

blocks.body: Remove the case from the phone before measuring, cleaning, or decorating. Never clean or wet the phone itself as part of this project.

blocks.question: Why make a paper template before placing the stickers?
options: It lets you test scale, balance, and opening clearances without committing adhesive.
It guarantees the stickers will never lift.
It proves that the case will protect the phone better.
It lets you cover camera openings temporarily during use.
blocks.explanation: A paper plan is reversible and exposes sizing or obstruction problems before adhesive is used.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Measure the case and define a safe canvas. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build and refine a paper layout
lessons.summary: Build and refine a paper layout

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Before peeling anything, test the design as movable paper shapes. For a 150 × 75 mm sample panel, a focal sticker around 20 × 25 mm could sit in the upper third, slightly off center. Supporting shapes of about 12–18 mm can balance it lower down, with 6–10 mm accents connecting areas without forming a rigid grid. These are starting dimensions, not rules. If your case is smaller, scale the shapes and spacing down while preserving the functional clear zones. A diagonal flow can make a narrow case feel lively; a loose triangle can make a compact group feel stable. Do not align every edge unless that deliberate order suits the design.

Use paper silhouettes or place the actual stickers, still on their backing sheets, over the template. Look at the page from a short distance and rotate it. Notice whether visual weight piles up at one corner, whether the focal element is hidden by neighboring shapes, and whether tiny gaps appear accidental. Give yourself permission to move or remove pieces. A good mock-up is not a promise to copy it exactly; it is a low-risk way to discover conflicts before adhesive is committed. Check every opening one more time, because an attractive arrangement can tem

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut paper silhouettes roughly matching sticker sizes, or place stickers on their backings over the template; begin with the focal shape.
Arrange supporting shapes in an open triangle or gentle diagonal around the focal element, leaving about 3–6 mm between neighboring shapes where space allows.
Add no more than four small accents, then view the template upright, sideways, and from arm’s length; record one revision before deciding the layout is ready.

blocks.body: Remove the case from the phone before measuring, cleaning, or decorating. Never clean or wet the phone itself as part of this project.

blocks.question: Your layout has a 10 mm sticker close to the camera opening. What is the safest next step?
options: Trim the camera edge of the sticker after applying it.
Keep the camera and functional openings inside a no-decoration zone and reposition or omit the sticker.
Cover the opening with clear tape so the sticker looks continuous.
Apply the sticker directly to the phone instead.
blocks.explanation: No decorative piece should intrude into camera, port, vent, control, or charging clearances.

lessons.title: Prepare the case and apply stickers carefully
lessons.summary: Prepare the case and apply stickers carefully

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Only move from planning to the case if its surface is compatible with the sticker adhesive and the case maker permits the cleaning method you plan to use. A gentle wipe with a barely damp cloth and mild soapy water can remove ordinary dirt from some cases, but some finishes should not be washed. Do not use alcohol, oil, adhesive remover, or other chemical cleaners in this beginner project. The cited sticker-preparation guide notes that moisture, oil, and dirt can interfere with adhesion and that a surface should air-dry completely before application [1]. That does not guarantee compatibility with this particular case or sticker.

After cleaning, wait until no dampness remains, then handle the case by its edges. Keep the template nearby and align it with the case outline. Apply one sticker at a time. A useful method is to position one edge first, check the alignment against your template, then lower the rest gradually while smoothing from the attached edge outward with a fingertip or a clean soft cloth. Avoid stretching a flexible case or pulling a sticker taut; tension can encourage edges to lift later. Do not use heat to force a bond, and do not apply a spray or clear coat. If a s

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: If case care instructions allow, wipe the detached case’s back with a soft cloth lightly dampened with mild soapy water; otherwise use a clean dry cloth only.
Let the case air-dry completely, then hold it by the edges and compare it with the template one final time.
Apply the focal sticker first by aligning one edge, lowering it gradually, and smoothing outward with light fingertip pressure; repeat with supporting shapes and accents.

blocks.body: Remove the case from the phone before measuring, cleaning, or decorating. Never clean or wet the phone itself as part of this project.

blocks.question: After permitted gentle cleaning, what should happen before sticker application?
options: Apply stickers while the case is slightly damp so they can slide.
Rub the surface with oil to make it glossy.
Let the case air-dry completely and handle it by the edges.
Warm the case with a heat gun.
blocks.explanation: The opened specialist guide recommends a clean, dry surface and complete air drying; product compatibility still varies [1].

lessons.title: Inspect, refine, and document the result
lessons.summary: Inspect, refine, and document the result

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Give the applied layout a calm final review before reinstalling the case. Confirm every sticker is inside the planned boundary and that no loose corner points toward an opening, side, or grip area where it may be caught. Check the camera view and controls with the case detached: the case must remain an ordinary fitted case, and the stickers must not intrude into its fit or function. Do not test for drops, water resistance, heat resistance, or any other protection. Decoration is not evidence of performance. If a sticker visibly lifts or makes the case awkward to handle, remove it only if the adhesive releases without force and without damaging the surface; otherwise stop using the decorated case and consult the case or sticker maker’s care guidance.

A useful refinement is subtraction. If the composition feels crowded, remove a small accent rather than adding more. If a visual gap looks accidental, move a piece only when it can be repositioned safely under its own product instructions. Recheck the full surface after each change. For the sample design, a good result might contain one 20 × 25 mm original focal shape, four supporting pieces, and three accents, while preserving the meas

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect all sticker edges and compare the design with the marked margins and opening buffers under good light.
Check the detached case’s camera opening, buttons, ports, vents, and charging interface for unobstructed access, then check that the empty case still fits its shape normally.
Write a short design note naming one successful choice and one possible future change; allow any adhesive rest time specified by its maker before normal handling.

blocks.body: Remove the case from the phone before measuring, cleaning, or decorating. Never clean or wet the phone itself as part of this project.

blocks.question: Which layout strategy best supports a clear focal point on a narrow case?
options: Use equal-sized stickers everywhere with no blank space.
Put every accent in the same corner.
Add more pieces until no case color remains visible.
Choose one distinct focal shape, arrange a few supports around it, and leave open space.
blocks.explanation: A limited hierarchy and visible blank areas support a readable arrangement, especially on a small surface.

name: Felt Screen-Cleaning Cloth Holder
tagline: Sew a compact, soft felt pocket that stores one commercially made dry screen-cleaning cloth.
outcome: Measure a commercial cleaning cloth and add a practical allowance for a loose-fitting felt sleeve.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Felt Screen-Cleaning Cloth Holder

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Sew a compact, soft felt pocket that stores one commercially made dry screen-cleaning cloth. The holder is a storage organizer only: it does not clean screens, protect devices, or make craft fabric su

lessons.title: Plan the pocket around the cloth
lessons.summary: Plan the pocket around the cloth

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful holder fits the folded cloth with a little breathing room. Too tight a sleeve makes removal awkward and can drag the cloth across the opening; too loose a sleeve lets the cloth slide out when the holder is carried. Begin with the actual commercial cloth you intend to store, not a guessed universal size. Fold it as you normally would for storage, then measure its width and height. For this sample project, the pocket body is sized for a folded cloth near 8 x 11 cm (3.1 x 4.3 in). If yours differs, use the formula below rather than forcing it to fit.

The front and back are simple rectangles. Add roughly 1 cm (3/8 in) of ease to each cloth dimension, then add 1 cm seam allowance at each side. The finished internal pocket dimensions are therefore approximately cloth width plus 1 cm and cloth height plus 1 cm; each cut piece is about 2 cm wider and 3 cm taller than the folded cloth. The extra height includes the bottom seam and a top opening. These are starting dimensions, not a guarantee: felt thickness and stitch placement affect usable space. Test the paper pattern first.

Choose a felt that is soft but stable and does not shed loose fibers. This project deliberately avoids

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Fold the clean commercial cloth the way you expect to store it; measure the folded width and height in centimetres and write both numbers down.
Draw a paper rectangle using cut width = cloth width + 2 cm, and cut height = cloth height + 3 cm; label the intended top edge.
Place the cloth beside the paper pattern and simulate the pocket by folding the lower section upward; check that the cloth can slide in and out with a little clearance.

blocks.body: Cut away from your body on a clear, stable surface; close scissors when setting them down and keep them away from the table edge.

blocks.question: What is the best starting point for sizing the holder?
options: Guess a common phone size
Measure the commercial cloth in its intended folded shape
Cut felt first and stretch it to fit
Make a sealed pouch regardless of cloth dimensions
blocks.explanation: Measure the cloth in the actual storage fold, then add ease and seam allowance to the pattern.

lessons.title: Mark and cut clean felt pieces
lessons.summary: Mark and cut clean felt pieces

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Once the paper fit is comfortable, use that pattern to make two matching felt rectangles. The back remains full height. The front may be slightly shorter if you want the cloth edge visible and easy to grasp; for this beginner version, cut both pieces the same size and let the back extend about 2 cm above the front when folding the front upward. This creates a simple back tab without a separate flap or fastener. Lay the felt flat rather than pulling it, because stretched or skewed felt can leave edges that do not line up. Trace lightly, or place the pattern on felt and hold it with clips. Avoid marker inks that could bleed or transfer.

Cut along the outside of the marks in a calm, continuous motion. Scissors that are too dull can chew the felt, so pause if the edge becomes ragged. You do not need perfect factory-straight edges: a consistent outline is easier to stitch and inspect than a hurried one. Round the two bottom corners of each rectangle slightly, using a paper coin-sized curve as a guide if helpful. The top edges stay straight and unrounded because they form the pocket mouth.

Before folding, place the felt pieces one on top of the other and compare their edges. If a corne

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Lay the paper pattern on felt, align it with a straight edge when possible, and trace two rectangles or secure the pattern with clips before cutting around it.
Cut each layer on a stable surface, away from your body, then compare the pieces and gently trim only obvious uneven projections.
Rub an offcut gently against clean white paper and inspect for shed fibers or color transfer; remove any loose snippets from the project area.

blocks.body: Cut away from your body on a clear, stable surface; close scissors when setting them down and keep them away from the table edge.

blocks.question: Which edges should be sewn for this simple folded pocket?
options: All four edges including the mouth
Only the top edge
One side only
Both sides and the bottom, leaving the top open
blocks.explanation: The opening must stay unstitched so the cloth can be inserted and removed.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Mark and cut clean felt pieces. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fold, align, and sew the pocket
lessons.summary: Fold, align, and sew the pocket

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The full-size felt rectangles now become a shallow sleeve. Put the intended back piece on the table with its outer face down. Fold the bottom upward to create a pocket front, leaving roughly 2 cm of back above the front. Test the fold with the paper pattern and cloth nearby, but keep the cloth out of the work until the needle is safely put away. The open top must remain unstitched. Align the side edges and bottom corners, then hold the layers with clips near the edge. A clip is safer than placing pins through the future seam, and it can be moved as you sew.

Thread the needle with a manageable length, about 45 cm at a time. Very long thread tangles and frays. Tie a small knot at the end. Starting at one bottom corner, pass the needle through both layers from inside the pocket toward the outside so the knot sits between the felt layers. Use simple straight hand stitches about 5 mm apart, keeping them roughly 4–5 mm from the edge. Each stitch should catch both layers. Consistent spacing matters more than speed. At a corner, make one stitch close to the turn, then rotate the work and continue up the side. Stop when you reach the top of the pocket front.

Do not stitch across the openi

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: With the back piece outer face down, fold the bottom upward to make a pocket front, leaving about 2 cm of back above it; align sides and clip the layers.
Thread a hand needle with about 45 cm of thread, knot the end, and begin at a lower corner by passing the needle through both layers so the knot is between them.
Sew up one side, across the bottom, and up the other side with straight stitches about 5 mm apart and 4–5 mm from the edge; leave the top opening unsewn.
Secure the final stitches at the top end of the side seam, weave the tail between felt layers, trim it short, and return the needle to its dish.

blocks.body: Cut away from your body on a clear, stable surface; close scissors when setting them down and keep them away from the table edge.

blocks.question: You notice loose felt fibers inside before loading the cloth. What should you do?
options: Use the felt sleeve to wipe the device first
Spray the holder with cleaner
Remove loose debris and assess; replace shedding felt rather than risk contaminating the cloth
Hide the fibers by adding glue inside
blocks.explanation: The holder is only a storage organizer. If the felt sheds or transfers color, replace it and keep the commercial cloth separate.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Fold, align, and sew the pocket. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Inspect, fit, and make a storage routine
lessons.summary: Inspect, fit, and make a storage routine

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Before the commercial cloth goes near the sleeve, inspect the finished work under good light. Check all three stitched edges from both sides. Look for missed layers, loose loops, sharp thread ends, felt crumbs, or decorations that could detach. Run a finger along the outer seam only; do not test it against a device screen. The inside should be free of loose debris. If there is a small gap, repair that section with a few hand stitches. If the seam is broadly uneven or the opening is too narrow, remove the relevant stitches and resew; do not force the cloth through.

When the needle and scissors are put away and the holder is clean and dry, fold the commercial cloth to its measured storage shape and slide it into the pocket. It should enter and come out smoothly without scraping, bunching, or needing a hard pull. The sleeve is not meant to seal out dust. Keep it in a clean, dry drawer or bag and avoid carrying it loose with coins, food crumbs, cosmetics, damp items, or craft scraps. If the cloth becomes dirty, follow the cloth maker's care directions and let it dry fully before storing.

Remember the distinction between the holder and the cloth. Felt is the craft material that stores

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect both sides of the empty sleeve for gaps, loops, sharp thread ends, loose felt fibers, and a clear open mouth; repair or remove any snagging thread.
After putting tools away, insert the folded, clean and dry commercial cloth, then remove it once using an ordinary gentle pull.
Choose a clean, dry storage place away from crumbs, loose craft fibers, damp items, heat, and powered devices; write a one-sentence care reminder for the holder.

blocks.body: Cut away from your body on a clear, stable surface; close scissors when setting them down and keep them away from the table edge.

blocks.question: The pocket puckers as you stitch. What is the likely first adjustment?
options: Pull each stitch tighter
Loosen thread tension and use more even spacing
Stretch the felt while sewing
Close the opening with glue
blocks.explanation: Puckering often follows overly tight thread or uneven stitches; carefully redo the affected section with controlled tension.
