name: Foldable Travel Phone Rest
tagline: Build a lightweight, fold-flat tabletop phone rest from corrugated cardboard.
outcome: Measure and mark a consistent cardboard base, back panel, lip, and brace using millimetres.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Foldable Travel Phone Rest

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Build a lightweight, fold-flat tabletop phone rest from corrugated cardboard. A hinged back panel, three-position brace, and low front lip create a simple adjustable display for stationary, non-chargi

lessons.title: Plan the footprint and prepare the board
lessons.summary: Plan the footprint and prepare the board

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful stand starts with a stable footprint, not with a guess about the phone's weight. This design uses a 105 mm wide base that is 145 mm deep. The back panel is 105 × 105 mm and folds at the rear edge of the base. A separate 25 × 115 mm brace swings behind the back panel and fits into one of three slots on the base. A low 105 × 18 mm lip keeps the phone's lower edge from sliding forward. The dimensions are starting points for a typical small phone; the learner should check the intended phone's width and case thickness before cutting. The structure is a tabletop craft object, not a certified stand or protective accessory. Keep the phone unplugged and never use the stand in a vehicle.

Inspect the cardboard first. Corrugations (the wavy inner layer) should be dry and reasonably flat. Make the main base and back panel from one continuous rectangle, 105 × 250 mm. Mark a fold line 145 mm from the front edge; the rear 105 mm becomes the backrest. When the backrest folds up, its lower edge stays connected to the base. The grain direction of the flutes can affect folding. Test a small offcut rather than assuming which direction will crease cleanly. A rounded, gently compressed crease i

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure the phone's width and case thickness, then draw a paper template at that size. Mark the proposed 105 mm base width and 145 mm depth beside it.
Inspect a clean cardboard area and mark one 105 × 250 mm rectangle; mark the transverse fold 145 mm from its front edge.
Prepare the work area, cutting mat, ruler, and blunt scoring tool. Choose scissors for manageable cuts; ask an experienced adult to handle any craft-knife work.
Cut out the continuous rectangle with scissors where practical, then score the 145 mm fold line gently with a blunt tool against a ruler.

blocks.body: This is for dry, indoor, stationary viewing on a stable tabletop only. Never use it in a moving vehicle, on a lap near an edge, or as a mount or load-bearing support.

blocks.question: What is the main job of the shallow front lip?
options: It catches the phone's lower edge on a level tabletop.
It seals the phone against spills.
It holds the stand to a car dashboard.
It covers the phone's charging port.
blocks.explanation: The low lip is a simple stop for stationary tabletop viewing, not a protective or vehicle-mount feature.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the footprint and prepare the board. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build the folding hinge and front lip
lessons.summary: Build the folding hinge and front lip

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The hinge must fold in a predictable direction and tolerate repeated opening without relying on a narrow strip of damaged cardboard. Gently test the scored line. Bend the 105 × 105 mm back panel upward from the base so it forms an obtuse angle rather than being sharply creased flat. If the liner cracks, do not hide the damage under decoration. Lay a strip of paper masking tape across the back of the hinge, centered over the fold, with about 15 mm of tape on each panel. Burnish it with a fingertip or the rounded back of a spoon. The tape acts as a flexible bridge; it does not make the assembly indestructible.

The front lip is a separate 105 × 18 mm strip. Its purpose is only to interrupt forward sliding on a level table. It is not a clamp and should not cover controls or ports. Make the lip by folding its final 6 mm toward itself to create a glue tab. Dry-fit it along the front edge before applying glue. The lip should stand no higher than about 12 mm above the base after its tab is attached. Small, continuous glue coverage on the tab helps avoid a single loose corner, while excess glue can warp paperboard. Press the joint under a flat scrap and light weight during the glue label's

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Fold the back panel upward along the scored line once, then reopen it and inspect the hinge from both sides.
Apply a 105 mm strip of paper masking tape across the rear hinge, centered so roughly 15 mm adheres to each section; smooth without stretching it.
Cut a 105 × 18 mm strip for the front lip and fold a 6 mm glue tab along one long edge; dry-fit it at the front of the base.
Spread a thin layer of craft glue on the tab, attach it to the base's front edge, and press under a flat scrap with light weight until set per label.

blocks.body: This is for dry, indoor, stationary viewing on a stable tabletop only. Never use it in a moving vehicle, on a lap near an edge, or as a mount or load-bearing support.

blocks.question: The hinge liner begins to split during the first fold. What is the best response?
options: Keep folding sharply until it becomes flexible.
Stop flexing and bridge a small split with paper tape on the rear face.
Wet the cardboard until it bends easily.
Cover the front of the phone with tape to hold it still.
blocks.explanation: A small split can be bridged after stopping; extensive damage calls for a replacement base, not more bending.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build the folding hinge and front lip. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Make the adjustable brace and slots
lessons.summary: Make the adjustable brace and slots

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The brace turns the flat base and hinged back panel into a shallow triangular arrangement. Cut a 25 × 115 mm strip from sound cardboard. A single layer may flex, so laminate a second strip of the same size with a thin film of craft glue, align the edges, and let it set under a flat weight. This creates a stiffer craft brace but does not establish a safe load rating. Avoid using a wet phone, heavy object, or forceful lean to test it. A paper phone template is enough for preliminary geometry checks.

Attach the brace to the back panel with a short paper-tape hinge near the panel's upper-middle area. The brace should swing freely and lie flat against the back when the stand folds. It is 115 mm long so its free end can reach a set of three slits in the base while the back panel is angled. Slits are receiving openings, not wide cutouts. Place them on the base centerline, each about 8–10 mm long, at positions 55, 70, and 85 mm forward of the rear hinge. A slit that is too wide lets the brace wobble; one that is too narrow may tear when inserted. Begin with a short opening and widen only a little if needed. Keep every slit away from the base edge and inspect both faces for tears.

The bra

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut two 25 × 115 mm brace strips, align their corrugations in the same direction, and laminate them with a thin coat of craft glue under a flat weight.
Tape one end of the brace to the back panel's rear face, about 35 mm below its top edge, leaving the rest free to swing.
Mark the base centerline and three 8–10 mm slits at 55, 70, and 85 mm forward from the rear hinge; cut each slit carefully on a mat.
Raise the back panel and insert the brace end into the middle slot; test whether it reaches without stretching the hinge or bending the base.

blocks.body: This is for dry, indoor, stationary viewing on a stable tabletop only. Never use it in a moving vehicle, on a lap near an edge, or as a mount or load-bearing support.

blocks.question: Which statement about using the finished rest is accurate?
options: It is suitable for charging if the brace is tight.
It is a drop-tested protective case substitute.
It is for stationary, non-charging viewing on a stable indoor tabletop.
It can be used in a moving vehicle if held firmly.
blocks.explanation: The design is a small tabletop craft object, not a charger stand, vehicle mount, or protective accessory.

lessons.title: Test, refine, and fold for travel
lessons.summary: Test, refine, and fold for travel

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Test the object in stages, beginning with no phone. Put the open rest on a level, dry indoor tabletop. Try each brace position, then gently touch the upper edge of the back panel with one finger. The stand should not slide, collapse, or show a spreading tear under this light check. This is a qualitative craft check, not a load test. If the base rocks, check whether it was cut square and whether glue or tape has created a bump underneath. Correct a small bump by trimming only loose material or repositioning tape. If the stand remains unstable, stop and rebuild the affected panel with larger, sound board.

Next, place the unplugged phone or its paper template behind the lip and against the back panel. Keep hands close enough to catch the phone without pushing the structure. Do not test near a table edge. Try one angle at a time. A screen angle that looks comfortable is not automatically stable; stability comes first. If the phone slips, inspect whether the lip is too short for the phone's case or whether the board is tilted too upright. A wider or slightly taller lip can be remade, but it must not cover ports or controls. Do not add a strap, adhesive to the device, or material over v

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Set the open stand on a level indoor table with no phone; test all three slots using only a gentle fingertip touch at the back panel's top edge.
Place an unplugged phone or its paper template behind the lip and against the backrest, holding near it without pressing down; try the middle slot first.
Compare the other two slots one at a time, then choose the least steep position that gives comfortable viewing and keeps the phone settled.
Fold the brace flat, close the back panel onto the base, and record one successful feature and one planned improvement; inspect the hinge before any later use.

blocks.body: This is for dry, indoor, stationary viewing on a stable tabletop only. Never use it in a moving vehicle, on a lap near an edge, or as a mount or load-bearing support.

blocks.question: Why are the three base slits kept short and narrow?
options: To turn the base into a decorative pattern.
To create small receiving points while preserving more of the base material.
To make room for a charging cable underneath the phone.
To let liquid drain through the cardboard.
blocks.explanation: Short slits are brace sockets. If a slit tears, reinforce or remake the area rather than cutting a large hole.

tagline: Make a compact, adjustable-angle tabletop rest from corrugated cardboard for stationary, non-charging tablet viewing.

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a compact, adjustable-angle tabletop rest from corrugated cardboard for stationary, non-charging tablet viewing. A broad folded base, two side cheeks and a low front stop cradle the tablet withou

lessons.title: Measure, sketch and prove the geometry
lessons.summary: Measure, sketch and prove the geometry

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful stand starts with clearance rather than a guessed universal size. Tablets differ in width, thickness, case shape and button location. Measure the tablet you intend to use, including any case that will remain on it. Do not make the stand fit tightly: a little extra width makes placement easier, while broad contact patches reduce the chance that a rough edge touches the device. The sample plan below suits a tablet up to 24 cm wide and about 1 cm thick. If yours is larger, scale the width and support spacing before cutting; do not assume a larger device is safe just because it fits.

The design uses a 26 cm wide, 18 cm deep base, two triangular side cheeks and a low front lip. The tablet leans against the cheeks at a modest backward angle, and the lip keeps its lower edge from sliding forward. A second, higher pair of rear contact points can be tested using two alternate notches, but this is an adjustment prototype, not a precision hinge. Corrugated board bends more predictably when a fold is deliberately scored; maker guidance also recommends pre-folding score lines and checking corrugation direction when designing cardboard displays [1]. Here the stand is deliberately limit

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure the tablet's outside width and thickness with a ruler; note whether the case is on. Add 2 cm to the measured width for the usable inside span.
On paper draw a 26 x 18 cm base, two side-cheek templates each 11 cm tall by 9 cm deep, and a 26 x 2.5 cm front lip.
Mark an 8 cm front zone on the base and place the cheeks symmetrically, with their front feet 7 cm behind the base's front edge and their rear feet near the back edge.
Tape the paper pieces into a rough upright mock-up and use a paper rectangle matching the device to check viewing angle and lip height.

blocks.body: This design is for stationary, non-charging viewing on a stable tabletop only. Never use it in a vehicle, while walking, on a bed edge or where a fall could injure someone.

blocks.question: A 23 cm-wide tablet has a case that stays on. What inside span should the sample plan use?
options: About 25 cm
Exactly 23 cm
About 18 cm
About 11 cm
blocks.explanation: The plan uses tablet width plus 2 cm for the inside span; dimensions must be based on the cased device.

lessons.title: Transfer the plan and shape the cardboard
lessons.summary: Transfer the plan and shape the cardboard

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Choose a flat panel with intact outer liners. Avoid wet, oily, crushed or sharply creased sections because defects make the two supports behave differently. Corrugated cardboard contains a wavy inner layer called fluting. For these short side cheeks, orient the flutes vertically when the cheek is upright, so the channels run from its bottom toward its top. This is a practical orientation choice, not a strength rating. The top edge of each cheek will meet the tablet's back, while its lower corners sit on the base. Cut two matching pieces from the same panel when possible.

A score is a controlled crease, not a cut through the material. Use a blunt tool along a ruler to compress the fold line, then bend gently away from the scored face. The aim is a clean hinge with both paper liners intact. If the outer liner tears, the fold may become weak or uneven; make a replacement rather than hiding damage with more pressure. Score a small test on scrap first because board thickness and flute spacing vary. Use scissors for thin board if they cut cleanly. For thicker board, adult knife use on a cutting mat is safer than forcing scissors or holding material in the air.

The two cheeks in this pl

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place paper templates on the cardboard and trace the 26 x 18 cm base, two 11 x 9 cm triangular cheeks, and the 26 x 2.5 cm lip; mark a centreline on the base.
Cut parts on a mat using scissors for thin board or an adult's craft knife and ruler for thick board; for a knife, use several light passes with the blade directed away from hands
On scrap, press a blunt scoring tool along a ruler to make one shallow line; fold the sample slowly and inspect both liners.
Mark and lightly score the base's two side fold lines 1 cm from each long edge, then fold each narrow edge upward only enough to make a shallow boundary rail.

blocks.question: What should you do before scoring the real support piece?
options: Press hard with a knife blade
Test moderate blunt-tool pressure on scrap
Soak the fold line
Fold sharply without a crease

blocks.body: A sleeve should fit the particular object without squeezing it. Portable batteries vary in shape, so the worked example is a starting point, not a universal template. lessons.title: Join the panels and turn the lining

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: Hand stitching is slow but gives a beginner direct control. Thread a needle with a manageable length, about 45–60 cm, and knot one end. Use a small, even running stitch along the 12 mm seam line. A stitch about 3–4 mm long is a useful target; keep spacing consistent and avoid pulling so hard that the fabric puckers. On the lining panel, stitch the sides and bottom while leaving the marked 50 mm turning gap open. Secure thread at both ends of that gap so the seam does not unravel during turning. On the outer panel, stitch the sides and bottom continuously. Backstitch a few stitches at the start and finish of each seam for security. Join the outer and lining at the top by placing their upper edges together and sewing across, aligning side seams carefully. Keep the opening unobstructed. Before turning, inspect every seam from the wrong side. Small gaps can be repaired now with a few close stitches. Clip only the bulky seam allowance at corners, stopping several millimetres before the stitches; never cut the stitching. Turn the assembly slowly through the lining gap. Ease fabric through with fingers and use a capped, blunt tool gently to define corners. Do not use a sharp point. After

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Hand-sew the lining panel sides and bottom on the 12 mm line with 3–4 mm running stitches, leaving the marked 50 mm gap open and securing thread at each gap end.
Sew the outer panel sides and bottom on the same 12 mm seam line, using short backstitches at the start and finish.
Align the outer and lining top edges right sides together, match side seams, and stitch across the top edge without closing the mouth.
Check seams, trim only bulky corner allowance without cutting stitches, turn through the lining gap, and close that gap with folded-in edges and small stitches.

Slide the battery in and out once without pressing on buttons, ports, or corners. It should enter and leave freely. Remove it immediately if there is resistance, and enlarge or remake the sleeve rather than forcing it. Remove the battery again after the fit check. This object is not meant to cushion drops or shield heat, and no performance claim follows from the presence of fabric or filler. Gently slide the cool, disconnected, undamaged battery into the sleeve once, then remove it; stop immediately if it catches or needs force.

blocks.explanation: A three-sided paperboard pocket supports the image from behind and keeps its top edge accessible.

lessons.title: Attach the easel and test the display
lessons.summary: Attach the easel and test the display

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The display stands on a broad cardboard kickstand, not on a narrow pointed tab. Cut a cardboard rectangle about 3 by 6 inches. Fold it lengthwise at the 3-inch midpoint to make two 3-by-3-inch halves. One half attaches to the back of the display; the other opens outward as a support leg. The fold is a hinge, so score only the cardboard surface lightly with the blunt back of a spoon or a pencil shaft; do not use a blade. A shallow crease helps the panel fold while leaving its outer layer intact. If the cardboard cracks, use a fresh piece.

Position the stand vertically on the rear centerline, with its top edge about 1 inch below the top of the frame. Glue one half flat to the backing, leaving the free half able to open. Reinforce the attached half with two whole craft sticks placed horizontally across it, one near the top and one near the bottom. Keep the sticks entirely on the stand flap and backing, never across the fold. Let all adhesive set. Open the free flap to a moderate angle, around 25 to 35 degrees from the backing, and place the display on a clear level tabletop. Adjust the angle before the glue is fully cured if needed.

Testing is gentle and limited: the object should r

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut a 3-by-6-inch cardboard rectangle and fold it across the 3-inch midpoint; make a light crease with a pencil shaft or spoon back without cutting through the outer layer.
Center one half vertically on the back, about 1 inch below the top edge, and glue it flat; reinforce that attached half with two horizontal whole sticks, avoiding the fold line.
After adhesive has set, open the free flap about 25 to 35 degrees, place the display on a stable tabletop and insert the photo through the top slot.

blocks.body: Use intact, smooth craft sticks only. Do not cut or snap wooden sticks in this project; reject splintered, cracked or moldy pieces.

blocks.question: The display leans backward on a level table. What is the best first adjustment?
options: Hang it from a nail
Add a heavy weight to the frame
Push hard on the frame until it bends
Open the free kickstand flap farther and retest gently
blocks.explanation: Adjust the cardboard support geometry on a stable surface; if it remains unstable, relocate it or repair the backing rather than adding load.

name: Painted Empty-Jar Desk Vase
tagline: Turn a clean, empty glass food jar into a small dry-indoor desk vase with a simple color-blocked landscape.
outcome: Select an intact, stable jar and explain why a dry-display use is appropriate for an untested painted surface.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Painted Empty-Jar Desk Vase

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Turn a clean, empty glass food jar into a small dry-indoor desk vase with a simple color-blocked landscape. The design uses paint intended for glass, a paper sizing guide, and a removable paper collar

lessons.title: Choose the jar and map the design
lessons.summary: Choose the jar and map the design

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Begin with the finished use, not with paint. This small jar is a dry desk accent, so select a shape that can stand without rocking and leave enough opening for one or two dried stems. A jar close to 7 cm across and 11 cm tall gives a useful upright silhouette without becoming a heavy centerpiece. Reject any jar with a crack, a chip, a sharp lip, a damaged base, or a smell that remains after washing. Do not attempt to repair damaged glass.

The sample design has a painted lower field and two quiet landscape bands near the shoulder. Keep the mouth and bottom ring clear. This preserves a clean handling edge and lets the jar sit directly on its glass base rather than on a painted ridge. Measure around the widest straight body with flexible tape; if you have only a ruler, wrap a paper strip around once, mark the overlap, then measure the strip flat. The circumference tells you how much guide paper is needed.

Wash using mild dish soap and water, rinse, and let the jar dry completely. A damp or greasy surface can make paint slide or form bare spots. Never use heat to hurry drying. Make a paper template first: it is easier to correct a paper line than to scrape at paint on glass. Plan two

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect the empty jar under bright light, checking the rim, body, and base. Choose a stable jar near 7 cm wide and 11 cm tall.
Wash with mild dish soap and water, rinse thoroughly, then air-dry mouth-down on a clean towel until no moisture remains.
Measure the straight body circumference and mark a paper strip at that length; note a 6 cm-high painted field beginning 2 cm above the base.
Sketch a broad lower color field and two simple curved hill bands on the guide; choose two colors with visible contrast.

blocks.body: Inspect the jar in good light before and after washing. Do not use glass with cracks, chips, sharp edges, or damage around its mouth; do not sand, cut, or modify glass.

blocks.question: Which jar is the safest starting choice for this desk vase?
options: A jar with an intact rim and flat, stable base
A chipped jar if the chip faces the wall
A cracked jar if paint will cover the crack
A jar that rocks slightly but looks attractive
blocks.explanation: Inspect all glass surfaces and the base before crafting. Decoration cannot make damaged or unstable glass safe.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Choose the jar and map the design. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Prepare boundaries and apply the first color
lessons.summary: Prepare boundaries and apply the first color

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The goal is controlled coverage, not a thick shell. Glass is smooth, so use only paint whose label names glass as a suitable surface, and use it exactly as directed. This course does not prescribe sanding, oven curing, or a generic clear sealer: these can create dust, heat stress, or unsupported durability expectations. Keep the paint manufacturer's product instructions beside the work area. If a product requires a method, ventilation, or equipment you cannot provide, do not use it; select a simpler compatible craft paint.

Place the dry jar upright on a protected table. Mark the lower edge of the design from your guide. Low-tack tape can help create a straight horizontal edge, but tape adhesive can pull a fragile coat if removed late or forcefully. Press only the edge lightly and test on a small inconspicuous area if the label and surface permit. Paint the broad lower field in one direction using a soft brush and a thin coat. Brush from the shoulder down toward the base, stopping above the base contact ring. Rotate the jar by its clear neck, not by touching wet paint.

Let the first coat dry as the label specifies. A thin coat may look translucent; that is not a reason to lay on a

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cover the table, set the jar upright, and apply low-tack tape along the lower boundary about 2 cm above the base.
Stir the glass-compatible water-based paint as its label directs, then brush a thin coat over the lower field, stopping short of the base ring.
Leave the jar upright in a dust-free place for the full label-specified interval before touching or adding another coat.
Add a second thin coat in the same field only if the first coat is dry and the color still looks patchy; remove tape gently as directed by the paint label.

blocks.body: Inspect the jar in good light before and after washing. Do not use glass with cracks, chips, sharp edges, or damage around its mouth; do not sand, cut, or modify glass.

blocks.question: Why should the outside jar be fully dry before painting?
options: Wet glass makes the paint glow brighter
Moisture can cause paint to slide or leave bare spots
Drying prevents the jar from becoming glass
The paint must be mixed with water on the glass
blocks.explanation: Wash away residue, rinse, and dry completely so moisture does not disrupt the paint layer.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Prepare boundaries and apply the first color. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Add the landscape bands and refine edges
lessons.summary: Add the landscape bands and refine edges

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A simple landscape can look intentional without precise illustration. Use the guide to locate two broad bands near the top of the painted field. The sample places a muted middle band about 1 cm tall and a narrow accent band about 5 mm tall, leaving some of the lower color visible. Those measurements are design targets, not a requirement to measure every brushstroke. The main aim is visual balance: the wider lower field anchors the vase, and the two smaller bands provide a transition toward clear glass.

Before painting on the jar, practice a few curved strokes on scrap paper. Hold the brush comfortably and turn the jar slowly with your free hand while keeping the brush in place; this often produces a smoother horizontal line than reaching around the whole circumference. Keep the jar on the protected tabletop and do not lift it while paint is wet. Use very little paint on the brush. A dab of color can be widened after it dries, but a thick wet ridge can slump and is harder to correct.

If you want the hill effect, let one side of the middle band rise by about 1 cm, then descend gradually. Continue the line around the jar at roughly the same height. The far edge need not meet perfect

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On scrap paper, practice two gentle curved strokes and mark the planned middle band about 1 cm tall on the guide.
After the lower field is dry, paint the middle band around the jar, turning the jar gradually while keeping the brush lightly loaded.
When the middle band meets its recoat condition, add a narrower accent band roughly 5 mm tall or leave the glass clear for a quieter design.
Rotate the dry-enough jar slowly and inspect every side; remove allowed tape gently, then make only small dry-surface corrections.

blocks.body: Inspect the jar in good light before and after washing. Do not use glass with cracks, chips, sharp edges, or damage around its mouth; do not sand, cut, or modify glass.

blocks.question: What is the best response if the first paint coat looks translucent?
options: Apply one very thick coat immediately
Heat the jar in an oven
Wait the label-specified interval, then add a thin coat if needed
Pour clear sealer inside the jar
blocks.explanation: Allow each layer to dry as directed. If opacity is still needed, add a second thin exterior coat.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Add the landscape bands and refine edges. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Dry, inspect, and set up the desk display
lessons.summary: Dry, inspect, and set up the desk display

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Finishing means checking suitability, not claiming a coating is indestructible. Leave the completed jar undisturbed for the paint label's full drying or curing period. Dry-to-touch and fully cured can mean different things, so follow the stated wording and time. Do not stack objects inside it, wash it, expose it to water, or use heat to accelerate curing. A clear craft sealer is optional only when a product label explicitly says it is compatible with the selected paint and glass; it does not turn this dry-display project into a waterproof vase. The simplest safe finish is often to stop after the paint dries.

Check that the jar still sits flat on the table. Look for loose edges, wet-looking patches, drips, and contact between paint and the base. If paint has reached the base ring, leave the jar stationary until dry and choose a different flat location for display rather than trying to pry paint off with a sharp tool. If paint remains tacky beyond label guidance, keep it away from children and pets and follow the label's cleanup or disposal instructions. Do not put dried stems into a jar with a narrow mouth if forcing them could chip the rim. Trim stems away from the jar, not over i

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Leave the vase undisturbed through the paint label's stated drying or curing period, with airflow and no direct heat.
Inspect for cracks, chips, loose paint, drips, and a flat base; keep the jar stationary while checking its painted body.
Choose a level indoor desk spot away from moisture and edges, then display the empty jar or place one or two dried stems inside without forcing them.
Record one successful feature and one specific improvement idea, such as narrowing the accent band on a future jar.

blocks.body: Inspect the jar in good light before and after washing. Do not use glass with cracks, chips, sharp edges, or damage around its mouth; do not sand, cut, or modify glass.

blocks.question: Which use matches the limits of this course project?
options: Hold water for a fresh bouquet
Store snacks after sealing the interior
Serve as a drinking glass after the paint dries
Display empty or with a few dry stems indoors
blocks.explanation: The finish and jar are not certified for food or water contact. Use it only as a dry indoor decoration.

name: Air-Dry-Clay Ring Dish
tagline: Shape a small, softly irregular ring dish from air-dry clay, refine its shallow basin and rim, dry it patiently, then add a simple original painted pattern.
outcome: Measure and portion a clay blank about 110 mm across and maintain a nearly even 6–7 mm wall and floor thickness.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Air-Dry-Clay Ring Dish

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Shape a small, softly irregular ring dish from air-dry clay, refine its shallow basin and rim, dry it patiently, then add a simple original painted pattern. The finished object is a decorative dry-sto

lessons.title: Plan the scale and prepare a workable blank
lessons.summary: Plan the scale and prepare a workable blank

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A successful small dish starts with a simple profile rather than decoration. This project aims for an outside diameter near 110 mm, a low rim about 12–16 mm above the center, and clay thickness close to 6–7 mm. These are design targets, not factory tolerances. A nearly even thickness matters because a thick center and very thin lip lose moisture at different rates and can distort or crack. A shallow dish is also easier to shape and less likely to become a brittle, steep-sided cup.

Choose a clear board and a smooth bowl whose inside diameter is about 100 mm. The bowl only supports the clay while it takes shape; it is not part of the finished object. Cover it with plastic so the clay can be lifted without pulling at its damp surface. Keep unused clay wrapped while you work. Clay that begins to feel stiff or develop a dry skin is harder to smooth, and forcing it can create splits.

Use the ruler as a guide, not as a reason to repeatedly press and thin the clay. Roll from the center outward with gentle, even passes, turning the board rather than stretching one side. If you see an edge that is much thinner than the middle, pause and even it out while the clay is still workable. A softl

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Clear the board, set out the ruler, bowl, plastic and roughly 180 g of clay, then sketch a motif on paper.
Knead the clay briefly until it feels uniformly pliable, then keep the unused portion wrapped.
Roll a slab to about 6–7 mm thick and roughly 115 mm wide, turning the board between passes.

blocks.body: Read the specific clay and paint packaging and follow its age, ventilation, cleanup and disposal directions; do not eat or taste materials, and wash hands after working.

blocks.question: What thickness is the target for the rolled clay blank?
options: About 6–7 mm
About 1 mm
About 25 mm
Any thickness is equally suitable
blocks.explanation: Roll near 6–7 mm and check more than one area; consistent thickness is more useful than exact precision.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the scale and prepare a workable blank. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Shape a shallow basin and refine its rim
lessons.summary: Shape a shallow basin and refine its rim

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The bowl support gives the slab a predictable curve, but pressure control creates the finished profile. Place the clay over the plastic-covered support with its center aligned to the bowl. Use the flat of your fingers to coax the middle downward and the outside upward in small increments. The dish should have a broad, gentle basin, not a sharp crease where the floor meets the rim. A crease is a stress point and can also look like an accidental fold after drying.

Work around the circumference rather than pushing one side all the way up at once. This distributes the curve and helps the rim stay level. Check from tabletop height; a rim that rises dramatically on one side can make rings slide toward the low side. Slight variation in the edge is part of the handmade look, but the dish should sit with its base centered and not tip when the support is removed later. Keep the rim low. A height around 12–16 mm above the center is enough to make a visual boundary for rings without turning the object into a deep vessel.

Smooth with a fingertip that is only slightly damp. Too much water can make the surface slick and soft, and may leave one patch wetter than another. Blend shallow finger mar

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Lay the slab over the plastic-covered bowl and center it, then press the middle down with broad fingertip pressure.
Raise the outer 15–20 mm gradually around the bowl until the rim is about 12–16 mm above the center.
Smooth finger marks with a barely damp fingertip and blend any tiny split with a pea-sized crumb of same-clay slip only as needed.

blocks.body: Read the specific clay and paint packaging and follow its age, ventilation, cleanup and disposal directions; do not eat or taste materials, and wash hands after working.

blocks.question: How should the dish be dried?
options: In direct sunlight so it finishes quickly
At room temperature, away from direct heat and sun
In an oven on a low setting
Beside an open flame
blocks.explanation: Use a shaded room-temperature location and wait longer rather than forcing a faster dry.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Shape a shallow basin and refine its rim. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Dry slowly and judge readiness
lessons.summary: Dry slowly and judge readiness

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Air-dry clay loses water as it sits, and a craft piece may shrink slightly. Uneven thickness or a sudden hot, sunny drying spot can make one region change faster than another. That difference can pull the form out of shape or contribute to cracks. Let the dish dry gradually at ordinary room temperature, away from direct sun, heaters, radiators, open windows with strong drafts, and flame. The exact time depends on the clay, thickness and room conditions, so use the stated time only as a planning guide. A small dish may feel firm within a day but can still hold moisture inside.

Allow the form to become stable on its support before moving it. Then lift it with both hands beneath the base rather than pinching the lip. Place it on a clean, level surface where air can reach it. If it is still damp and the underside is against the table, reposition it carefully when it can hold its shape so that the underside also has a chance to dry. Never flex a stiffening dish to test it; that can create a crack.

Look for changes, not a single magic test. A damp area may look darker or feel cooler than the rest. The piece should be uniformly dry in appearance and feel before painting. If there is dou

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Leave the dish supported in a shaded, room-temperature place until it is firm enough to move without bending.
Lift the dish with both hands under its base and move it to a level, clean drying surface; reposition carefully later if the underside remains damp.
Wait until color and feel are uniform throughout, inspect for cracks and stability, and extend drying time whenever uncertain.

blocks.body: Read the specific clay and paint packaging and follow its age, ventilation, cleanup and disposal directions; do not eat or taste materials, and wash hands after working.

blocks.question: Which use matches this project's intended boundary?
options: A tabletop place for a few dry rings
A bowl for snacks
A cup for water
A holder for wet cosmetics
blocks.explanation: Keep the finished object indoors and dry; it is not a serving dish, cup or washable container.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Dry slowly and judge readiness. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Paint, review and set dry-use boundaries
lessons.summary: Paint, review and set dry-use boundaries

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Only decorate the dish after it is fully dry. Put paper under it and use a small amount of craft acrylic paint. A simple design often looks more intentional than filling every area: for example, paint a narrow muted band near one edge, then add three spaced dots in a second color. Leave some natural clay visible so the shallow form remains easy to read. Keep the pattern original and geometric; this course does not use branded characters or copied artwork.

Use a soft brush and thin coats. A thick coat can obscure the surface and may dry unevenly. Let one color dry before adding another, following the paint label. If paint beads or rubs off, stop and check whether the clay is truly dry and whether the paint is suitable for the surface. Do not scrub the clay or add more water. You may choose to leave a small test area unpainted until you know the first coat adheres.

An optional craft sealer can change sheen and reduce ordinary surface scuffing, but it does not turn air-dry clay into a waterproof or food-safe material. If using one, confirm it is compatible with your paint and clay, use it according to its label, and allow full drying with appropriate ventilation. Skipping sealer is

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place fully dry clay on paper and apply a thin first coat of one or two craft acrylic colors using the planned simple motif.
Let each coat dry as its label directs, then add optional compatible craft sealer only if desired and label directions can be followed.
Set the dish on a stable indoor tabletop, test that it rests steadily, and use it only for a few clean, dry rings.

blocks.body: Read the specific clay and paint packaging and follow its age, ventilation, cleanup and disposal directions; do not eat or taste materials, and wash hands after working.

blocks.question: A rim develops a small split while still pliable. What is the best first response?
options: Add a large puddle of water and rub hard
Bake it to close the split
Gently press the split together and blend with minimal same-clay slip if needed
Pull the rim outward until the split disappears
blocks.explanation: Use light pressure and minimal moisture, then support the form and dry gradually.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Paint, review and set dry-use boundaries. What did you learn and verify?

name: Fabric-Wrapped Storage Box
tagline: Turn a clean, sturdy small cardboard box into a tidy tabletop organizer with a removable fabric identity and neatly finished edges.
outcome: Measure a rectangular box and calculate fabric allowances for its base, walls, and folded top edges.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Fabric-Wrapped Storage Box

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Turn a clean, sturdy small cardboard box into a tidy tabletop organizer with a removable fabric identity and neatly finished edges. This course teaches measuring, dry fitting, folding, gluing in manag

lessons.title: Choose, measure, and plan the wrap
lessons.summary: Choose, measure, and plan the wrap

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A clean result starts with a box whose shape is predictable. Choose a small open-top box with four straight walls and a flat bottom. Check that the bottom sits on a table without rocking and that each wall remains upright when you gently touch it. This is a light-duty craft container, so reject a box that is soft, wet, crushed, stained, musty, or held together by staples. Removing a lid is fine only when the box can remain square afterward; do not reinforce it in a way that disguises structural damage.

For the sample box, target inside dimensions are 18 cm long, 13 cm wide, and 8 cm high. Measure the outside length and width too: wall thickness means the inside and outside numbers differ. The wrap calculation uses the outside footprint. If the outside length is 18.6 cm and outside width is 13.6 cm, the fabric traveling around the outside perimeter needs 2 × (18.6 + 13.6) = 64.4 cm, plus a 2 cm overlap allowance, so cut length 66.4 cm. To cover the bottom and fold over the rim into the inside, use width equal to box height + inside depth allowance + bottom allowance: 8 + 2 + 2 = 12 cm. This narrow band method leaves the broad interior cardboard visible; the optional liner finishes

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect the empty box, measure its outside length and width and inside depth, and record the numbers in centimetres.
Calculate perimeter plus a 2 cm seam overlap; calculate strip width as wall height plus 2 cm for the inside turn and 2 cm for the bottom turn.
Lay the fabric flat, smooth it without stretching, mark the calculated rectangle with pencil or removable tape, and cut one test paper template first.

blocks.body: Use this project as a dry indoor organizer for lightweight objects only. It is not load-bearing furniture, a stool, a step, a toy safety device, or a protective shipping container.

blocks.question: For an outer band traveling around a box, which measurement determines the needed strip length?
options: Add outside length and outside width once, with no overlap
Use twice the sum of outside length and width, then add a small overlap
Use inside length multiplied by box height
Cut fabric until it stretches around the box
blocks.explanation: The outer strip follows the perimeter 2 × (outside length + outside width), plus the planned overlap. Verify with a paper dry fit.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Choose, measure, and plan the wrap. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Dry-fit and prepare clean folds
lessons.summary: Dry-fit and prepare clean folds

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Dry-fitting means arranging materials in their final positions before glue is opened. It is the best moment to catch a reversed pattern, an awkward seam, or a corner that gathers too much cloth. Put the box on the paper template and mark the four corner lines. At each corner, the fabric must transition from one wall to the next without a thick wad. For the side-band method, keep a small square of fabric at each bottom corner rather than cutting right to the cardboard corner. A short relief cut lets the bottom flap turn without pulling the side band out of position; stopping 3–5 mm short of the corner leaves enough material to hide the cut edge in the fold.

If you want a fully fabric-covered inside, make a separate liner from paper first, then use it as a pattern for fabric. A simple liner has a base rectangle and four walls; its tabs overlap at the corners. Do not rely on a snug fabric liner to strengthen a weak box. The sample course uses the paper/card liner option, which adds a clean-looking interior without thick extra fabric. Test the paper liner dry and trim it until it sits flat with no buckling.

Before gluing, choose the orientation of any woven pattern. Decide where the

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Wrap the paper template around the box and mark the back seam and all four vertical corner lines.
Mark shallow corner reliefs where the bottom and wall turns meet; cut only the paper template, stopping a few millimetres short of each corner.
Dry-fit the fabric strip with the overlap at the back and mark an unobtrusive inside edge; test the optional paper liner separately.

blocks.body: Use this project as a dry indoor organizer for lightweight objects only. It is not load-bearing furniture, a stool, a step, a toy safety device, or a protective shipping container.

blocks.question: Why should a paper corner template be tested before cutting fabric?
options: Paper strengthens the box permanently
It makes the adhesive dry faster
It reveals where folds and relief cuts will land before the fabric is committed
It proves the box can hold heavy objects
blocks.explanation: A paper test fit is low-cost and adjustable. It helps locate seam and fold lines before glue or fabric cutting.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Dry-fit and prepare clean folds. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Attach the fabric in controlled sections
lessons.summary: Attach the fabric in controlled sections

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Use the adhesive only if its label permits paper or fabric craft use and the work surface is ventilated as directed. Test a small dab on a fabric offcut and scrap cardboard. Let the test set according to the label and check for visible staining, stiff patches, or poor adhesion. If the test is unsatisfactory, stop and choose a compatible water-based craft adhesive; do not add more glue to hide a stain. White craft glue can wet thin fabric or warp cardboard when used heavily, so spread a thin, even film only over the next small working area. A small glue spreader gives more control than squeezing a thick line.

Begin at the back seam. Apply glue to a short section of the box wall, press the fabric into place from the center outward, and smooth with clean fingers or the back of a spoon. Do not pull hard: tension can bow the cardboard or distort the weave. Work around one wall at a time. At corners, fold the fabric as if wrapping a small gift: one flap lies flat, and the neighboring flap turns over it. Trim only excess hidden inside the fold, keeping enough cloth to cover the cardboard edge. A helper may hold the box steady, but no one should touch wet adhesive and then handle food or

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Test the selected labelled craft glue on a fabric offcut and scrap cardboard, then wait for the label's stated set or drying interval.
Spread a thin film on one short back-wall section, place the fabric, and smooth from the center toward both edges without stretching.
Continue one wall at a time, folding at each corner and using the template reliefs as guides; turn 2 cm over the rim and under the base.
Fit and attach the optional paper liner only after the outer wrap has dried as directed; smooth it from the center of the base outward.

blocks.body: Use this project as a dry indoor organizer for lightweight objects only. It is not load-bearing furniture, a stool, a step, a toy safety device, or a protective shipping container.

blocks.question: The glue test patch makes the cotton look dark and stiff. What is the best next action?
options: Apply a thicker layer so the stain is even
Heat the fabric until the spot disappears
Switch to a solvent adhesive without testing
Stop, consult the label, and test a compatible water-based craft adhesive on a fresh offcut
blocks.explanation: A stained or stiff test is a warning. Stop and choose a label-compatible product, then test again rather than masking the effect.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Attach the fabric in controlled sections. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Dry, inspect, and refine the organizer
lessons.summary: Dry, inspect, and refine the organizer

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Set the box on a protected, level surface and leave it undisturbed for the full adhesive-label drying time. A box that feels dry at one edge may still be damp under a folded seam. Do not stack objects on it, close it in an airtight container, or put it near heat to speed drying. When dry, inspect every surface in good light. Look for glue visible on the fabric, lifting corners, loose raw edges, softened cardboard, skewed walls, and an unstable base. Check the inside as well as the outside because a rough fold can snag paper or fingers. If an edge lifts, use only a tiny amount of compatible glue under that edge if the label allows, press it with a clean scrap of paper, and allow the full drying interval again.

Test the box on a stable tabletop with a few lightweight paper items or fabric scraps. Do not test by standing on it, dropping it, carrying heavy objects, or using it as a safety container. Its intended job is simple organization, not protection. Keep it dry and away from heat. Do not use it for food, cosmetics, liquids, batteries, or active electronics. If it is used to hold a disconnected cable or accessory, keep the accessory unplugged and disconnected.

A label can improv

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Leave the finished box undisturbed on a level protected surface for the adhesive label's full drying time.
Inspect corners, rim, seam, base, liner, and wall alignment in good light; correct only small loose edges with compatible glue and a fresh drying period.
Place a few lightweight dry paper items inside on a stable tabletop, then label the intended use and record actual dimensions.

blocks.body: Use this project as a dry indoor organizer for lightweight objects only. It is not load-bearing furniture, a stool, a step, a toy safety device, or a protective shipping container.

blocks.question: How should a slight fabric wrinkle be handled while the adhesive is still repositionable according to its label?
options: Gently lift the area and smooth from its center outward without stretching
Pull hard on both ends until it is taut
Cut the wrinkle out while the fabric is attached
Pour water on the wrinkle
blocks.explanation: Only reposition when the product instructions allow it. Smooth gently; if it has set, allow drying and assess rather than forcing it.

name: Cardboard Mini Keepsake Cabinet
tagline: Make a small, dry indoor display cabinet from clean corrugated cardboard.
outcome: Measure and mark a consistent 18 × 24 × 10 cm cabinet body with a shallow base, top, sides, and back.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Cardboard Mini Keepsake Cabinet

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a small, dry indoor display cabinet from clean corrugated cardboard. The sample cabinet measures 18 cm wide, 24 cm tall, and 10 cm deep, with two shallow shelves, a hinged front door, and a simpl

lessons.title: Plan the cabinet and mark the panels
lessons.summary: Plan the cabinet and mark the panels

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Start by choosing clean, flat cardboard. Corrugated board has a fluted inner layer between two paper faces; it is stiffer in one direction than another. For this small upright cabinet, keep the corrugations running vertically in the two side walls and back where possible. That orientation helps the walls resist their own slight bending. The design uses a simple open-front box rather than a complex miniature door frame: the front door will overlap the opening and attach to one side with a flexible paper hinge. This leaves fewer delicate cutouts and makes the first build easier to align.

The target outside size is about 18 cm wide, 24 cm high, and 10 cm deep. Panel thickness varies, so these are planning dimensions rather than a precision tolerance. Make a back panel 18 × 24 cm. Make two sides 10 × 24 cm, and top and bottom panels each 18 × 10 cm. The top and bottom fit between the side walls; when assembled, the outside width may be close to 18 cm depending on how you place the joints. If your board is unusually thick, prioritize a square opening and matching side depth over chasing an exact outside measurement. The door is 18.5 × 24.5 cm so it can overlap the opening by a small ma

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Choose a clean, dry cardboard sheet and identify the direction of its corrugations by looking at an exposed edge. Mark the direction on a scrap diagram.
Draw a panel plan for a back 18 × 24 cm, two sides 10 × 24 cm, and top and bottom 18 × 10 cm. Label inside faces and intended flute direction.
Measure, mark, and cut the five body panels, then mark a 18.5 × 24.5 cm door and two 16 × 8.5 cm shelves on spare board or thin card.

blocks.body: This is a small dry indoor decorative craft, not load-bearing furniture, a toy tested for children, or a protective device. Place it on a stable tabletop and keep it away from edges, heat, water, and active play.

blocks.question: Why is it helpful to dry-fit the cabinet panels before applying glue?
options: It reveals alignment or size problems while the parts are still easy to adjust.
It makes cardboard waterproof.
It proves the cabinet can hold heavy objects.
It eliminates the need to let glue dry.
blocks.explanation: Arrange all body pieces without adhesive first, check the opening and edges, and correct mismatches before assembly.

lessons.title: Build a square, reinforced body
lessons.summary: Build a square, reinforced body

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Assemble the body with the back panel flat on the table and the front facing upward. The two side walls stand on the back panel, and the top and bottom bridge between them. Dry-fit the parts before applying glue. This means arranging the pieces with no adhesive to see whether their edges meet and whether the open front remains rectangular. A dry fit is a useful checkpoint because glue reduces the time available to correct a twist. If one side is taller or a top edge is slanted, correct the cut now.

The cabinet does not need a hidden frame. Instead, add narrow card tabs inside the corners: cut eight strips about 2 × 8 cm, fold each lengthwise, and place one leg against each adjoining surface. The tabs spread the glued connection over more area and help the joint stay aligned. Apply a thin continuous layer of white craft glue rather than a puddle. Press the tab into the corner and hold it with gentle masking tape while it dries. Tape is a temporary clamp, not the permanent joint. Build the side-to-back joints first, then add the top and bottom. Keep the front edges even so the door can close without catching.

For the base, glue a second 18 × 10 cm layer underneath the bottom panel,

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Dry-fit the back, sides, top, and bottom on a flat surface, checking that the sides stand at right angles and the front opening stays clear.
Fold eight 2 × 8 cm thin-card strips lengthwise. Glue two strips inside each rear corner and one strip at each top and bottom side joint, using light tape to hold parts still.
Glue a second 18 × 10 cm base layer under the cabinet bottom with its flute direction turned across the first layer; set the body upright on a flat table to dry.

blocks.body: This is a small dry indoor decorative craft, not load-bearing furniture, a toy tested for children, or a protective device. Place it on a stable tabletop and keep it away from edges, heat, water, and active play.

blocks.question: Which shelf-support placement best helps make a level shelf?
options: Put one support higher so the shelf drains toward the door.
Measure both left and right marks from the same inside-bottom reference.
Place supports by eye and add more glue if the shelf rocks.
Attach one support only and balance the shelf on it.
blocks.explanation: Matching measurements from a common bottom edge is more reliable than estimating by eye.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build a square, reinforced body. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Add shelves, a hinge, and a simple door
lessons.summary: Add shelves, a hinge, and a simple door

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Plan the shelf heights before gluing anything inside. Measure upward from the inside bottom and make two pencil marks for shelf levels, for example 8 cm and 15.5 cm. The openings will not be identical after allowing for board thickness, and that is acceptable. Keep both marks level by measuring from the same bottom edge at the left and right sides. A shelf that slopes can let paper keepsakes slide, so compare the paired marks with a straight ruler. Cut shelf supports from thin card: four strips about 1.5 × 8 cm. Glue one support at each side wall for each shelf, placing the top of each support on the marked line. Let supports set before resting the shelf on them. A short paper lip on the shelf front helps prevent a flat token from slipping forward, but it is not a safety rail for small objects.

The door is a flat panel, not a fitted cabinet door with hardware. Lay it over the opening and confirm that it covers the edges while swinging clear of the body. Make a paper hinge from a 3 × 20 cm strip of sturdy paper or thin card. Fold it lengthwise into a narrow strip, then attach half its width to the inside edge of the door and half to the cabinet side. Leave a small flexible gap at t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure and mark shelf lines 8 cm and 15.5 cm above the inside bottom on both side walls; match left and right marks with a ruler.
Glue four 1.5 × 8 cm support strips on the marks, two per shelf; after they set, place the 16 × 8.5 cm shelf blanks on them and glue only where they touch.
Attach a folded 3 × 20 cm paper hinge between the door's inside edge and one cabinet side, leaving the fold free to bend; add a small backing patch at each hinge end.
Fold a 2 × 4 cm paper pull into a small loop and glue its ends near the door's free edge; leave the cabinet undisturbed through the labeled adhesive drying period.

blocks.question: The hinge fold has accidentally been glued flat. What is the safest useful response?
options: Pull hard until it tears free.
Keep opening it repeatedly until the glue cracks.
Stop, let the adhesive set, then add a separate flexible hinge with backing patches.
Wet the cabinet until the fold releases.
blocks.explanation: Do not force a stuck hinge; preserve the body and add a flexible hinge only after the existing bond is stable.

lessons.title: Finish, inspect, and use within limits
lessons.summary: Finish, inspect, and use within limits

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Finishing is optional. A plain cabinet can look intentional if you align a small title card and leave the cardboard texture visible. If you cover it, use dry paper panels cut to the body dimensions and glue them sparingly after the structure has dried. Paper can wrinkle when too much wet glue is used, and adding a wet covering layer to a soft joint can distort the cabinet. Test one small offcut first. Smooth from the center toward an edge with a clean scrap card, using light pressure. Avoid wet paint, spray finishes, glitter shedding onto keepsakes, and any coating whose ingredients or ventilation needs you do not understand. A paper surface is decoration, not a waterproof or protective coating.

Inspect the object while empty. Place it on a stable flat tabletop, let go, and look for rocking or leaning. Check that both shelves remain seated, that their supports are bonded, and that the base is not separating. Open and close the door slowly several times while one hand steadies the cabinet. A clean motion is a useful functional check; it does not prove durability for repeated use. If the door rubs, identify the contact point and trim a tiny amount from the door edge with safe superv

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Optionally cover the dry exterior with paper cut to fit, testing glue on a scrap first and smoothing each panel lightly from its center outward.
Set the empty cabinet on a stable table; inspect for rocking, lean, open seams, shelf movement, and door rubbing, then make one small repair at a time.
After complete drying, place only a few paper keepsakes on the shelves, each under about 20 g, and write one proposed improvement for a second version.

blocks.body: This is a small dry indoor decorative craft, not load-bearing furniture, a toy tested for children, or a protective device. Place it on a stable tabletop and keep it away from edges, heat, water, and active play.

blocks.question: What is an appropriate first use for the finished cabinet?
options: Store a glass of water on a shelf.
Use it as a wall-mounted shelf for a heavy trophy.
Keep medicine and batteries inside for daily access.
Display a few very light paper keepsakes on a stable tabletop.
blocks.explanation: Use the cabinet only on a stable tabletop for lightweight dry paper objects; this is not a tested capacity rating.

name: Paper Collage Wall Art
tagline: Design and make a dry indoor decorative collage: layered paper shapes mounted on a 20 × 25 cm recycled-card panel, with a simple folded-paper hanging loop or tabletop display option.
outcome: Plan a balanced abstract composition using a 20 × 25 cm portrait panel and a measured 1.5 cm safe margin.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Paper Collage Wall Art

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Design and make a dry indoor decorative collage: layered paper shapes mounted on a 20 × 25 cm recycled-card panel, with a simple folded-paper hanging loop or tabletop display option. You will practice

lessons.title: Plan a composition and prepare a clean panel
lessons.summary: Plan a composition and prepare a clean panel

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A strong collage begins with choices made before glue comes out. This project uses a portrait panel measuring exactly 20 cm wide by 25 cm high. Reserve a 1.5 cm margin on all sides, leaving a 17 × 22 cm design area. That border gives the composition breathing room and keeps the artwork away from fragile cut edges. Reused packaging card is welcome if it is clean, dry, flat and free of food residue. Avoid a panel with a deep crease, dampness, grease, loose dust or a damaged corrugated edge; glue cannot make a warped or dirty base reliable.

Choose an original abstract theme such as “wind crossing a garden” or “stacked windows,” not a copied character, logo or existing artwork. Select three main colors plus one small accent. Use paper with different visual weights: a broad background shape, medium shapes and a few small details. A useful arrangement has one dominant shape occupying roughly one-third of the design area, two or three supporting pieces and a small accent. This is a guide, not a rigid formula. Leave gaps where the background can show.

Before cutting, arrange the scraps dry. Photographing is optional; a pencil thumbnail is enough. Dry placement helps reveal crowded corner

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure and mark a 20 × 25 cm rectangle on clean, flat packaging card; trim carefully with scissors, or ask an adult to prepare the panel if the card is too thick.
Draw a light pencil guide 1.5 cm inside each edge and label three chosen colors plus one optional accent on scrap paper.
Arrange the scraps without glue into one large, two or three medium, and up to four small shapes; keep every shape inside the guide and leave some background visible.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and pass them handle-first. Younger learners need age-appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What is the usable design area after drawing a 1.5 cm margin inside a 20 × 25 cm panel?
blocks.explanation: A 1.5 cm margin on both sides reduces the width by 3 cm and the height by 3 cm, leaving 17 × 22 cm.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan a composition and prepare a clean panel. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut shapes and build a controlled paper layout
lessons.summary: Cut shapes and build a controlled paper layout

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Collage shapes do not need to be complicated. Begin with large, simple forms that can be cut without tiny points: an arch, a broad leaf-like oval, a band, a circle, or an irregular block. These are basic geometric choices, not templates from a particular artwork. The scale matters more than intricate cutting. With a 17 × 22 cm usable area, a dominant shape about 7 × 10 cm will read clearly, while small accents around 2–4 cm provide detail without becoming difficult to glue. Keep enough paper around a shape to hold it safely as you cut.

Layer order creates depth: lower pieces go down first, and upper pieces overlap their edges. Lay each piece in place and decide what it should cover before adhesive is applied. Do not make every edge line up. A few overlaps create continuity; too many can form thick ridges. Keep paper relatively flat and dry. Glossy laminated wrappers may resist glue and can curl, so test a tiny offcut first or omit them. Newspaper print may transfer or show through thin paper, so choose opaque scraps for the focal shape. The background should be attached before the decorative layers.

Glue is most controllable when it is applied sparingly and spread toward the edge

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trace or free-cut one dominant 7 × 10 cm form, two or three supporting pieces about 4–6 cm, and up to four accents about 2–4 cm.
Place the cut pieces on the panel dry, test two possible overlaps, then choose a lower-to-upper order and stack the unused pieces in that order.
Test a pea-sized amount of glue between two scrap pieces; observe the paper for buckling and the bond after the glue becomes tacky or dries as its label directs.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and pass them handle-first. Younger learners need age-appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: A scrap of printed wrapper smears when tested with the glue. What is the best next move?
options: Brush on more glue so the ink is sealed
Stop using that paper-glue pairing and switch to a tested opaque paper
Rub the ink until it dries
Add solvent to remove the smear
blocks.explanation: A scrap test is a decision point. If ink transfers or paper curls, change the material rather than adding adhesive or chemicals.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut shapes and build a controlled paper layout. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Adhere the layers and keep the panel flat
lessons.summary: Adhere the layers and keep the panel flat

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Cover the card before building the design. Place the background paper on clean scrap paper and spread a thin, even film of glue across the card-facing side. A brush or washable applicator gives better control than pouring glue. Pay attention to the perimeter, but do not create a wet ridge at the edge. Lower the sheet from one short side toward the other, smoothing outward with a clean dry scrap or fingertips that are not sticky. Gentle strokes move trapped air toward the edges; hard rubbing can stretch wet paper. Trim overhang only when the sheet is secure and no longer sliding.

Decorative pieces are attached in their planned order. Use small dabs or a thin film distributed across the reverse. For a narrow strip, place tiny glue dots along its length rather than coating the entire table-side area. A piece that lifts at one corner may need a little glue under that corner, not more adhesive everywhere. Press through clean scrap paper so fingers do not snag a damp edge. If glue beads squeeze out, lift them carefully with a dry scrap while still fresh; do not wipe with a wet cloth, which may spread moisture into the paper.

To reduce bowing, allow the panel to rest flat on a dry surfa

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Lay the background sheet face down on scrap paper, brush a thin even coat of paper glue over the card, and lower the sheet from one edge while smoothing gently outward.
When the background is secure enough not to slide, trim its overhang flush with the panel using blunt scissors, keeping fingers clear of the cutting line.
Glue the planned shapes from lowest layer to topmost, using a thin coat or small distributed dabs; press each through clean scrap paper for several seconds.
Let the panel rest flat until surface moisture is gone, then place clean paper above and below it and press under two flat books or boards for at least 2 hours or longer if damp.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and pass them handle-first. Younger learners need age-appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: Which sequence is appropriate for building overlapping collage layers?
options: Glue the smallest accents first, then cover them with the background
Glue all pieces into one wet pile
Attach the background first, then add shapes from lower layer to upper layer
Attach the hanger before the collage layers
blocks.explanation: Background-first, lower-to-upper placement makes the intended overlap order clear and prevents unnecessary lifting.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Adhere the layers and keep the panel flat. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Finish, display and inspect the artwork
lessons.summary: Finish, display and inspect the artwork

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A finished collage needs a display choice that matches its light construction. The most reliable option in this beginner project is tabletop viewing: lean the panel against a stable upright surface on a table, away from the edge and from places where it can be knocked. An optional folded-card foot can help it stand, but it is not a brace and must not support weight. To form one, fold an 8 × 5 cm card piece lengthwise so a 1 cm strip remains as a glue tab; the wider section becomes a shallow prop. Attach the tab at the rear lower center only after the artwork is fully dry. Test it on the intended tabletop and remove the foot if the panel tips.

A light paper loop is another option for display on an appropriate interior wall. Fold a 12 × 1.5 cm strip into a loop with about 2 cm overlap at the ends and glue the overlap to itself. After it dries, attach the flattened overlap to the back near the top center using a small patch of paper and glue. This decorative loop is not a rated hanger. Use only for this lightweight panel and only with a suitable wall fastener; do not hang over a bed, crib, walkway, heat source or valuable object. If there is doubt about the wall or fastener, display

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect every visible edge and the panel back; mark loose spots on a separate note rather than writing over the artwork.
Choose tabletop display first, or make the optional 8 × 5 cm folded foot with a 1 cm glue tab; glue the tab to the dry rear lower center and test on a stable table.
If choosing a wall display instead, form the optional 12 × 1.5 cm paper strip into a loop with 2 cm overlap, let it dry, then attach its flattened overlap at the rear top center an
Record one successful choice and one future improvement, then place the artwork in a dry indoor spot away from direct sun, heat, moisture and impact.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and pass them handle-first. Younger learners need age-appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: After two hours the center still feels damp. What should you do?
options: Use a hair dryer on high heat
Hang it immediately to let gravity flatten it
Add a second thick glue coat
Keep it flat between clean dry scrap and allow more time
blocks.explanation: Drying varies with paper, glue and room conditions. Wait until the panel is dry rather than forcing it with heat.
