name: Decorative Indoor Plant-Pot Cover
tagline: Make a removable, dry-use decorative sleeve for a small tabletop houseplant pot.
outcome: Measure a tapered inner pot at its widest top, bottom, and height, then add practical clearance for a removable cover.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Decorative Indoor Plant-Pot Cover

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a removable, dry-use decorative sleeve for a small tabletop houseplant pot. The sleeve is an outer cover only: keep the plant in its ordinary pot with drainage, remove the plant and inner pot for

lessons.title: Measure the pot and plan the fit
lessons.summary: Measure the pot and plan the fit

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A successful cover slips around the outside of an existing pot without squeezing it. It should not replace the pot or interfere with drainage. Choose a small, ordinary tabletop plant pot that can stand securely on the table by itself. Remove the plant only if you already know how to do so safely; the project can be measured around the outside of the pot while the plant remains in place. Protect the table with scrap paper and keep the plant away from glue and cut scraps.

Measure the widest outside circumference near the rim, the circumference near the bottom, and the pot's vertical height. A flexible tape gives the circumference directly. If you have only a ruler, wrap a narrow paper strip around the pot, mark where it meets itself, then lay it flat and measure the marked length. Do not estimate from the pot's stated volume. A pot may flare outward or curve, so note its silhouette and whether the base is narrower than the rim.

For the example design, imagine an inner pot with a 30 cm top circumference, a 24 cm bottom circumference, and 12 cm height. Add 1 cm of circumference ease at the top and bottom so the sleeve is removable. This yields a top edge of 31 cm and a bottom edge of

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Set the pot on a level table and measure its outside top circumference, bottom circumference, and height; write each measurement with units.
Add 1 cm ease to each circumference and choose a sleeve height about 2 cm shorter than the pot; calculate top and bottom pattern edges.
Draw the trapezoid on plain paper, centering the bottom edge under the top edge, and add a 2 cm seam tab along one short side.
Cut the paper test shape, tape the short ends into a loose sleeve, and check it around the pot at top, middle, and base.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and ask an adult to help younger learners. Do not use a craft knife or power tool for this project.

blocks.question: What is the correct role of this handmade cover?
options: A. A removable decorative outer sleeve around the plant's normal draining pot
B. A waterproof replacement pot
C. A hanging basket that supports the plant
D. A sealed container for watering the plant
blocks.explanation: The project is a dry decorative cachepot-style sleeve. The plant stays in an ordinary pot with drainage.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Measure the pot and plan the fit. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut and shape a clean sleeve
lessons.summary: Cut and shape a clean sleeve

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Once the paper pattern fits, transfer the measured body to clean cardboard. The example uses a single corrugated panel large enough to contain the trapezoid plus its seam tab. Keep the top of the pattern aligned with the same direction throughout the project. Cardboard can bend more easily across its corrugations than along them; try a gentle curve with a scrap first and orient the panel so it rolls around the pot without cracking. Do not crease sharply, because a crease creates a weak-looking flat spot and may make the sleeve rock or press unevenly against the pot.

Cut slowly with scissors suited to thin cardboard. If the cardboard is too thick or resists, choose a thinner clean panel rather than forcing the blades. A doubled cereal-box material can work for a small pot, but it changes the stiffness and can make a small sleeve less forgiving. Keep the cut edges away from the plant leaves and the potting mix. Remove loose fibers and inspect the panel for bent corners.

Before joining the ends, curve the panel gently around a round object close to the pot's diameter, or around the pot with the plant safely clear of the work. Hold it with small tape pieces on the outside. The panel

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Trace the approved paper pattern onto clean cardboard, including the separate 2 cm seam tab, then mark the top edge and inside face.
Cut the cardboard outline with scissors in short, controlled snips, keeping the supporting hand outside the cutting path.
Gently pre-curve the panel around a similarly sized round object, then overlap the seam tab on the inside and hold it temporarily with tape.
Test the untaped or lightly taped sleeve around the pot, lifting it off and returning it without scraping leaves or trapping the pot.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and ask an adult to help younger learners. Do not use a craft knife or power tool for this project.

blocks.question: Your measured pot is 30 cm around at the top and 24 cm at the bottom. Using the example's 1 cm ease at each edge, what are the pattern edge lengths before adding the separate seam tab?
options: A. 30 cm top and 24 cm bottom
B. 31 cm top and 25 cm bottom
C. 32 cm top and 26 cm bottom
D. 31 cm top and 24 cm bottom
blocks.explanation: The worked pattern uses 31 cm at the top and 25 cm at the bottom, then adds a separate seam tab.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut and shape a clean sleeve. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Add the decorative surface and rim
lessons.summary: Add the decorative surface and rim

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Decorate the sleeve while the cardboard is still easy to reach. Decide on a simple original design first: for example, a wide muted-color band near the bottom, a few hand-drawn leaf-like shapes that are not copied from a character or branded artwork, or alternating geometric blocks. Keep the pattern away from the plant itself and do not attach anything that could fall into the soil. A restrained design often makes small cutting inconsistencies less noticeable. Make a paper mock-up or arrange scraps dry before gluing so you can judge spacing and color.

Lay the panel flat with the outer face upward. Cut the wrap with enough material to turn slightly over the top and bottom edges, but do not make a thick wad that prevents the base from sitting flat. For the example, the 35 × 25 cm decorative piece gives a little margin around a panel roughly 33 cm wide including tab and 10 cm high. The exact required amount depends on your pattern and whether the wrap is paper or fabric. Dry-fit it before applying glue. Use a thin layer of craft adhesive on the cardboard, following its label. Too much glue can wrinkle paper, soak through fabric, or make the panel curl. Smooth from the center outward

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Choose and dry-arrange a simple original motif or color layout on the outer panel before using adhesive.
Cut the paper or fabric wrap with a modest margin around the panel and test-fold it over the top and bottom edges.
Brush or spread a thin layer of label-approved craft glue on the cardboard, smooth the wrap from center outward, and fold excess neatly inward.
Cover the top cut edge with a narrow card rim strip or a clean inward fold, then leave the sleeve flat to dry as directed on the adhesive label.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and ask an adult to help younger learners. Do not use a craft knife or power tool for this project.

blocks.question: The cardboard sleeve feels tight around the pot. What should you do?
options: A. Push the pot down firmly until it fits
B. Cut away a large section while the plant is inside
C. Reopen the seam and add a narrow matching strip, then retest
D. Glue the pot permanently into the sleeve
blocks.explanation: Increase the circumference gradually at the seam and test again with the plant safely stable.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Add the decorative surface and rim. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fit, use, and refine the finished cover
lessons.summary: Fit, use, and refine the finished cover

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
After the finish has dried, put the empty cover on the table and check that its base sits evenly. A decorative sleeve that rocks, leans, or curls upward can tip or scrape furniture, so correct the base before placing a plant nearby. Lay it on a flat surface and look for gaps under the edge. A tiny unevenness in thin cardboard may be corrected by trimming a small protruding fiber; do not add a thick pad that makes the base unstable. If the wall has warped, gently open the seam and reshape it, then secure it again only when the surface is dry. If it cannot stand reliably empty, retire it as a flat decorative sample rather than use it around a plant.

Next, set the normal plant pot inside the cover and verify that the pot remains seated on the tabletop. The sleeve should not bear the plant's weight in the sense of suspending it; it merely surrounds the pot. Lift the inner pot straight out and return it once. This demonstrates that the cover is removable for routine care. Check that no seam or decoration catches leaves and that you can still see the top rim of the plant pot. Use the original pot's drainage as intended. Penn State Extension explains that a pot with drainage is needed fo

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Set the empty sleeve on a level tabletop and check whether its entire lower edge rests evenly without rocking.
Place the ordinary plant pot inside, confirm the pot itself stands on the table, and lift it back out once to test removal.
Adopt a dry watering routine: remove the inner pot, water where it can drain, and return it after dripping stops; promptly empty any collected water.
Record one fit observation and one concrete revision for a future sleeve, such as changing ease by 0.5 cm or selecting a smoother wrap.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table, cut away from fingers, and ask an adult to help younger learners. Do not use a craft knife or power tool for this project.

blocks.question: Which watering routine best protects the handmade cardboard cover?
options: A. Leave the inner pot sitting in any collected water
B. Remove the inner pot for watering and return it after drainage stops
C. Seal the inside with an unverified chemical coating
D. Block the inner pot's drainage holes
blocks.explanation: A removable outer cover should not interrupt drainage; keep it dry and remove pooled water promptly.

name: Ribbon and Photo Memory Display
tagline: Build a lightweight, dry-indoor tabletop memory board from recycled cardboard, wrapped ribbon, and removable paper photo tabs.
outcome: Measure and cut a flat 12 by 16 inch display face from sound recycled corrugated cardboard and identify a safe, stable work surface.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Ribbon and Photo Memory Display

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Build a lightweight, dry-indoor tabletop memory board from recycled cardboard, wrapped ribbon, and removable paper photo tabs. The 12 by 16 inch board displays up to six small prints or copied snapsho

lessons.title: Plan the board and prepare safe materials
lessons.summary: Plan the board and prepare safe materials

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The design is a portrait board measuring 12 inches wide by 16 inches high. Six picture spaces will sit in two columns and three rows. A ribbon lattice crosses the face, but paper photo tabs—not adhesive—hold the prints. The measurements are a practical sample, not a preservation specification. If a photograph is precious, make a copy for display and store the original appropriately. Keep all construction glue on the back and on the easel pieces.

Before cutting, inspect the cardboard. A slightly corrugated package panel is useful because its broad face is easy to mark, but it must lie flat enough to support the ribbon. Avoid dampness, torn edges, food residue, unknown stains, or loose staples. Measure from a straight factory edge where possible. Accurate marking now prevents a lopsided grid that later forces photos into the ribbon intersections. The board face is intentionally modest in size: larger boards need a better engineered support and are outside this beginner project.

Use a paper mock-up to choose colors and positions. Put the six prints on the table and preserve a narrow visual margin around each. Do not force every picture to match; select a consistent orientation or al

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Clear a table, put the cardboard flat, and inspect both sides for moisture, dirt, sharp staples, and crushed folds.
Measure and mark a 12 x 16 inch portrait rectangle; cut slowly along the ruler-guided marks with paper scissors.
Mark vertical ribbon lanes at 2, 6, and 10 inches from the left edge, and horizontal lanes at 2, 6, 10, and 14 inches from the top.
Arrange six paper placeholders, each up to 4 x 6 inches, over the grid and pencil a small no-ribbon zone where each image needs clear space.

blocks.body: Use scissors pointed away from the body, cut while seated at a clear table, and ask an adult to help younger learners.

blocks.question: What is the planned size of the display face?
options: 12 x 16 inches
16 x 24 inches
8 x 10 inches
4 x 6 inches
blocks.explanation: The board face is 12 inches wide by 16 inches high, with a 2 inch perimeter margin.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the board and prepare safe materials. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Weave and anchor the ribbon grid
lessons.summary: Weave and anchor the ribbon grid

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The ribbon should lie flat and feel snug, not stretched like a strap. Estimate each run by following the marked lane across the board and around the back edge, adding about 3 inches at each end for wrapping and trimming. These are generous working allowances; exact ribbon use changes with thickness and the route around the board. Cut one sample length first and test it before cutting the remaining pieces. Leave clean square ends, and keep scissors away from fingers while trimming frayed fibers.

Each ribbon run passes from the front over an edge to the back. The reverse side carries the small overlaps, so the visible face stays tidy. A paper tape tab on the back is only a temporary positioning aid; it is not a structural guarantee. Secure the end by folding it under and using a small amount of paper-safe glue on cardboard, or by trapping it under a folded cardstock tab. Do not glue across the front where it may seep into a photograph. At crossings, alternate over-under order when practical, then flatten the intersection with a fingertip. Do not pull so hard that the board bows inward.

Work one direction at a time. Keep the ribbon aligned to the pencil marks and inspect the board a

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut one ribbon test run along a vertical lane, adding about 6 inches beyond the front span for back wraps; test-fit it without stretching.
Cut the two remaining vertical runs and four horizontal runs, adding roughly 6 inches to each measured front span for wrap and trim.
Lay each vertical strip along its mark, wrap its ends to the back, and temporarily hold them with small low-tack tape tabs.
Lay the four horizontal runs across the face, alternating over-under at crossings, then fold and secure each end on the back with a small glue spot or cardstock tab.

blocks.body: Use scissors pointed away from the body, cut while seated at a clear table, and ask an adult to help younger learners.

blocks.question: Why are photographs held by paper pockets rather than glued directly?
options: So the display can be used outdoors
So copies can be removed or rearranged without adhesive on the image
To make the board load-bearing
To waterproof the print
blocks.explanation: The corner tabs are intended to retain lightweight copies while allowing removal; they do not certify preservation.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Weave and anchor the ribbon grid. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Make removable photo tabs and build the easel
lessons.summary: Make removable photo tabs and build the easel

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
For a casual display, removable corners are preferable to sticking a photograph directly to the board. This project uses small handmade cardstock pockets. They are not archival or museum-grade: paper, ink, adhesives, light, humidity, and long display times can all affect photographs. Use copies when preservation matters. A public museum mounting guide describes photo corners and paper-channel supports as methods for securing paper objects; this course borrows only the general idea of supporting an image at its edges, not its conservation materials or museum procedure. The simple pockets here are a craft adaptation, not a conservation claim.

Cut corner-tab blanks from cardstock, fold each blank into a small triangular pocket, and test it on scrap paper first. The pocket should catch only a small corner of the print, leaving most of its image visible. Do not tape the pocket to the print. A tab can be positioned under a ribbon crossing or tucked behind the ribbon so that ribbon and paper share support. Check that the photo can slide out without tearing. If it catches, enlarge the pocket opening or replace the tab.

The easel is a folded rear support for stationary viewing. Cut a 5 by

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut eight 1 x 1 inch cardstock squares and fold each diagonally; make a short second fold on one edge to create a shallow corner pocket.
Place four pockets around each selected print corner and tuck their outer edges under nearby ribbon; do not glue the image or its corners.
Cut a 5 x 12 inch rear easel strip; score it 2 inches from one end with a blunt tool and fold along the score.
Glue the 2 inch flap to the rear center of the board, add a cardstock side brace if needed, and leave it flat until the adhesive label's set time has passed.

blocks.body: Use scissors pointed away from the body, cut while seated at a clear table, and ask an adult to help younger learners.

blocks.question: What should you do if the ribbon makes the board bow?
options: Pull every strip tighter
Stand it up immediately so the easel straightens it
Release a nearby rear anchor and reattach with slack
Add a heavy object to the front
blocks.explanation: Ribbon should be snug but not tensioned; release and re-anchor rather than adding weight.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Make removable photo tabs and build the easel. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Test, refine, and care for the display
lessons.summary: Test, refine, and care for the display

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Open the easel and place the display on a level, stable tabletop. First test it without photographs. The base should sit flat, the board should lean without a sharp crease collapsing, and the easel should not slide away. Add photographs only after the empty stand is steady. Then load one light copy at a time and inspect whether ribbon, pockets, and board remain flat. This is a gentle tabletop check, not a laboratory test or a certified stability rating. Never test it by hanging weight, placing it in a vehicle, or setting it near an edge.

Look at the display from normal seated viewing distance. Check whether ribbon crosses a face or caption. Move the paper pocket rather than pulling hard on a photograph. The visual design may improve when the most colorful print is balanced by a quieter image, but no single arrangement is required. Keep the maximum print size at 4 by 6 inches and do not add heavy objects, ornaments, glass, or containers. If the surface bows, remove the prints and reduce tension or replace a damaged board. If the easel rocks, check that its flap is centered and both rear edges rest evenly; a thin, flat cardstock shim under a short edge may help on a tabletop, but do

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Open the easel and stand the empty board on a stable, level table away from the edge; gently check that the foot and board contact the surface.
Add one copy at a time, then check that pockets hold it and ribbon does not hide important image details.
Refine the arrangement by moving copies and tabs, then note one measurable change such as shifting a lane 1/2 inch or reducing a print size.
Lift the board by both side edges, remove photographs before storage, and keep the display dry and indoors.

blocks.body: Use scissors pointed away from the body, cut while seated at a clear table, and ask an adult to help younger learners.

blocks.question: Which use is appropriate for the cardboard easel?
options: Stationary viewing on a stable tabletop
Supporting a heavy glass frame
Display inside a moving vehicle
Hanging from a wall hook
blocks.explanation: The display and easel are small dry-indoor tabletop decor, not structural fixtures.

name: Recycled-Cardboard Door Sign
tagline: Turn clean corrugated shipping cardboard into a light, dry-indoor name or message plaque with a folded stand-off back, paper face, and hand-lettered decoration.
outcome: Measure and mark a 20 × 12 cm plaque and a 2 cm fold tab on clean corrugated cardboard, checking square corners with a ruler.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Recycled-Cardboard Door Sign

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Turn clean corrugated shipping cardboard into a light, dry-indoor name or message plaque with a folded stand-off back, paper face, and hand-lettered decoration. This is a display craft, not a load-bea

lessons.title: Plan a readable plaque and prepare the board
lessons.summary: Plan a readable plaque and prepare the board

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Begin with a message that fits the space: a first name, a short room label, or a brief original phrase. Aim for one main line of lettering and a few simple accents rather than a crowded collage. The model uses a 20 cm by 12 cm face. Reserve about 1.5 cm around the edge as a quiet border; this leaves a central writing area approximately 17 cm by 9 cm. Sketch the message on scrap paper at roughly the same scale. Tall letters around 2 cm high are easier to read from a few steps away than tiny lettering. Choose a dark color for words and lighter colors for decoration so the message remains the focus. Do not copy a branded character, logo, or protected artwork; draw your own dots, stripes, leaves, stars, or geometric shapes.

Select a piece of clean, dry corrugated cardboard with its flutes running horizontally across the eventual 20 cm width. The corrugation acts like a set of channels; the plaque is more likely to bend if you cut a narrow strip that separates the face from those channels. A horizontal grain also makes it easier to fold the rear tab along the 20 cm edge. Check the board for staples, tape ridges, grime, dampness, and strong odors. Reject questionable material rather tha

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On scrap paper, sketch a short original message in a 17 × 9 cm central area, leaving a 1.5 cm margin inside the planned 20 × 12 cm face.
Inspect the cardboard and orient its visible corrugation channels horizontally across a clean area at least 20 × 14 cm.
Use a ruler and pencil to mark a 20 × 12 cm rectangle and a 20 × 2 cm tab along one short edge, making a 20 × 14 cm blank.

blocks.body: Work seated or standing at a stable, well-lit table. Keep the cutting area clear and cut only cardboard that scissors can handle without excessive force.

blocks.question: What is the measured size of the visible face in the sample design?
blocks.explanation: The face is 20 × 12 cm. Adding a 2 cm folded tab along one edge makes the total cardboard blank 20 × 14 cm.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan a readable plaque and prepare the board. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut cleanly and fold the rear tab
lessons.summary: Cut cleanly and fold the rear tab

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A neat plaque starts with a controlled outline. Place the cardboard flat on a stable work surface. Use scissors only if the board is thin enough that the blades close smoothly without twisting the wrist or crushing the flutes. Cut slowly around the outside of the marked 20 × 14 cm blank. Keep fingers away from the scissor path and move the cardboard to approach each edge comfortably. Small cuts are often easier around corners than one long bite. Do not try to cut through thick board by repeatedly squeezing with force. A crushed, fuzzy edge indicates the tool is struggling, not that more pressure is the right answer. Stop and ask an adult to prepare the piece with a suitable hand tool, or switch to thinner layered board. The safety source notes that eliminating a blade task or choosing a safer suitable tool is preferable where possible; where blades are used, a stable surface, controlled pressure, and keeping body parts out of the path matter. This course does not require the learner to use a utility knife.

Mark the fold line lightly across the width at 12 cm from the top. Corrugated cardboard does not behave like cloth: forcing a sharp fold can split its outer paper. Instead, gent

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut the 20 × 14 cm outline with scissors only while they move smoothly; rotate the board to keep fingers outside the cut path.
Measure 12 cm down from the top edge and lightly mark a straight fold line across the 20 cm width.
Flex the tab gently along the line, then fold it behind the plaque without sharply creasing or crushing the board.

blocks.body: Work seated or standing at a stable, well-lit table. Keep the cutting area clear and cut only cardboard that scissors can handle without excessive force.

blocks.question: Your scissors crush the corrugation and require strong squeezing. What is the safest next choice?
options: Force the scissors through in several hard squeezes
Stop and ask an adult to prepare the cut, or switch to thinner board
Hold the cardboard in your lap and pull the scissors toward you
Use a kitchen knife without a cutting mat
blocks.explanation: Do not force scissors or improvise with a knife. The CCOHS recommends choosing an appropriate tool and stable surface and avoiding excessive pressure; this course lets an adult prepare resistant board.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut cleanly and fold the rear tab. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cover the face and attach a display loop
lessons.summary: Cover the face and attach a display loop

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Cut the face paper to about 21 × 13 cm, giving roughly 0.5 cm extra on each side of the 20 × 12 cm face. Center it on the cardboard before adding glue. Fold each extra edge over the perimeter and test that the four corners overlap without creating a bulky wad. Trim only the paper if needed; leave the cardboard rectangle unchanged. This wrap hides small rough edges and provides a calmer surface for lettering. If you prefer visible cardboard texture, use a 20 × 12 cm paper panel centered on the face and leave the border uncovered. Test a small dot of glue on scrap first. Some thin papers wrinkle when saturated, so use a thin, even layer rather than puddles. Smooth from the middle toward the edges using fingertips or the side of a clean ruler. Wipe away excess glue before it dries, and set the plaque flat under a clean sheet of scrap paper while it dries. Do not put a heavy object on it; pressure can crush the corrugation or squeeze glue out unevenly.

For hanging, the optional yarn loop is only a light display aid. Cut an 18 cm piece, bring its ends together, and make a small knot so the loop is about 6 cm high. Place the two yarn ends on the rear tab near its center, roughly 5 cm ap

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut a 21 × 13 cm paper face, center it on the 20 × 12 cm plaque, and dry-fit the 0.5 cm edge allowances around the panel.
Apply a thin even layer of school glue, smooth the paper from center outward, wrap its edges to the back, and leave the plaque flat to dry.
For the optional loop, make an approximately 6 cm-high loop from the 18 cm yarn, place its ends about 5 cm apart on the rear tab, and cover the ends with a 3 × 5 cm paper patch.

blocks.body: Work seated or standing at a stable, well-lit table. Keep the cutting area clear and cut only cardboard that scissors can handle without excessive force.

blocks.question: Why is the face paper cut about 21 × 13 cm for a 20 × 12 cm plaque?
options: It makes the plaque suitable for outdoor rain
It creates a 2 cm structural hanging strap
It provides about 0.5 cm of wrapping allowance at each edge
It guarantees the sign cannot bend
blocks.explanation: The paper is 1 cm larger in each dimension, giving approximately 0.5 cm per edge to fold behind the face.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cover the face and attach a display loop. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Letter, test the display, and refine
lessons.summary: Letter, test the display, and refine

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Once the paper face is dry to the touch, lightly place the lettering with pencil before coloring. Check that the longest word fits inside the 17 × 9 cm central area and that the letters do not collide with the border. Use one dark color for the words and reserve other colors for small accents. Make original decorative marks such as a simple repeated line, a cluster of circles, or a geometric corner motif. If adding colored-paper shapes, use only a few pieces no larger than about 3 × 5 cm; too many raised layers can pull the face unevenly. Avoid wet marker over damp glue because the paper may buckle. Leave the backing visible and undecorated unless you need to hide a small patch; the smooth front is the viewing side.

Check the plaque on a flat tabletop before considering a wall or door display. The 2 cm tab should rest behind the lower edge without creating a sharp bend. If the plaque leans, adjust the angle of the tab gently and support it against a stable object. Do not treat the tab as a kickstand for a high shelf, and do not place the sign where it can fall onto someone. If using the optional loop, inspect the glue patch after drying and give it a gentle hand check while holdin

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Lightly pencil the message within the 17 × 9 cm writing area, then trace it with a dark marker, crayon, or colored pencil after the glue is dry.
Add up to four small original paper accents or simple drawn patterns, leaving the outer 1.5 cm border mostly clear.
Test the plaque flat on a tabletop, check that its rear tab rests evenly, and choose a stable lean display unless a suitable pre-existing hook is certain.
View the sign from a few steps away, identify one readability or balance issue, make one small correction, and allow all glue to dry before moving it.

blocks.body: Work seated or standing at a stable, well-lit table. Keep the cutting area clear and cut only cardboard that scissors can handle without excessive force.

blocks.question: Which glue method is most likely to keep the paper face smooth?
options: Pour a thick puddle of glue across the center
Apply a thin even layer and smooth from the center toward the edges
Use hot glue across the entire face
Glue only the corners and stretch the sheet tight
blocks.explanation: A thin, even layer with center-to-edge smoothing reduces bubbles and excess wetness. Allow the face to dry flat.

name: Explosion-Style Keepsake Gift Box
tagline: Build a dry indoor decorative keepsake box with three nested paper layers, a removable lid, and original messages or drawings.
outcome: Measure and mark concentric nine-panel cardstock layers using a ruler, square, and consistent grid dimensions.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Explosion-Style Keepsake Gift Box

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Build a dry indoor decorative keepsake box with three nested paper layers, a removable lid, and original messages or drawings.

lessons.title: Plan the layers and mark accurate grids
lessons.summary: Plan the layers and mark accurate grids

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
An explosion-style box opens because its layered walls are hinged to a central square. The center remains in place while each outer panel rotates down and outward. This version uses three square blanks rather than copying a particular published template: 30 cm, 27 cm, and 24 cm. Divide each into a three-by-three grid. Their panel sizes are 10 cm, 9 cm, and 8 cm, respectively. When centered on one another, the inner layer sits in the middle of the next layer with a visible border around it. The center squares all measure 10, 9, and 8 cm, so check placement rather than assuming they align automatically. The lid is built separately to fit the assembled center walls.



Before marking, measure each sheet twice and check that its edges are square. A small error repeated on every line can make the finished stack twist. Make pencil marks along opposite edges, connect them with a ruler, and use the table edge or a square to check each line. Keep marks light so they erase after cutting. Do not cut the grid lines: they are fold guides. Use scraps to test how much pressure creates a crease without breaking the surface. If your stock cracks, switch to lighter stock or reduce scoring pressure.

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure three square blanks: 30 × 30 cm, 27 × 27 cm, and 24 × 24 cm. Mark each centerline at one-third and two-thirds of its side: 10 and 20 cm; 9 and 18 cm; 8 and 16 cm.
Connect the marks with a ruler using faint pencil lines, then label the reverse of each blank 30, 27, or 24 cm.
On a cardstock offcut, draw one line and make a single light pass with the blunt scoring tool; fold both ways to test the crease.
Cut each blank to its measured square only if the sheet is larger; keep scissors on the waste side of the pencil line.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table; pass them closed and handle-first. Supervise younger learners.

blocks.question: What should remain intact at the center of each cross-shaped layer?
options: The central square and its four hinge edges
Only one attached arm
A fully cut-out center
The four corner squares
blocks.explanation: The four side panels hinge from the uncut center square; cutting the center apart would prevent a connected reveal.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the layers and mark accurate grids. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Score, cut, and form the opening layers
lessons.summary: Score, cut, and form the opening layers

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Each gridded blank has four corner squares, four side squares, and one center square. Keep the center intact. To make each layer open as a connected cross, remove the four corner squares along their outside edges. Then the four side squares remain attached to the central square along their inner edges. Those four inner edges are the hinges. Score only those hinge lines: one line on each side of the center. A gentle crease lets the side panels lie down while remaining joined. This is different from cutting the outline of the center, which would separate the panels and defeat the opening action.



Use the blunt scoring tool and ruler to follow the pencil line. The goal is a shallow channel, not a trench. Fold each side panel outward once and return it upright. Avoid repeatedly flexing the same crease because paper fibers weaken with every bend. Do the same for all three sizes. Keep the scraps: they make small note tabs or can be used as test pieces, but do not glue scraps into the hinges. Place the largest cross first on the table. Center the medium cross on it, then the small one. Measure the border on each side rather than judging only from one corner. A little asymmetry is easy t

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On each sheet, cut away the four corner squares along the outer boundaries of those squares; do not cut into the center or side squares.
Score the four grid lines that border the center square with one light pass, using the ruler as a guide; fold each arm away from the center and reopen it once.
Repeat the corner cuts and four hinge scores on the medium and small blanks; lay them flat in descending size order.
Place the 27 cm cross centered on the 30 cm cross, then the 24 cm cross centered on the 27 cm cross; measure the visible border at left, right, top, and bottom.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table; pass them closed and handle-first. Supervise younger learners.

blocks.question: Which is the safest way to create a fold guide?
options: Cut halfway through with a knife
Make one or two gentle passes with a blunt tool
Scratch repeatedly until the surface is white
Wet the fold until it bends
blocks.explanation: Use a blunt scoring tool with light pressure, checking a scrap first; do not cut through or wet the paper.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Score, cut, and form the opening layers. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build a simple fitted lid and attach the stack
lessons.summary: Build a simple fitted lid and attach the stack

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The lid blank begins as a 14 × 14 cm square. Mark a 3 cm border from each edge so the center is 8 × 8 cm. Each corner contains a 3 × 3 cm square. Cut one edge of each corner square from the outside edge to the central square; remove only a narrow slit, not the whole corner. These four cuts create tabs that overlap to form shallow lid walls. Score the four inner lines around the 10 cm center and fold the border upward. Overlap one tab inside each adjacent wall, using a small amount of glue. Dry-fit the lid over the central square before gluing. It should sit over the 8 cm top center without being forced. Cardstock thickness changes the fit slightly. If tight, trim a narrow sliver from each inner wall edge evenly; if loose, add a thin folded paper shim to two opposite inside walls.



Adhesive placement matters. Use small amounts on tabs and on flat surfaces only. Excess glue can wrinkle paper and seep through to the visible side. When bonding the three crosses, place the largest layer on the table and apply glue to the central square of the medium layer. Align centers, press gently, and repeat for the small layer. Do not glue the arms together; all panels must move independently. Ke

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On the 14 cm lid square, mark 3 cm in from all four edges; connect marks to define an 8 × 8 cm center, then cut one 3 cm slit inward from an outside edge at each corner.
Score the four lines around the 8 cm center, fold the 3 cm walls upward, and overlap each tab against the inside of the adjacent wall using a small glue-stick patch.
Center the three crosses in descending size order; glue only the flat central square of the medium cross to the largest, then glue the small center to the medium center.
Place the lid over the central stack for a no-force fit check; trim a narrow, equal amount from opposing inside wall edges only if needed, then let the assembly dry lid-off.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table; pass them closed and handle-first. Supervise younger learners.

blocks.question: Where should glue go when the nested crosses are attached?
options: Across all four arms
On every hinge crease
Only on the flat center squares
On the outer edges of the largest cross
blocks.explanation: The flat centers bond the layers.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build a simple fitted lid and attach the stack. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Personalize, test the reveal, and refine
lessons.summary: Personalize, test the reveal, and refine

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Decorate only after the structure works. The panels are small, so plan content before applying glue. A useful arrangement gives each layer a purpose: the largest arms can hold a short greeting or broad color blocks; the middle arms can contain four brief memories; the smallest arms can hold a tiny drawing or a final note. This is an example, not a required theme. Use original handwriting, abstract shapes, or your own drawings. Do not reproduce branded characters or another artist’s protected artwork. Cut photographs to no more than 8 × 8 cm so they fit comfortably on the 8 cm inner panels. A photograph can be mounted on a slightly larger flat mat, but keep it thin and leave a clear margin near the fold. Avoid buttons, beads, heavy charms, and thick foam: they add bulk and may stop the lid closing.



Before gluing each decoration, place it on the panel and open the box fully. Check that it does not cross a hinge, overlap a neighbor, or project beyond the lid footprint. Apply adhesive sparingly to the back of the paper piece, press from center outward, then smooth without rubbing across a crease. Add one piece at a time and test again. Let the project dry open. To present it, set it

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Sketch a decoration map naming what will go on each of the 12 visible arms; leave at least a 5 mm clear strip along each hinge.
Attach flat paper decorations one at a time with a light glue-stick layer; smooth from the center outward and keep each piece within its panel.
After the adhesive dries, open each arm outward and close it once; lift and replace the lid, then open all layers fully on a stable table.
Write a small note in the center, place only flat lightweight keepsakes inside, and leave the assembled box open until all adhesive is fully dry.

blocks.body: Use scissors seated at a clear table; pass them closed and handle-first. Supervise younger learners.

blocks.question: The lid catches on a raised decoration. What is the best response?
options: Press down hard until the lid closes
Pull the lid sideways
Add a heavier object to flatten the box
Lift it off, move or flatten the decoration, then test gently
blocks.explanation: Find the exact point of contact, adjust the decoration or lid fit, and retest without force.

name: Pull-Tab Surprise Message Card
tagline: Make a dry indoor greeting card with a hand-built paper slider.
outcome: Plan a card layout around a 3.25-inch slider travel and reserve enough paper for the card fold, window, and pull tab.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Pull-Tab Surprise Message Card

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a dry indoor greeting card with a hand-built paper slider. Pulling a broad tab moves a concealed message into a framed window. The course teaches a measured guide channel, a paper stop, a cover l

lessons.title: Plan the card and prove the motion on scraps
lessons.summary: Plan the card and prove the motion on scraps

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A pull-tab card works because a narrow strip travels in a controlled path behind a stationary face. Your design uses a folded 5.5 × 8.5-inch card, with its fold on the left when closed. The front face is 5.5 × 4.25 inches. The message starts hidden behind a 2.5 × 0.75-inch window and moves sideways about 3.25 inches. The slider and the message must remain separate from the cover: only the slider moves, while the window frame stays fixed. This distinction matters because even a beautiful front panel will fail if glue reaches the moving paper. A modest reveal is easier to control than trying to move a large panel through a tight slot.

Before cutting the actual card, draw the front face full size on scrap. Mark the fold edge, window, pull-tab exit, and the proposed start and end positions of the message. Keep the window at least 1/2 inch from the outside edges, leaving a stable border. The pull tab emerges from a horizontal slot near the right edge. Keep its route straight and give the moving strip a little clearance rather than making the channel fit like a clamp. Paper thickness, cutting tolerance, and minor skew can otherwise turn a slider into a jam. Test the movement using scrap

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut a 5.5 × 8.5-inch rectangle from cardstock and mark a crease 4.25 inches from one short edge; fold to make a 5.5 × 4.25-inch card.
On scrap, sketch a 2.5 × 0.75-inch reveal window 1 inch below the top and 1.5 inches from the fold edge; mark a straight pull route toward the outer edge.
Draw a short message on a 1 × 6-inch scrap slider and slide it behind the drawn window by hand to check where the words appear at both ends.
Choose two simple original decorations, such as dots and rays, and mark areas outside the guide route where they will go.

blocks.body: Use scissors with blades pointed away from fingers; an adult should operate a craft knife on a cutting mat. Never cut toward the supporting hand.

blocks.question: Why does the sample channel leave about 1/16 inch of clearance around the 3/4-inch slider?
options: To leave a little room for hand-cut variation and smoother travel
To let the message card fall out when pulled
To make space for wet glue
To widen the window automatically
blocks.explanation: A small clearance helps a paper strip move despite slight cutting variation; too little clearance creates friction.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the card and prove the motion on scraps. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build a low-friction guide and sliding message
lessons.summary: Build a low-friction guide and sliding message

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The card mechanism has three functional layers: the card front with an opening, two narrow rails that create a channel, and a moving strip behind those rails. For this beginner version, make the two rails from smooth cardstock strips about 1/4 inch wide and 3.5 inches long. Position them parallel, with a clear gap of about 13/16 inch between their inner edges. The 3/4-inch-high slider then has roughly 1/16 inch of clearance. If they converge, the strip may bind near one end.

The channel must not be glued shut. Apply adhesive only to the outer half of each rail or to its underside, away from the open space where the slider travels. For a beginner, a narrow glue-stick swipe on the underside works better than squeezing liquid glue beside a moving strip. Let the fixed rails set before inserting the slider. Keep the blade pointed away from your fingers and work over a cutting mat or protected surface. Save the removed piece as a measurement check. Do not enlarge the opening casually: the surrounding frame keeps the front layer tidy and hides the channel.

Attach the mechanism backing to the back of the front face, aligning the slider path under the reveal. The message must move into view through the window; test that alignment before fixing the backing. Apply adhesive to the outer perimeter of the backing and to solid rail areas only. Add liquid to lubricate the channel

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A mechanism should be tested before its working parts are hidden by decoration. Hold the card flat on the table and move the tab with a gentle fingertip pull. Travel should be smooth, the message should align with the opening, and the stop should prevent accidental escape. Try several slow cycles, returning the tab to its starting position each time. A card that works once but catches on the return stroke is not ready to decorate. Look at the path from the side: the front and backing should lie flat, and no rail should be visibly lifted. Use the symptom location to diagnose the fault. A catch at the same spot often points to a local glue ridge or a bent paper edge; increasing resistance along the whole track can mean the rails are too close.

If the mechanism fails, take the smallest safe repair. Open the card, remove the slider, and inspect for adhesive or a curled edge. A dry narrow scrap can help lift a loose rail; replace that rail with a straighter piece if necessary. If the channel is pinched, reposition one rail outward slightly. It keeps the card standing upright

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Start by deciding where the banner will be displayed. This example is designed for a dry indoor wall or a party table backdrop, not outdoors where wind, rain and sunlight can degrade cloth or pull at attachments. Nine pennants make a useful short strand while leaving room to practice consistent spacing. Each triangle has a 15 cm top and an 18 cm vertical drop. Its two sloping sides are about 20.9 cm, so a 23 cm-deep fabric layout leaves useful handling room. The folded binding strip is 8 cm wide before folding; once folded lengthwise, it forms a roughly 4 cm band that encloses the raw top edge.

Choose lightweight woven cotton because it is easy to mark and does not stretch substantially as you sew. Prewash thrifted fabric if you intend to launder the finished banner, then dry it completely. Mix fabrics by value and scale: place a busy print next to a quiet solid so the shapes remain legible at a distance. Lay nine paper triangles in sequence before cutting cloth. This is a planning decision, not a rule about party colors; the point is to decide the order while pieces can still be rearranged. Use the measurement grid and the checkpoints below rather than relying on guessed symmetry

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The binding is the long folded strip that captures the raw top edge of every triangle. Cut one 8 cm-wide strip that is 210 cm long. If your fabric is not wide enough, use two strips with diagonal joining seams. To make such a seam, place strip ends at right angles with right sides together, stitch diagonally across the overlap, then trim the excess and press the join open. A diagonal join distributes the small thickness change instead of creating a bulky straight ridge. Keep the seam allowance modest and inspect that the joined strip is still long enough. This course does not require a commercial bias-strip maker: the banner is decorative and the straight-grain strip works when handled gently. Bias-cut tape is more flexible around curves, but these pennant tops are straight.

Fold the strip in half lengthwise, wrong sides together, and press or finger-crease the fold. Open it, fold each long raw edge toward the center crease, then close the strip again. That creates two folded layers whose outer edges meet. You may instead use a suitable 2.5 cm double-fold tape, but check the width against the sample sandwich before stitching. lessons.title: Position and stitch the pennants

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Open one short section of the folded band just enough to locate its center crease. That keeps the strip from creeping as the growing group of pieces gathers on one side. Use the measured centers as the reference, but also check the visible clear gap: neighboring pennants should have about 4 cm between their top corners. Small variation is acceptable; a deliberate change in spacing should be corrected before stitching.

Sew continuously along the open edge of the folded tape, about 3 mm from its edge, so the needle passes through both tape layers and the enclosed pennant top. Keep fingers out of the needle path and guide the material without pulling. At each pennant, slow down and confirm the layered fabric is still inside the binding. blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A reusable banner should be checked before each display and stored clean and dry. First hang it loosely at a low, reachable height on a suitable indoor display point, away from heaters, candles, door swings and places where people or pets can snag it. This is not a load test: do not pull on the loops or suspend weight from the banner. If the points do not hang vertically, look for an off-center top placement or a twist in the binding. If the spacing seems uneven, measure the clear gaps between top corners and decide whether the difference is a design choice or an accidental shift. Minor unevenness does not make the craft unusable; a beginner's repair should improve stability without concealing damage.

For care, follow the fabric's washing instructions. Remove the banner from its display and hand wash or use a gentle cycle only if the fabrics can tolerate that method. Place it in a laundry bag if loose threads might catch. Air-dry fully, reshape the triangles by hand, and store the piece loosely folded or rolled in a clean dry place. lessons.title: Plan and prepare square sheets

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Choose the favor before folding. This sample tray starts with a 20 cm square and its lid with a 21 cm square. That extra centimetre is a starting allowance, not a promised fit: paper thickness, crease placement, and wall shape all matter. Select a light, shallow item such as a note, sticker sheet, or wrapped token. Measure its footprint and height. Leave clearance so the contents do not push against the lid. Do not use the project for loose food, sharp objects, or anything that needs protective packaging.

Make each square by measuring the shorter side of a rectangular sheet, marking the same length along the longer side, and trimming the excess. Check opposite edges and compare the two diagonals. Equal diagonals are a useful sign that the sheet is square. Put the patterned face down so it will show outside after folding. Keep pencil marks light and on the reverse. A small center mark can help the corner folds meet consistently.

Paper responds differently to folding. Thin paper is easy to crease but may sag; stiff or coated paper may crack if repeatedly bent. Test one crease and any marker or adhesive on scrap first. Use a spoon back or bone folder gently rather than scraping hard

lessons.title: Fold and form the tray

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The tray begins with a crease map. Fold opposite edges together to find the center in each direction, then open the sheet. Bring each corner to that center and crease the short flap. Next fold opposite straight edges toward the middle, crease, and unfold. These intermediate creases are guides for the walls. Align edges before pressing; a drifting fold makes opposite walls uneven. Crease from the middle outward, using firm but controlled pressure. Unfolding is intentional: the paper retains the lines that later guide its shape.

Open the short end flaps and raise one end along its crease. Pinch the two side folds inward so the paper forms triangular supports. Fold the raised end flap over those supports and down into the tray. Repeat at the other end. The tucked triangles support the ends; they are not scraps to remove. Work along existing creases instead of pulling the paper upright by force. Stiff paper may resist, so lower the wall and reform the fold gradually.

Set the empty tray on a level table. The base should rest flat, with four similar shallow walls. A loose interior flap may be held with a tiny tape tab, but broad adhesive can wrinkle paper. This remains a presentation o

items: Fold opposite edges together, crease the midpoint, unfold, and repeat in the other direction.
Fold all four corners to the center and crease each flap.
Fold opposite straight edges to the center, crease and open; repeat for the other pair.
Raise one end, pinch side folds inward, tuck the end flap over its triangle supports; repeat at the far end.

blocks.question: What if the lid buckles as it is lowered?
options: Push harder.
Lift it and adjust opposite walls gradually.
Glue it shut.
Cut the assembled box.
blocks.explanation: Remove pressure, inspect alignment, then adjust gently.

lessons.title: Make and adjust the lid
lessons.summary: Make and adjust the lid

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Make the lid from the 21 cm sheet by repeating the same center, corner, and wall folds. The larger sheet creates an initial allowance for the lid to sit outside the tray, but it cannot guarantee exact clearance. Thick paper and uneven folds change the fit. Form the lid walls gently and check that all four corners remain intact. Compare the lid with the tray before decorating. If one wall is visibly taller, reopen that section and use the existing crease as a guide; cutting a folded edge can weaken its corner.

Lower the lid over the empty tray with the corners aligned. If it catches, lift it rather than pushing down. Note which sides touch. A tight lid can be eased by reforming opposite walls slightly outward. A loose lid can be folded slightly inward or paired with a removable paper band. Change one small amount at a time and retest. Symmetric adjustment keeps the cap centered. Do not crush the base to make the parts fit.

Place the intended lightweight favor inside and close the lid once. It should not press on the contents or bow upward. The box is not for mailing, stacking or rough transport; carry it level and support it underneath if needed. If the tray is uneven, correct it

items: Repeat the tray's crease pattern on the 21 cm sheet.
Raise and tuck lid walls; compare corners and wall heights with tray.
Lower lid over empty tray; adjust opposite lid walls slightly until it sits without pressure.
Place the light favor inside and close the lid; remove it before decorating.

blocks.question: Which favor best suits the box?

Unwrapped food.
Small note or sealed wrapped token.

lessons.title: Decorate and finish responsibly

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Decorate after the fit is settled. Choose one simple original motif: dots, geometric lines, initials, or a small abstract shape. Do not copy a character, logo, or another artist's distinctive illustration. Keep decoration on outside faces and away from the rim where the lid slides. Thick layers change the fit; wet marker or glue can warp paper. Test color on scrap and let it dry according to its label. If color bleeds or remains tacky, use a dry paper accent instead. Keep loose glitter and adhesive away from the favor.

An optional band can add a removable closure. Wrap the 2 cm strip around the closed box without stretching it. Mark the overlap, remove it, and trim a little at a time. Join the strip to itself with a small adhesive dot. It should slide on and off without denting the walls. If it pinches, lengthen it with a paper splice or omit it. Do not use staples or wire; sharp fasteners can catch fingers or snag contents.

Erase pencil marks gently and stop if the surface roughens. Let adhesive dry fully before closing the lid. Set the empty box on a stable tabletop, then test it with the intended lightweight favor. Check that the base sits flat, tucked corners stay down, and t

Apply dry pencil, tested marker, or one lightweight paper accent; let it dry.
Optionally fit the 2 cm band, mark overlap, trim gradually and join band to itself.
Inspect the empty box, then test once with the lightweight favor.

To check bleed, smear or buckling.
To prove waterproofing.

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Design a coordinated set of twelve writable recipe cards, four category dividers and a simple folded paperboard presentation sleeve. The set is a dry indoor stationery gift, not a food-contact product

lessons.title: Plan a useful card set
lessons.summary: Plan a useful card set

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A gift set feels considered when the cards share a system but remain easy to use. This project makes twelve portrait-oriented cards, each 4 inches wide by 6 inches tall. That gives enough room for a recipe name, a short ingredient list and method notes without creating a bulky oversized stack. Four dividers use the same width and extend half an inch beyond the cards, leaving a visible tab. The categories are adaptable: choose four that make sense to the recipient, such as breakfast, mains, sides and sweets. Do not assume a recipient's diet or write health claims into the design.

Begin with a paper prototype. Draw a 4-by-6-inch rectangle on scrap and reserve a 0.5-inch top band for the title. Leave a 0.5-inch margin on the other edges. Lightly rule a writing area with two columns: a 1.4-inch ingredient column and a 2.0-inch method column, separated by a narrow gutter. A 4-inch width leaves only 3 inches after side margins, so these numbers are approximate guides, not rigid boxes; make sure the measured columns plus gutter fit the 3-inch usable width. Leave the lower 0.5 inch for source, date or notes. The card remains blank for the recipient to fill in.

Choose three colors: one ba

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On scrap, draw one 4-by-6-inch portrait card and mark a 0.5-inch title band, side margins and lower notes strip.
Select four category names and three coordinated colors; sketch one small motif that can be repeated without covering writing space.
Test the chosen stock and pen on a scrap: write a heading, draw one ruled line, and check whether ink feathers or shows through.

blocks.body: Keep scissors pointed away from the body and pass them handle-first. Younger learners should work with an attentive adult.

blocks.question: Why test the actual stock with the intended pen before making all twelve cards?
options: To confirm legibility and whether the mark feathers or shows through
To certify the card as food-safe
To make the paperboard waterproof
To avoid measuring the cards
blocks.explanation: Testing a scrap is a practical way to spot feathering and readability problems without wasting the full supply.

lessons.title: Measure and make the cards and dividers
lessons.summary: Measure and make the cards and dividers

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Accuracy comes from a stable reference edge and repeated measurement, not from rushing. Use the first card as a master template. On each sheet, mark the outer edges lightly in pencil and connect marks with a ruler. Cut slightly outside the pencil line, then trim to it; this is easier to control than trying to follow a long cut in one motion. If your ruler has centimeter markings, 4 by 6 inches is approximately 10.2 by 15.2 centimetres. Use one unit system consistently and do not mix rounded conversions from one edge to another.

The dividers are 4 inches wide and 6.5 inches tall. Their top half-inch extends above the cards, making a visible tab. Write each category on that exposed portion. Cut four dividers from the lighter paper, then reinforce each by attaching it to a matching card-stock back. The finished divider should remain flat and not curl. Align its bottom edge and sides with the backing; leave the extra half-inch at the top exposed. Use thin adhesive coverage rather than a wet puddle, which can wrinkle paper.

Make twelve cards from the heavier stock. If sheets are too small, join panels only for dividers, not for the writing cards, because a seam can snag a pen and spli

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Mark and cut twelve 4-by-6-inch rectangles from heavyweight stock, using a master template and trimming each edge against a ruler.
Cut four 4-by-6.5-inch lightweight-paper panels and four matching 4-by-6.5-inch backing panels; glue each decorative panel to its backing, aligned at sides and bottom.
Pencil each category name on the exposed tab and add a small motif in the corner below it; ink after checking the four labels as a set.

blocks.question: What is the planned finished size of each recipe card?

6 by 9 inches
4 by 6 inches

lessons.title: Add a writing system and folded sleeve
lessons.summary: Add a writing system and folded sleeve

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The cards should invite use rather than turn into miniature posters. Add the same small header on each card: recipe name, then compact prompts for yield, ingredients and method. Use pencil guides first. If you make rules, draw them lightly with a ruler and leave ample blank height for handwriting. A 0.5-inch title band and 0.5-inch bottom notes strip are starting proportions, not a law; a recipient who writes large may need fewer rules. Test a filled sample with your ordinary pen. Check that a name, a few ingredients and several method lines fit without touching the edges.

The sleeve is an open-ended wrap, not a sealed box. Place the 4-inch card width along the 12-inch dimension of the 12-by-9-inch paperboard. From one short edge, mark fold lines at 4 inches, 8 inches and 8.5 inches. The first two 4-inch panels wrap around the front and back of the card stack; the remaining half-inch is a glue tab. The 9-inch dimension accommodates a 6.5-inch divider plus about 1.25 inches of clearance at top and bottom. When folded, the blank remains open at both ends and cards can slide out. Test this geometry around the actual stack before gluing. If your paperboard differs or the stack is thic

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On each card, pencil the same compact prompts and add only the planned border or motif; test one sample by writing a mock title and several lines.
On the 12-by-9-inch paperboard, mark vertical fold lines at 4, 8 and 8.5 inches from one short edge; mark a light centerline across the 9-inch dimension if useful.
Dry-fit the folded blank around the stacked cards and dividers; trim excess only if needed, then score the confirmed fold lines gently with a ruler and blunt tool.
Fold on the scores, apply a thin line of paper glue to the 0.5-inch tab, and attach it inside the opposite panel; hold gently until it grips, then leave flat to dry.

blocks.body: Keep scissors pointed away from the body and pass them handle-first. Younger learners should work with an attentive adult.

blocks.question: The writing test looks crowded. What is the best adjustment?
options: Add another decorative border
Remove or simplify rules and widen the method area
Write smaller until it fits
Glue a second card over the writing area
blocks.explanation: The card's purpose is writable space. Reducing decoration is the safer design correction.

lessons.title: Finish, inspect and prepare the gift
lessons.summary: Finish, inspect and prepare the gift

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Finishing is an inspection, not a race to add more decoration. First check that all glue is dry to the touch and that the sleeve seam stays closed during ordinary tabletop handling. It is not designed to be carried as a protective case, shipped, or exposed to moisture. Slide the cards out and back in once. If an edge snags, identify whether it is a rough cut, a protruding glue ridge or a divider tab that is not aligned. Correct only that point. Do not seal the open ends.

Count twelve cards and four dividers. Verify that the category names match your plan and that no card has an accidental mark in the writing area. Use a fresh sheet as the recipient's first blank card if you want a hand-written note; keep the note separate from the usable recipe cards. If you include a sample, label it clearly as an example written by the maker, not as tested culinary or food-preservation guidance. This course teaches paper craft only. The set is not certified for food contact, and adhesives or ink should not touch food.

A good gift lets the recipient personalize it. You may add a small cover label reading “Recipes to keep,” but avoid borrowed logos, branded characters or copied artwork. Keep the

items: After full drying, slide the stack in and out once, then count twelve cards and four dividers and inspect the sleeve seam and cut edges.
Compare the finished set with the plan, remove stray pencil marks, and write a separate gift note that explains the set is blank reusable stationery.

blocks.body: Keep scissors pointed away from the body and pass them handle-first. Younger learners should work with an attentive adult.

blocks.question: Which is an accurate description of the finished sleeve?
options: A load-bearing storage box
A water-resistant food wrapper
A shipping package for fragile objects
An open-ended decorative stationery wrap for dry indoor use

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a reusable tabletop memory jar with a removable paper sleeve and a set of thoughtfully worded prompts. The finished jar stores folded notes about shared moments, personal milestones, gratitude, a

lessons.title: Plan a jar that fits its notes
lessons.summary: Plan a jar that fits its notes

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A memory jar works best when the container is easy to reach and the writing slips are large enough to read after folding. Choose a stable, clean, dry container with a wide opening. A roughly 10 cm diameter and 12 cm height is a useful sample, not a required standard. Check that the lid opens without force and that no rim is chipped or sharp. This is a dry indoor keepsake, not a food-contact item. Decide whether notes will be private, shared by invitation, or made as a gift. That choice affects the label: a gentle invitation such as “Open when you want to remember” is less demanding than an instruction to share every note.

Use a scrap strip to measure around the container at the point where the sleeve will sit. Add about 1.5 cm to that circumference for an overlap, then cut a 10 cm tall sleeve so it ends about 1 cm below the rim and 1 cm above the base. For a 10 cm round container, the circumference is about 31.4 cm; a 33 cm sleeve can fit with a small overlap. Container shapes vary, so the scrap-strip test is more reliable than assuming the sample dimension. A sleeve should not cover the lid seam or make the container harder to grip. Test one paper slip before preparing a full bat

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect and measure the container; wrap a scrap strip around the sleeve area and mark where its ends meet.
Transfer the strip length to sturdy paper, add 1.5 cm overlap, and mark a 10 cm sleeve height with top and bottom clearance.
Draft six prompts on scrap, mixing memory, sensory detail, learning, gratitude, and future reflection; include permission to pass.

blocks.body: Use only a clean, dry, stable container with a smooth, undamaged rim. Do not use glass if a suitable plastic or paperboard container is available; never cut glass.

blocks.question: Why measure around the container with a scrap strip before cutting the sleeve?
options: It accounts for the actual circumference and leaves room for overlap.
It makes the container food safe.
It guarantees that the jar cannot tip.
It prevents all paper from tearing.
blocks.explanation: A measured scrap strip transfers the real circumference; adding a small overlap gives the sleeve a fastening seam.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan a jar that fits its notes. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut, fold, and label the paper pieces
lessons.summary: Cut, fold, and label the paper pieces

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The slips are the working part of the project, so prioritize legible writing and easy retrieval over decorative complexity. Use a ruler and pencil to mark a batch of rectangles about 7.5 cm by 12 cm. This dimension leaves room for several handwritten lines and folds into a compact piece that usually fits a wide-mouth container. Test a single slip in your chosen container before cutting the rest. If it catches at the opening, trim its width slightly; if it becomes too small to write on, use fewer folds or choose a wider container. Do not stuff the jar to its maximum capacity. A loose stack is easier to add to and remove from.

Create two groups: blank memory slips and prompt slips. For a simple system, use the same size paper but mark prompt slips with a small dot in one corner. That mark remains visible after folding and helps distinguish a question from a written memory. If color is used, do not depend on color alone; a pencil symbol or short label also works for people who do not distinguish colors easily. Write prompts in large, dark, high-contrast lettering. Good prompts are concrete yet flexible: “What small detail from this week would you like to keep?” invites a specific ans

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Mark and cut six or more slips about 7.5 x 12 cm; test one folded slip through the container opening.
Separate at least six blank memory slips from six prompt slips; put a small drawn dot or word on each prompt slip.
Write prompts in dark, readable lettering and fold each slip in half, then once more only if it still opens comfortably.

blocks.body: Use only a clean, dry, stable container with a smooth, undamaged rim. Do not use glass if a suitable plastic or paperboard container is available; never cut glass.

blocks.question: A folded slip catches at the opening. What is the best first response?
options: Push it through with a pen.
Trim a test slip slightly, reduce folds, or remove excess contents and retest.
Glue the slip into the jar.
Cut the container opening wider.
blocks.explanation: The safe fit correction is to reduce slip width or folds, or lessen crowding. Do not force or modify the container.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut, fold, and label the paper pieces. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Make a removable sleeve and assemble the jar
lessons.summary: Make a removable sleeve and assemble the jar

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A removable sleeve adds a personal gift finish without permanently covering the container. Place the measured paper around the jar and check that its ends overlap by about 1.5 cm. Before fastening, remove it and decorate the paper on a flat surface. Use an original pattern: repeating dots, bands, leaves drawn from observation, geometric shapes, a small date, or a handwritten title. Avoid copied characters, logos, or artwork. Keep the design around the sleeve rather than applying liquid finishes to the container. A sleeve can be removed for repair or reuse, and it should never interfere with a lid, opening, or the user’s grip.

Fasten the overlap with two short pieces of removable paper tape, one near the top and one near the bottom. Place the sleeve back on the container and check that it sits level. If tape is not suitable, use a small amount of ordinary paper glue on the overlap only and leave the sleeve off the jar until fully dry according to the product label. Do not substitute hot glue, solvent adhesive, or an aerosol coating. The container remains a dry keepsake; decoration does not make it food safe or more protective.

Prepare the contents in an uncluttered sequence. Put b

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Remove the measured sleeve, decorate it flat with an original title and simple pattern, leaving edges clear.
Wrap the sleeve and secure only its overlap with two short tape pieces, or use paper glue and wait until fully dry.
Add a few folded slips and a brief optional-use instruction card, then close and reopen the lid once.

blocks.body: Use only a clean, dry, stable container with a smooth, undamaged rim. Do not use glass if a suitable plastic or paperboard container is available; never cut glass.

blocks.question: Which prompt best respects different experiences and privacy?
options: What was your happiest family holiday?
Tell everyone your most private secret.
What small detail from a recent day would you like to remember? You may pass.
Why was this year perfect?
blocks.explanation: An inclusive prompt lets the writer choose the memory and explicitly preserves the option not to answer.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Make a removable sleeve and assemble the jar. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Test, refine, and give thoughtfully
lessons.summary: Test, refine, and give thoughtfully

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful final check asks whether the jar is comfortable to use, not whether it looks professionally manufactured. Set it on a level tabletop and gently tap the table beside it, not the container. It should remain upright. Open the lid normally, add one folded note, and retrieve a different note. The sleeve must not cover the lid seam, slip into the opening, or make the jar difficult to hold. Read each prompt once and consider whether a person can choose not to answer. Replace any question that assumes a happy event, a particular relationship, a holiday, or a willingness to share. A memory jar can include mixed feelings; there is no requirement to write only cheerful notes.

If giving the jar to someone else, include blank paper and a note explaining that they may use it privately, share selected notes, or not use a prompt. Do not write another person’s private story without permission. If the jar is for a group, provide a separate collection envelope and explain who may read notes before anyone contributes. This project is not a confidential storage system. For sensitive information, choose another way to preserve it. For an individual gift, a prompt can focus on ordinary details:

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Place the jar on a level table and check that it stands upright with the sleeve clear of rim, base, and lid seam.
Add and retrieve folded notes, then read every prompt for assumptions, legibility, and an explicit option to pass.
Prepare a gift card describing private use and optional sharing; offer blank slips and invite the recipient to adapt the prompts.

blocks.body: Use only a clean, dry, stable container with a smooth, undamaged rim. Do not use glass if a suitable plastic or paperboard container is available; never cut glass.

blocks.question: What does decorating the container or sleeve establish about food use?
options: That it is safe for dry snacks only.
That it can store liquids if the lid closes.
That it is safe for any household purpose.
Nothing about food safety; use it only as a dry craft keepsake.
blocks.explanation: A decorated container has not been certified or tested for food contact, so keep it to dry paper notes.

lessons.title: Choose the story and prepare the paper

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: A memorable mini-book is selective: a few moments with space around them usually read more clearly than a crowded stack of memorabilia. This design uses a 4.25 × 5.5 inch closed cover. Each interior sheet measures 8 × 10.5 inches before folding, making two leaves with a 5.25-inch height and 4-inch width. Three nested sheets form six spreads, or twelve visible page faces. blocks.heading: Overview

Place the three folded interior sheets inside one another with their folded edges together. Keep the sheets nested rather than stacking them as separate signatures: this simple structure has one central fold and no hidden sewing channel. Put the folded cover around the stack. Because cover and interior heights differ slightly, the cover should extend beyond the leaf edges; check the stack before punching. The ribbon holes sit on the cover’s spine area, about 1 inch from the top and bottom edges and about 3/8 inch from the fold. Punch through cover and pages together only if the punch can cut the stack cleanly without crushing it. Otherwise punch each layer separately using a pencil mark as a guide. Leave ribbon slack; the closure is only to keep pages together, not compress them. On opening, pages should turn freely and the covers should not buckle. On every edge of the image
On the flat corner tabs attached to the page

Keep the inner margin about 1/2 inch from the fold and the outer margin about 1/4 inch from the page edge. A 3 × 4 inch image fits on a 4 × 5.25 inch page, but use a smaller image if you want a caption below it. Paper photo corners are a useful low-adhesive approach: fold a small square diagonally, fold the triangle’s two points inward, then place it over one image corner. Rotate page layouts modestly so the book feels varied, but keep type siz
