lessons.title: Describe and prepare the surfaces
lessons.summary: Describe and prepare the surfaces

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Before attaching anything, learn to describe texture in a way another person can use. Look at each piece in ordinary indoor light. Note whether it is matte or reflective, smooth or visibly ridged, tightly woven or open, flat or raised. Then touch it lightly with a fingertip. Describe pressure gently; do not rub rough or shedding samples across skin. Use concrete language: “parallel raised ribs,” “soft short pile,” or “fine crosshatch weave.” These are observations, not claims about fiber content or performance. A scrap that looks like cotton is not automatically identified as cotton.

Preparation should preserve the surface rather than disguise it. Trim loose threads with scissors if the material can be cut safely. Do not pull a thread hard, because that can unravel a woven edge. For a fraying fabric, fold a narrow edge under or plan to hold it with two paper tabs. If small paper is curled, flatten it between clean books while you prepare the rest; do not add water. For flexible mesh or netting, place it over a plain paper backing sample only if the backing is separately identified and the paired layers are clearly noted. Otherwise, use a contrasting card beneath the open weave and

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: For each sample, write two short observations: one visual feature and one gentle-touch feature, using specific descriptive words.
Trim loose fibers only where ordinary scissors cut cleanly; fold a fraying edge inward by about 5 mm where it can be folded without bulk.
Choose a paper tab, thread tack, or tiny labeled craft-glue dot for each sample; test the chosen method on a spare offcut first.
Set out the samples in a deliberate order, alternating smooth/raised and light/dark appearances; keep the chosen order on your notes.

blocks.body: Use clean, dry, odor-free scraps. Reject moldy, oily, dusty, contaminated, brittle, or unidentified chemical-coated material; do not sniff, sand, burn, or wet-test scraps.

blocks.question: A candidate scrap has an unknown coating and a chemical odor. What should you do?
options: Heat it briefly to identify the coating
Reject it and choose a clean, known, dry alternative
Wash it and use it while still damp
Cover the odor with glue
blocks.explanation: Do not sniff closely, heat, wet-test, or otherwise experiment with unknown coatings. Replace the sample.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Describe and prepare the surfaces. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Attach samples and make readable labels
lessons.summary: Attach samples and make readable labels

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Attach the samples one at a time, starting in the upper-left cell and following your planned order. Use only the attachment method tested for that sample. A sample should lie flat enough to inspect, but it need not be stretched taut. Stretching fabric changes its shape and can make a sample appear smoother or wider than it naturally is. For a paper tab, place a 1 × 3 cm strip across one edge or corner so that about 1 cm covers the sample and the remainder lies on the board. Add a small amount of paper glue under the tab, not across the texture. Use a second tab opposite the first if the sample lifts. For fabric that resists glue or would be obscured by tabs, use a couple of loose tacks through the cardboard. Keep stitches short and snug, not tight enough to pucker. If a needle is used, work slowly and keep its point directed away from hands.

Labels should identify a material as observed, not overstate what it is. Write a short sample name in large clear letters, such as “ribbed knit scrap,” then a one-line note like “soft loops; raised vertical ridges.” If the source is unknown, use “unknown woven scrap” rather than guessing. Leave the sample itself visible; never cover an interes

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Attach the first sample using the tested method, centering it in its 8 × 5 cm cell and leaving planned label space.
Continue in grid order, using one or two tabs, a few loose thread tacks, or the smallest effective glue amount for each sample.
Write each sample name and one concise visual or tactile observation on paper labels, then attach labels in a consistent position.
Set the board flat in a ventilated, undisturbed area and wait for the craft-glue label directions to be satisfied before lifting it.

blocks.body: Use clean, dry, odor-free scraps. Reject moldy, oily, dusty, contaminated, brittle, or unidentified chemical-coated material; do not sniff, sand, burn, or wet-test scraps.

blocks.question: What is the most useful label for a scrap whose fiber content is unknown?
options: 100% cotton, guaranteed
Waterproof cloth
Unknown woven scrap; fine diagonal ribs
Premium fabric
blocks.explanation: Name only what you know and describe observable texture rather than inventing composition or performance.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Attach samples and make readable labels. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Inspect, refine, and use the reference board
lessons.summary: Inspect, refine, and use the reference board

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A finished board should be judged by whether it supports clear comparison, not whether every square is perfectly identical. Inspect it after the attachment has dried. Look for lifted corners, stray threads, unreadable labels, glue visible on the sample face, and edges that could catch a hand. Turn the board slowly and inspect the back as well. Any thread end should be tied or trimmed safely, and no needle should remain. Do not pull hard on a sample to test it; a gentle touch at an edge is enough for this non-load-bearing display object. The backing is not a handle, shelf, or stand, and the board is not intended to carry weight.

Use a simple viewing test: place the board flat on a stable tabletop, step back about an arm's length, and ask whether you can locate a named sample and distinguish it from its neighbors. Then compare your tactile notes with the actual feel. A strong note names a feature that can be checked. Replace “rough” with a more useful description such as “short raised ridges with a dry, firm feel under light touch.” Avoid claims such as waterproof, washable, durable, hypoallergenic, or protective unless you have a suitable test and evidence; this craft project provi

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: After glue has dried, inspect the front, back, corners, labels, and every sample edge without forcefully tugging.
Set the board flat on a stable tabletop and perform an arm’s-length legibility and comparison check on all eight labels and samples.
Make one targeted correction, such as adding a paper tab, replacing a confusing sample, or rewriting an unclear label; record the change on the back.
Store the board flat and dry, then use its named textures as reference when planning a later paper or fabric composition.

blocks.body: Use clean, dry, odor-free scraps. Reject moldy, oily, dusty, contaminated, brittle, or unidentified chemical-coated material; do not sniff, sand, burn, or wet-test scraps.

blocks.question: The tested glue darkens one fabric scrap. Which response best preserves its texture?
options: Add more glue across the surface
Use heat to dry the spot quickly
Stretch the fabric tightly over the board
Stop using glue on that material and try a paper tab or suitable thread tack
blocks.explanation: A stained test is evidence that glue is unsuitable for that scrap. Switch methods or select a replacement.

name: Personalized Reusable Packaging Set
tagline: Make a coordinated set for wrapping small dry gifts: a reusable fabric drawstring pouch, a fold-flat paperboard gift sleeve, and a removable personalized tag.

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a coordinated set for wrapping small dry gifts: a reusable fabric drawstring pouch, a fold-flat paperboard gift sleeve, and a removable personalized tag. The project uses simple straight seams an

lessons.title: Plan the fit and prepare the pieces
lessons.summary: Plan the fit and prepare the pieces

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful reusable set begins with one known gift, not an arbitrary template. This lesson makes a pouch for a sample item no larger than 10 cm wide, 14 cm tall, and 3 cm thick, such as a small notebook or boxed keepsake. The pouch finished flat will be about 24 cm wide by 28 cm high, with room above the object for a gathered mouth. Its panels are cut 26 × 34 cm because the side seams use 1 cm allowances and the top includes a 5 cm turn-over for the drawstring channel. The paper sleeve is designed around a dry, rigid object up to 7 × 10 × 2 cm; it is a presentation sleeve, not a crush-resistant box. If your gift is larger, measure it and redraw both pieces before cutting.

Choose two fabrics that look good together but are easy to distinguish, such as a solid outer cloth and a small-print lining. Avoid stretchy jersey for this first project because it can curl and distort while sewing. Before cutting, inspect the fabric for holes and make sure it is clean and fully dry. Lightly press creases only if an adult-safe iron is already available and the learner knows how to use it; pressing is optional and is not part of the required tool list. For board folds, a shallow score guides the fo

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure the chosen dry gift at its widest, tallest, and thickest points; record the sample limits of 10 × 14 × 3 cm and 7 × 10 × 2 cm separately if making both sizes.
Cut two fabric rectangles, each 26 × 34 cm, and mark the top edge on both pieces with a small removable thread or pencil mark.
On scrap board, test a light score with the blunt tool and fold along it; identify the easier grain direction by a gentle bend test.

blocks.body: Cut on a stable table, direct scissor points away from hands and body, and close or store scissors when not cutting. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What is the first useful action before cutting the pouch panels?
options: Measure the gift and identify which component it needs
Cut both panels at whatever size the fabric permits
Add decorations before deciding dimensions
Use the sleeve dimensions for every piece
blocks.explanation: Measure the object first, then apply the stated panel dimensions or revise them before cutting.

lessons.title: Sew a lined drawstring pouch
lessons.summary: Sew a lined drawstring pouch

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The pouch is made as a tube first, then its lower end is closed. Put the two fabric rectangles right sides together, where “right side” means the face you want visible. Sew both long side edges with a small, even backstitch or running stitch backed by occasional stitches, keeping a 1 cm allowance. Leave the top open. A consistent seam matters more than tiny stitches: use stitches around 4–5 mm and avoid pulling thread so tightly that the cloth puckers. Tie off thread tails securely. Fold the top edge down 1 cm toward the wrong side, then fold another 4 cm to create a channel. The channel should be wide enough for the chosen cord to slide through freely; test the cord before sewing the channel seam. Sew around the lower edge of the folded channel, leaving roughly a 2 cm opening near one side seam. This opening is where the cord enters and exits.

Turn the tube right side out and put the lining inside the outer layer, aligning the top edges. The side seams can sit beside each other rather than directly on top of one another to reduce bulk. If the fabric is bulky, use a thinner cord or make a wider channel rather than forcing the cord through a tight tunnel. Attach a safety pin to the

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: With right sides facing inward, sew both 34 cm sides and the lower short edge with a 1 cm allowance; leave the top open and secure the seams.
Fold the top edge inward 1 cm, then another 4 cm; pin or clip carefully and stitch near the lower folded edge, leaving a 2 cm opening at one side seam.
Turn the pouch right side out, nest the lining inside, feed the 70 cm cord through the channel and back out the opening, then knot its ends.

blocks.body: Cut on a stable table, direct scissor points away from hands and body, and close or store scissors when not cutting. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: How should the top channel be checked before its final seam is completed?
options: Close it completely so no opening remains
Test that the cord slides through and leave a 2 cm entry opening
Make the channel narrower than the cord
Cut a slit through the fabric after sewing
blocks.explanation: A cord-sized channel and a small deliberate seam gap allow the cord to pass without forcing it.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Sew a lined drawstring pouch. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fold the presentation sleeve and make a tag
lessons.summary: Fold the presentation sleeve and make a tag

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The paperboard sleeve wraps a small flat gift in a continuous band with a broad front panel, a back panel, and a short overlap. It is intentionally open at both ends, so it does not enclose objects or stop them from falling out. Cut a rectangle 24 cm wide × 18 cm high. Across the 24 cm direction, mark vertical fold lines at 7.2 cm, 9.4 cm, 16.6 cm, and 18.8 cm from the left edge. These create panels of 7.2 cm front, 2.2 cm side, 7.2 cm back, 2.2 cm side, and a 5.2 cm overlap flap. The 18 cm height leaves extra margin around a 10 cm tall item; center the item and trim only after a paper test if the sleeve looks too tall. Score each line with a blunt tool against a ruler using light pressure, then fold away from the visible printed face if it is the cleaner side.

Wrap the band around the sample gift, keeping the 7.2 cm panels on the broad faces and 2.2 cm panels on the narrow sides. The overlap flap should cover the first panel by at least 2 cm. If it does not, adjust the band around the object or redo the panel dimensions; do not stretch or crease the gift to force a fit. Use a short removable tape tab inside the overlap, or use a simple slit-and-tab closure if the board holds its

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut board to 24 × 18 cm and mark folds at 7.2, 9.4, 16.6, and 18.8 cm across the width.
Score each marked line lightly with a blunt tool and ruler, then fold each line in turn to form a rectangular loop around the sample object.
Secure the overlap with a removable paper tab or paper tape, then cut a 6 × 8 cm tag and add a name or original geometric motif.

blocks.body: Cut on a stable table, direct scissor points away from hands and body, and close or store scissors when not cutting. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of scoring the paperboard?
options: Cut most of the way through the board
Make a shallow guide that helps the board fold neatly
Make the sleeve waterproof
Replace all measuring and marking
blocks.explanation: A shallow score guides the fold.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Fold the presentation sleeve and make a tag. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Coordinate, test, and refine the reusable set
lessons.summary: Coordinate, test, and refine the reusable set

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A finished set should be easy to use again. Lay the pouch, sleeve, and tag together and check that one accent color or repeated shape links them. Add a small fabric scrap accent to the pouch with a few hand stitches, or draw a simple line motif on the tag. Keep embellishments flat so they do not catch on the cord or rub away against the board. Do not attach loose beads or anything that could be swallowed by a young child or pet. Wait for any marker or glue to dry as directed by its label. Test the pouch by placing only the intended dry gift inside, gathering the cord, lifting it just enough to move it from table to table, and setting it down. This is a fit and seam check, not a carrying-capacity test. Do not fill it with heavy objects or present it as a safety pouch.

Test the sleeve around its intended flat gift while the gift rests on a stable tabletop. It should slide on without forcing, remain in place when gently nudged, and open without tearing. The board sleeve is for presentation only; it should never be used as a stand or support. Inspect all fold lines for cracks, the cord channel for loose stitches, and the pouch interior for exposed needle ends. Remove and store the gif

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Add one coordinated flat accent to the pouch or tag using stitches or a small original drawn motif, then let any labeled product dry fully.
Place the intended dry gift in the pouch, gather the cord, and gently move it between nearby tabletop positions before setting it down.
Fit the flat gift into the sleeve on a stable table, check the overlap and folds, then remove the gift and flatten the sleeve for storage.

blocks.body: Cut on a stable table, direct scissor points away from hands and body, and close or store scissors when not cutting. Younger learners need appropriate adult supervision.

blocks.question: The finished sleeve has only a 1 cm overlap around the gift. What is the best response?
options: Force it closed and press the gift inward
Add bulky decorations over the join
Measure again and recut with a longer overlap or adjusted panels
Call it a protective shipping container
blocks.explanation: A fit issue should be corrected through measurement and resizing, never by forcing or overstating performance.

name: Modular Cardboard Display Stand
tagline: Design and build a compact, dry indoor tabletop display stand from reclaimed single-wall corrugated cardboard.

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Design and build a compact, dry indoor tabletop display stand from reclaimed single-wall corrugated cardboard. Three interlocking components—a broad foot, upright spine, and shallow ledge—make an adju

lessons.title: Plan the parts and test your board
lessons.summary: Plan the parts and test your board

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
The stand uses three flat parts that cross through snug slots: a horizontal base, a vertical back, and a short front ledge. The base is 18 cm wide by 10 cm deep. The back is 18 cm wide by 20 cm high. The ledge is 18 cm wide by 4 cm high. The central spine occupies a 4 cm-wide region of the back and base, leaving material on both sides. This is a deliberately modest display for a lightweight paper card. The broad base gives the stand a footprint, but it does not turn cardboard into furniture or make the object safe for a heavy frame. Center the spine in the 10 cm base depth, leaving 5 cm of base in front and 5 cm behind its plane; the arrangement should sit flat, not lean precariously.

Corrugated board has flat paper faces with a wavy interior. Inspect the edge to see the flute channels, then draw a small arrow parallel to them on the inside face of every panel. Orient the spine's flute channels vertically when the stand is assembled, so the back's vertical dimension follows the channels. The base channels run front-to-back. Reused panels may have folds, labels, or crush marks; place the best uncreased area where a slot will be cut. Test a slot on scrap first because board thicknes

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect two clean board areas and mark flute direction with arrows; reject damp, moldy, torn, heavily crushed, or stapled areas.
Draw paper templates for base 18 × 10 cm, back 18 × 20 cm, and ledge 18 × 4 cm; label front, rear, top, and flute arrows.
On scrap, mark a 4 cm-long test slot, then estimate its width from the measured board thickness; make the cut using scissors or adult-supervised knife technique.
Choose the cleanest face for the front and mark intended front/back directions on the paper templates before transferring anything.

blocks.body: This is a lightweight decorative tabletop stand, not load-bearing furniture, a shelf, a protective device, or a tested product support. Use only for a light paper card in stationary viewing.

blocks.question: What is the correct response when the back slot will not slide into the base with gentle pressure?
options: Push hard until it seats
Separate the parts and widen the slot a tiny amount after checking a scrap fit
Fill the slot with wet glue
Tap the stand against the table
blocks.explanation: A close but non-forced fit is the goal. Tune the slot in small increments or remake damaged stock.

lessons.title: Mark, cut, and refine the three parts
lessons.summary: Mark, cut, and refine the three parts

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Transfer each template to the board with a pencil and ruler. Use square corners and light lines so the finished edges remain easy to read. Keep the base's 18 cm width parallel to the back's 18 cm width. Put the base slot at the center of its width: mark the midpoint at 9 cm, then mark a 4 cm-long line centered there, running front-to-back. This slot crosses the 10 cm depth at its midpoint, so the base extends 5 cm forward and 5 cm behind the back plane. The back gets a matching slot from its bottom edge, centered across its 18 cm width. Make this slot 4 cm long, so when inserted into the base it reaches the base's mid-plane. With board thickness measured as t, slot width is t plus only a small clearance—start at t + 1 mm on scrap. Cardboard compresses and varies, so the test fit matters more than a false appearance of precision.

The ledge is a separate 18 × 4 cm strip. It crosses the back through a short centered slit about 2 cm above the base. Mark a horizontal slit along the back's 18 cm width, centered at 9 cm and sized to the ledge thickness plus approximately 1 mm, then fit the ledge so about 2 cm projects forward and the remaining 2 cm sits behind the back. This little lip c

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Transfer and cut the 18 × 10 cm base rectangle, then mark its centered 4 cm front-to-back slot at the board-specific test width.
Cut the 18 × 20 cm back and its 4 cm bottom slot, centered across the width and matching the base slot's measured width.
Cut the 18 × 4 cm ledge and mark a centered slit across the back about 2 cm above the base; fit the ledge through it with equal projection front and rear.
Compare the three cut parts against their templates, mark any rough edge that needs a tiny trim, and recheck slot width using the scrap sample.

blocks.body: This is a lightweight decorative tabletop stand, not load-bearing furniture, a shelf, a protective device, or a tested product support. Use only for a light paper card in stationary viewing.

blocks.question: Where should the base slot sit across the base's 18 cm width?
options: At 3 cm from the left edge
At the rear edge
Centered at 9 cm
Anywhere, because the ledge balances it
blocks.explanation: Half of 18 cm is 9 cm, so the spine is centered across the base width.

lessons.title: Interlock the stand and add the paper stop
lessons.summary: Interlock the stand and add the paper stop

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Assemble on a flat table. Slide the back's bottom slot over the base slot with both parts held near the joint, not at a distant edge that could buckle the board. Press gradually until the back's bottom edge meets the base's upper face. The base should remain flat and the back should look centered when viewed from the front. If the joint resists, separate the parts and adjust the slot width by a very small amount with scissors. Never lever one panel against the other; the surface liner can split before the joint appears to move. A joint that slips freely is also a signal to stop and remake a part, not to pack the gap with a hard object.

Insert the ledge into its slit at the marked height. Center it so the ends line up with the back's side edges. Look at the stand from the side: the base is level, the back is approximately vertical, and the ledge points straight forward rather than tilting. Since this is a simple cross-slot prototype, it has no hidden brace or engineered angle. Its usable load is limited to a lightweight paper card held stationary. Do not use a framed print, glass, a tablet, or a phone as a test object. The card should rest with its bottom edge behind the lip and it

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: On a level table, slide the back slot over the base slot using gentle pressure close to the joint; stop at the base surface.
Insert the ledge into its horizontal slit, center its ends with the back, and align it roughly 2 cm above the base.
Place a plain card up to 15 × 18 cm against the back with its lower edge behind the ledge; use no frame or electronic object.
Remove the card, inspect joints and liner faces, then optionally add light paper decoration outside all slot edges and allow it to dry fully.

blocks.body: This is a lightweight decorative tabletop stand, not load-bearing furniture, a shelf, a protective device, or a tested product support. Use only for a light paper card in stationary viewing.

blocks.question: Which item is appropriate for the project's stability check?
options: A lightweight paper card, stationary on a stable table
A framed glass picture
A phone connected to a charger
A stack of books to test capacity
blocks.explanation: Use only a lightweight paper card for still tabletop viewing; no test here establishes a load rating.

lessons.title: Check stability, improve, and store
lessons.summary: Check stability, improve, and store

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A careful test is a sequence of observations, not a strength demonstration. First remove the card and inspect the table contact points. The base should touch the surface without rocking. Next assemble the back and ledge, then place the paper card in its intended position. Observe from front and side for a short period while your hands remain ready nearby. Do not push, shake, stack objects, or leave the stand near an edge. If it tips or rocks, remove the card immediately. This project has no certified capacity; a failed stability check means the stand should not be used until you make a modest correction and repeat the paper-only check. It may be simpler to use a smaller card or rebuild a cleaner base than to add weight.

Diagnose the symptom before changing anything. A base that rocks with no card likely has a warped panel or uneven cut. Replace the base or trim a tiny high corner only if that does not make the footprint narrow. A back that leans because the slot is loose needs a replacement part with a closer-fitting slot; wedges can split the liner and are not a sound fix. A card that slides while the stand remains flat may need the ledge centered or a smaller card. Record the ex

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: With the stand empty, inspect the base from two sides and check whether it rocks on a level table.
Place only the suggested lightweight paper card against the back, watch for sliding or lifting, and remove it immediately if any part tips.
Write down one symptom, likely cause, one adjustment, and the result after repeating the same paper-only check.
Remove the card, slide the ledge and back free without twisting, and store the dry components flat; inspect again before future use.

blocks.body: This is a lightweight decorative tabletop stand, not load-bearing furniture, a shelf, a protective device, or a tested product support. Use only for a light paper card in stationary viewing.

blocks.question: Why make a test slot on scrap before cutting the final joints?
options: To make the cardboard waterproof
To determine how the actual board thickness affects the fit
To guarantee the stand supports any frame
To avoid measuring the parts
blocks.explanation: A scrap test helps tune a snug slot to the specific board while protecting the finished panel.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Check stability, improve, and store. What did you learn and verify?

name: Craft-Project Planning Journal
tagline: Make a reusable paper planning journal that turns a craft idea into a practical, budget-aware project plan.
outcome: Create a compact 12-page journal from two letter-size sheets, with aligned folds and a secured center binding.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Craft-Project Planning Journal

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Make a reusable paper planning journal that turns a craft idea into a practical, budget-aware project plan. You will build a 12-page folded booklet, create repeatable project-record pages, and use a w

lessons.title: Make a useful project brief before choosing supplies
lessons.summary: Make a useful project brief before choosing supplies

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A planning journal earns its space by helping you make decisions before you buy or cut anything. Begin with one object and one intended use. Keep this course's practice example modest: a dry indoor paper desk tray for lightweight, nonhazardous stationery, sized to sit on a stable tabletop. It is not a shelf, a phone stand, or a container for food, liquids, hot objects, or electrical equipment. A precise limit prevents the plan from quietly becoming a claim about strength or safety that has never been tested.

Use a project brief with four parts: what you want to make, who or what it is for, where it will be used, and what it must not do. Add two or three measurable constraints, such as maximum footprint, approximate budget, and whether you already own the materials. A brief is not a shopping wish list. It is a filter: if a new embellishment adds cost but does not support the intended use, defer it. Ohio State University Extension recommends researching intended use and preparing a budget and shopping list before purchasing craft supplies; this course applies that idea in a small, repeatable journal format.

The journal has 12 numbered faces, not 12 separate sheets. Two letter-size

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Write a one-sentence project brief naming the object, intended user, and dry indoor location; use the sample lightweight stationery tray if needed.
List three constraints: maximum footprint, a spending limit in your own currency, and one material you already have.
On the first working face, draw a simple top view and side view of the proposed object; label only its overall target dimensions and the parts you have not resolved.
Create a ‘not for’ box on the risk-review face and record prohibited uses plus any unknowns that require a safer redesign.

blocks.body: Use scissors in a clear, well-lit work area; carry them closed and pass them handle-first. Young learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: What is the best first entry in a project brief?
options: A detailed shopping list of attractive supplies
The object, intended user, and place of use
A promise that the finished object will last for years
A decorative title and color palette only
blocks.explanation: A clear brief identifies the proposed object and context before materials or decoration are chosen.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Make a useful project brief before choosing supplies. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Fold and bind the planning journal
lessons.summary: Fold and bind the planning journal

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
Make a quick prototype from scrap first. For the standard booklet in this lesson, use three letter-size sheets, not two. A letter-size sheet is 8.5 inches wide by 11 inches high. Fold each sheet crosswise so the short edges meet; each folded sheet forms two leaves, and three sheets form six leaves with 12 interior faces. Nest the folded sheets and check the fold direction before adding a separate cover. Number the interior faces in reading order before decoration. Use the first faces for the project brief, constraints, materials, and risk review; later faces hold the sequence, time plan, test observations, and revision. Mark estimated quantities as estimates and revise them after a paper mock-up. The purpose is not to make every project predictable. It is to make assumptions visible early enough to change them cheaply.

For the standard version, fold three sheets and nest them. The finished closed page is 5.5 × 8.5 inches; the open spread is 11 × 8.5 inches. Paper thickness makes the innermost edges extend slightly beyond the outer sheet. Align the fold lines and outer corners, then trim only the exposed fore-edge together to 5.5 inches wide when closed. Do not trim the folded spin

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Fold three letter-size sheets crosswise, matching the short edges, and press each crease gently with a blunt scoring tool.
Nest the three folded sheets, then open the stack and mark the center crease as the spine; number the 12 interior faces in reading order using light pencil marks.
Measure and trim only the exposed fore-edge to a closed width of 5.5 in, keeping the folded spine intact; cut slowly with scissors in manageable passes.
Cut a cover about 11.25 × 8.75 in, fold it at 5.625 in, and test-fit around the closed pages; secure with two clips or a thin glue-stick layer after the fit is right.
Optionally punch two aligned holes on the spine crease, about 1.5 in from each end, and tie a short thread through them with a small knot inside.

blocks.body: Use scissors in a clear, well-lit work area; carry them closed and pass them handle-first. Young learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: Three letter-size sheets folded crosswise create how many interior page faces?
options: 6 faces
8 faces
12 faces
16 faces
blocks.explanation: Each folded sheet forms two leaves; three sheets make six leaves, each with two faces: 12 interior faces.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Fold and bind the planning journal. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Turn an idea into a materials and action plan
lessons.summary: Turn an idea into a materials and action plan

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A useful plan connects each material to a job and a quantity. Avoid entries such as ‘some paper’ or ‘glue.’ For the practice desk-tray plan, write ‘one sheet of medium-weight recycled card for a 20 × 15 cm footprint mock-up’ and mark the size as a proposal to verify. This is not a tested construction recipe: the course teaches you to record and question dimensions, not to claim that a paper tray will support a particular load. The materials page should include what you already own, what must be acquired, why it is needed, and a lower-cost substitute. If a substitute changes thickness or size, mark a new test as necessary. A project that depends on unavailable materials is not ready to begin.

Write the action plan in verbs, one action per numbered line. Put measuring before cutting, dry fitting before gluing, and a review checkpoint after assembly. Under each action, add four short prompts: what to do, why the order matters, what you will check, and what you will do if it fails. A troubleshooting plan should be a safe alternative, not pressure to continue. For example, if a fold cracks, stop and replace the sheet or redesign with fewer folds; do not wet the paper or apply heat to f

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Fill the materials page with item, quantity, purpose, and an alternative; use the journal materials as a model and then draft a separate list for your chosen craft.
Write four to six numbered project actions, each with an action, reason, checkpoint, and safe fallback in the margin or on the facing page.
Record reading, active work, and drying/resting time separately; label each number E, C, or R for estimated, checked, or revised.

blocks.body: Use scissors in a clear, well-lit work area; carry them closed and pass them handle-first. Young learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: A substitute material is a different thickness from the planned one. What should the journal say?
options: Treat it as identical because the color matches
Change the plan silently after beginning
Use more adhesive to compensate
Flag the change and re-check dimensions or sequence with a small mock-up
blocks.explanation: A material change can affect fit and handling. Record it and verify only the relevant planning assumption before proceeding.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Turn an idea into a materials and action plan. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Review, test assumptions, and revise the journal
lessons.summary: Review, test assumptions, and revise the journal

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body:
A plan should be reviewed before supplies are cut. Read it once as if you were a first-time maker who has not heard your explanation. Can that person find the finished dimensions, distinguish a sketch from a verified measurement, and understand what to do if a step goes wrong? Check that every proposed dimension uses the same unit. If the drawing says 20 × 15 cm while the materials list says 8 × 6 inches, convert carefully or choose one unit system for the page. Do not hide uncertainty by rounding away a mismatch.

Use a paper mock-up to check layout and sequence, not to certify performance. For the journal itself, open and close the cover, turn through pages in order, and confirm that the fold and binding do not block writing. For the sample desk tray, draw a full-size footprint on scrap and place it on the intended tabletop to verify only that the footprint fits. Do not load, hang, or treat a paper mock-up as furniture. Record the exact observation and the limit of what it tells you. An honest note reads, ‘The traced 20 × 15 cm outline fits the clear area; no strength or load test was performed.’

When something fails, describe symptom, likely cause, and a safe fix. ‘Pages snag a

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Run a page-order and usability check: open every spread, find each planned section, and confirm there is writing room beside the prompts.
Compare the sketch, material list, and steps for matching dimensions and units; circle any value that is still only an estimate.
Test one non-hazardous planning assumption with a scrap mock-up, such as whether the drawn footprint fits the clear tabletop; write the observation and what it does not prove.
Add a final symptom-cause-fix note and one next-version improvement, then complete the six-item self-checklist.

blocks.body: Use scissors in a clear, well-lit work area; carry them closed and pass them handle-first. Young learners need suitable adult supervision.

blocks.question: Which is an appropriate time record?
options: Reading 30 min; active work 90 min; adhesive resting 20–30 min (estimates)
Finished in five minutes, guaranteed
Two hours total including unknown drying, with no note
Only count the time when glue is wet
blocks.explanation: Separate reading, active work, and resting time, and label estimates as estimates rather than observed results.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Review, test assumptions, and revise the journal. What did you learn and verify?

name: Personal Craft Portfolio and Display Box
tagline: Design and make a compact, personalized paperboard portfolio with a separate tabletop display box.
outcome: Measure a sample paper craft and calculate a portfolio pocket with a usable clearance allowance.
certificateTitle: Rreal Certified: Personal Craft Portfolio and Display Box

modules.title: Project Lessons
modules.description: Design and make a compact, personalized paperboard portfolio with a separate tabletop display box. A folded portfolio stores sketches, small paper crafts, and notes; its matching shallow box presents

lessons.title: Plan the portfolio and map your board
lessons.summary: Plan the portfolio and map your board

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: The portfolio is a flexible organizer for lightweight paper pieces, not a rigid case. Begin with one sample item and design the pocket around its real size. In this course the sample is a 4 × 6 in card. Add 1/4 in (6 mm) to each dimension so it can slide without scraping: the pocket's inside target becomes 4 1/2 × 6 1/2 in (11.5 × 16.5 cm). The pocket front will be 4 1/2 × 5 1/2 in; leaving the top open gives the card a finger-width entry. The back panel is 4 1/2 × 6 1/2 in. The cover opens like a book, so a 1/2 in spine allowance makes the closed portfolio about 5 × 7 in. Your board's flutes may bend more easily in one direction; test this on an offcut instead of forcing a crease. A blunt scorer creates a crease line without cutting through the board. A scored fold closes more neatly and is less likely to split than a hard crushed fold. Sketch the net at full scale before cutting. Mark every line as cut, score, or fold, and label the face that will show. This small map prevents accidental cuts through a hinge. Reserve enough board for the separate 6 × 8 in display base, two 1 in side walls, a 1 in bottom lip, and a rear stand. If your piece is too small, reduce the display dimensi

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure the sample card, then write the card size and 1/4 in clearance on your plan.
Draw a full-size portfolio net: 5 × 7 in cover panel, 1/2 in spine, and 4 1/2 × 6 1/2 in back-pocket area with a 4 1/2 × 5 1/2 in pocket front.
Test a score and fold on an offcut, then label cut lines, score lines, and the portfolio's outside face.

blocks.body: Work on a stable, uncluttered table with good light. Keep drinks away from the craft materials; these objects are dry indoor decor, not food-contact certified.

blocks.question: For a 4 × 6 in sample card, why does the course specify a larger pocket interior?
options: To allow about 1/4 in clearance on each side
To make the portfolio a shipping-safe case
To create space for a battery
To make the pocket mouth permanently closed
blocks.explanation: A small clearance makes a pocket usable while preserving the stated sample dimensions; it does not create certified protection.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Plan the portfolio and map your board. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Cut, fold, and assemble the portfolio
lessons.summary: Cut, fold, and assemble the portfolio

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: Make the portfolio slowly and dry-fit before gluing. Cut only the outer silhouette and relief notches shown on your net. Where a knife is needed for thick board, make several light passes instead of pressing hard; if you cannot keep the board stable, ask a capable adult to cut the piece or redesign it with scissors and thinner board. Keep the blade path clear of your supporting hand. Score the spine line, then bend the board gently over the table edge. The cover should open without springing sharply. Line the inside with smooth paper if the corrugation catches the sample card. Apply adhesive in a thin, even layer and leave a narrow margin at the open pocket mouth; glue squeezed into the opening can trap the card. Press flat under a clean, light book only while drying, and avoid weights that crush the corrugation. Add a closure only after testing the pocket. A ribbon loop can catch around a small paper tab on the front cover; attach the loop to the outside rear panel with a paper patch so the elastic does not pull directly on one small point. Do not stretch the loop tightly. The finished object should close while empty and while holding the sample card, but it is not meant to be stu

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Cut the mapped outline and notches with scissors or supervised controlled knife passes on a cutting mat.
Score the 1/2 in spine, fold gently, and dry-fit the pocket front over its backing with the top left open.
Glue the pocket sides and bottom, leaving the top unglued; attach a paper loop patch and optional loose ribbon closure.
Add a paper liner and original decoration after a fit test, then let adhesive dry as directed.

blocks.body: Work on a stable, uncluttered table with good light. Keep drinks away from the craft materials; these objects are dry indoor decor, not food-contact certified.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of scoring the portfolio spine before folding?
options: To cut the spine fully apart
To make a controlled fold that is less likely to split
To waterproof the cardboard
To increase the pocket capacity
blocks.explanation: Scoring guides the bend; test on scrap because board thickness and flute direction vary.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Cut, fold, and assemble the portfolio. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Build the matching tabletop display box
lessons.summary: Build the matching tabletop display box

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: The display box is a shallow paperboard stage for one lightweight piece, not a storage chest or support for valuable objects. Use a base measuring 6 × 8 in (15 × 20 cm). Add a 1 in front lip and two 1 in side walls, leaving the top open. The back will stand upright with a separate triangular brace. Cut a 6 × 8 in base, a 6 × 1 in front strip, two 8 × 1 in side strips, and a 6 × 5 in back panel. The extra 4 in on the back panel includes a 1 in overlap flap plus a 4 in visible area; score the flap boundary so the panel can attach to the rear edge. For the stand, fold a 2 × 5 in strip into a shallow triangular prism: a 1 in glue tab and two panels about 2 in wide make a prop approximately 2 in deep. The measurements are intended for a compact display and can be adjusted if your board is notably thick. Leave the open upper edge clear so a 4 × 6 in artwork card is easy to place. Assemble with paper tape hinges first. Tape supports the joint while adhesive dries and lets you correct squareness. Keep the back close to perpendicular to the base, then add the triangular prop from the rear panel to the base. The display must sit on a level tabletop and hold only paper or similarly light deco

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Measure and cut one 6 × 8 in base, one 6 × 1 in front lip, two 8 × 1 in side strips, and one 6 × 5 in back panel with a scored 1 in attachment flap.
Tape the front and side strips to the base as temporary hinges, check the corners, then glue and hold the joints flat.
Fold the back-panel flap and attach it at the rear edge; make a 2 × 5 in stand strip into a triangular prop and tape/glue it between back and base.
Place the lightweight sample card in the box and set it on a stable tabletop for a stationary fit check.

blocks.body: Work on a stable, uncluttered table with good light. Keep drinks away from the craft materials; these objects are dry indoor decor, not food-contact certified.

blocks.question: When cutting thicker board with a knife, what is the safer approach?
options: Hold the board in your lap and pull toward yourself
Press hard once to finish quickly
Secure the board, clear the hand from the path, and use controlled passes under appropriate supervision
Snap off a blade segment over the table
blocks.explanation: Use scissors where suitable; if a knife is required, secure the material and keep all body parts outside the planned travel path.

blocks.prompt: Review your progress on Build the matching tabletop display box. What did you learn and verify?

lessons.title: Refine, label, and assess the finished set
lessons.summary: Refine, label, and assess the finished set

blocks.heading: Overview
blocks.body: The last lesson checks function and finish instead of adding decoration for its own sake. Set the portfolio and display beside each other. Use one repeated color and a shared title label to make them read as a set, but keep the portfolio closure and display opening accessible. Inspect the portfolio spine for splitting, pocket mouth for adhesive, and closure patch for lifting. Inspect the display corners and brace with the card in place. Do not test by hanging, shaking, standing on, or loading the box. It is a stationary tabletop display, not a load-bearing object. If the back falls, identify whether the brace is too short, the adhesive joint is loose, or the base is uneven; repair the specific cause with a wider board brace or fresh paper patch. Avoid adding a heavy object as ballast. If the portfolio bulges, remove excess contents rather than forcing the closure. A final learner note can record one dimension that worked and one improvement for a second edition. A successful capstone is not judged by professional finish; it is judged by clear construction decisions, accurate fit, safe process, and an honest test. Take a photograph for personal reference if desired, but no photograp

blocks.heading: Core Actions
items: Inspect the pocket, spine, closure patch, tray corners, and brace; write down any fault before decorating further.
Refine one issue using a broad paper patch, a corrected brace, or a smaller paper insert, then repeat the stationary fit test.
Apply a shared label or two-color motif, record final dimensions, and complete the reflection exercise.

blocks.body: Work on a stable, uncluttered table with good light. Keep drinks away from the craft materials; these objects are dry indoor decor, not food-contact certified.

blocks.question: Which display-box use matches the design and safety limits?
options: Hold a heavy ceramic sculpture on a vehicle dashboard
Store food for later
Support a lightweight paper card on a stable tabletop
Hang a plant from its rear panel
blocks.explanation: The box is a dry indoor tabletop display for lightweight paper only.
